2. The function of the Board will be to advise Government on all 
matters relating to food and relief in the State of West Bengal. 


3. The term of office of the members shall be one year for the present 
with effect from the date of the Resolution. 


4. The Board will meet once a month. 


5. Eleven members will form the quorum. 


6. The Secretary shall convene meetings of the Board with the approval 
of the Chairman. Notice of the meeting will be given by the Secretary ہ‎ 
week before the commencement of the meeting along with the agenda. At 
the end of each meetjng the date for the next meeting should be fixed. 


7. All suggestions for inclusion in the agenda of the meeting should be 


sent to the Secretary of the Board. 


8. The proceedings of the meeting will be duly circulated among all 
members of the Board and will be confirmed at its next meeting. 


9. The Chairman may nominate one of the members to be the Vice- 
Chairman who will perform such duties and functions as may be entrusted 
to him by the Chairman from time to time. The Vice-Chairman will preside 
over meetings of the Board in the absence of the Chairman. 


10. The Board may co-opt technical experts as and when necessary. 
The co-opted members shall have the right to participate in the deliberations 


of the Board. 


11. The+Chairman of the Board by resolution may appoint Standing 
Committees or ad-hoc Committees for the consideration of any special 
matters. Persons who are not members of the Board may be appointed as 


members of such Committees. 


12. Government may appoint additional members at any time, if 


considered necessary. 


13. The Chairman may invite any person to be present at a meeting of. 
the Board or of a Committee and to take part in its deliberations. The 
Chairman may also invite any peraon at the suggestion of any member of the 


Board.

OagnrrEn that the Resolution be published in the Calcutta Gazette and 
copies thereof be forwarded to the Chairman and Members of the Board. 


OrpERED also that a copy of the 


Resolution be forwarded to all 


Departments of this Government for information.

LABOUR DEPARTMENT 


ORDER 


No. 6447-LR./1R/7L-2/67.—22nd December 1958.—Whereas under the 
Giovernment of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 4966-18. /TR / 
112/67, duted the 17th December 1957, the industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Clive Mille Co., Ltd., 491 1 Garden Reach Road, Calcutta, and their 
workmen represented hy National Union of Jute Workers, 8 Commercial 
Buildings, Ist Floor, 20 Netaji Subhas Road, Calcutta-1 and Bengal Chatkal 
Mazdoor Union, 1/1, Garden Reach Road, Culeutta-24, regarding thé issues 
mentioned in the said order being matters specitied in the second schedule 
to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), was referred to the 
Third Industrial Tribunal for adjudication ; 


And whereas during the pendency of praceedings before the suid 
Industrial Tribunal, Shri Narendra Nath Banerji, a workman of the said 
Company, made a complaint in writing to the said Industrial Tribunal 
against the said Company alleging that the said Company had punished the 
said workinan concerned in such . Aa 


And wherenas in exercise of the powers conferred by section 383A of the 
Industrial Tribunal, Shri Narendra Nath Banerji, a workman of the said 
hax adjudicated upon the said complaint and submitied its award to the 
State Government; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the 
Industrial Tisputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased 
herehy to publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE 
In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, filed by Shri Narendra Nath Banerji, Markman, against 
Messrs. Clive Mills Co., Ltd., in connection with Covernment order 
No. 4966 /1(1)-1.R./1R-7L-2/57, dated 17th December 1957. 


BEFORE THE THIRD INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL

Disputes Act.

Petitioner, 
versus 


Messrs. Clive Mills Co., Ltd., 48/1, Garden Reach Road, Calcutta

ANNEXURE 
in the matter of an application under section 33A filed by Shri 8. M. Hannif 
against the Saturday Club Ltd., 7 Wood Street, Calcutta-16, in 
connection with the Covernment order No. 132-1.R., dated 11th 
January 1958. (Case No. 32/58 under section 33A.) 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT : 
Sirrt M. N. GAN, Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
For the workman: None. 
For the Company: Shri J. K. Ghosh, Advocate. 


AWARD 


S. M. Hannif, an employee of the Saturday Club Ltd., filed a complaint 
under section 33A of the Jndustrial Disputes Act alleging that he was 
discharged without any enquiry and without payment of his dues, and that 
the Company violated the provisions of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. He was accordingly entitled to proper relief in the case. The 
complaint was made against Mr. .٭)‎ S. Green, the Secretary of the Club, 
and not against the Club. The Club contests on merits as also on technical 
grounds. It contends that the complaint is defective for it is made against 
the Secretary of the Club, and not against the Club, and that there was no 
violation or the contravention of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
Heard Shri J. K. Ghosh, Advocate, on behalf of the Club. The 
complainant and his lawyer are aheent. The complaint was filed against 
the Secretary of the Club and not against the Club itself. It is, therefore, 
defective in form. It appears that the Club informed the Tribunal of the 
facta of his dismissal when the order was passed. This was done in the 
helief that it was sufficient compliance with the provision of law. Later, 
on proper legal advice, the Club filed an application under section 33(2) (b) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act for approval of this Tribunal of the order of 
discharge passed against the complainant. This was done shortly after the 
complaint was filed, and in the circumstance the delay does not appear to be 
unreasonable or unduly long. In any case, there has not been any 
violation of provision of law of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act 
in discharging the complainant. That being so, the complaint is not legally 
maintainable. It fails. The Club, however, undertakes to pay one month’s 
wages in addition to complainant’s normal dues, if any. 


এ. N. GAN, 


Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
The 9th Dacem ber 1958.

S. C. MUKHERJEE, Asst. Secy.

Exhibit 1(a) is the explanation offered by these four workmen to the 
charge-sheet, dated 8th September 1954. 11 will appear thut these work- 
men denied the charges levelled against them and their main grievance in 
substance was that the Company employed contractors’ coolies to work inside 
the factory just to fill up the vaccum created by the retrenchment of 52 
heads which was nothing short of unfair labour practice. This was followed 
by an enquiry. The enquiry into these charges was held on 13th October 
1954. The proceedings of enquiry are marked Annexure C in this case. 
The statements of Mr. Samuel, Wien. Mr. Jacob, Supervisor, were record- 
ed in this case, as also of Raghunath, Jogeswar, Basudeo and Ram Sevak, 
Parameswar, Ram Lakhan, Doulat. A perusal of their statements, to say 
briefly, will go to prove the charges against them. The evidence further 
points to the fact that these workmen shouted and behaved very indecently 
with the Production Manager, and stopped the lorry coolies employed in 
removing the packed biscuit tins from the factory to the lorry and were 
responsible for a good deal of chaos and confusion in their work. There 1s 
an endorsement at the end of this proceeding that the workmen were afforded 
opportunities to cross-examine the witnesses but they declined, nor did they 
adduce any evidence on their behalf. If these workmen being apprised of 
the enquiry and after attending the same did not avail of the opportunities 
afforded the workmen should thank themselves and take the consequences, 
and no blame attaches to the Company in the circumstances. In this behalf, 
the ruling reported in 1947 L.L.d., (IT), page 395 (Upper Ganges Electric 
Employees’ Union and Upper Ganges Valley Electric Suppy Company Ltd.) 
at page 40 lefthand column at the bottom, may be referred to, Therefore 
the Union cannot contend with any show of reason that the Company 
violated the principles of natural justice in this case. The Company, as tt 
appears from record on receipt of workmen's explanation, held an enquiry 
which wos attended by them and found them guilty under clauses (a), (£) 
aud (h) of the Standing Orders of the Company. Thus by applying the test 
laid down in the Allahabad High Court case of Radha Raman Bajpai and 
others and Labour Appellate Tribunal of India and others reported in 7> 
L.L.J., 11, page 15 (at page 16), the Court considers (1) that the workmen 
were found guilty of misconduct by the employer, (2) that the correct 
procedure was followed in arriving at the finding and (3) that the misconduct 
could be visited with dismissal aud as the punishment could not be regarded as 
arbitrary or unauthorized hy the Company’s standing orders, the same cannot 
he interfered with. Having regard to the above ruling the Court could 
rightly refuse to consider the evidence adduced in Court. Still I would 
observe that Madan (P.W. 1.) admitted in his cross-examination that coolies 
earry goods from stores to lorry and the workmen could not produce any 
witness who carried finished products to lorries. If the Company in 
i954 employed lorry coolies in having finished goods carried to stores from 
the factory, instead of employing the retrenched men of 1952, the workmen 
cannot make a legitimate grievance of it, because this is an internal manage- 
ment with which the Union cannot interfere. The Company has got every 
right to rationajise and economise its establishment expenses. Fifty-two 
workmen employed in Production Department were not employed in carrying 
finished products from factories. Jt is common ground that 52 men were 


discharged in 1952 as Company’s business declined and a new machine was 
installed at the factory which curtailed the labour. The difference on the 
retrenchment in 1952 of 52 men was made up and the Union, it appears. 
tried to rip open the old sores and threw various obstacles in the way of 
contractors’ coolies carrying the finished products from factory to the stores

Company has got the common law right to discharge or dismiss an 
employee which is popularly known as the right to hire and fire, but there 
ure certuin statutory restrictions which may be enumerated as follows سب‎ 
(1) that an industrial worker must be placed in such a position that the 
security of his service may not depend upon the caprice or arbitrary will 
of the employer, (2) that industrial peace should be maintained, (3) that 
industry hoa be efficiently managed [ ride the case of Lipton Ltd., reported 
in 1996 ...ا‎ Vol. (1), page ٦ As is well known, the decision of the 
Company at a domestic enquiry 18 liable to be interfered with only if— 


(1) there is want of bona fides, or 


(1)) it is a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice or violation 
of the principles of natural justice, or 


(11) there is basic error on facts, or 
(iv) there has been ہ‎ perverse finding on the materials. 


The decision of the management is also liable to be reversed if it is held by 
the Court that the punishment is so unjust that remedy is called for in the 
interests of justice, The view taken by the Company in this case as the 
result of the enquiry was a possible view and the Court will not be justified 
in interfering with the decision of the management. If the Company with 
a view to rationalise employed contractors’ men in the work objected to by 
the Union, I do not think the Company can be blamed. Thus on a_ very 
careful consideration of the charges, workmens’ replies and the enquiry 
proceedings, I um unable to say that the Company’s decision is vitiated by 
any of the aforesaid vitiating elements. The view taken by 1108 
Company at this enquiries was a possible view and I do not think the 
Court is competent to interfere with it. In the circumstances, these work- 
men must be found to deserve no relief. This disposes of the case of serials 
1, 2, 3 and 4 in the Order of Reference. 


Next, [ take up the cases of Dandasi and Apalswami, serials 7 and 8. 
The charges against them will appear -from Exts. A7 and A8 and in shoit 
they are that on 9th November 1956 they left their places of work at about 
ا‎ p.m. and were found fighting with each other, and Dandasi caught the 
supervisor Shri Subhas Chandra Dey by the neck. It appears that Dandasi 
admitted to have caught the said Supervisor by the neck and Apalswami also 
admitted that he caught Dandasi by neck and snatched the jute from him. 
Some witnesses, viz., Basudeb, Parameswar also proved the unhappy 
incident. The proceedings of enquiry in this connexion may be referred to 
und the Company nghtly found them guilty of misconduct under clause 
15(i)(a) and (i)(f) of the Standing Orders and dismissed them with effect 
from 9th November 1956, the date of suspension (166 orders Exts. K-K1). 
A very careful perusal of the proceedings in this case convinces one that 
the enquiry was properly conducted and the workmen were given 1109 
facilities and the finding of the Company is not vitiated by any of the afore- 
said vitiating elements. The Court is therefore not inclined to interfere 
with the possible view taken by the Company and the punishment imposed 
upon them. This disposes of the cases of serials 7 and 8.

As the decision of the Company is a possible view and not vitiated by

Next, I take the case of Shri Kalijoy Biswas, serial 6, employed as an

but that 26 was a case of gross negligence and carelessness and irresponaibility 
as he started further downward motion of the machine from its normal 
position which was none of his business. The Union has tried its level best 
to exonerate Kalijoy and to shift the blame on to Moti, and it was argued 
that the main switch should have heen kept off while Kalijoy was handling 
the other switches, but as this was not done, the valuable machine was 
burnt. The Union calls this an accident but really speaking, Kalijoy being 
an expert electrician should have taken due precaution before handling 
the valuable machine and certainly he mishandled the machine and thereby 
damaged it involving the Company in loss, and thus the charge of gross 
negligence must be said to have been brought home to him. It appears from 
the proceedings of the enquiry that the Company held a due enquiry 
wherein the statements of Sachin Babu, Sagarat Kahar, Deonandan Shaw,

deposition in this Court, so ws to challenge the finding of the Company. 
Thus the Court cannot interfere with the finding of the Company, nor with 
the punishment imposed on him.

The case of serial 11, Shri Ram Sagar Singh is not pressed on behalf

As regards serial 12, it appears that the workmen was absent without 
notice and therefore the Company terminated the service under clause 
16(i)(k) of the Standing Order. Exhibits L-L] may be referred to in this

1955, states that Suha Alam was absenting himself since 1111) instant with- 
out leave or information and therefore he was asked to show cause. Added 
to that is the Company’s letter Ext. L1, dated 26th March 1955, wherein

dismissed. Other letters are marked as Exts, 13-9 and 1511) wherein he 
was charged with absenting: himself on various dates in spite of warnings 
issued to him and undertaking given by him not to he guilty of such

it 1s very difficult for the Company to carry on with a workman of this type 
who is found habitually guilty of such unauthorised repeated absence. In 
the circumstances, the dismissal of this workman cannot but he found to be 
justified. The Company cannot wait indefinitely for this workman. This 
view is laid down in 1997 L.1..J., I, page 234, and 1998 L.J..J., I, pages ۸(۱ 
and 372, which need not be reiterated here. 


Last of all, I take up the case of serial 13, Shri Ershad. It appears from 
Exts. G-G2 that the Gompany~ approached the Appellate Tribunal for 
permission to retrench.51 workmen of whom No. 20 is Md. Ershad Ali on 
the ground of considerable fall in the sale of bread. During the pendency 
of the proceedings before the Appellate Tribunal the same became 

unctus oficio, The cause for retrenchment is stated as fall in production. 
This is a matter connected with internal administration of the Company. 
As already said the Company has got every right to rationalise the manage- 
ment and econamise its expenses. With that end in view the Company 
retrenched Ershad Ali and the Court cannot interfere with it. 


To sum up, once more I would briefly refer to the contentious urged on 
behalf of the Company. The sheet-anchor of the contention of the Union 
is that the Company victimised all these workmen as there was no love lost 
between the Company and the Union since the Union was formed in 
September 1952 and took up to Tribunal the question of retrenchment of 
52 workmen in 1952 and next the main grievance of the Union is that the 
Company employed contractors’ (P. Sett & Co.) coolies to get the job of 


1৮1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 1, 1959 7 


carrying finished products trom the factory to the storea done which the 
workmen agreéd to do. This employment of contractors’ men for carrying 
purposes instead of getting the same done by the retrenched workmen is 
severely characterised as an unfair labour policy. This was the whole rub 
between the Company and the Union and the workmen in a body persistently 
obstructed contractors’ men in this act of carrying the finished products. 
For the [ nion, it is contended that the workmen were fully justified in 
offering obstruction to the systematic unfair course of action. The Union 
also shows that there are certain criminal proceedings against serials 1, 2 
and 6 of the workmen. but the findings of the Criminal Court are not really 
relevant in this case. The Company has every right to manage its business, 
to teorgunise, rationalise it in a manner 80 as jo economise the expences 
and the Court is not cémpetent to interfere with Company’s internal manage- 
ment. The Court cannot justly call it an unfajr labour practice. In this 
connexion, I have already referred to the Lipton’s case. Thus the contention 
of the Union in this behalf ia effectively repelled. 


Next, the argument on behalf of the Union was that the Company was 
out to crush the Union and these workmen who took gctive part in unionism 
were singled out for victimisation, On a very careful ৪0011) of the ۵ء‎ 
evidence on record, there is no cogent evidence to show that the Company 
was vindictive and proceeded to victimise the workmen.. Thus to sum up, 
the Court cannot interfere with the orders passed by the Company at the 
domestic enquirits held with due notice to the workmen concerned 7٣ 
they deliberately refrained from cross-examining the Company’s witnesses 
and the decisions of the Company being not vitiated by any of the vitiating 
elements aforesaid stgnd. ; 


In the circumstances, the ‘dispiisealé and discharge of the workmen are 


found justified and they ‘are not entitled do any relief. 
This is my award.

To—All Heads of (Offices and Heads of Departments (both (Central and 
State) under the audit control of the Accountant-(Gieneral, West Bengal. 


Subject: Acceleration of settlement of cases of Final Payment of Provident 
Fund money. 


No. TM /Fund-I /708.—24th December 1958.—Attention of all Heads of 
Offices and Departments is invited to this office circular No. 7, 
dated 30th November 1957, in connection with the final payment of 
Provident Fund money. It was requested therein that the instructions 
issued in this uffice notification No, 'T'M(Fund 1) /687, dated 21st December 
1956, may be scrupulously followed in order to help this office in expediting 
final payment of Provident Fund money. It has been noticed that on 
many otcasions the cases of impending retirement are not reported three 
months in advance; nor the cases of death or dismissal or any other 
contingency which makes the fund money payable, are reported promptly. 
It is again brought to notice that the Provident Fund account of a subscriber 
should be closed as early as possible by effecting the final payment, when 
the occasion therefor arises. The instructions issued from this office from 
time to time, may, therefore, be strictly followed. 

In this connection it is necessary to point out that the cases of final 
payment are also being وی سے‎ for want of correct and complete particulars 
about the subscriber and also the prescribed certificates. The particulars 
that would be necessary in dealing with the cases of final payment are 
furnished in the annexure for the guidance of the departmental officers. 
It may be ensured that all these particulara are made available while 
forwarding the applications for final withdrawal of Provident Fund money. 


Y. P. PASSI, 
Dy. Accountant-General (0). 


Particulars required for final closure of Provident Fund Accounts. 
(1) Name of the subscriber. 

(2) Fund account number. 
(3) The actual date of retirement, resignation, death, etc.— 


(a) In case of resignation it should be stated whether the resignation 
as been accepted. 


(b) In case of dismissal or discharge from service, whether an appeal 
as been preferred; if so the final orders passed with dates. 
If no appeal has been filed, whether the appeal time is over. 


(4) Amount of the last Fund deduction with the number and date of 
the Treasury Voucher or the number of bill with date of its encashment 
from which it was deducted. 


(6) A certificate stating whether any advance from the Fund was granted 
to the subscriber during the 12 months immediately preceding the date of 
hap nape of the contingency (as at item 3 above) and if so, full particulars 
of the advance. 


(6) (a) A certificate stating whether any withdrawal from the Fund was 
yranted to the subscriber for payment of Insurance Premia during the 
12 months immediately preceding the date of happening of the contingency ; 
if so, full particulars thereof; 


(b) The numbers and other details of the policies of the subscriber that 
are financed from the Provident Fund. 


(7) A certificate stating whether any final withdrawal for house building 
purpose waa granted to the aubscriber from the Fund during the previous 
12 months in terms of 0.0. No. 5163-F., dated 19th December 1955. 


(8) A written, dated application from the subscriber or other claimant} 
claimants claiming payment of the balance in the Fund account. 


(9) The name of the Treasury at which payment is desired. 


(10) A certificate stating whether any non-refundable advance was 
granted for meeting the cost of (i) house-building, (ii) higher education 
and (iii) daughter’s marriage during 12 montha prior to the date of happen- 
ing of the contingency [applicable to subscribers of Central Government 
only}. 


(11) In case of death of the subscriber, the following further information 
may he given :— 

(a) Whether the nominee is alive (if particulars of nomination are 
available with the departmental officer). 

(b) Whether the subscriber married or re-married after the submission 
of the declaration. 

(c) If there is no nomination or the declaration is null and void, an 
exhaustive list of the members o e Iamily os defined in 
Provident Fund Rules, surviving as on the date of death of the 
subscriber together with their names, ages and sex. {In care 
of রাবি: কা oe "02 হস they are married or 
unmarried. married, the date of marria

Account and Audit Rules of Cram and Anchal Panchayats. 


Draft Rules. 


1, Short title.s—These rules may اد٦‎ called the West Bengal Anchal and 
Gram Panchayats*(Account and Audit) Rules, 1959. 


2. Definition.—In these rules, unless there is anything repugnant in 
the subject or context,— 


(a) ‘‘the Act’? means the West Bengal Panchayat Act, 1966 (West 
Bengal Act I of 1957); * 


(6) ‘*Form’’ means a form appended to these rules. 


3. Custody of Cram Panchayat Fund and Anchal Panchayat Fund,— 
The Adhyaksha of a Gram Panchayat or the Pradhan of an Anchal 
Panchayat shall deposit all receipts of the Gram Panchayat Fund or the 
Anchal Panchayat Fund, as the case may be, in the Savings Bank of the 
nealest post office. The Savings Bank account shall be maintained in the 
name of the Gram Panchayat or the Anchal l’anchayat, as the case may be, 
and the Postal Pass Book shall remain in the eustody of the Adhyaksha or 
the Pradhan, as the case may be, who shall operate the account. The 
Adhyaksha or the Pradhan, as the case may be, shall not keep in his 
personal custody at any time an amount in excess of Rs. 50 belonging to 
7 — Panchayat Fand or Rs. 100 belonging to the Anchal Panchayat 
“und. 


4 Books of Accounts and Rogisters to be maintained by Cram 
Panchayat and Anchal Panchayat.—(a) Cash Boek.—All receipts and 
payments (including advances) aball be recorded in a cash book, an Form 
No, I on the same day on which the money is received or paid. The Cash 
Kook shall be balanced daily. 


(6) Register of immovable properties.—A record of all immovable pro- 
perties in the possession of the Gram Panchayat or the Anchal Panchayat 
shall be kept by the AdAyaksha or the Pradhan, as the case may be, in 
Form No. IJ. Also all public rights-of-way by land or water shall he 
entered separately in this register, giving the plot numbers, If a path over 
which the public has a right-of-way has not been formally acquired by Gov- 
ernment or by the Gram Panchayat or the Anchal Panchayat, an entry shall 
be made accordingly.

PROCEDURE FOR RECEIPTS, PAYMENTS AND COLLECTION OF MONEYS. : 


7. Procedure for Receipts.—When 9, sum is received in cash or by cheque 
by a Gram Panchayat or an Anchal Panchayut a receipt in Form XV duly 
signed by the Adhyaksha or the Pradhan, as the case may be, shall be' grant- 
ed to the person paying the ۰۱ 


৪. Procedure for payments.—!’ayments from a Gram Panchayat Fund 
‘ut an Anchal Panchayat Fund shall be made only against bills showing the 
full details of the charges and shall be signed by the person to whom the 
money 18 due after a certificate has been endorsed on the bill by the 
Adhyaksha or the Pradhan, as the case may be, that the work charged for 
has actually been completed. At the time of making payments the 
Adhyaksha or the-Pradjan;,aa the case may be, shall take a receipt, stamped 
where nefessury,"¢rom the piyee and endorse the bill with the words “paid

endorsement গু be dated and signed by the Adhyaksha or the Pradhan, 
as the case may be: In 0989 of payment to illiterate persons the bill shall 
be attested by a competent witness along with the Adhyaksha or the 
Pradhan, as the case may be, and the payee shall put hia left thumb 
impression legibly on the receipt. 


9, Collection of dues. -*i1) The Anchal Panchayat shall, at a meeting, 
appoint Sarkars who would be entrusted with the task of collecting the 
lanchayat dues for a specified period. The remuneration to be paid to 4 
Sarkar shall be at the rate of such percentage as may be fixed by the District 
Panchayat \fficer from time to time on realisations made by him. The 
Pradhan or Upa-pradhan or any other member of the Anchal Panchayat 
muy he engaged for collecting dues, but no remugeration shall be paid te 
him Ever — other than the Pradhan, the Upa-Pradhan or a’ member 
of the Anchal Panchayat appointed as Sarkar for collection of dues, shall, 
m advance, deposit such security in the Anchal l’anchayat Fund Savings 
Bank Account as may he fixed by the District Panchayat ()fficer and shall 
he given a Daily Collection Book in Form IV and a Book of Receipts in 
Form No. XIII. The amount collected each day by the Sarkar shall he 
entered by him in the Collection Book in respect of each single transaction 
0) the same day and receipts against payments shall also be granted by 
him on the same day. On the first day of a month and also on any day 
when the Sarkar has Rs. 26 or more in hand he shall preduce the Daily 
Collection Book and the Receipt Book to the Pradhan and make over the 
amount to the Pradhan for credit to the Anchal Panéhayat Fund and obtain 
the Pradhan’s signature in the Daily Collection Book. The Pradhan shall 
post the collections in the relevant Register on the same day. 


(2) The Anchal Panchayat may take disciplmary action against a 
Narkar by discharging or dismissing or suspending him or forfeiting his 
security deposit, Hefore taking any such disciplinary action, the proce- 
jure laid down in adb-rule (2) of rule 50 shall he followed. 


10. (6858 of pounds and ferriés.—(1) The lessees of pounds or ferries 
911 at least 15 days before the commencement of the period of every lease 
place their signatures in column 9 of the Register of Pound and Ferry Rents 
in Form No. IX and pay to the (rfam Panchayat in advance at least one 
quarter of the annual rent.

(2) Every entry in the’Register of Pound and Ferry Kents shall be 
verified by the Adhyaksha who shall put his initial with date in the 
reievant column against each entry. 


(3) When a lease is cancelled and the pound or the ferry is Jet out afresh 
or abolished, the demands up-to-date shall be worked out and compared with 
the collections up-to-date. 


11. Advance.—(1) If any work involving expenditure is to be carried out 
by a member of a Gram Panchayat who does not directly or indirectly 
participate in the profits of the work or is not concerned or does not parti- 
cipate m any contract connected with the work, or by a contractor under 
the supervision of a member of the Gram /’anchayat, an advance may be’ 

aid by the Gram Panchayat either to such member or to the contractor. - 
‘he person to whoy, an advance is paid, shall keep proper account of the 
amount advanced and shall submit an account duly supported by vouchers 
to the Adhyaksha within three months from the date of receipt of the 
advance. No fresh advance shall be naid until the previous advance is 
adjusted. 


(2) The payment orders shal] be used as vouchers. Advances paid tu 
the same person for more than one work shall be entered og separate entrics 
both in the cash book and in the register of advance..° * 


12. Audit of Accounts.—(1) A complete audit of the accounts of the 
Gram Panchay@t and of the Anchal Panchay all be carried out at the 
office of the Gram Panchayat or of the Anc anchayat, as the case may 
be, by the Supervisor of Panchayats and a report on ৪61) audit and the 
working of the Gram Panchayat or Anchal Panchayat during the past year 
shall be submitted by him to the Inspector of Panchayats and to the District 
Panchayat Officer not later than the 3lst July of the ensuing year. At the 
time of the audit the Adhyaksha or the Pradhan, as the case may be, shall 
produce 21100007069 of the Gram Panchayat or the Anchal Panchayat, 
respectively, and also the cash balance in hand which shall be counted by the 
Supervisor of Panchayats. 


(2) When any person appointed under section 69 of the Act inspects a 
Gram Vanchayat er an Anchal Panchayat the Adhyaksha or the Pradhan, 
as the case may be, shall, if required so to do, produce before him the cash 
balance in hand and the prescribed books of accounts and registers. 


13. Remission to be sanctioned by Anchal Panchayat and Cram 
Panchayat at a meeting.—No remission shall be sanctioned by an Anchat 
Panchayat or a Gram Panchayat except at a meeting.

Ext. A was admitted without any objection from the Union. There

This Company manufactures (i) 0. I. pipe, and (ii) buckets. ~ In 
manufacturing these products, looge tools and spare parts are necessary. 
They are not necessarily capital expenditure. They do not add jo the 
value of’ block asset8, i.e., plant and machineries. They cannot be 
identified in the product itself. It ie common knowledge that ‘loose tools 
and gpare parts aré acéepted hy the Income.Tex ৮8007011668 under the

apeaking, outlay is to be. capital when it is made for thé initiation of a

whether any expenditure is revenue or capital depends on a .variety of 
cireufustances. The main test is permanency, i.e., whether the capital of 
the Company or its asaets or its goodwill is permanently increased by 
reason of such expenditure.”’ 


There is nothing on record of this case to show or suggest that these 
expenses were not factory expenses. It is, therefore, idle to contend on 
the part of the Union that in calculating the available surplus profits the 
factory expenses shown agninst these two items amounting to Ra. 7,333 
should be omitted. This nmount, in my opinion, should not be deducted 
out of the profits. Shri Sen contends that only statutory depreciation 
amounting ہا‎ Rs. 28,944 should be deducted from the Gross Profits and 
that nothing should he deducted on account of rehabilitation. Shri Sen 
accepts that Income Tax amount to Rs. 11,475 and dividend on capital of 
Rs. 1,84,06044 at 6 per cent. amounting to Rs. 8,079 should be deducted. 
According to this calculation a surplus of Ra. 464 is only left out of 
profits, Bonus of two months’ wages, as in claim, requires Rs. 4,400 
08015. A small margin of profits left as surplus is not even adequate to 
may half month’s bonus to the workers. And then, the needs of the 
industry in a partnership concern where the partners work in running the 
business cannot be totally ignored. Salaries paid to partners under such 
circumstances, who work os whole time servants, have also to be paid out 
of profits. In this case a partner was actually paid a salary of Rs. 1,800, 
i.e,, Rs. 150 0 month. If this amount is deducted from the gross profit, 
halanee would be a deficit under the Full Bench Formula. The workers 
are, therefore, not entitled to any profit bonus in the year in question. 


There is nothing on record to prove that the workers ure entitled to 
get any bonus either دم‎ a condition of service or as Puja (customary) 
bonus. The Union’s claim fails and is dismissed.

issue 1: This relates to revision of grade and scales of pay of 
subordinate staff. Before entering into the dispute it is necessary to state 
certain facts as are either admitted or established in evidence for proper 
appreciation of the case. The Asiatic Society (hereafter called the Society) 
was formed ‘for enquiring into the History, Civil and Natural, the 8511 
quities, Arts, Sciences and Juiterature of Asia”. In furtherance of its 
Ghject the Society publishes books and sells them to the public. Tt main- 
tains a library and a hall for reading purpose as 818 for holding mectings 
by the public on payment of charges. The source of income of the Society 
for general administration is derived from ( 1) subscription from members, 
(2) interest from investments, (3) advertisements, (4) rent from lands and 
holdings and (2) grant from (Government of India. Even sums received as 
admission and a8 compounding fees from members are not available for the 
general expenditure of thé Soriety, but only interest acruing from their 
investment if any. So alao income derived hy «ale of books cannot be 
utilised in general administration.

The administrations direction and management of the affairs al the

initially before they are considered in the Council und in the general 
meeting. 


The Society employs, in its office and library, subordinate staff of which

The Union alleges that the starting pay, the maximum rates of 
incremennts in the existing pny scales are all madequate. It claims that

Socjety with retrqspective effect from 28th August 1957 the date of filing 
the charter of 06811081068. 


The Society opposed the claim. It 22910601060 that grades and scales 
of pay as have been existing in the Society are quite just and proper and 
admit 00 revision. The Society is not a profit-making concern and its pay 
scales cgnuot, therefore, be compared with those in 0 7 i concerns. 
Tts source of income for general administration is wholly limited. Although 
there ore several funds of the Society, these are for specific purposes and 
they are watertight and the money from these funds cannot be utilised for 
meeting general office expenses. The Society is run principally on subscrip- 
tion from the members, interest from investments and Government grants. 
Hesides it has notgbeen, possible for the Society Yo undertake any of its 
valuable work for want of finance, During the last 8 years the Society 
has been passing* throth great financial diffitulties. As resyjt of “this 
not only many of its im@ortant activities have been curtailed but Also its 
net assets are being Pain year after year. The Society’ tried utmost 
{o get increased granis from the Government but without any success. It 
tried to improve the service conditions of the workmen according to its 
ability. Besides basic pay and J).A., as already stated, the subordinate 
staff enjoy many advantages in the shape of rent free accommodation, 
liheral leave rules, free medical advice, bonus, provident fund and gratuity. 
They compare favourably with what is being paid in similar concerns. 
The Spciety has no prospect of having any large income in the future and ‘n 
such view of the matter there is no scope of enhancing the acales of pay 
of the subordinate staff, The Society has filed a statement (Ext. D) showing 
safdry, D.A., interim relief, total emoluments of each of the subordinate 
staff with their designation, besides abstract statements of receipts and 
disbursements of the Society for the vears 1945, 1956 and 1957 (Exts, A to 
42) and Annual Reports of the Society for the years 1955, 1966 and 1957 
(Exts. C to (2), 


On giving careful consideration to the matter I accept the Society’s 
contention that in its present state of finance there is no scope for revision 
of the grades and scales of pay. The Rules and Regulations of the Society 
(Ext. RB) show that the source of income for general administration froin 
which the subordinate staff are paid ia wholly limited to (1) subscription 
from membera, (2) interest from investments, (3) advertisements, (4) rent 
from lands and holdings and (5) grant from Government of India. It 
further dppears that even sums received as admission and as compounding 
fees from members are not available for the general expenses of the Society 
but only its interest. (Vide rule 63.) Likewise income devised 
from sale of books cannot be utilised in general administra- 
tion. (Vide 1), W. 2). The funds are earmarked 107 specific 
purposes and no money can be diverted from them to the general adminis- 
tration. In the circumstances, the Society can rightly claim that it cannot 
go further in the matter of improvement of the scales. The account papers 
filed reveal that as a result of the expenditure exceeding the income derived 
in the years 1955, 1956 and 1957, the fixed assets were being depleted year 
after year. The amount of depletion in the veara 1955, 1996 and 7 
were respectively Rs. 660-44-8 pies, Is. 4,682-13-6 pies aud Rs. 19,915.64 nP.

have been discussed aud settled by the Hou’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal 
in Buckingham (Carnatic Mills Co., Ltd. vs. workers of the Company (1952 
L.A.C. 490). The floor level of wages of an industrial worker must be 
such as would enable him to maintain three consumption units including 
himself in a state of efficiency with provision for education, medical 
expenses and amenities. This is the minimum which the worker must 
huve irrespective of the capacity of the industry or of his employer to pay. 
The upper limit of wages must be set by what may be (81190 the capacity 
of the industry to pay not of a particular unit thereof but on the industry- 
cum-region basis, Between these two limits lies fair wage depending 
upon the following factors :— 


I. Productivity of labours; 

II. Prevailing rate of wages; 

111. Level of national income and its distribution; and 
IV. Place of the industry in the economy of the country.

was, after all, a hypothetical sum arrived at by taking the average. 
According to the Labour Appellate Tribunal the national income figures may 
perhaps be relevant for the purpose of seeing if the total emolument of an 
industrial worker is violently out of proportion to the per capita national 
income. The only relevant consideration in this case is, therefore, the 
prevailing rate of wages. In the absence of any evidence by the Union 
about the same in comparable industries, the existing scales cannot be 
condemned. Then it has been held that basic wages should not be fixed

the Industrial J)isputes Act, 1947 (XTV of 1947). The said Fifth Indus-

The reference was received here on 4th December 1957. The Union filed 
its written statement on 27th December 1957. The Company filed written 
objection on 4th February 1958. After several adjournments the case was 
taken up for hearing on 8th December 1958. The evidence including the 
argument was concluded on that date. The award was reserved. 


The only issue contained in the order of reference for determination 
stands as follows :— 


(1) Provident Fund. 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 8, 1959 147 


AWARD 


According to the Wnion, the business in question is 8 profitable one, and 
the Company makes a substantial profit out of it. This Union placed a 
charter of demands on the Company which ended in a reference to the 
Fourth Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Company, just to avoid 
increase of wages and dearness allowance, pleaded before the said Tribunal 
that it had introduced a Provident Fund Scheme for the workmen since 
October 1956, and the fact of the existence of a Provident Fund Scheme 
for the workmen, contends the Union, weighed with the Tribunal in giving 
its award which was published on 2nd May 1957. But the Company, most 
unfairly, withdrew the existing Provident Fund Scheme since May 1957 
and রি the contributions made by the employees to the said fund up 
to that date. The Unign found no justification for the Company's stopping 
the Provident Fund Scheme, and it took up the matter with the Labour 
Conimissioner. As attempts at conciliation yielded no result, the matter 
has been ultimately referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. The Union 
claims that the employer may be directed by the Tribunal to continue the 


Provident Fund Scheme legally and in accordance with the provisions of 
law. 


The Company contends that it 1s a small concern manufacturing 
varnishes and paints, and 1t makes a very smal] margin of profit in this 
business. The Government of India by its memorandum dated 17th 
September 1956, asked the Company to introduce a Provident Fund Scheme 
for its employees. It further directed that deduction from the wages of 
employees for the Provident Fund should be started forthwith with effect 
from the Ist October 1956. The Company, accordingly, started the 
Provident Fund Scheme for the employees, and complied with the Govern- 
ment direction in the matter. Having complied with the (iovernment 
direction, the Company, however, by ite letter dated 16th October 1956 
sought for clarification from the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, 
West Bengal, whether the Company in question would really fal] within 
the scope of the Employees’ Provident Fund Act of 1952. But, not having 
any reply to the aforesaid letter from the Commissioner, the Company 
sent a reminder to him on 217٦ January 1957. Eventually the Regional 
Provident Fund Commiasioner by his letter, dated 7th May 1937 
No. R-1227/WB/2814, informed the Company that the factories manu- 
facturing paints and varnishes were excluded from the Provident Fund 
Aci of 1952 as they did not fall within the category of “Heavy and Fine 
Chemicals”. So the previous letter of the Regiona] Commissioner of 
Provident Fund asking the Company to introduce a Provident Fund 
Scheme for its employees forthwith was asked to be treated as cancelled. 
That letter was dated 1th September 1956. The Company, accordingly, 
stopped the working of the said Provident Fund Scheme and refunded the 
~ontributions made to the anid fund by the employees. The Company, 


however, further pleads that it is not in a position to continue the 
Provident Fund Scheme. 


Now, turning to the evidence on record, I find that every bit of the 
Company’s version with regard to the Provident Fund matter has heen 
substantiated by documentary evidence marked as Exts. A, টি aud ٭)‎ series. 
The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner on 17th Septemher 1956 
called upon the Company to start the Provident Fund Schevae with effect 
from 181 October 1956, The Company at once complied with the direc- 
tion. Thereafter the Company was again informed as per the Ext. 1 
that companies such as the present one was, were excluded from the category 
of ‘‘Heavy and Fine ۳۳ and, as such, exempted from the liahility 


148 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 8, 1959 [Parr l 


een سور‎ আজ امس‎ ০০ ee দর = ہے سس‎ ee miei ০০০০ ١! TER ES aie URC  ےیوعأ‎ Bee 


of introducing any Provident Fund Scheme. The previous Government 
order in the matter was revoked. This was on 7th May 1957. The 
Company accordingly stopped the working of the Prevident Fund which 
it had started at the instance of Government, and refunded the money 
collected in the fund from the workers. So, where is the mala fide on the 
part of the Company? The Union has stressed the fact that the award of 
Shri M. N. Gan, the Tribunal before whom the issues of wages and dearness 
allowance were mooted, was published in May 1957, and the Company 
just to weigh down the claims of the Union had placed before the said 
Tribunal the privilege of the then Provident Fund Scheme in vogue in the 
Company. It contends that the factor of the existing [Provident Fund 
benefit weighed with the Tribunal in its consideration of wages, etc., and 
as a result it refrained from granting such increment of wages, etc., as it 
would otherwise have had granted. But, immediately after the award of 
Shri Gan was published, the eisting Provident Fund Scheme was with- 
drawn by the Company. But this seems to be a distortion of facts. It 
is only a fortuitous coincidence that the award of Shri M. N. Gan and the 
withdrawal of the Provident Fund came in close sequence of events. The 
Company could not help it. Government exempted it from the liability 
of introducing Provident Fund, and the Company merely acted accordingly. 
So there was no mala fide on the part of the Company. Besides, the 
allegation or the suggestion that the fact of the Provident Fund in vogue 
in the Company weighed with the Tribunal in granting less wages and 
dearness allowanre to the employees seems to be without much substance. 
I have gone through the said award carefully, but I find not even a casual 
reference to the existence of Provident Fund in the said award. This 
matter did not evidently weigh with the Tribunal when granting increment 
of wages, etc., in his award. The learned Tribunal discussed the matter 
and considered it from different angles. He does not appear to have 
attached much importance to the Provident Fund Scheme which was in 
vogue in the Company. Even if he did, the Company cannot be blamed 
in the matter. It merely followed Government direction. Even if it had 
stressed upon this factor of Provident Fund before the Tribunal for resist- 
ing the claim for increased wages, etc., that cannot be set up as a ground 
for bringing home the allegation of mala fide against the Company. So, 
I am unable to accede to the Union's prayer as made out, in its written 
stafement thut the Tribunal should give a direction to the Company to 
continue the Provident Fund Scheme legally and in accordance with the 
provisions of law. That is not called for or justified by the circumstancea 
elicited in this case. So the prayer of the Union is rejected. The issue is 
found against the Union. 

Before I part with the records of the case, I must point out that I have 
not gone into the question whether the Company 18 solvent enough to 
start or continue the Provident Fund Scheme, or what should be the amount 
of contribution, if it is continued. The present issue stands delimited and 
in a narrow compass, as made out by the Union in its written statement. 
The representative of the Company rightly resists the stretching out of the 


Part IT] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 8, 1959 149 


issue io cover and comprehend the broad point of introduction of Provident 
Fufid with an eye to the financial position of the Company. He cuntends 
that it would be a matter outside: the scope of the present issue as chalked 
out by the Union in its written statement. I accept his contention. So 
the matter is decided os abave. This is my award.

No. 57/M.8R-52/58.—5th January 1959.—In exercise of the power con- 
ferred by clauses (b), OF und (h) of section 44 of the Bengal Municipai 
Act, 1982 (Bengal Act XV of 1942), the Governor is pleased to make, after 
previous publication as required by sub-section (1) of section 505 of the 
said Act, the following amendments in the rules published with notifica- 
tion No. 4063M., dated the lst September 1934 (hereinafter referred to'as 
the said rules), in their application to the general elections of Commis- 
sioners of the Halisahar, Budge Budge, Bashirhat, Rajpur, Nabadwip, 
Chakdah, Rishra and Ghatal Municipalities to be held before the second 
yeneral election of the Commissioners of the said municipalities after the 
commencement of these amendments, namely :— 


Amendments 
In the said rules— 
(1) in rule 17, 
(a) in sub-rule (1)— 
(i) for the expression “45 days” substitute the expression 0 
days’; and 
(ii) کس‎ the expression “36 days” substitute the expression 3 
ays’; 
(b) in sub-rule (3)— 
(i) for the expression “32 days’ substitute the expression 2 
days”; and 
(ii) for the expression 26 dayg’?, substitute the expression 8 
days’’; and 


(৫) in sub-rule (5), or the expression “25 days” substitute the 
expression “18 days’; 


(2) in sub-rule (1) of rule 20, for the expression “‘15 days’’ substitute 
the expression “8 days’; 


(3) in rule 21, for the expression ‘‘ten days” substitute the expression 
“eight days’. 
By order of the Governor, 


A. NIYOGI, Jt. Secy. 


No. 1214 M1M-76/58.—6th January 1959.—In exercise of the power 
conferred by clause (gz) of section 8 of the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 
(Bengal Act XV of 1982), the Governor is pleased to alter the number of 
Commissioners of the Bhatpara Municipality in the district of 24-Parganas 
from 15 to 26. 

This notification shall have effect for the purpose of and from the next 
reconstitution of the Commissioners of the said municipality. 


By order of the Governor, 
B. P. BASU, Dy. Secy.

Fund money.

Offices and Departments is invited to this office circular No. 7, 


dated 30th November 1957, in connection with the 


Provident Fund money. 
issued! in this office notification No. 


final payment of 


It was requested therein thut the instructions 


M(Fund I) /587, dated 21st December 


1966, may be scrupulously followed in order to help this office in expediting 
final payment of Provident Fund money. It has been noticed that on 
many occasions the cases of impending retirement are not reported three 


months in advance; nor the cases of death or dismissal 


or any other 


contingency which makes the fund money payable, are reported promptly. 
It ia again brought to notice that the Provident Fund account of a subscriber 
should he cloned as early as possible by effecting the final payment, when 
the occasion therefor arises. The instructions issued from this office from 
time to time, may, therefore, be strictly followed. 


In this connection it is neressary to point out that the cases of final 
payment are also being delayed for want of correct and complete particulars 


about the subscriber and also the prescribed certificates. 


The particulars 


that would he necessary in dealing with the cases of final payment are 
furnished in the annexuse for the guidance of the departmental officers. 


11 may be ensured that all these 


articulars are made available while 


forwarding the applications for final withdrawal of Provident Fund money. 


Y. P. PASSI,

Particulars required for final closure of Provident Fund Accounts. 


(1) Name of the subscriber, 
(2) Fund account number, 


(3) The actual date of retirement, resignation, death, etc.— 
(a) In case of resignation it should be stated whether the resignation 


has been accepted. 


(b) In case of dismissal or discharge from service, whether an appeal 
has been preferred; if so the final orders passed with dates. 
If no appeal has been filed, whether the appeal time is over. 


(4) Amount of the last Fund deduction with the number and date of 
the Treasury Voucher or the number of bill with date of its encashment 


from which it was deducted. 


۵ A certificate stating whether any advance from the Fund was granted 
to the subscriber during the 12 months immediately preceding the date of 
happening of the contingency (as at item 3 above) and if so, full particulars 


of the advance. 


(6) (a) A certificate stating whether any withdrawal from the Fund was 
granted to the subscriber for payment of Insurance Premia during the 
12 months immediately preceding the date of happening of the contingency ; 


if so, full particulars thereof; 


(b) The numbers and other details of the policies of the subscriber that 


are financed from the Provident Fund. 


(7) A certificate stating whether any final withdrawal for house building 


purpose was granted 


to the subscriber from the Fund during the previous 


12 months in terms of G.O. No. 6163-F., dated 19th December 1955. 


(8) A written, dated application from the subscriber or other claimant/ 
¢laimants claiming payment of the balance in the Fund account. ‘ 


(9) The name of the Treasury at which payment is desired. 
(10) A certificate stating whether any non-refundable advance was 


granted 


for meeting the cost of (1) house-building, (ii) higher education 


and (iii) daughter’s marriage during 12 months prior to the date of happen- 
ing of the contingency [applicable to subscribers of Central Government * 


only). 


(11) In case of death of the subscriber, the following further information 


may be given:— 


(a) Whether the nominee is alive (if particulars of nomination are 
available with the departmental officer), 


(b) Whether the subscriber married or re-married after the submission 


of the declaration. 


(c) If there is no nomination or the declaration is null and void, an 


exhaustive list of the members of the family as 


defined in 


Provident Fund Rules, surviving as on the date of death of the 
subscriber together with their names, ages and sex. [In case 
of daughters, it should be stated whether they are married or 
unmarried. If married, the date of marriage and whether 
husbands are alive should be stated. ]

ORDER 


No. 5617-I.R. /1R /18L-29/58.—30th December 1958.—Whereas under 
the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 4394-I.R. / 
TR /18L-15/57, dated the 2lst November 1957, the industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Ananda Bazar Patrika (Private) Ltd., 6 Sooterkin Street, 
Calcutta, and their employees represented by the Ananda Bazar, Hindusthan 
Standard, Desh Employees’ Union, 6 Sooterkin Street, Calcutta, regardin 
the issue mentioned in the said order being a matter specified in the thir 
schedule to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947) was referred 
to the Fourth Industrial Tribunal for adjudication: 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1959 248 


, An whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said 
{ndustrial Tribunal Shri Kanai Lal Sarma, a workman of the said Compuny, 
made a সা in writing to the said Industrial Tribunal against the said 
Company, wleging that the said Company had discharged the said workman 
concerned in such dispute; 


And whereas in exercise of the powers conferred by section 383A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the said Industrial Tribunal 
bas adjudicated upon the said complaint and submitted its award to the 
State Ciovernment;: 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased 
rereby to publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE 


۲٢ the matter of a complaint under section 33۸ of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, filed by one Shri Kanai Lal Sarma of Messrs. Ananda Bazar 
Patrika (Private) Ltd. against the said Company arising out of the 
original dispute referred under Covernment order No. 4394-1,R., dated 
2151 November 1957. (CaSe No. 35 58/33A.) 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 


PRESENT: 
Suri M. N. GAN, Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
For the Union: Shri 13. K. Bose, Advocate. 


For the Company: Shri ৩. 0. Sen, Advocate. 


This is a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, by 
Shri Kanai Lal Sarma against his employers, Mesars. Ananda Bazar Patrika 
مامتا‎ Ltd., the Opposite Party, in which it is alleged that the Opposite 

arty had violated the provisions of section 33(2) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act in dismissing him from the service during the pendency of an 
adjudication proceeding between the parties before this Tribunal, and that 
without following the Standing Orders and ignoring the principles of 
natural justice. The complainant, therefore, has asked for his reinstate- 
ment, The Opposite Party contests and contends that the complaint 18 not 
maintainable, inasmuch as there has not been any contravention of the 
provisions of section 33(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, and that the 
complainant waa properly charge-sheeted and given opportunity in a 
proper enquiry to appear and to defend him against the charge, and was 
found guilty of misconduct for which he wae dismissed from service with 
offer of payment of one month's wages as required under section 9302) of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, and was also informed that an application under 
the Industrial ])isputes Act was being filed before this Tribunal for approval 
af the action taken against him. 


Point for decision 
1. Whether this complaint is maintainable? 


Findings 


In fact, such application was filed betore this Tribunal on 9th May 1958, 
three days’ after the complaint was filed, and within about a week's time 


246 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1959 [Pari T 


سے 


from the date of dismissal. The learned Advocate on behalf of the Company, 
contends that this complaint is not maintainable as there has not been any 
erntravention of section 33(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The learned 
Advocate on behalf of the complainant, however, points out that there has 
been clear violation of provisions of section 33(2) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act when the Company, a» in this instant case, has not filed an application 
before taking any action against the complainant as required by the proviso 
of section 33(2) ot the Industrial Disputes Act. He, however, concedes 
that actual payment of wages need not be made before taking any action in 
dismissing an employee from service. An offer or tender was sufficient 
compliance of the provisions of the sub-section, but. he emphatically urges 
that an application, as required by the proviso to that sub-section, should 
be filed before the employee is actually dismissed trom service. Td is not 
necessary that actual approval is taken before the order of dismissal is made. 
The leained Advocate, on behalf of the Company, refutes these arguments 
by pointing out that section 33(2) of the Industria] Disputes Act contains 
penal provisions, the words of which should be strictly construed and that 
nothing should be introduced which is actually not there in the section. 
There is no period of limitation prescribed for filing of this application and, 
in his opinion, 21 could be filed within a reasonable time of the date of order 
of dismissal, And an application should be filed only when an action has 
been taken and not before that. The words ‘‘propose” or ‘‘before’’ cannot 
be assumed to exist before the word action and ‘‘tn be’’ before taken in the 
rovisions of the sub-section. Any other interpretation, in his submission, 
is sure to defeat the purpose for which the provisions have heen enacted. 


In this particular case, admittedly, the complainant was informed of 
the order of dismissal on 26th April 1958. It would appear from the said 
letter that the order of dismissal was to take effect from 30th April 1958. 
The complainant was oftered one month's wages in lieu of notice and was 
advised to callect this amount from the office. He was also told that an 
application would be filed before this Tribunal for approval of this action 
taken as required by section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. In actual 
fact, this application was filed, as stated above, on 9th May 1958. The 
question is whether this is sufficient compliance of the provisions of section 
$3 of the Industrial Di-putes Act, if not, whether the complaint lies. 


In my opinion, there 1s no scope for intermetation of the words of a 
stuu‘e on equitable grounds. The words must be given their plain and 
simple meaning. Chapter VIT of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 
contains ‘“‘miscellaneous’’ provisions. 11 starts with section 32 which 
provides for punishment of the Company's officials for certain offences 
eommitted hy the Company. Section 33 provides, among others, that the 
conditions of service, etc., would remain unchanged, under certain cir- 
cumstances, during the pendency of the proceedings. In some cases, the 
employer is absolutely prohibited from taking any action against an employee 
except without express permission in writing of the authority before which 
the proceeding is pending. In some other circumstances, the employer has 
been given the freedum to act without such permistion. Only approval of 
the action is required of the authority, and not his express permission in 
writing. The sub-section 33(2), with which we are concerned رز‎ this 
dispute, has conferred such freedom to employers to act in certain ¢ir- 
cumstances. The sub-section 33(3), however, limits the said freedom in 
caren against the protected workmen. Having reward to the scheme and 
objects of the Act and its other provisions, the provisions of section 33, sub- 
section 2, must be read subject to sneh limitations and qual‘ficationaas arise 
from the context. The crucial limitations, in my opinion are (i) the employer 
must act in 00001021006 with the Standing Ordera, (11) in case of discharge or

issue No. 1: Wages and dearness allowance.—TI am not here consi- 
dering the wages and dearness allowance for whole of the State of West 
Bengal, but wages and dearness allowance of the workers of this particular 
concern which is located in Calcutta. In fart, cost of living differs from 
place to place and so far as Calcutta is concerned, 11 18 common knowledge 
that the cost of living is higher than any moffusil districts. Same is the 
condition of dearness allowance, which is paid im order to meet the ever 
rowing and fluctuating price in the cost of living. Dearness allowance 
is not unalterably fixed and dearness allowance is flexible and changes with 
the cost of living index. The cost of living is soaring high since the days 
of war, famine, partition of Bengal and nobody knows when it will come 
to a stabilized standard figure. I would therefore give my award so far as 
wages and dearness allowance are concerned as follows:—

workman. Next point is whether the reference is otherwise maintainable

Now, turning to the evidence on record, 1 think that the report of the

ats English translation as follows سے‎ 


“I, sergeant Dhan Singh, went to check the Texmaco Railway gute

Durwan Bansnurain Singh in his statement in the enqmry proceeding 
stated that he was sitting on a stool on the siding where coal, iron, ete., 
remained stacked. He saw the sergeant passing by, but he never doubted 
that the sergeant hand picked up the register from the gate which waa to 
be signed hoth by the sergeant and the Durwan on duty, He also admitted 
that Surajmani Tamang came to him, but he was never told about the 
Register. 


Taking the evidence as a whole, I am clearly of opinion that the finding 
«of the Enqury Committee was perverse. It was influenced by the fact 
that the accused Bansnarain pleaded no animus against the sergeant. As 
euch, the statement ot the sergeant was totally believed. Of course, the 
‘absence of animus, no doubt, inclines one to accept the evidence 01 the 
prosecution. Hut it should also be judged whether the prosecution is 
over enthusiastic in making out the offence alleged. In this case the 
sergeant was in the military service before. He mas be a stickler of 
<liscipline. In his zeal for maintaining discipline he may have been landed 
Into an error of judgment. That seems to have happened here. That 
Bansnarain pleads no animus on the part of the sergeant would also tncline 
one to accept his statement as 01 a turthful and straightforward person. 


That the sergeant in this case was 060৮ on incriminating Bansnarain is 
clear enough. In his report to the authorities immediately after bis 
inspection he makes no secret of this. He says as per the Ext. 3 that 
Bansnarain is very negligent in his duties and that he had been warned on 
Previous occasions also. Thefts also occur due to their negligence and 
sleepigg on duty. He requests the authorities that Bansnarain should be 
given adequate punishment. This taints his report with prejudice against 
Bansnarain Singh. Let me see whether his subsequent conduct corro- 
borates this. 


In his first report to the authorities which is contemporaneous with the 
event, I do not find any mention that he flashed his torchlight on 
Bansnarain and found him asleep. In his subsequent statement hefore 
the Enquiry Committee, Ext. 4, he first mentions about this flashing of 
forchlight on Bansnarain for about two minutes. Certainly this is an 
important piece of evidence which should not have been missed in_ his 
original statement. Bansnarain denies all this. So it is clear that the 
story of this torchlight focussing is merely an invention. It has been 
introduced only to strengthen the prosecution story.

Next, according to the prosecution, the sergeant took away the register

Next, what did Surajmani Tamang see? He saw Bansnarain ٣۴ 
on the stool. Now, this dozing is said to be the same thing as sleeping 
on duty, and on the basis of this Bansnarain Singh, an old worker, is 
punished with dismissal on a charge of ‘‘major misdemeanour’’. (۶ 
course, ‘‘aleeping on duty’’ has heen termed as a major misdemeanour in 
1009 Standing Orders of the Company. But it is for the Tribunal to see 
how much amount of by inning is necessary m a particular case. I have 
to see whether there has been negligence of duty on the part of the watch- 
wan for his closing of eves. If the closing of one’s eves while sitting on 
a stool, at dead of night, is a major misdemeanour, and if it is to be put 
on the same level as sleeping, I should say that the position of Durwans

prescribed for the Durwan. Here there was a stool on which ۸] 
sat. The sergeant does not take exception to that. May he that the 
carpenter had left the stool there. But sitting on a stool has not been 
tound by the Company to be an offence. Then, what was the watchman 
guarding? It was a railway yard. There were stacks of coal, brass, 
scrap iron, etc., which could not be stolen in the twinkle of an eye. So 
I may hold that the degree of vigilence required on the part of Bansnarain 
in the present case was not very high and rigid. Even if the Durwan 
dozes, such things as coal, scrap iron, brass, etc., cannot be stolen in a 
1106. So, to hold Bansnarain Singh guilty of a major misdemeanour for 
dozing having regard to all the facts and circumstances, is really difficult. 
It is still more difficult to find him guilty on the evidence that was before 
the Enquiry Committee ax also on the evidence before me. So I hold that 
the order of dismissal on Bansnarain is liable to be set aside. It has been 
disapproved also in the case under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act which has been tried analogously with the present case. Jn this case 
under section 33A, I grant the necessary relief to the workman. He has

Before I part with the records of the case I would refer to the argument 
01 the learned counsel of the management that since it is wanting in 
bona fides, and as the Tribunal cannot sit in appeal over the propriety of 
the management’s order, the Tribunal should not interfere under section 
338.4 of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947. Of course, the question of 
bona fides is importaut here as elsewhere in all industrial adiudicationa, 
But this is not the only thing to be considered in such a case, Of course, 
the Tribunal does not sit in appeal over the management’s decision. But 
if it is perverse, the Tribunal can very well reverse it, otherwise there is 
no point in the Tribunal’s assuming jurisdiction in such cases. The 
learned counsel seems to have lost sight of the fact that under section ۸ 
unlike section 33 of the Act, the matter in dispute mooted before the 
Tribunal is nothing more nor less than a reference, and the decision by 
the Tribunal is an award binding on the parties as such. So the entire 
thing in all its bearings has got to be scrutinised by the Tribunal in a 
case under section 33 just as in the case of a reference made by the 
Government.

The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by

the industria] dispute between Messrs. All India Spring Manufacturing 
(0.১ 185 Netaji Subhas Road, Caleutta-], and one of their workmen,
