Schedule 


Whether the dismissal of Shri Subal Mondal was justified. To what 
relief is he entitled ? 


AWARD 


This is a case arising out of alleged legal and unjustified 01181018৮48] of 
one Shri Subal. Mondal previously employed in Messrs. <All India Spring 
— Co. (hereinafter referred to as the Company for the sake of 

revity). 


The Union’s case in short is as follows :— 


The Company carries on business as manufacturer of various types of 
metal springs. The employees of the Company had various grievances 
regarding their pay-scales, etc., and raised a dispute which was adjudicated 
upon by an award published in the Calcutta Gazette on 27th June 1907, 
and the same became enforceable on 27th July 1957. The said award, 
inter alia, enhanced the pay-scales of the employees. After the publication 
of the award Shri Mondal was charge-sheeted on 9th August 1957 for 
having incited other workmen not to accept their wages if the said award 
werc not given effect to with effect from the date of its publication in the 
Caleutto Gazette. The Company made a show of enquiry into the alleged 
charge on several dates and ultimately perversely found the workman 

uilty of the charge and dismissed him with effect from 26th August 1957. 
کت‎ Union therefore seeks the reinstatement of this workman together with — 
ack wages. 


The Company, on the other hand, denies the allegations of the Union 
and contends that the Company held a due ad into the charges fram 
against the workman and gave him all reasonable facilities to defend himself. 


260 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 16, 1959 [Parr I 


পু 


On 219 August 1957 during the enquiry the workman filthily abused the 
Works Manager Shri J. Kodal for which a separate charge was framed @nd 
issued to him on 22nd August 1957, and the enquiry was held on 26th 
September 1957 when the workman was examined and he also examined hi» 
witnesses, and they were asked to sign the proceedings of the enquiry which 
they refused to do. In the circumstances, the Company justifies the 
dismissal of the workman and resists Union's claim tor reinstatement with 


back wages. 
Deoision 


It is common ground that there was an award whereby the pay-scales 
of the employees were enhanced to a certain extent and that the award was 
published in the Calcutta Gazette on 27th June 1957. By virtue of 
section 17A of the Industrial Disputes Act the award became enforceable 
on the expiry of 30 days from the date of its publication. So the award 
became enforceable on 27th July 1957. There is not much dispute that 
some of the employees of the Company inclusiye of this workman did not 
accept the wages for the month of July on the 7th of August following. 
Admittedly, monthly wages of employees are paid on the 7th day of the 
month succeeding that for which the wages hecome due 


Admittedly enquiries were held into charges framed against the work- 
man, so the Court in following the ruling reported in 1967 1.1... ,ا‎ 
‘page 15 (Radharaman Bajpai ۴ others vs. Labour Appellate Tribunal] and 
others) proceeds to consider three questions, viz., (1) whether the workman 
was found guilty of misconduct by the employer, (2) whether the correct 
procedure was followed by the employer in arriving at the finding and 
(9) whether the misconduct could be visited with dismissal. The Company 
charge-sheeted the workman (vide charge-sheet Ext. A, dated 9th August 
1957) whérein the charge is that the workman was engaged in activities 
detrimental to the interests of the Company and instigating innocent 
workers against the management as a result of which majority of them 
did not receive payment of their wages for the month of July, and there 
wasa further charge that he adopted go-slow tactics himself and also 
Avcited other local workers to do the same. This was followed by Ext. B, 
dated 14th August 1957, a notice asking him to attend an enquiry with 
his witnesses to be held on 2ist August 1957 at 4 p.m. There is, how- 
ever, denial on behalf of this workman of the service of this charge-sheet. 
On 2187 August 1957 statements of the workman were recorded wherein he 
stated that he did not accept his wages on 7th August 1957 on the 
impression that the award should have been given effect to with effect from 
the date of its publication in the Calcutta Gazette (27th June 1957), and 
be further stated that other employees held the same opinion and that he 
‘wa: 1101 guilty of laches in his work. The enquiry was thus held partially 
و‎ 2181 August 1957 and further enquiry was resumed on 22nd August 
1957 wherein the statement of Shri J. Kodal was recorded. It may he 
‘stated in this connexion that the workman made several mistakes in giving 
the dates of enquiry as 10th July 1957 and service of notice of enquiry 
Shr Kodal has stated at the enquiry that it is Subal, the workman, who 
incited other workmen to create a trouble over the date on which the award 
should be made operative and that Subal also adopted go-slow tactics. 
It appears from the statement of Kodal that Subal also cross-examined 
Shr Kodal as to his outturn of work. During this enquiry Subal was 
confronted with the production register and Shri Kodal’s allegation is that 
Subal got furnious and filthy abused him (Kodal) It is remarkable that 
no other witness was examined to prove the charge of the workman's 
anciting other workmen not to accept their wages as alleged in the charge. 


Part 1( THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1959 2617 


As regards the charge of go-slow tactics there is nothing else excepting 
the uncorroborated testimony of Shri Kodal. The production register 
(Ext. H) does not really prove the charge of go-slow tactics as there is 
nothing to indicate what quantum of works Shri Subal did previously, and 
what he was doing during any month. There are no data to fix the charge 
upon Subal. If work were given to several workers in a lump, there ia 
nothing to show what quantity of work was done by whom. So, in alk 
fairness, the charge of go-slow tactics cannot be taken as proved. After 
this there was the second charge-sheet, dated 23rd August 1957, Ext. . 
wherein the charge was that during the enquiry on 22nd August 1957 he 
filthily abused Shri Kodal and was thus guilty of disorder a indiscipline 
— this the enquiry was scheduled to he held at 3 p.m. on 4th September 
1957, 


Then let us refer to the proceedings of enquiry held on 4th September 
1957 at 3-30 p.m. It appears from a perusal of the proceedings of this 
enquiry held on 4th September 1957 that one of the partners Shri Gourhari 
Das conducted this enquiry. This enquiry was also attended by two other 
workmen, named Agnu Thakur and Kulamani. At this enquiry, as stated 
by Shri Gour Das (0.P.W. 3) in Court also, he asked the workman Subalk 
as to his relationship with the Works Manager, Shri J. Kodal, and eventually 
asked him to apologise to him considering the relationship as Kodal was the 
uncle-in-law of the workman. This proceedings only shows that there was 
only an attempt on behalf of Shri (001 Das and other workmen to effect 
an amicable compromise between the workman and the Works Manager, 
Kodal and there ia no evidence to substantiate the charge of the workman’s 
filthily abusing Shri Kodal. It may also be stated in this connexion that 
the workman emphatically denied the charge of huving committed any 
offence but he simply admitted that he called Shri Kodal a liar us he 
brought against him a false charge of inciting other workmen not to accept 
their wages and so Subal said that he was not at all sorry, nor was he 
prepared to offer any apology. Dispassionately considered, the proceedings 
did not prove that the workman filthily abused the Works Manager andi 
there was simply an attempt to restore good feelings hetween the workman 
and the Works Manager as they were relations. ‘here was an adjourned 
hearing on 25th September 1957 at 3 p.m. on which date one Bijoylak 
Burman stated that Subal went out saying ×۸ বাচ্চা, আমাকে কাজ শেখাচ্ছ।” 
So Bijoy was not present at the time of the actual occurrence, but he is m 
later arrival and he did not give his evidence in this Court. Shri Subal, 
it appears, did not examine any witness and refused to sign the proceedings 
of enquiry. Thus all that we find from the proceedings of enquiry on 
different dates is the hare statement of J. Kodal on the first dute of enquiry 
and that there was an attempt on the part of the partner Gour Babu and 
some workmen for restoration of good feelings between the father-in-law 
and the son-in-law. As regards the charge of go-slow tactics, I must state 
that there is only the uncorroborated testimony of Kodal which does not, 
strictly speaking, substantiate the charge of go-slow tactics. Thus the 
evidence recorded during the enquiries really falls far short of proving the 
charges against the workman. It may also be pointed out that the proceedings 
of the enquiry were not duly recorded and there is nothing therein to indicate 
that the workman was given opportunity to cross-examine the Company's 
witnewses, Jn order to prove the charge of inciting other workmen not to 
accept the wages as alleged, the evidence of workmen so incited should 
have heen recorded. If other workmen do not come to state that Subal 
incited them not to accept the wages, where is the proot that he incited 
other workmen? The evidence of Shri Kodal on whose report the charge 
was levelled against the workman, was admittedly a member of the Board 
of Euquiry and thus the prosecutor himself was a judge which is against 


262 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1859 [Purr I 


the fundamentals of tairplay and justice. A judge musi be completely 
detached from the charge into which he is required to hold an enquigy. 
۸ء5۸‎ in the evidence recorded during the domestic enquiries cannot be 
made up by the evidence recorded in Court. Admittedly, on Shri Kodal’s 
report charges were drawn up against the workman and so obviously he was 
interested in the result of the enquiry and thus following the principles 
laid down in 1956 1.1.3. U1, pages 67 and 433, T hold that this enquiry was 
vitiated by violation of principles of natural justice and the decision therein 
had no judicial sanctity. It is therefore found that neither correct procedure 
was followed at the enquiries nor is the finding of guilty based on sufficient 
evidence and thus the decision of the Company at the domeatic enquiries 
should be interfered with as there was perverse finding of guilty when there 
$s no evidence to substantiate the charge. 


As regards the Union’s allegation of victimisation J have reasons to 
believe on a consideration of the facts and circumstances and the evidence 
on record that the Company singled out this workman for the purpose of 
wiclimisation as he took a leading part in forming the Union and ar he 
was its Assistant Secretary. It 18 also in evidence that during conciliation 
proceedings the Company was prepared tu pay him any amount but not to 
reinstate him. This also shows that the Company did not take in good 
grace the trade union activities of this workman and was determined to 
8961 him. Workmen have legitimate rights to ventilate their grievanres 
and have them redressed in a constitutional manner and there was no 
justification for Company’s wrath falling on thia workman as the Union 
succeeded in getting an award over their demands. Thus ٤ am convinced 
on a careful consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and 
evidence on record that this is a clear case of victimisation and that the 
findings of enquiry are perverse and mala fide and thus vitiated and must 
be interfered with. It is therefore held that the dismissal of Shri Subal 
is not justified. 


As regards relief, the normal relief is reinstatement and I think there 
is no justification for denying him the normal relief of reinstatement in this 
ease. That being so, he should be granted his full pay inclusive of all 
allowances from thé date of his dimissal till the date of his reinstatement. 
The Company is directed to reinstate him if he reports for duty within 
10 days of the publication of the award and the Company is further directed 
to pay him his full wages for the period of his unemployment treating the 
continuity of service as unbroken. 


This is my award. 
Dictated and corrected by me. 
NW. C. CHATTERJEE, N. C. CHATTERJER, 
Judge. Judge, Farst Labour Court.

(08106, petitioner alleged that the opposite party did not hold any enquiry 
and afford him any opportunity to defend himself; that there had gv 
contravention of the provisions of section 38(2) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act; and that the dismissal was unjustified, mala fide and o glaring instance 
of unfair labour practice. The petitioner accordingly prayed for reinstate- 
ment with back wages for the period of forced unemployment. 


The opposite party, on the other hand, contended that the application 
under section 38۸ was not maintainable in law as the Company did not 
in any way violate section 33 of the Industrail Disputes Act. As to merits 
the opposite party maintained that the dismissal was justified and bona fide. 

Points which so arise for determination are as follows:— 

(1) Is the application under section 383A maintainable? 
(2) Is the dismissal justified ? 


270 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1959 [Parr | 


Decision 

Point 1: ‘The opposite party contends that as the petitioner was 
offered one month’s wages and as the opposite بت‎ made an application 
uuder section 33(2) seeking approval of the Tribunal of its actign of dis- 
missing the applicant, this was sufficient compliance with the proviso and 
there has been no contravention of section 338 and as such the complaint 
under sertion 388A is not maintainable. I[t is, on the other hand, main- 
tained on behalf of the petitioner that there has been contravention 
as the offer of one month’s wage was made and the application 
under section %33(2) was made after dismissal, and as the opposite purfy 
did not proceed with the said application under section 33(2) but he got 
it struck off without obtaining approval. On giving careful consideration 
to the matter 1 am unable to uphold the contention of the opposite party. 


The relevant facts from the point of view of determination of this point 
are the date on whica the petitioner was dismissed and that on which the 
employer made an offer of his wages for one month to him and submitted 
an application to the Tribunal for approval of the petitioner’s dismissal. 
The petitioner was dismissed on 5th May 1958. He was offered » month's 
wages on 6th May 1958, that 1s, a day after the dismissal, and the applica- 
tion for approval was made on 13th May 1958. The language of tue 
proviso to section 33(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act is ‘‘no such workman 
shal] be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been paid wages for one 
month and an application has been made by the employer to the authority 
before which the proceeding is pending for approval of the action taken’ 
by the employer’. The words ‘unless’? and ‘‘has 0890 in this proviso 
are extremely siguificant, and they clearly indicate that the workman in 
question could be discharged or dismissed only after the wages had been 
paid and the application had been made. If 2৮ was intended otherwise, & 
period of time from tae date of discharge or dismissal would also have 
been prescribed for compliance with the aforesaid conditions and things 
would not have been left in an uncertain and fluid state. To hold that the 
discharge or dismissal would be regular even though the wages were offered 
or the application made after auch discharge or dismissal would, it is 
clear, amount to doing violence to the natural meaning of the proviso and 
particularly the words ‘‘has heen’? which have been used twice in it. [ 
accordingly find that there has been contravention of: the mandatory 
provision of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. A further fact 
of which I have to take notice is that the application which was submitted 
by the employer on 13th May 1958 was not pursued by him, with the result 
that it was struck off on Ist July 1958. There is thus no approval by this 
Tribunal of the dismissal of the worker in terms of section 33(5) and, aa 
there is no approval, the workman’s complaint under section 338A becomes 
clearly maintainable. 

For action without prior approval, section 33(2) as 1 construe it lays 
down three essential conditions or safeguards for the workman :— 

(1) The employer shal) have to act in accordance with the provisions 
in the standing orders; 

(2) The aggrieved workman has to be paid one month's wages before 
discharge or dismissal; and 

(3) The employer must make application before discharge or dismissal 
seeking approval from the Tribunal of the action proposed to be 
taken by him. The approval is then to be obtained. 


This is also essential as the powers of the Tribunal under sub-section 
(5) seem to be Jimited either to according approval or refusing it. The 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 16, 1959 271 


Nee ee A rar 
সপ 


Tribunal cannot in particular order reinstatement under sub-section (5). 
J hold this view on the basis of the decision of the Supreme Court on the 
rape of the old section 33 08 reported in 1953) L.A.C. 26% in case of 
Atherton West & Co. Ltd. versus Sweet Mill Mazdoor Union. So, not 
only approval has to be sought for but also to be obtained in order to comply 
with the provisions in section 33, Only on fulfilment of الد‎ these essential 
conditions the workman will be debarred from seeking redress under section 
315 while contravention of any of the aforesaid conditions will give the 
workman right to apply under section 383A, سد‎ the contention of the 
opposite party that the mere filing of an application even if it be after 
the discharge or dismissal, without obtaining approval, would constitute 
sufficient compliance with the proviso cannot in any view of the matter be 
upheld since it would make the submission of the application meaningless 
and a 08810] provision made in the Act in the interest of the worker 
entirely nugatory. 


Sub-section (2) of section 33 has to be read along with sub-section (9), 
These would leave no room for doubt that the application contemplated in 
the proviso would not be complete unless it has been prosecuted up to the 
last ending in approval of the action. To hold otherwise would defeat the 
object of — the employer to seek approval of its action. Besides 
it would make the remedy provided to the workman under section 8۸ 
whoHy nugatory and the provision in sub-section (5) infructuous. If mere 
fling of an application can constitute compliance of the provision of 
section 33, an unscrupulous employer after taking action against the work- 
min will simply make an application under section 33(2) just for the sake af 
depriving the workman of his right to make a complaint under section 33A 
and will then sit tight over the matter without proceeding to have approval. 
There would be no meaning in requiriug the employer to make an uppilca- 
tion seeking approval, unless he bas the obligation to prosecute the applica- 
tion successfully ending in approval. 


Formerly there could have been no discharge or dismissal without prior 
permission. With the introduction of the present section 33, previous 
permission was maintained only for action in case of misconduct counented 
with the dispute; while the employer was given liberty to take action in 
accordance with the standing ordera for misconduct not connected with the 
dispute without reference to the Tribunal subject to the conditions already 
indicated. As im the present case the application was allowed to be struck 
off without upproval, I find that there has been contravention of the provi- 
sion of section 38. The decision in the case of Laksman Roo and others 
versus State of Madras reported in 1956(I1) 1414৭. 487 cited by the opposite 
party has no application to the facts of the present case. This was a case 
under the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood prior to the amendment in 
1956 when in all cases prior permission was essential under section 33. In 
1018 case the employer sought his level hest to obtain such previous permis- 
sion but it was the Tribunal which refruined from deviding the matter 
on merits. In these circumstances, 16 was held that there was sufficient 
compliance with the provision of section 88 by the filing of the applica- 
tion so that there would be no foundation for a complaint under section 
83A. In the present case, the employer himself got his application struck 
off without proceeding to a successful conclusion. In these circumstances, 
it canyot be said that the workman is debarred from making the complaint. 
ln the present ruse I also find, as stated below, that there has been no 
cunipliance with the provisions in the standing orders. I, therefore, hold 
that the complaint under section 38۸ is in order and maintainable.

Standing orders of the opposite party (Ext. G) require that the person 
charged with has to be given opportunity to defend himself. Principles 
of natural justice also so require. In the present case I find there has heen 
contravention of them. 


Even accepting that there has been enquiry on 26th March 1948, it 
appears that there was no basis for the finding of guilt on the materials 
before the management. Of the 8 witnesses examined on 2010) March 1958,

the finding of guilt on those materials. The finding of guilt is, in my 
opinion, clearly perverse. From the manuer in which the management 
proceeded in the matter there can be no doubt that it was not acting bona 
716 but was playing into the hands of its employees who purported to have 
made the statements on 26th March 1958 apparently to serve their own 
purpose. The fact that after dismissal the opposite party did not proceed 
with the application under section 33(2) to hearing would also suggest lack 
of bona fides. I am, therefore, of opinion that the dismissal is unjustified 
and wrongful. The opposite party is accordingly directed to reinstate the 
Petitioner with continuity of service and full wages for the period of

2. The,reference was received here on 10th February 1958. The Union

AWARD 


4. The preliminary legal point which has been raised_by the manage- 
ment is that the Howrah District Engineering Mazdoor Federation which 
represents the workmen in the present case has lost its representative 
character, its registration having been cancelled by (sovernment as per the 
publication of the West Bengal Labour Gazette of June 1958 at page 112, 
with effect from 2nd May 1958. Against this the Union contends that 
iere has been a settlement reached in the office of the Labour Officer, Govern- 
ment of West Bengal, Howrah, on 8th October 1958. The Company has 
also been made a party to the said settlement without there being anv 
objection. So, how can it be contended that the Union has lost its 
representative character, says the Union, as far back as 2nd May 1958? It 
1৭ further contended that simply becouse of cancellation of registration of 
the Union the dispute in the order of reference cannot be affected. Shri 
3070] (thosal, President of the Iron and Steel Equipment Workers’ Union, 
a registered body, has heen authorised by 121 workmen of this establishment 
to represent them in the dispute. He wants that he should be permitted to 
carry on the dispute. 


Now, turning to section 36 of the Industrial Disputes Act which deal» wilh 
the representation of parties, as re clause (1) :¢ 1৭ clear enough that a party 
to a dispute in a proceeding under this Act can be represented by an officer 
of « registered Trade (10101) of which he is a member or by any officer of ۵ 
Federation of Trade Unions to which the worker’s Trade Union is affiliated, 
and where the worker i» not a member of any Trade Union, then by an 
officer of any Trade Tnion connected with the industry in which the worker 
employed and authorised in such a manuer as has been prescribed. But 
in the present case the Trade Union which had been representing the work- 
men in question lost its registration before the date of hearing, i.e., on 
end Mav 1958. The publication in the West Bengal Labour Gazette places 
this matter beyond any dispute. So it may very well be taken that the 
Howrah District Engineering Mazdoor Federation is no longer competent to 
represent the workmen in question. Then, the Iron and Steel Equipment 
Workers’ Union which seeks to represent the workmen, does not appear to 
he a body affiliating within its fold the Howrah District Engineering 
Mazdoor Federation. There is no evidence on this point. So, the require- 
ments of both the suh-clauses (a) aud (b) of section 36(1) of the Act appear 
to be wanting here. Regarding the sub-clause (c) the evidence is nil. So 
the legal position is that the workmen do not stand represented by any 
Vnion in the present case. If any other Union has meanwhile sprang up. 


280 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 16, 1959 [Parr | 


and the workinen in question do subscribe to it, then they should have 
epprouched Gayernment in the matter just to have the order of retegence 
corrétted accordingly by the substitution of thei: representative Union in 
place of the previous one which has lost its registration as 98101985161, But 
that has not been done. But, apart from the question of section 36*%of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the workmen গজ could ‘@eme before 
the Tribunal in the matter of their dispute. That is als» not done. Of 
course, in the face of the reference not being revoked, it would be dificult 
tor the Tribunal to allow them to do so unless each of the workers concerned 
was properly identified. 


So, reguid being had to all these facts and circumstances, [ find that the 
present reference cannot be maintamed in law. The Tribunal is not com- 
petent to decide the issues in the present circumstances. It accordingly 
rejects the refrence in tts present form. This is my award.

AWARD 
Decisions 


Issue No. 1: The Union states that pursuant to a joint conference held 
at the chamber of the Hon’ble Labour Minister, Government of West 
Bengal, on 27th January 1956, in convection with a strike, the factory of 
the Company resumed work on 30th January 1956. Though there was no 
recorded minutes of proceedings signed hy the parties, the Union after 
resumption of work after the said conference placed the points for dis- 
cussion before the Hon’ble Labour Minister for confirmation by letter, 
dated 4th February 1956, a copy of which is enclosed and marked 
Aimexure ‘‘A’’ to the Union's written statement. It is stated that it was 
agreed as it was mentioned in the letter, Annexure ‘“‘A’’ that the workers 
of the Glass section in case of furnace being found to be not in order would 
he put in rotation. It is further stated that in violation of the agreement 
arrived at the aforesaid conference the Company refused either to work 
the Glass section ip rotation or to pay lay-off benefit to the workers. The 
Company also did not make any consultation with representative of the 
Union in the matter of furnace, etc. The Union, therefore, claims full 
wages for the period of unemployment for workmen or in any case lay-off 
benefits as provided in the Industrial Disputes Act.

The question at issue is, if the laid-off workers as mentioned in the list 
in the order of reference are entitled to any wage or lay-off compensation 
under the Industrial Disputes Act. The Union's case is that as according 
to the agreement in the conference before Hon’ble Labour Minister the 
Company was to lay-off workers in ‘‘rotation’’? in consultation with 
representative of the Union, and as the Company did not do so, the workers 
are entitled to wages or at least lay-off compensation for the period of lay- 
off under the Act. The Company's case is that there was no agreement 
for laying-off workmen in rotation. There was necessity for lay-off and 
that as the workers had to be laid-oft as a consequence of an unjustified 
and illegal strike for a period of three and half months and for adoption 
of go-sluw movement prior to the date of strike, the workmen are 1001 
entitled to any benefit in the form of wage or compensation during the 
period of lay-off.

payment for the periods of lay-off. 


The learned Advocate for the Company pointed out that the laid-off 
workers were not entitled to any payment for the period of Jay-off in view 
of section 25(E)(iii) of the Industrial Disputes Act, as the lay-off was a 
result of the strike and slowing down of production on the part of the work- 
men in the entire establishment. The learned spokesman for the Union 
pressed that section 25(E) (iii) is not applicable to the present case and was 
applicable only to the case of lay-off which was due to a strike or slowing 
down of production on the part of the workmen in another part of the 
establishment. I have no doubt that in the present case as there was 1) 
slow down before the date of the strike on the 19th Octoher 1955, which 
prevented the Company from completing the furnace as they intended. and 
there was a strike of the majority of the workmen, which resulted in a 
closure of the entire establishment, and the essential workers could not 
also be made to work during the period of strike, section 29 (19) (121) would 
be applicable, to the case of laid-off workmen in the present case. The 
werkers will not, therefore, he entitled to any compensation for the period 
of lay-off as laid down in section 25(C) of the Act. The matter can 16 
viewed from another point and it will be found that the claim of the work- 
men for compensation for the period of lay-off is not also justified. The 
atrike from the 19th of October 1955 was, as has been mentioned ahové, 
illegal owing to the pendency of the proceeding before the Seventh 
Industrial Tribunal between the Company and their workmen. The strike 
was also a sit down strike from the 2181 Oetober 1945 till the 28th ۷ھ"‎ 
1955. The Company declared a lock-out on the 21st October 19055, after the 
workmen staged this sit down strike. This lock-out is to be deemed to he 
lawful under section 24(3) of the Act, as it was declared in consequence 
of an illegal strike. The lock-out was formally lifted on 2nd November: 
1955, but the workers did not attend and willing workers were prevented

AWARD 


4, Without going into the merit of the issues raised, I take up the 
legal objection, viz., how far this case, as framed, is maintainable, a8 it 
goes to the very root of the Tribunal’s jurisdiction. Tf the Tribunal lacks 
jurisdiction, then its award on the issues specified in the reference would 
e null and void. The learned Counsel on behalf of the management 
eontends that under section 19(6) of the Tudustrial Disputes Act, as 
amended, an award does not automatically lapse after a period of one year, 
as mentioned in sub-section 3. It continues to be binding on the parties 
until “a period of two motths has elapsed from the date on which notice دز‎ 
given by any party ৮০0 by the award to the other party or parties, 
intimating its intention to terminate the award, As no such notice 01 
intimation was given in the present case, the award of Shri P. K. Sarkar. 
Judge, Industrial Tribunal, as per the Government order No. 2748-Lub., 
dated Gth June 1949, still operates, und continues to be binding on the 
parties. In that view of the matter, the present reference relating to 
identical issues cannot be sustained in law. He relies ov section 3 of the 
Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, in support of his 
contention. 


Shri D. L. Sen Gupta, Advocate, on behalf of the workwen, contends 
that the said section 3 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act 
ts ngt applicable here because it is not retrospective. He relies on the 
decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal given in, Calcutta Appeal Nos. 15) 
and 164 of 195], dated 30th August 1991, in connection with the case of 
Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. Referring to the decision 
of the Hon’ble Judges of the Labour Appellate Tribunal he contends that 
the awards of Shri P. K. Sarkar has lapsed after one year. Section 19(6) 
of the amended Act which came into force on 20th May 1930 could not 
stop automatic termination of the previous award because this section was 
not made retrospective. If it was meant to be retrospective having created 
an obligation, it should have been made expressly or impliedly so. 


Turning to the evidence on record 1 find that the award of Shri P. K. 
Sarkar was admittedly alive, and in operation on 20th May 1950 when 
section 19(6) came to be a law. This section made it imperative that an 
award should continue to be binding till it is terminated by the parties by 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1959 291 


a ×سسدد اد‎ — = = জর می دہ ےہ‎ — জপ হত 


proper notice, Now, the question is whether this new section should 
govers also the award of Shri P. K. Sarkar which was passed مھ‎ far back 
as in dune 1949, If the award of Shri Sarkar was already in operation for 
one yeur next before the date when section 19(6) came to be in operation. 
it could easily be 80101 that the said section could not govern that award. 
The section aforesaid could not touch an award which had died a natural 
death-by the lapse of one year from the date it came into force under 
Government notification. In other words, ‘this section 19(6) vould not. 
revive a defunct award and make it continue to be binding on the parties. 
But in the present case the position is pot that. It can very well be assumed 
that it was the law with effect from 20th May 1950 that an award must not 
automatically lapse after one year, but must continue to be binding until 
1৭ termination by notice is caused by the parties. The award required to 
be terminated to ceuse to be binding. Under the old law an award had 
automatic termination. Under the new law of 1990) the old law is rescinded 
or rather modified. Regarding the force of the new law, section 3 of the 
Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, is relevant. Under 
this new Act the said section 19(6) came to be operative. Section 3 of the 
aforesaid new Act runs as follows :— 


“The provisions of this Act and of the rules and orders made there- 
under shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent 
therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force 
or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any such law”. 


So the force of this section is that section 19(6) introduced hereunder should 
override any other legal provision inconsistent therewith. In that view of 
the matter automatic termination under the old law stands superseded by the 
uew section 1900), So awards which were subsistent on 20th May 1950 
tequires to be terminated under this new section. If it is contended that 
even the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act is no longer the law, 
since it is abrogated, by the Act of 1956, 1 do not think thut this contention 
is tenable because in the new Act also section 19(6) has been reproduced 
verbatim as hefore, 


Regarding the contention of the Union that section 3 of the Industrial 
Disputes (Appellate Tmbunal) Act cannot be construed or interpreted as 
having retrospective effect, I um unable to agree. Acts which create an 
obligation or which take uway a vested right are required to be made 
expressly or by implicaton retrospective. But in the present case, section 
19(6) does not create any obligation or take away any vested right. It 
merely confers a privilege on the parties to terminate the award by their 
own action after the expiry of one year by a notice. It is not open to the 
(non to coutend that the new Act creates an obligation upon the work- 
men by making the award to continue. If any obligation under the award 
8 cast under the new Act, that is cast on the management. But the 
management does not oppose it,—rather, it opposes the objection against 
the automatic lapse of the award. So the section 3 need not be retrospective 
expressly. 


Regarding the observation of the Hon’ble Judges of the Labour Appelate 
Tribunal in the case of Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. 
concerning the scope of secton 19(6) of the amended Act, the objection 
there came from the Company, and the matter was whether there could be 
any waiver of such a legal right. Even accepting the interpretation of the 
lon’ble Judges in its broadest aspect, I must say that the section was 
required to be restrospective on its face only when it created a new obligation 
or took away a vested right. It does not do either in the present case. So 

see no reason why section 1900) should not govern the award which was 


292 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1959 [Parr I 
Da mere nn | 


passed before it came into being, but which was subsisting on the date of 
its operation and thereafter. The Government notification, whick was 
stressed, to make the award operative only for a year does not go far 
enough. Awards are no more than recommendations. They become binding 
only under orders of Government. When Government said that the award 
would remain in operation for one year, it merely reiterated the provision 
of the Statute. But when the statutory provision itself was amended, I do 
not think that the said Government order could he invoked to make the 
award lapse after one year contrary to the existing law. 


Having regard to all these facts and circumstances, I find that the old 
award not being annulled by a notice under the law, is atill operative. 
Unless it is terminated, the present reference cannot be maintained. This 
is for obvious reasons because in case the previous award is in operation, 
I canot give a new award which may militate against it. That will also 
embarrass the parties as to which of the awards to follow. So I have no 
option but to reject the present reference. But then I have to see if the 
issues are identical. I find that they are so. There are in this case issues 
relating to dearness allowance, casual leave and duty hours of workmen in 
the Head Office as in the award of Shri P. K. Sarkar. Of course, here the 
Head Office has been mentioned, but that makes no substantial change. 
The issue No. 2 about the continuity of service is also covered by the award 
of Shri 9. N. Modak, published in I..A.C. 1953, as admitted in paragraph 17 
of the Union’s written statement. That award also has not been terminated. 
So I give an award that the present reference in the absence of termination 
by notice is liable to be rejected, and I reject it accordingly.

in the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Smith

Suri G. PALIT, Judge, Fifth Industrial Tribunal. 
Present for the Union: Shri D. L. Sen Gupta, Advocate. 
Present for the Company: Shri N. D. Manna, Counsel. 


1. By Government order No. 379-1.R./IR/11L-342/56, dated the 1 
February 1958, the aforesaid dispute has been referred to the Fifth 
Industrial Tribunal, presided over hy me, for adjudication under section 10 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947). The said Fifth 
Industrial Tribunal was constituted under Government notification 


No. 808-I.R./IR/3A-2/57, dated 11th March 1957. 


2. The reference was received here on 5th February 1958. The Union 
filed written statement on 28th February 1958. The Company filed written 
objection on 2nd April 1958. After several adjournments the case was 
taken up for hearing on preliminary ground on 3rd December 1958. 10 
both sides. The order was reserved. 


8. The issues which arose for determination as per the order of 
reference are‘as follows ;— 


(1) Revision of wages and scales. 
(2) Additional bonus for 1956. 
(3) Revision of piece-rate wages. 


AWARD 


4. The learned Counsel on behalf of the management has rained an 
objection that the present reference is bad in law, and cannot be maintained 
because there is an award given by Shri P. K. Sarkar, Judge, Industrial 
Tribunal, in respect of this very Company, as per Government order 
No. 2748-Lab., dated 6th June 1949. As the said award has not been 
admittedly terminated in pursuance of section 19(6) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, as amended in 1950, it still subsists. In the face of thia 
subsisting award the Tribunal is not competent to pass any fresh award 
touching the issues which are substantially indentical. 


The learned Advocate on behalf of the Union contends that the award 
of Shri P. K. Sarkar relating to this Company was passed in June 1949 
under the old Act. As that Act provided under section nt that an award 
would lapse after one year from the date it is enforceable under (tovern- 
ment order, the award in question has lapsed, and it should he taken 08 
terminated automatically. At that time there was no such provision as in 
section 19(6) of the subsequent Act requiring the parties to terminate an 
award by a notice. 


Turning to the legal position of the case, I find that I must concur with 
the contention of the management. Section 19(6) of the Industrial 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1959 297 


Disputes Act, as amended in 1950, requires on award to be terminated by 
eithes of the parties concerned by notice, and till such termination is 
effected the award continues to be binding on the parties. This provision 
was introduced on 20th May 1950 under Act No. XLVITI of 1950 styled as 
Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act of 1950. On 20th May 1950 
the award of Shri P. K. Sarkar was admittedly subsisting. It is also 
admitted that there has been given no notice by either of the parties to 
terminate the said award. As section 19(6) hits all awards which had 
been subsisting on 20th May 1950 as also awards given thereafter, the 
award of Shri P. .کا‎ Sarkar must have been hit by this section. If it is 
৪0 hit, then in the absence of its termination by the parties as aforesaid, it 
should be taken as subsisting and binding on the parties. In that case 7 
fresh reference relating to the same subject matter substantially cannot lie 
for obvious reasons because if the Tribunal entertains such a reference and 
gives an award contrary to the subsisting one, then there will result a clash 
and the parties will be in an embarrassing position os to which of the 
awards to follow, and which of the two to subsist. So, unless the previous 
award is put to a termination or annuled, a fresh award on the same point 
in respect of the same Company cannot be given in law. 


Next, coming further to the legal question, I find in section 3 of the 
Industrial Jasputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act that provisions therein of the 
Act have been made to be effective notwithstanding anything inconsistent 
therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any 
instrument having effect by virtue of any such law. Now, if the award of 
Shri P. K. Sarkar was to become defunct on automatic termination after 
one year from the date 11 wag made enforceable, under the old law, then 
the said law in question is in direct conflict with the present law under 
section 19(6) asx introduced by the Act of 1950 aforesaid. So section 19(6), 
in such circumstances, ought to prevail. The learned Advocate on behalf of 
the Union further contends that section 19(6), as amended in 1950 does not 
appear to be expressly retrospective. If it was meant to be retrospective, 
it should have been made so either expressly or by necessary implication 
because, he contends, it was going to take away a vested right of the work- 
men or was going to create a new obligation. He refers to the decision 
of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in the case of Bengal Chemical 
and Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. in, Oaleutta Appeal Nos. 151 and 164 
of 1951. Of course, I must admit that section 19(6) has not been made 
retrospective in so many words. If it is taken along with section 3 of the 
Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, then to a certain extent 
this retrospective character of the section becomes manifest because section 3 
is sweeping and comprehensive in its scope. Besides, section 19(6) does 
not take away any vested right. It does neither create nor cast any 
obligation touching the parties. What is the vested right of the Union 
that is being taken away? An automatic lapse of an award cannot be 
construed as a vested right of the Union. There is no obligation imposed 
on the parties. What is imposed is merely a privilege which the parties 
did not have before. The termination of an award has been left in the 
hands of the parties by means of a notice. If the lengthening of the life 
of an award means the lengthening of obligation, then complaint, if at all, 
may come from the management. But here the management does nol 
complain,—rather it takes the award as continuing and does not oppose 
such continuance. In the care before the Tabour Appellate Tribunal, as 
mentioned ubove. it was the Company which contended that the award was 
at an end hy the lapse of time. So in that view of the matter also it 
cannot he said that the old award of Shri P. K. Sarkar, Tribunal, has 
lapsed automatically after one year from the date it was made enforceable, 
and it is not required to he formally terminated by a notice under section 


298 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1969 [Parr 1 


19(6) of the Act. The Judges of the Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal stressed 
the fact that by Government notification an award was made operatives for 
one year, and that it must lapse automatically after that period. That the 
award will last for one year from the date it 1s made enforceable under 
Government order also finds place in the new Act of 1950. But, that it will 
lapse after one year is neither in the (fovernment order nor in the Act. 
All that follows from the Act is that an award will remain in operation for 
one year. Its ‘‘automatic termination’? after one year is a sort of inference 
which can very well be negatived by an express provision of law as under 
section 19(6) of the amended Act. 


So, regard being had to all the facts and circumstances, I find that 
section 19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act, after amendment in 1990), 
hits the award of Shri P. K. Sarkar, Tribunal, and in the absence of its 
termination done by the parties, that award ia still operative. That being 
so, the present reference is liable to be rejected. 


Here a question may arise, whether the present reference is liable to be 
rejected in toto or in part. If [ place the issues concerned in the last 
reference side by side with the issues for determination in the present 
reference, I find that the issues Nos. (1) and (3) in the present reference 
tally with those in the aforesaid award of Shri P. K. Sarkar. But the 
issue No. (2) in the present reference, viz., ‘‘additional bonus for 1920 
is a new one. So the point for decision is whether the present reference 
should be liable to be rejected only with regard to the issues which are 
identical with the issues in the past reference, or the present reference as 
a whole should be abrogated. My decision is that a particular reference is 
one integral whole, and there can be no two separate awards in respect of 
one single reference. There may be ‘“‘interim awards’’ given, but not 
separate awards. A reference cannot be split up in parts for separate awards. 
So, 1 cannot pass one award ‘n respect of the issues (1) and (3) saying that 
the reference is not maintainable in law, and the other on merit in respect 
of the issue No. (2). I am afraid, this is not permissible in law. So | 
reject the entire reference as bad in law. This is my award. 


Dictated and corrected by me.

The order of reference described the employers as ‘‘Messrs. Das Brothers 
(Printing) Ltd., 14 Garanhatta Street, Calcutta.’”” The Company, in its 
written statement, pleaded that the description of the و‎ পিল 0৪ 
mentioned in the order of reference, was not ‘correct inasmuch as, there 
was no such Compuny carrying on business at 14 Garanhatta Street, Calcutta. 
It was pleaded thut in view of this tact, the proceedings upon the order of 
reference, were not maintainable in law. The Company also stated in its 
written statement that Messrs. Das Brothers carry on business and maintain 
a printing press at 14 Garanhatta Street, Calcutta, and unless the said 
industry was brought on record by a fresh order of reference, adjudication’ 
on the present order of reference was not maintainable. The Government, 
by order No. 5112-I.R./IR/13]-4/67, dated 27th December 1957, issued a 
corrigendum by which it was stated that the Company Messrs. Das Brothers 
(Printing) Ltd. as mentioned in the order No. 1o086-].R./1R/131.-4/87, 
dated 17th May 1957, and its addendum No. 3817-I.R./IR,18L-4/57, dated 
27th September 1957, should be read ‘Messrs. Das Brothers’’. The name 
of the employer was, therefore, amended by the order of the Government, 
dated 27th December 1957. 


The learned Advocate for the Company raised the issue that the present 
reference was incompetent, in view of the erroneous description of the 
employer on the order of reference, although it was amended subsequently. 
A fresh Issue is, therefore, framed as follows :— 1 


Issue No. 7! Whether the order of reference 1s competent. 


AWARD 
Decisions 


issue No. 7: The learned Advocate for the Company argued at the time 
of his address that the name of the Company was wrong on the order of 
reference, dated 17th May 1937, as 9150 on the order of addendum, dated 
27th September 1957, and the name was amended to ‘‘Messrs. Dag 
Brothers’’, which was a correct description of the Company, on 27th 
December 1957. The learned Advocate for the Company stoted that this 
order of amendment, dated 27th December 1957, amounted to a cancellation 
of th® original order of reference and referred to the decision of the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court in the case of State of Bihar versus D. N. Ganguli and 
others, reported in 1962(11) L.1L.J., 684, in support of his contention, The 
objection of the learned Advocate is unworthy of support. The gase of 
State of Bihar mentioned above relates to one of rescinding or cangelling 
an order of reference and the Hon’ble Supreme Court decided 05 the 
Government could not rescind or cancel the order of reference 
In the present case, the order of reference was neither rescinder 
nor cancelled; it was only amended in respect of the description of the 
name of the employer. The (sovernment has got the powers under section 21 
of the General Clauses Act to amend an order of reference. The case of 
the Hon’ble Supreme Court mentioned above did not relate to the question 
of the power of the Government to amend or add to a reference made under 
section 10(1) of the Act and this fact hag been mentioned by the Hon'ble 


part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 183, 1959 303 


ہے হার‏ موسوم ps‏ سود ہد =e = a শস্্‏ سح _ سید 


(921 at page 644 of the Report (left-hand side column), The question 
as to Whether the Grovernment could amend or add to the order of reference 
at এ section 10 of the Act has been considered by the Hon'ble High Court 
at Caleutta in a case reported in the ‘‘West Bengal Lahour Gazette,’’ June, 
1997, page 10 and the decision was that the Government had the power to 
amend an order of reference made by it and a corrigendum to that effect 
was valid. There can be no doubt that this Tribunal is bound by an inter- 
pretation of Jaw made by the Calcutta High Court [vide decision of the 
Bombay High Court in 1905 )11( 15151 5 202]. That being so, it is decided 
that the amendment of the order of reference as. made by the Government on 
Mth December 1997 was conrpetent and the present order of reference is 
maintainable, 


This issue is accordingly answered.

the salary grades and seales of each individual Tel of the Company

DECISION 
Assuss 1 and 2 are taken up together for consideration. 


The dispute relates to the subordinate staff. Shri Sheikh Ekramuddin 
who wus a member of the subordinate staff was dismissed on 28th January 
1957 prior to the date of reference while the Head Clerk and the only other 
clerk filed a joint سر‎ before this Tribunal stating that they were not 
members of Weat Bengal Club Employees’ Union and did not authorise the 
৭811 Union to take up their cause. The dispute so relates only to existing 
1] members of the subordinate staff. There was previously an award in the 
matter by Shri P. K. Sarkar which was published in the Calcutta Gazette, 
Hetraotdinary, on 18th March 1949. The workmen of the Club were 
represented at the time by a different Union. After the said award the 
Manayement of the Club granted increment in basic wages twice at the 
rate of Ra. 2 to all the members of the subordinate staff in 1955 and 1956. 
Their existing wages and D.A. after such increments are admittedly as 


follows :— 

Pay. D.A. 

Rs. Rs. 
lL. Sheikh Karim, Abdar .. 44 30 
2. Sheikh Enamuddin, Abdar we 89 30 
3. Maju, Abdar we OO 30 
4. Md. Yasin, Billiard Marker ww. 44 30 
9. Sheikh Shakawat, Billiard Marker oe 60 30 
.ت6‎ Bana Nayak, Sweeper ১০০29 30 
7. Haladhar Suin, Mali ... 834 30 
§. Wahed Ali, Cook wa ৭8 30 
9. Kanan Bahadur, Durwan ... 28 30 
10. Pulin Behari, Peon ar. 90

Of the aforesaid employees, Mashalchi Kamaluddin, I am _ told, left 
service two months ago and in 119 place one Abdul Aziz has been appointed 
on the same salary of Rs. 26 plus D.A. of Rs. 15 per month. 


In the written statement before the Tribunal the Union demands 
incremental pay scales for the aforesaid categories of workmen as 9180 
D.A. at the flat rate of Rs. 40 per month. The Union alleges that due 
to various factors the cost of living has increased abnormally high since 
the award, while there has been no corresponding rise in wages of the 
members of the subordinate staff. Hence the demand as above. 


The Club opposes the claims. It is stated that the wages and D.A. 
granted to the employees compare favourably with those of any other Club 
of the same standing and that it is not financially possible for the Club 
to bear any increase in the shape of wages and D.A. Regarding incremental 
pay scales the Club says that such claim cannot be entertained on the issue 
referred to as also having regard to the fact that no such demand had been 
made in the charter of demands leading to the reference. 


Regarding claitn for incremental pay scales I agree with the Club that 
on the present reference the claim cannot he entertained, more so, when 
such demand was not made in the charter of demands. The claim of the 
Union in the charter of demands it appears was only for an increment in 
their wage (Ext. 3). The claim of the Union in this respect must ৪০ fail. 


312 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 16, 1959 [Parr ] 
je rN rrr 


The Club it appears has also no financial oapacity to bear burden of 
incremental pay acales. As to the wages the Union has not filed anything 
to show that what is being paid as wages to the different members of the 
subordinate stafi by the Club 10 compare untavowably to those in Clubs 
of similar standing. Except Mashalchi the total emoluments in the shape 
ot wages and D.A. do not go below Its. 58 for any one. Compared to the 
minimums in the pay scales demanded by the Union for these workmen, 
it appears that the existing basic wages are generally higher than the said 
minimums. Then there has been an increment in the basic wages in 1954 
and 1996. In the circumstances I do not think that any revision in the 
existing basic wages is called for. Regarding D.A. this has remuined 
undisturbed since the award in 1949 except for the sweeper. It cannot be 
disputed that since then there has been great rise in the cost of living 
index which justifies claim for increase in D.A. The main consideration 
in the matter of D,A. is neutralisation in the cost of living. At the same 
time D.A. must be related to the capacity of the employer to pay. Club’s 
contention that it has no capacity to pay any additional ]).A., cannot he 
sustained. From the balance sheets produced (Ext. A series) it appears 
that its gross income increased gradually froin the year 1964. It further 
appears that it has been earning profits on all its undertakings. During 
the year ended 3ist December 1907 there remained a balance of Rs. 670) 
being excess of income over expenditure after making provision for reserve 
tor building renovation to the extent of Rs. 1,000, for bad debts to the 
extent of Rs. 1,000, for legal expenses to the extent of Rs. 1,200 and ৪177 
gratuity to the extent of Rs. 640 (vide Ext. Ad). So with little adjust- 
ment hen would be no difficulty for the Club to grant additional D.A, 
Considering all the relevant factors D.A. is increased to Rs. 33 per month 
which I think to be fair, There is no justification to treat the Masulchi 
differently in this respect. His D.A. is accordingly raised to Rs. 33 per 
month as for others of the subordinate staff. 


The issues are answered accordingly. 


Issue 83: The Union demands both Provident Fund and Gratuity under 
this head. The Club in its balance sheet for the year ended 31st Deceniber 
1957 made provision for Gratuity of the staff. So, the Club cannot in 
fairness oppose such claim. The Club is accordingly directed to pay 
Gratuity at the rate of 15 days’ pay for each year of service subject to a 
maximum of 16 months. Ten years’ service as the minimum will entitle 
the workmen to earn the Gratuity. 


As for Provident Fund I do not think it will be fair to direct ‘ta 
introduction now having regard to the limited resources of the Club. 


issue 4: The Union demands as follows: (1) fitteen days’ 0৮৭18] 
leave with pay and (2) fifteen days’ sick-leave with pay to accumulate up 
to six months. The Club says that on the basis of the award of 1949 it 
has heen granting 7 days’ casual Jeave with pay to the workmen and 0 
days’ privilege leave. It is said that no other Club grants 30 0৪ 
privilege leave and so the existing provision for casual leave should not be 
disturbed. There is nothing on the side of the Union to justify claim for 
additional casual leave. So, the present system of 7 days’ casual leave 
with pay should continue. 


Regarding sick-leave it appears that provision was also made in the 
previous award of 1949 but both the parties lost sight of the said provision. 
Be that as it may, I direct that the Club should grant sick-leave for 15 
days of which 7 days on full pay and 8 days on half pay to the employees. 
The Club may require a certificate from a registered medical practitioner 
in case it has reason to doubt about the fact of illness.

Issue 6 Shri Sheikh Ekramuddin was bearer No. 1 and a cook in the

Qn giving careful consideration to the evidence and circumstances آ‎ 
find nothing to sustain the case of the workmen. That there had been 
two iucidents, one on 1111) November 1956 and the other on 19th 7۲٣ 
1957 19 not disputed. On 1111) November 1956 the President of the Club 
Mr. 70665 (1).W, 1) left the Club at about 11 p.m. and then again 
returned to the Club with some friends soon after 11-30 p.m. to pick up 
his car and to take coffee and found that the Club had already been closed 
and that all the bearers including bearer No. 1 Ekramuddin had 16, 
Kkramuddin a8 alxo other bearera were to have been on duty up to the 
mid-night. The President got the Club opened by the durwan and sent 
him to bring bearer No, 1 Ekramuddin. Ekramuddin did not come forth- 
with, Aceording to Ekramuddin (P.W. 2), he was at the time 
faking meal and so could not return forthwith and he thus sent word 
through durwan that he would be coming after finishing his meal. Be 
that as it may, as the Club was closed and as Ekramuddin was not avail- 
able, President lett the Club and on the next date (12th November 1956)

Ekramuddin received the charge sheet on that very day (12th November

Ekramuddin admitted the charges except under item 8 which amounte

said 97) ay The committee considered the report of the President

the materials the management was justified to award punishment by 
suspension for 7 days und the warning. Regarding awarding of 7 days’ 
suspension I find no serious — as the Club under the standing 
orders formulated under the award could suspend a workman pending

pending the enquiry cannot be accepted as contravening the provisions

of mala fide on the part of the management. 


Regarding the incident on 19th January 1957 it is not also disputed

compliance (Ext. D). The evidence shows that in the Club communi-

im on his requisition for discussion with others. Disclaimer of

he committee found him guilty of the charge and having regard to the

on 19th January 1957 (Ext. D6). The sequence of events us already noted 
clearly indicates that the management proceeded against him on both the

AWARD 


This is a reference arising out of alleged illegal and unjustified dismiysal 
of 24 workmen previously employed in (1) Messrs. Sree Hosiery Mills and 
(2) Sri Sankar Industries (hereinafter described as the Company for the 
sake of brevity). 


The case of the Union in a nutshell is as follows :— 


The workmen concerned were employed in Sree Hosiery Mills for about 
$5 years. The Company was very unkind in its dealing towards its work- 
men, No attendance register was maintained, nor were overtime wages paid 
aml there was no leave with pay. To add to that, the Company dismissed 
workmen at its sweet will. To ameliorate the conditions of service the Union 
placed a charter of demands which was pending before the Labour Com- 
missioner on 19th June 1957. The Company discharged one Shri Motilal 
Das illegally and unjustly. During the pendency of that dispute the 
Company further discharged Madhusudan Sen, Nilmani Das and Kamal 
Krishna Dhar. The Company did not stop there, but declared a lock-out 
on ond from 116) July 1957 which the Company ugreed to lift on 20th July

| Decision 


Before the points for determination as stated in the Government Order 
of Reference are taken up, it is necessary to take up another preliminary 
point raised on behalf of the Company that these people do not fall within 
the purview of the definition of a workman as given in section 2(s) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. If this point is found in favour of the Company, 
the reference will be wholly incompetent, and in that case, the points for 
reference do not call for any decision, but if the finding be otherwise, the 


points for reference will have to be determined. So I take up this 
preliminary objection first. 


In deciding this point the main difficulty is presented by the absence 
of any written terms and conditions of employment between the parties. As 
is well known the tests of a workman are laid down in various case-laws. 
First, I may refer to the case of Dharangadhra Chemical Works Lid. and 
State of Saurashtra and others reported in 1957 L.L.J. Vol. I, page 477. 
The prema face test is the existence of right of control in respect of the 
manner in which the work is to be done and that the correct method of 
approach is to consider, having regard to the nature of the work, if there 
was due control and supervision by the employee and in doing so all the 
circumstances of a case have got to be considered. In this connexion, the 
House of Lords in the case of Short versus J. & W. Henderson, Ltd. [(1946) 


মিন 427, 429] laid down the four indicia of a contract of service as 
ollows :-—~ 


(a) the master's power of selection of his servant, 
(b) the payment of wages or other remuneration, 
(c) the master’s right to control the method of doing the work, and 
(d) the master’s right of suspension or dismissal. 


The pronouncements of Fletcher Moulton, L.J., at page 549 in Simmons 


7 
versus Health Laundry Company [1910) 1 K.B. 543, 549, 550], may also 
be profitably referred to as follows :— 


‘Tn my opinion it is impossible to lay down any rule of law 
distinguishing the one from the other. It is a question of fact 
to be decided by all the circumstances of the case. The greater 
the amount of direct control exercised over the person rendering 


220 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 15, 1959 [Parr ] 


the services by the person contracting for them, the stronger the 
grounds for holding it to be a contruct of service, and similarly 
the greater the degree of independence of such control the greater 
the probability that the services rendered are of the nature of 
professional services and that the coutract is not one of service,”’ 


In this connexion, I may refer to a recent case-law reported in 1958 L.1J., 
Vol. II, puge 786 (Maharaja Beedi Factory and North Arcot District Beedi 
Workers’ Union and সু wherein the previously decided cases have 
been reviewed and the principle has been reiterated as follows :— 


‘‘Whether or not the test of control and supervision, inclusive of the 
control over the time of the labourer, is the sole test to apply, 
that test must be satisfied before the relationship of master and 
servant is established. That relationship must be established 
before a person could be said to be ‘‘emploved’’ within the 
meaning of section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act. In 
applying this test the followimg factors must be considered: 
(1) what the industry is, (2) what the activity of the labourer 
is in that industry, and (3) what is the control exercised in 
relation to that activity by the person for whom that aotivjty is 
carried on. The factual position and the economic realiti®®s in 
a given case could not be ignored in applying the test which is 
by no means an easy one in its application.’’ 


In the light of the principles enunciated above and the evidené& on 
record I would hold that these persons are not contractors but they are 
‘‘workmen’’ fulfilling the necessary tests. To be brief the Company (Sree 
Hosiery Mills) admittedly supervised works of these persons, maintained’ 
attendance registers Ext. I-1 for the period from July 1955 to december 
1956, and Ext. 1-2 for the period from July 1957 to December 1957, took 
disciplinary action against some of them as per charge-sheets (Ext. B series) 
and this contention was never raised by the Company at any previous stage 
during the long conciliation proceedings. If the Company really helieved 
these people to be independent contractors and treated them as such, they 
could have raised thia contention before the Conciliation Officers and thus 
cut short the matter. This contention is really an afterthought and is 
negatived. The learned Advocate for the Company cited the ruling reported 
in 1958 L.L.J., Vol. 11, page 744 (Palanjappa Mudaliar and Additional 
First Class Magistrate, Kulliftalai, and others), but the facta in that case 
are quite distinguishable as the people in that case were under no obligation 
to come and work on any particular day, nor was there obligation on the 
part of the employer to provide work, nor were the men wnder any 
obligation to come at any time and go at any time, nor could they be 
prevented from working for a competing manufacturer. In this case the 
workers were required to come at about 10-30 a.m. or 11 a.m. and leave at 
6 or 30۔6‎ p.m. as the attendance register shows and this shows that their 
time was at the disposal of the Company which also supervised their works 
of cutting, neck-cutting, shouldering, ironing, etc., the genzies and also 
admittedly charge-sheeted them for bad and unsatisfactory work «and also 
granted them holidays on Sunday and these people could not work at any 
other time except with Company’s permission. The maintenance of 
attendance register, the drawing up of charges against them, the granting 
of holidays, ete., the exercise of supervision are circumstances Inconsistent 
with these people being termed independent contractors having no 
relationship of master and servant between thein. - 


Thus I hold that these people are workmen according to seotion 2(s) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act.

As regards the strike ] would generally observe that, of course, strike is 
a recognized weapon of workmen to be resorted to for assisting their 
bargaining power and for backing up their collective demands upon an 
unwilling employer and as it has an adverse effect upon production, it 1s 
to be resorted to as a last resort when all other avenues for settlement of 
a dispute as provided in the Statute, have been exhausted and proved 
abortive, so it is necessary to discourage its misuse, 


In this particular cuse the strike and lock-out during the period from 
th July 1957 to 24th July 1957 is considered unjustified as it was not 
hona fide launched as it was for exacting an advance amount from the 
Company which it was not obligatory upon it to pay and on other extraneous

Company was cympetent to proceed for their misconduct. The Union

T have gone through the entire evidence both oral and documentary in

If any authority be needed, I may refer to the following cases :— 

(1) Mahalaxmi Cotton Mills case, reported in 1952 L.A.C., page 370, 

(2) the case of United Commercial Bank Ltd., reported in 1954 L.A.C., 
page 498, 

€8) the case of Express Newspapers Ltd., Madras, reported in 1957 
L.A.C., page 73, and 

(4) the case of Western India Match Company Ltd., reported in 1957 
L.A.C., page 322. 


All the above cases lay down in substance that if the employer is not guilt: 
of any unfair labour practice, the workmen who had gone on an unjustified 
strike really courted unemployment and are not entitled to any wages for 
the strike period. The law on this subject seems to have been clearly laid 
down in the case of West Bengal Flour Mills Mazdoor Congress, reported 
in F.J.R., Vol. X (1956-57) page 240 as follows :— 
‘‘The workmen may have their fundamental right to do work and with- 
hold it at their pleasure. They were free to choose their own 
time to launch a strike; but this right has nothing to do with 


pant I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 16, 1969 325 


the right to get wages during the period of strike. One has no 
legitamate connection with the other. The benefits obtained out 
of a strike exclusively belong to the workmen in full measure. 
Ordinarily, they are not supposed to be compensated for any loss 
that may be sustained by them in the venture. The trike, 
being a deliberate act on the part of the workmen, they must 
be prepared to take all of its consequences. The workers no 
doubt suffered loss during the period of voluntary unemployment. 
Under the Standing Order 12 the Company is entitled to treat 
the workmen involved in u strike as suspended during the period 
of strike. The period of strike will be considered as dies non. 
Accordingly, the workmen are not entitled as of right to any 
wages for a period of strike in terms of their employment. 
Further, the relief asked for, is not a normal legal relief. It is 
granted on compassionate and equitable grounds. It is, however, 
invariably refused when the strike is forbidden by law and/or 
found to be otherwise unjustified. Also it is refused when it is 
found to be not bona fide or launched on extraneous consideration 
or where its purpose is not lawful and/or when it is conducted 
in a disorderly maner. It is not only the end but the means 
also must be reasonable and just.’’ 


Thus in fine I find that the strike in this case during the period from 
101 July 1957 to 24th July 1957 was unjustified and the lock-out justified 
due to disturbances caused by the workmen. 


To sum up, the reference is found to be incompetent as two different 
Companies having two different sets of workmen are made parties to it 
which has vitiated the reference for misjoinder of parties and that the strike 
and lock-out for the period from 10th July 1957 to 24th July 1957 were 
respectively unjustified and justified and that the workmen in this reference 
are entitled to no relief. 


This is my award.

No. 331/M.2B-4/58.—14th January 1959.—Whereas the Commissioners 
of the Darjeeling Municipality in the district of Darjeeling have made the 
following by-laws under section 499 of the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 
(Bengal Act XV of 19382), and have applied to the Stale Government for 
confirmation of the suid by-laws under section 506 of the said Act; 


And whereas— 


(a) notice of the intention to apply for such confirmation of the sdid 
by-laws has been duly given one month before the making of 
the application for corfirmation as required by clause (i) of sub- 
section (2) of section 506 of the said Act, and 


(b) for one month before the application a copy of the said by-laws has 
been kept at the office of the Commissioners of the said muni+ 
cipality and has been open during office hours thereat to the 
inspection of the inhabitants of the said municipality, without 
fee, as required by clause (15) of sub-section (2) of the section 506 
of the said Act; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powcr conferred by section 506 of 
the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1982), the Governor is 
pleused to confirm the following by-laws, namely :— 


In these by-laws—‏ .ل1

donkey,

$. The Licensing Officer may refuse to grant a jicense if ihe riding

5. Every license granted during a half-year under these by-laws shull 
be valid for the first half-year ending on the thirtieth day ot September 
and for the second half-year ending on the thirty-first day of March and 
no longer, on whichever date the License might have been granted. 


6. <A lense shall be granted subject to the following conditions :— 


(i) No riding horse suffering from gulls, sore-back or other open wound 
puch ax would render it unfit for bire, or from any infectious or 
contagious diseases or which is lame, weak, winded or otherwise 
in bad condition, or the use of which has been prohibited by the 
Licensing Officer, shall be let out on hire; and 


(ii) Every riding horse let out on hire shall be provided with proper 
suddle and bridle.

AWARD 


Thia is a complaint under section J3A of the Inductmal Disputes Act 
by Shri Bhup sb Chandra Dey. He was a Store Clerk in the Company 
On the advice of the physician he ayy lied for 4} months’ leave but the 


426 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 22, 1959 ([Pazr I 


management granted 2 months leave to him. According to the petitioner 
he applied tor extension of leave up to 16th November 1957 by his applica- 
tion, dated 101) October 1957, as he was not till then physically ‘fit to 
carry on work. The opposite party company, however, discharged him by 
notice, dated 3lst October 1957, said to be in violation of section 33 of the 
Industria] Disputes Act. Hence the complaint. 

The opposite party contends that the application is not maintainable in- 
asmuch as it has not disclosed contravention of any of the provisions of 
section ۰ 

Decision 

Foundation for a complaint under section 388A is contravention of the 
provisions of section 93. In the present case the petitioner has not been 
uble to show contravention of any of the provisions of section 33. Section 
33(1) is not attracted as according to showing of the petitioner the 
misconduct for which hegwas discharged is not connected with the dispute 
pending adjudication before the Tribuhial. কুল section 17302) 
18 not attracted as the opposite party had no standing orders at the time. 
The standing orders contemplated in sub-section (2) of section 33 are those 
contemplated and certified under the Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Act or laid down under an award. As the Company had مھ‎ such 
standing orders at the time, section 33(2) is not alao attracted As there 
has been no contravention of any of the provisions of section 33, it is obvious 
that the complaint under section 33A is not maintainable. It is awarded 
accordingly. The petitioner may, however, seek redress by wnoy of a 
reference under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act.

The Government of West Bengal, in the —— of Labour, by 
order No. 460-I.R./TR/10L-1380/57, dated 7th February 1958, referred 
under sections 7 and 10 of the Industria] Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of aid 
an industrial dispute between Messrs. Narsingh Sahay Modun Gopal, 
Managing Agent: The East India Electric Supply & Traction (Co. 
Ltd. 3 Jogindra Kaviraj Row, Caleutta-7, and one of their workmen, Shri 
Gaya Prasad represented by the Hindusthan Drivers’ Union, 3/1 Mangoe 
Larie, Calcutta-1, regarding matters specified in the second schedule of the 
Act, to this Court for adjudication : — 


Schedule. 
Whether the dismissal of Shri Gaya Prasad is justified. To what 


relief including reinstatement is he entitled? 
AWARD 


This is a case arising out of alleged illegal dismissal of a Driver namely 
Shri Gaya Prasad previously employed in Messrs. Narsingh Sahay Modun 


PartI] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 22, 1959 433 


১০ ভরত নিপতিত উরি জপ ০০ কমল এল হাল وب و وو!‎ 
০ তাজা ০০০১০ সি TT 


Gopal, Managing Agent: The East India Electric Supply & Traction Co. 
146৫, ৭ Jogindra Kaviraj Row, Calcutta-7 (hereinafter described as the 
Company for the sake 01 brevity). 


The Union’s allegation in brief is that Shri Gaya Vrasad was appointed 
as a Driver in August 1955 on « monthly salary of Rs. 105. The Company 
did not اسم‎ him any public holiduy, nor overtime allowances for overtime 
work. The workman পল fixation of working hours and overtime 
allowances which the management did not take in good grace, and ulti- 
mately dismissed him from service with effect from 4th November 1956. 
The Union, therefore, contends that this dismissal is utterly unjustified 
and illegal and seeks to recover arrears of pay for 4 days of November 1956, 
notice pay, leave pay and gratuity. In all lis claim is laid at Rs. 329 only. 


The Company, on the other hand, denies the allegations of the Union 
and contends that the workman was paid overtime wages as stated in the 
written statement and that the driver was not dismissed and that he is 
entitled only to the arrears of pay as claimed and nothing else. 


The driver examined himself in this Court and stated that the Company 
turned deaf ears to his demand for overtime wages. None was present on 
behalf of the Company al the time of 1111) مہ‎ the evidence of the driver 
stands uncontradicted. According to his evidence he was appuinted in 
August 1955 and dismissed on 4th November 1956. It is common ground 
that his wages for 4 days of November 1956 are outstanding and that his 
monthly salary was Rs. 105, so he is undisputedly entitled to 4 days’ wages 
01 November 1966. It appears that he was not given any notice prior to 
his dismissal, so he is entitled to one month’s pay in lieu of notice. 


As regards his dismissal, there is mone | to controvert the statement 
of the driver that he was illegally dismissed for his demanding overtime 
wages. 


In all fairness, the driver is entitled to another half month’s pay as 
compensation for his loss of service. So, he is found entitled 10 Rs. 105 
as notice pay, plus Ra. 62.50 nP. as compensation for loss of service, and 
Its. 14 for 4 days of November 1956, in all Rs. 171.50 nP. 


As the workman has not prayed for reinstatement hecause he is work- 
ing temporarily elsewhere, the same is not granted. Thus the Company is 
directed to pay Rs. 171,60 nP. to the workman within seven days of the 
publication of this award. 


This is my award, 
Tictated and corrected by me.

Judge. Judge, First Labour Court.

Schedule 


Whether the refusal of the Company to employ Shri Dilip Kumar Das
