AWARD 


This 1৮ a case arising out of alleged illegal and unjustified dismissal of 
one Shri Thilip Kumar Das previously employed in Messrs. Chandana Shoe 
Mart (hereinafter referred to as the Company for the sake of brevity). 


The case of the Union, in a nutshell, is as follows سے‎ 


Shri Dilip Chandra Das was employed as a salesman in the Company 
from October 1955 to 138th October 1957 on a monthly salary of Rs. 90. 
The Proprietor Shri Suresh Chandra Paul, unjustly discharged him on 1301) 
October 1957 without any chargesheet, enquiry or reason whatsoever. 
There were three tripartite conferences over this dispute which ultimately, 
however, ended in smoke. The Union therefure seeks the reinstatement of 
this workman together with wages for the period of his unemployment. 


The Company, on the other hand, denies the allegations in the written 
statement of the Union and contends that the allegations of disrnmssal are

ne 2۳ جج جیا‎ cies 


entizely false but the fact is that this workman wrongfully, unjustly and 
dishonestly left the job of his own accord on and from 18th October 1957 
without any previous notice. The Company further avers that the work- 
man was very careless in his work for which the Company was very often 
involved in loss and the Company later on discovered that a few pairs of 
shoes were missing. The Company has further stated that this employce 
has later on started ےج‎ Cycle Shop and is not keen about his work. In the 
শুনা 08 the Company asserts that the workman is not entitled to 
any relief. 


Today (2911) December 1958) was fixed for hearing of the case, but on 
this date, it appears that both parties have put in a joint petition of com- 
promise stating that the dispute has been fully and finally settled out of 
the Court and that the workman shall have no further claim on _ the 
employer either by way of reinstatement or compensation or any other relief. 


The terms of the petition of compromise appear to be fair, reasonable and 
lawtul and may be given effect to. This reference is thus disposed of in 
terms of the petition of compromise which do form a part of my award. 

This is my award, 


Dictated and corrected by me.

BEFORE THE FIFTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL.

Suri G. PALIT, Judge, Fifth Industrial Tribunal. 


By (Government order No. 4846-I.R./TR/10L-73/56, dated 11th 
December 1957, the aforesaid dispute has been referred to the Fifth 


PartI] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 22, 09 437 


Tndustrial Tribunal, presided over by me, for adjudication under section 
10 of the Judustrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947). The said Fifth 
Ludustrial Tribunal was constituted under Government notification No. 808- 


L.R./1R/3A-2/57, dated 11th March 1997. 


The reference was received here on 13th December 1997. The Union 
filed its written statement on 9156 January 1958. The Company after 
several petitions for time, filed its written objection on 7th August 1958. 
After several adjournments the case was set down for hearing on 4th 
Qctober 1958. It stood over to 20th December 1958 when the case was 
taken up tor hearing. The parties concerned did not take any steps on 
that date. There was already a petition filed by the management that the 
workers had directly entered into a settlement with regard to three issues 
in the reference out of the four. The Tribunal reserved its award. 


he issues which stood for adjudication as per the order of reference are 
as follows :— 


(1) Basic wages and scales of pay. 
(2) Dearness allowance. 
(3) Bonus for 1996. 


‘4) Whether the management was justified in dismissing Shri S. C. 
Ghosh and Shri A. Latiff. What relief are they entitled to? 


AWARD 


issue Nos. 1, 2 and 3: In the petition filed by the Company on 12th 
December 1958 it appears that the representatives of the Company and 
the workmen, after negotiations, met at a meeting and settled up all the 
disputes referred to the Tribunal themselves as also other disputes between 
the parties. A written agreement of settlement in this respect was signed 
by the workmen and the representative of the Company on ldih October 
1958. As per the paragraph 1(c) of the memorandum of settlement, it 
appears that all the issues و سی‎ before the Tribunal have been amicably 
settled. In the said settlement the workers who represent the entire body 
of the establishment, state that they are not in any way interested in the 
alleged disputes with regard to the issue No. 4 im the reference, and they 
do not support the alleged disputes in respect of Shri 8. 06 Ghosh and 
Shri A. Latif as per the aforesaid issue No. 4. So, it may very well be 
taken that the issue Nos. 1, 2 and 3 in the order of reference do not require 
any adjudication hy the Tribunal. They are accordingly disposed of 
without any direction. This order is based on the memorandum of settle- 
ment filed by the workers and the management jointly before the Tribunal, 
which forms a part of my present award in respect of the issue Nos. 1, 2 
and 3. It finds place in the Appendix A. 


Issue No. 4: Now, it may very well be contended whether even after 
the amicable settlement of the issue Nos. 1, 2 and 3, there should he 
adjudication required on the issue No. 4. Conceding for the sake of 
argument that this issue No. 4 still survives, I should find that the issue 
in question is liahle to be rejected after the disclaimer by the entire hody 
of the establishment of the case of Shri ১, 0. Ghosh and Shri A. Latif. 
The dispute over their dismissal now is no other than an individual dispute. 
Being an ‘‘individual dispute’’ if cannot come within the definition ot 
“Tndustrial Dispute’. That an individual dispute is not within the scope 
of jurisdiction of an Industrial Tribunal has heen held in series of decisions 
ay per 565 C.W.N., page 256, and 57 C.W.N., page 169, decided by the 
Hon’ble Caleutta Tigh Court. There was some conflict of decision as in 


438 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, TANUARY 22, 1959 [Parr 1 


স্পা সস 


the case reported in 1959 1,.14.থ.১ page 757, decided by the Hon’ble Labour 
Appellate Tribunal of India and the case decided by the Madras High 
Court us reported in 1965 L.L.J., page 477. The final word however, ٤ؾ‎ 
to be said by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in the case reported in 
1953 L.1..J., page 195. It was held that a single employee’s case may 
develop into an industrial dispute if it is espoused by the other employees 
of the establishment or at least by a substantia) body of them or 0 the 
Union representing those workmen. But in the present case the entire 
body of workmen of the establishment have dissociated themselves from 
the dispute in question. There is also no evidence before me that the 
Union composed of workmen of this Company had taken up this dispute 
from the beginning. If the Union had taken this up even from the 
beginning, it seems to have thrown the cases of these two workmen over- 
board at the time of hearing not having entered appearance before the 
Tribunal. So, in any view of the matter the issue No. 4 is answered 
against the two workmen concerned, namely, Shri ۸.۰ 0. Ghosh and Shri 
A. Latif. They are entitled to no relief from the Tribunal in the present 
circumstances. This 1s my award. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


G. PALIT, G. PALIT, 
Judge. Judge, Fifth Industrial Tribunal.

1. The representatives of the Company and the workmen met at a 
meeting on 15th October 1958 to negotiate for settlement of all the disputes 
pending between the Company and the workmen. After detailed discussions 
a negotiations between the parties, it has been mutually settled as 
follows ::— 


(a) The existing quantum of salary or remuneration of the workmen 
will continue and there will be no incremental pay scale. 


(b) The Company may, in consideration of the merits of the permanent 
workmen and, in its absolute discretion, give increase in wages 
varying from thirteen naye paise to twenty-five naye paise with 
effect ivan 186 November 1958. The Company may also in its 
discretion give temporary workers such increment as it may be 
found possible or warranted. The Company may also confirm 
such of the temporary workers as it may consider necessary to 
retain them in service. It also will have the right and discri- 
tion to discontinue with the services of such of the temporary 
workers as in its discretion may be declared surplus. 


(c) It is also agreed and: confirmed that the dispute under four issues 
pending before the Fifth Industrial Tribunal have been amicably 
settled and finally concluded between the parties.

Act, 1947, the industrial dispute between Messrs. Royal Calcutta 
Golf Club, Tollygunge, Calcutta-33, and their workmen represented 
by the Royal Calcutta Golf Club Muazdoor Union, 48 Dharamtalla 
Street, Calcutta-33, regarding the matters specified in the schedule tu the 
Third Industrial Tribunal, constituted under section 7A of the Industrial 
isputes Act, 1947, by notification No. 808-I.R./IR/3A-2/57, dated the 
1111) March 1967, for adjudication. 


2. After usual summons the parties put in appearance and filed their 
written statements. Then after addition of issue No. 4 the parties filed 
supplementary written statements. The pleadings were completed on 10th 
April 1958. The parties were thereafter directed to file lists of documents. 
Then after adjournments the dispute was heard and award was reserved. 


3. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference after amendment are as follows :— 


(1) Wages and Dearness Allowance for all categories of workmen. 
(2) Working hours for kitchen staff and bearers of the club. 


(3) Whether the Management was justified in discharging the eight 
female workmen named below. To what relief are they entitled 


(1) Sm. Bala, (i) Shrimati Subash II, (iii) Sm. Makam, 
(iv) Sm. Johora, (v) Sm. Noni, (vi) Sm. Subash را‎ 
(vii) Sm. Mongla, (viii) Sm. Satya. 


(4) Puja Bonus for 1956. 
Decision. 


The Royal Caleutta Golf Club (hereafter called the club) is a club which 
lins as its object the promotion of the game of (Gjolf and affording to its 
Members the usual convenience of a Golf Club. According to the elub its 
actual effective membership varies between 600 and 700 and the total 
membership including life members and absent members is 1,239. The club 
has arrangement for supply to its Members on payment tea, snacks, break- 
fust and Junches on requisition but: not dinner. It also maintains a bar 
from which the members con have drinks on payment. According to the 
club, it has on its pay roll 102 employees of different categories. 


There had been an award in respect of an industrial dispute between the 
cub and their workmen represented by the Royal Calcutta Golf (lub 
Workers’ Union on 20th September 1948. Subsequently the present union 
—Royal Calcutta Golf Mazdoor Union (hereafter called the union) was 
formed. ‘The union on behalf of the workmen presented a Charter of 
Demands in 1955 but the Government declined to intervene on the ground 
that the existing conditions were unsatisfactory and intimated the union 
accordingly by its letter, dated 22nd June 1955 (Annexure A to club’s 
written statement). Thereupon the union filed a case in the High Court 
under Article 226 for redress but the case was dismissed. Then the union 
on the allegation that there has been change in the service conditions since 
the award, presented similar Charter of Demands as in 1955 to the Manage- 
10800 of the club on 24th October 1956 (Annexure A to union’s written 
statement and Ext. 1) with copy to the Labour Commissioner. Thereupon 
conciliation proceedings started. During the pendency of the conciliation 
proceedings, the Management of the club laid off 8 female coolies named in 
issue No. 3 with effect from 15th January 1957 with intimation that 
Permission to discharge them was being sought for from the authority

issue 2: The case of the union under this head is that the club employs 
the workers for 14 to 15 hours on Saturdays, Sundays and on all other 
holidays. The workmen have got no fixed hours of work either in a day 
or in a week. By this method the club wrongfully employs them to work 
equivalent to 1 to 2 men’s work without paying them extra wages. The 
union accordingly demands that the working hours should not exceed 8 hours 
a day and 48 hours in a week. 


The club denies that the workmen are employed for 14/15 hours a dav 
and pleads that the hours of work for kitchen staff and bearers are limited

uswilly attending on week days. There is so a negligible load of work for 
the staff during week days. The club submits that the hours of work uie 
not excessive and less than those laid down for employees covered by the 
Shops and Establishment Act. 


On giving careful consideration to the matter it does not appear that 
anv revision in the existing arrangement is required. The factory hours 
are not applicable to a club. Shops and Establishment Act has also no 
application to 1 club. In the absence of laws prescribing hours of work, 
the hours of work have to he regulated by various considerations such as 
conditions of work, hours of work in comparable industries, amount of

Issue 32 In the written statement before this Tribunal the union 
alleged that the 8 female workers named in this issue were workmen under 
the cluh doing work ax coolies for periods varying hetween 15 and 30 yeurs. 


৮ 


448 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 22, 1959 [Parr 1 


ue to presentation of Charter of Demands and dv(ivities of active members 
ot the union, the club Management became enraged and discharged the 
8 female workers on false and malicious grounds. The union accordingly 
prayed tor reinstatement with wages for the period of unemployment. 


The club denied charge of mala fide. It pleaded that it used to employ 
temporary female workers for certain jobs on the Course. For some yeurs 
it has been the endeavour of the club to abolish the system of employing 
temale workmen. This fact has been mentioned by Shri P. K. Sarkar in 
his award, dated 25th September 1948. The club in order to obtain 
maximum efficiency of work changed the then existing system of work 
which rendered the female workers concerned redundant to requirements. 
In the circumstances the club submitted that the discharge of the femule 
workers was not illegal and was carried out in the interest of the club 
work and was a normal function and, therefore, wholly justified. 


On the evidence and circumstances, I am unable to accept the union’s 
case that the discharge was by way of victimisation or mala fde. It appears 
from the award, dated 20th September 1948, of Shri P. K. Sarkar that the 
club even then expressed its desire to do away with the system of employing 
the female coolies. Jt further appears that in pursuance of the said policy 
the club discharged on 23rd January 1948, five female covlies, namely, 
Kusum, Tarangini, Saraswati, Rani and Kiron out of 20 female coolies in 
its employ at the time, and that union’s demand for their reinstatement 
could not be acceded to by the Tribunal of Shri P. K. Sarkar as the discharge 
took place subsequent to the date of reference and as the club took the plea 
of want of jurisdiction of the Tribunal in the matter. It further appeurs 
that out 01 the remaining 15 female coolies, 7 lett employment of the club 
leaving only the 8 female coolies on the work. According to Satyabula 
(P.W. 3) they were the only 8 female coolies who were working im the 
club for last 5/6 vears. So the case of the union that because of presentation 
of Charter of Demands which it has already been noted, took place on 24th 
October 1956, these 8 female workers were discharged, cannot be sustained. 
Thotgh the Secretary of the union P.W. 1 said that out of the 8 female 
workers, three—Satyabala (P.W. 3), Noni Bala (P.W. 6) and Subhas No. 1 
have heen members of the executive committee of the union, P.W. 3 und 
P.W. 4 who have heen examined before this Tribunal, did not claim to have 
had any union activities. The evidence of the Secretary (P.W. 1) that 
those 3 female workers had discussion regarding the Charter of Demands 
with the Management subsequent to presentation of the Charter of Demands 
and also during conciliation proceedings, is given direct lie by Satyabala 
herself (P.W. 3). Satyabala admitted that she had never occasion to 
discuss about workers’ demand with the Management. She also admitted 
that she had no quarrel with the Management. P.W. 6 Nonibala did not 
impute any motive to the Management or made any complaint agaist the 
club. It will, therefore, appear that the discharge in question was made in 
normal and natural course in pursuance of a policy adopted long ago and 
that there was no lack of bona fides on the part of the Management of the 
club in the matter. There has been no irregularity or illegality in 
the matter either as contended by the union during hearing. During 
the pendency of the conciliation proceedings there had been no discharge 
but only lay-off from 15th } anuary 1957 by the notice, dated 14th 
January 1957 (Ext. 2 series). Section 33, as it then stood, did not attract 
o lay-off. Besides in the notice of lay-off the club gave the reasons and 
stated that permission was being obtained from the authority concerned to 
discharge them (vide Ext. 2 series). It will, therefore, appear that there 
was no irregularity or illegality in the matter. Subsequently after the 
conciliation proceedings were over, the club discharged the wofkers frow 


1970 11] TUE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 22, 1969 449: 


a a উল 
ঠা April 1957 (vide Ext. 3 series). So the club did not violate the 
progision of section 98. 


Now the question is whether the discharge is justified. The reayon 
assigned for the same in the notice (Ext, 2 series) is that the workers have 
heen rendered surplus to the requirements due to the abolition of the 
evstem of work on which they have been employed as 8150 on account of 
the fact that there is no other alternative work to offer to them at the time. 
When the work has been continuing and when the anid work is being carried 
on by male workers, it cannot be said thut the female workers became 
redundant to the requirements. The club no doubt adopted a policy of not 
employing female workmen but these cun have application in fairness dnly 
when vacancies arise in future and uot with reference to those already in 
employment. There will be no justification tor retrenchment of the existing 
workmen if the work on which they are employed does not cease to exist but 
contimues. To have the same work done by male workers in replacement 
of female workers already in employment is not the same thing as change 
in the system of work but only a change in the personnel. This, however, 
is not permissible. When the work is there, there would be no justification 
to replace the female workers by male workers even assuming that the inale 
workers would be more efficient. When the female workers were doing 
the work for these long years, they cannot be sacked to make room for male 
workers under the cover, of abolition of system 01 work. When it is a case 
of retrenchment us per notice of the club, if has also obligation to follow 
the principles of “last come, first go’’ on the basis of category irrespective: 
of sex of the workers. In the circumstances, ] am unable to uphold the 
retrenchment. The discharge by way ot retrenchment is accordingly held 
to be unjustified. I, therefore, direct the club to reinstate the workmen 
with continuity of service on their reporting for duty within 15 days froin 
the date of publication of the award. As, however, there has been no 
mala fide on the part of the Management of the club in the matter, and as 
the club has not the benefit of the service of the workmen, I do not saddle 
the club with hahility for full wages during the period of unemployment 
of the workmen. The workmen are allowed 1/3rd of their total emoluments 
for the period. The club is directed to make the payment within a mouth 
from the date the award becomes enforceable. 


Issue 4: This issue was added subsequently on 18th September 1957. 
Thereupon the parties were directed to file supplementary written state- 
ments which they did. The issue as referred to speaks of Puja Bonus for 
the year 1956. In the Charter of Demands presented on 24th October 1956 
(Ext. 1) on the basis of which reference has been made, the union also 
claimed such Puja Bonus equivalent to 2 months’ pay. So the bonus 
elaimed and referred to is one for customary bonus as distinguished from 
bonus out of available surplus os per Full Bench Formula. Union’s claim 
at the hearing for a bonus out of profit for the year 1956 cannot, therefore, 
be sustained within the scope of the issue referred to. Claim for customary 
bonus can be upheld only on 118 being a condition of service. To ruise an 
inference of its being a condition of service, the puysment must have been 
made for a long period and continuously, especially in years of loss. The 
(20707) has no evidence to prove so. According to the club it is not a 
condition of service of workmen in ita employ. P.W. 2 Charu Chandra Das 
admitted that what they used to 1eccive as bonus waa 0 variable amount 
paid as Christmas Bonus between March and August. He could not, how- 
ever, say the source of the money paid as bonus and whether it was a 
bakshis paid by members during Christmas time. P.W. 4 Md. Mostab 
admitted that it was bakshis in connection with Christmas every ০7. 
Hira evidence also reveals that the said bakshis was paid in 1957, apparently 


450 THE CALCUITA GAZETTE, JANUARY 22, 1949 [Parr I 
লিলি জলজ 
the bakshis relatng to Christmas of 1956. The evidence also reveals that 
the said bakshis is not paid to all the employees but only to the mewbers 
of the house staff. I, therefore, accept the evidence of P.W. 1 and find 
that it is not a condition of service. The claim for Puja Bonus muot, 
therefore, fail.

|. Is the dismissal of Shri Satish Chandra Jagnik justified? To what

AWARD 


This is a case arising out of alleged illegal dismissal of one Shri Satish 
Chandra Jagnik previously employed in Messrs. Shree Ambika Jute Mills 
Litd., Belur, Howrah (hereinafter described as the Company for the sake 
of brevity). 

The Union’s case in short is that Shri Satish Chandra Jagnik entered 
the service of the Company in April 1951 as a lapping clerk in the Finish- 
ing Department where he continued as such up to June 1954 and then in 
July following he was transferred to the Mechanical Department and was 
asked to work both in A and B shifts in which capacity he worked up to 
12th July 1956. Ordinarily the Management had to maintain two clerks, 
one for A shift and another for B shift, but during the material period from 
July 1954 to July 1956 this clerk worked single-handed and managed al! 
the clerical works of both the shifts. Accordingly the workman insisted on 
having his overtime wages for which he eventually incurred the displeasure 
of the Manager though the Manager in the beginning gave him assurance 
that overtime wages would be paid to him. Suddenly on 181 August 7 
the Manager served a charge sheet on this workman on false allegations of 
(1) indiscipline and insubordination, (2) negligence and enrelessness in 
work and (8) excess payment and loss to the property of the Company. 
The workman gave his reply, dated 3rd August 1957, contradicting the 
allegations. Thereupon an ex-parte enquiry was held into the charges and 
he was dismissed by order, dated 13th June 1957, and this dismissal is 
contrary to the Standing Order, rule 14(c) of the Company. To add_ to 
that, the Companv brought a false charge against him and prayed for prose- 
۴٦ہ‎ under section 59 of the Factories Act and this prosecution was 
nothing but a counterblast to {he workman’s demand for overtime wages. 
Ou toese allegations the Union seeks the reinstatement of the workman 
together with other reliefs as he is found entitled 10. 


The Company, on the other hand, in its written statement denies the 
material allegations in the written stutement of the Union and contends, 
inter alia, that the conduct of this workman was most unsatisfactory, 
perfunctory and much below the standard of efficiency during the period 
particularly from July 1954 to July 1956 and he was a habitual late comer 
since November 1954 and the Management received innumerable complaints 
for his groas negligence resulting in severe monetary loss of the Company 
and several warnngs were given to him but to no effect. The Manngement 
out of compassion in view of the age of the petitioner did not take any 
drastic steps against him but allowed him to attend as o special mensure 
from 7 a.m. to 12 noon and from 3 to 6 p.m., and the Company asserts that 
thia concession allowed hy the Management is now being utilised by the 
workman only to set up a 18186 plea of working in double shifts to base 
thereon his false claim to overtime wages. The Company had no mala fides 
in the matter, nor did the Company adopt any unfair labour practice. The

Management therefore duly charge-sheeted him and dismissed him on 


enquiry in the interests of discipline. The Management therefore contends 
that this workman is entitled to no relief whatsoever. 


Decision 

There is no dispute in this case that the workman was originally appoint- 
ed as a lapping clerk in the finishing department of the Company in 1951 
where he worked till sometime in 1954 and then he was transterred to the 
Mechanical Department in July 1954 where he worked till July 1956. The 
whole trouble between the parties centres round the allegation of non- 
yayment of overtime wages which the workman claims on the basis ot his 
দি worked in both A and B shifts. Admittedly, A shift in the Mulls 
continues from 6 a.m. to 11 a.m. and then again from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. It 
is common ground that to suit the convenience of this particular workman, 
the Management compassionately due to his old age changed the timings 
of his attendance from ¢ a.m. to 12 noon and from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m. 
Admittedly, each shift is for 8 hours a day. The gravamen of the griev- 
ance of this workman is that he worked in both the shifts single-handed but 
he wars not granted any overtime allowances though he was given an 
assurance that he would have it. The Company’s case on the other hand as 
already referred to above, is that he worked partly during the ordinary 
timings of A and B shifts as he attended from 7 a.m. to 12 noon and from 
3 p.m. to 6 p.m. which he utilises as a basis tor his false claim to overtinre 
allowance. [t is evident that the special timings during which the 
Management agreed to allow this workman to attend دراو‎ overlapped 
the timings of both A and B shifts, In support of his claim the workman 
is under a delusion that the attendance register supports him. Curiously 
enough, there is not a single application on his part to show that he ever 
specifically demanded overtime wages for working in both A and B shifts 
extending over 16 hours a day. If his main grievance were non-payment 
of overtime allowance, we would expect that there should he at least one 
application in writing during the long two years to show his demand for 
the same. The workman in support of his claim examined one Shri Ram 
Chandra Roy whose evidence does not really help him hecause this witness 
(P.W. 3) was a workman in the factory of the mechanical department of 
the Company, thereas the workman concerned was working in the office and 
thai the witness had no personal knowledge about what works the workman 
concerned did and what works he did not do. Towards the end of his cross- 
examination this witness hroke down when he admitted that the workman 
Satish Jagnik used to work both in A and B shifts because he found the 
workman at work at 6 a.m. and found him also at work at 12 noon which 
Ix not inconsistent with the special timings of his attendance in the Milla. 
Thus I hold that the workman has not been able to prove that he worked 
চা সপ for both A and B shifts during the period from July 1954 to 
uly 1956.

The second charge sheet relates mainly to allegation of the workman’s 
falsely and maliciously complaining to the Chief Inspector of Factories 
that he was not being paid overtime wages and he was culled upon to show 
cause why he should not be prosecuted under section 59 of the Factories 
Act. The workmun, however, showed cause as per Ext.-F, dated 2nd 
August 1956, and Ext.-F1, dated 14th June 1957, and his replies ure 
substantial denials of the allegations made in the charge sheets and asser- 
tions that he served very satisfactorily and that he was never late in 
attendance and that he never issued any unauthorised gate passes and that 
he worked for 16 hours a day for both the shifts. The Manager Shri Sunil 
Krishna Ghose (0.P.W. 1.) in his deposition before the Court has stated 
that he duly enquired into the allegations and was satisfied of the charges 
levelled against this workman and ultimately passed orders dismissing him 
from. service with effect from 17th June 1957. One thing that strikes me 
in this case is that there are no written proceedings of enquiry into the 
charges. The Company has, however, produced evidence both oral and 
documentary in this case on the basis of which the Court hae duly consi- 
dered the charges and on an independent enquiry held by this Court which 
the Court is entitled to do (vide the case of Vithal Shetty and Chokshi Silk 
Mills) reported in 1956 ٢:ا...‎ Vol. I, pages 132-158) safely pronounce 
thai the Company was quite justified in passing the orders of dismissal in 
this case and that no prejudice appears to have heen caused to the workman 
by the absence of any written proceedings of — enquiry. 
The absence of written proceedings of enquiry in cnses 
where the workman is not prejudiced in his defence does 
not effect materially the result of the enquiry. This view has been pro- 
nounced in the case of Assam 011 Company vy. Appalsami, reported in 1954 
L.L.J., Vol. II, page 323, at page 233 where it is laid down as follows: — 


“Rules of procedure are only handmaids of justice and any departure 
from such rules of procedure laid down in the Standing Orders 
would not be material, unless it is shown that the workman 
concerned had materially been prejudiced by the aduption of an 
irregular procedure.”’ 


This case has been referred to in the recent case of Chunilal 1). Singrani 
and বি S. T. Undertaking, Bombay, reported in 1958 1..1,.J 7 Vol. ا‎ 
page 699.

As regards the allegations of his working in both A and B shifts the evidence

by any element of mala fides or unfair labour practice or perverse finding

As regards the punishment, there are decided cases to show 11780 the 
punishment is in the sole discretion of ihe Management as laid down in the 
case of Caltex (India) Ltd., Appellant, +. I. Feimandes and another, 
পপ reported in A.I.R. 1947 9.0. 326 wherein it is lnid down as 
follows :— 


“Once the Industrial Tribunal came to the conclusion in the present 
case that the enquiry which was conducted by the appellants 
was fair and no principles of natural justice had been violated 
in the conduct of the enquiry and the appellants bona fide came 
to the conclusion that dismissal was the only punishment which 
should be meted out by them to the first respondent, the Lndus- 
trial Tribunal had no power to substitute another punishment 
for the one which was sought to he meted out.’’ 


The punishment is also well called for by his past bad record of service 
and warnings given to him in vain (vide the yuling reported in 1955 ۰ 
Vol. Il, page 348, Tungabhadra Industries Lid. and 1), Ranga Reddi). 


In the circumstances, the punisament awarded by the Company to the 
workman, having regard to his past bad record of service, stands and the 
Court cannot interfere with the punishment. 


To sum up, the Manager rightly found the workman guilty of misconduct 
as per clause 14(c)(vi) (habitual late attendance) and (ix) (habitual negli- 
gence or nezlect of work) of the Standing Orders of the Company and thus 
fiis dismissal is found justified and he is found entitled to no relief.

Considering all the circumstances as mentioned above, I have no doubt 
that Ext. A, Est. B(1), Ext. D(1), xt. C and Ext. F which are all con- 
tempuraneous documents show that Shn Raphael Kuzur and his four gom- 
panions were not dismissed by the Management and driven away from the 
Garden, as alleged by the Union, but that there was an allegation against 
these five persons that they assaulted Sukda and Janglu in connection with 
the trouble over Shri Saniaro JI, daughter of Shri Muta Munda and on 
account of this allegation, there were mass meetings of the workers along 
with the members of the Works Committee on 18th August 1954 and 29th 
August 1954, in which the general body of the workers expressed serious 
resentment at their conduct and wanted them to leave the Garden forth- 
with. The evidence further shows that these five persons begged for mercy, 
but not being excused, took fmght and left the Garden forthwith with the 
members of their families, being the rest of the workmen mentioned in the 
orde: of reference. Before they left, they received all their dues from the 
Munagement, as shown by Ext. G to Ext. G(4). All the workmen includ- 
ing Shri Raphael Kuzur signed on their receipts. 11 these workmen hail 
been driven away by the Management by force, nothing prevented them 
fror refusing to sign on the receipts, Ext. G series. It appears from the 
evidence on record that the Management tried to help these workers as far 
ae practicable, and taat is why they supplied them with the transport of a 
lorry to take them away from the Garden at their request. The evidence 
on record clearly justifies the truth of the Company’s case on the matter of 
the termination of the services of the workmen in question. The evidence 
01 Shri Raphael Kuzur and Shri Somra Ornon are unworthy of credit, in 
view of the fact that they tried to suppress salient facts which they had to 
admit under stress of cross-examination. The learned Advocate for the 
Union argued that the story of the existing Works Committee was incredi- 
ble and laid emphasis on the evidence of 0.P.W. 1 Dr. Samar Sinha Roy 
whe said that the election to the Works Committee was done by show of 
hands in a meeting and no voters list was prepared for the purpose. 
0.۲۰۷۰ 2 Shri Dharani Prosad Bhowmick stated that a voters list was 
prepared for the Works Committee election and copies were sent to the 
Government. The election to the Works Committee is to be done under 
Rule 2(A) of the Bengal Industrial Disputes Rules, 1947, and there are 
elaborate provisions Jnaying down the procedure for holding the election. 
The election is made hy a Returning Officer appointed by the Tabour Com- 
missioner of the Government of West Bengal. In the face of the Govern- 
ment notification, Ext. K, dated 28th December 1957, publishimg the names 
of the members constituting the Works Committee of the Ethelbari Tea 
Estate, these questions on the procedure for the election are not relevaut 
to the present proceeding, inasmuch as, the present enquiry is not for 
setting aside the election on the ground of illegal procedure in the election. 
In view of the notification, Ext, K, it is to be presumed that the Official Act 
of the holding of the election was done according to law. This plea is not 
also supported by evidence in view of the fact that both the witnessea for 
the Union, in spite of pre-verifications, admitted the existence of the Works 
Committee. They also admitted that they were members of the Works 
Committee. Any adverse allegation as to the existence and functioning of 
the Works Committee in this Ten Garden in 1954, is, therefore, unworthy 
of acceptance und should be, and 18 rejected. 


The evidence on record does not support the plea that Raphael ۰٣ 
anc his companions made an attempt to set up a Union as claimed or they 
had any union activity in retaliation whereof the management discharged 
them from service. The evidence showa that the management tried to have 
the matter between Rapheel Kuzur’s group and another opposing group 


PaatI] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 22, 1959 467 


of workmen concerning the assault on Sukda and Janglu, settled and 
formed a sub-committee for that purpose. This fact explains why no 
charge-sheet was given to Raphael Kuzur and his companions and no 
enquiry was made on their conduct. The evidence on record proves beyond 
doubt that the termination of service of the workmen in question was not 
the result of any victimisation or malafide vonduct on the part of the 
management and also that the workmen in question abandoned ×ط‎ 
employment under the Company following two meetings of the workmen, 
along with the Works Committee. The fact that there was silence over the 
matter for more than two years, and the claim on these two issues was 
raised along with the claim of bonus in issue No. 3 at the end of 1956, takes 
away from the bonafides of the Union’s story. It appears that all the work- 
10161) have settled down in other gardens but Raphael Kuzur has been draw- 
ing 0, much less remuneration than he used to do at Ethelbari. In view of 
all circumstances and the evidence on record as discussed above, I do not 
find that the story of the Union as to the termination of the services of the 
12 workinen mentioned in issue No. 1 is worthy of acceptance. That being 
so, if is decided that’ the termination of services of the workers mentioned 
in Issue No. 1, being (1) Shri Raphael Kuzur, (2) Shri Muta Munda, (3) 
Shri Ram Munda, (4) Shri Palhad Kherwar, (5) Shri Mahali Munda, (6) 
Shri Saniaro, (7) Shri Saniaro IL, (8) Shri Sanicharoa, (9) Shri Karmi and 
10) Shri Biran, was justified. The Management states that Shri Balku 
and Shri Sudhu were not their workmen and in view of the decision of the 
15886 No. 1, the question as to whether they were workers in the Garden 
does not really arise. Issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. It is clear that 
in the circumstances, the question of entitlement to any relief or compensa- 
tion for the workmen mentioned in Issue No. 1 does not arise and Issue No. 
॥ 18 answered accordingly. 


issue NO. 3: It appears from Ext. 6 that Shri Raphael Kuzur received 
the bonus for 1958. As his service was terminated at the end of August 
1954, he 18 entitled to bonus for 1954 pro rata for the period of his service 
during the year. The representative of the Company stated before me that 
the Company was willing to pay honus for 1954 pro rata according to the 
Company’s Bonus Scheme to Shri Raphael Kuzur, because the other 
members of the staff of the Garden got bonus according to the Company's 
scheme. It is awarded that Shri Raphael Kuzur shall get bonus according 
ly the Company’s Scheme pro rata for the period of his service in 1954. 
This bonus shall be paid according to the same scheme on which the other 
members of the clerical staff were paid. 


As to the four members of the sub-staff, being Shri Muta Munda, Shri 
Ram Munda, Shri Palhad Kherwar and Sari Mahali Munda, they shall get 
bonus for 1958 and 1954 on the same srheme as the other members of the 
subordinate staff were paid for these years. 


As to the payment of bonus to the other workmen, being mazdoors, the 
Company is willing to pay them bonus ez-gratia according tu the scheme of 
payment to the other workmen for 1953 and 1954. It is awarded that the 
Company shall pay as ez-gratia to these workmen bonus according to the 
Scheme on which other workers were paid bonus in 1953 and 1954. The 
entitlement to bonus of the sub-staff and the mazdvors will vary according 
lo the period of their work according to the scheme of bonus payment and, 
therefore, the question wether Shri Balku and Shri Sudhu were workmen 
snd put in any work during the relevant period does not really arise. If 
they did not do any work, they will not be entitled to any bonus. If they 


468 THE OAJCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 22, 1909 a I 


really did any work, they. will he entitled to some bonus according to the 
cheme of bonus payment, The Scheme of bonus payment for 1953 and 
19): on which payments are to be made to the subestaff and the workers 
is the Delhi Bonus Agreement, dated 8th January 1956, and the other 
workers of these categories were also paid bonus on this scheme. 
This Issue is accordingly answered.

DEPARTMENT OF LOCAL SELF- 
GOVERNMENT AND PANCHAYATS 


NOTIFICATION 


No. G697/M.2A-4/69.—27th January 19459.— 
Whereas in the opinion of the Governor, the 
affairs of the South Dum Dum Munivipality, in 
the district of 24-Parganas, wre not properly 
managed ; 


And whereas the Governor considers it desirable 
in the public interest to declare that the said muni- 
cipality shall have un Executive (Officer for the 
period hereinafter mentioned ; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred by sub-section (1) of section G7A of the 
Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 (Bengal Act XV of 
1932), the Governor is pleased to declare that the 
said municipality shall have an Executive Officer 
for a period of two yeurs with effect from the date 
of uppointment of such an officer. 


2. In exercise of the powers conferred by sub- 
sections (2) and (3) of section G7A of the said Act, 
the Governor is further pleased hereby tu appoint 
Shri Amulya Kumar Hoy, retired Wub-Deputy, 
Collector, to be the Executive Officer of the South 
Dum Dum Municipality, in the district of 24-Par- 
ganas, referred to above and to direct that the 
Executive Officer shall, during the period of his 
office, exercise and perform the powers and duties 
vested in the Commissioners of the said munici- 
pality whether at a meeting or otherwise, by 
clauses (i), (12) and (iii) of sub-section (2) of sec~ 
tion 69 and by sections 112, 129, 180, 131, 156, 
198, 140, 141, 142, 154, 155 except sub-section (3), 
156, 167, 159, 160, 161, 162, 163, 178 and 189 of 
the said Act and the power of the said Commis- 
sioners to grant leave to their officers and servants 
under the rules framed by them in exervise of the 
hited conferred on them by section 75 of the said 

ct. 


By order of the Governor, 
A. NIYOGI, Jt. Secy.

The manner in which the Committee will discharge its duties is as 
follows :— 

The members will not visit the hospitals individually, the Committee 
will form itself into groups of not less than three members, each 
group in turn will, according to a roster to be kept for the 
purpose, visit the hospital on a fixed day and at a fixed time in 
each month. In addition to these visits at fixed times the 
members will pay unexpected visits to the hospitals. Members 
while paying surprise visit should on arrival at the hospitals 
iminediately contact the Superintendent and in his absence his 
Deputy before entering the wards. If all the three members of 
the group are not present, the remaining members can go round 
without the absentee or absentees, as the case may be. The 
members constituting the group should inspect the internal 
arrangements and offer such suggestions regarding the 
administration of the institution as they think proper. 


A visitors’ book will be kept in the hospitals in which the recom- 
mendations of the Committee will be recorded. The Superin- 
tendent will note on the margin the action taken دہ‎ each 
recommendation with any other remarks or explanations that 
he may wish to offer. He will transmit a copy of the entries 
without delay to the Director of Health Services, West Bengul, 
for consideration. The Director of Health Services will tuke 
such further action us may seem necessary and will bring to the 
notice of Government any matter which he thinks sufficiently 
important. 


The Committee as a whole will meet at least once a quarter, review 
the feport of the visiting groups and discuss the remedial 
measures adopted. The Superintendent of the Medical College 
Hospitals should attend the meetings of the Visiting Committec.

action taken or proposed to be taken on the points raised in those 


resolutions. 


The members will hold office for three years or until the 6১1 


reconstitution of the Committee.

the hospitals during three successive months without sufficient 
reason will automatically cease to be a member, aud (tovernment

should be submitted by the Superintendent to Government onve 
every quarter for noting the numes of habitual absentees.

Subject: Crant of advance to Central Covernment employees on the eve of 
important festivals. 


Reference: Finunce Ministry Oftice Memorandum No. 16-C(16)-E. LIA) { 7, 
dated the 20th December 1957, and Office Memorandum No. F. 16-005)- 
15110801685 dated the 5th September 1958. 


The undersigned ia directed to state that the President is pleased to 
decide that Ministries/Qffices of the Government of India may sanction 
udvances on the eve of important festivals to their non-gazetted employees 
on the following terms and conditions :— 


(i) The amount of advance will be Rs. 75 or one month’a basic pay 
as defined under Fundamental Rule 9(21)(a)()), whichever 1s 
لد‎ 


(ii) The advance will be recovered in not. more than four equal monthly 
instalments, the first instalment commencing with the next 
month’s pay bill, i.e., the pay bill of the month following that 
in which the advance ia drawn. The amount of each instalment 
shall be rounded off to the nearest rupee, any balance being 
recovered in the last instalment. 


(111) The advance may be granted to non-gazetted Central Government 
servants in receipt of hasic pay not exceeding Ra. 300 per month 
(including similar categories 0 staff in Industrial Establishments 
under the Gfovernment of India). The concession is also admis- 
sible to the work-charged staff who are entitled to pension or Con- 
tributory Provident Fund benefits but not to the staff paid from 
contingencies. 


(iv) The advance should not he granted to temporary staff who are not 
likely to contimue in service for a period of at least six months 
beyond the month in which the ndvance is drawn. 


(v) The advance is admissible only to those on duty or on leave on 
avernge pay or earned leave on full pay at the time the advance 
is drawn. 

(vi) The advance will he admissible only on one ocension in a calendar 
year for members of each community serving in ane establishment. 
More than one occasion may, however, be fixed for a community, 
if the competent authority is satisfied that in his opinion it is 
deairnble to do so taking into aceount the staff ৪ of 
his estublishment. The ‘tcompetent authority” for the purpose 
of fixing the festival occasions will he the Head of Department / 
Industrial Katablishment concerned. Such authorities may fix 
the festival occasions after taking into consideration the impor- 
tance attached locally to such festivals and in consultation with 
recoguised associations of staff where such exist.

19. (1) Not less than 44 days before the election day the Election 
Officer shall fix for the nomination of candidates a date which shall not be 
less than 35 days before the election day. On or before the date of nomina- 
tion so fixed every candidate for election shall cause to be delivered at the 
municipal office between the hours of 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. to such person as 
may be authorised in this behalf by the Election Officer a nomination pauper 
in Form B annexed to these rules. 


۱ (2) No nomination paper shall be valid unless it is duly filled in and 
signed and unless it is accompanied by a receipt for the deposit of the amount 
required by section 25 of the Act. 


(3) Not less than 32 days before the election day the Election Officer 
shall publish a notice in Form C annexed to these rules at the municipal 
office, fixing the time at and the date on which the nomination papers shall 
be scrutinised by him, such date being not less than 26 days before the 
date fixed for the election. 


(4)(a) At the time and on the date so fixed, the Election Officer shall, 
at the office of the municipalily, scrutinise all nomination papers in the 
presence of the candidates or their agents if they appear, and shall register 
as candidates all those whose nomination papers are found to be valid. 


(b) A nomination paper which is liable to be rejected on the ground of 
any irregularity in respect of the nomination paper, shall not affect the 
validity of the nomination of the candidate if he been duly nominated 
by means of another nomination paper in respect of which there is no 
irregularity. 


(৫) No’ nomination paper shall he rejected on the ground of alight 
technical defects such as the wrong spelling of a name or description of the 
ward so long as the intention is clear, or on the ground of any disparity 
between the signature of any person and his name as appearing in the 
electoral roll ne the identity of such person is satisfactorily established. 


(0) On completion of the scrutiny of nominations, the Election Officer 
shall forthwith examine symbols selected by the candidates and, if such 
symbols are found to conflict with each other, he shall allocate symbols in 
conformity as far as possible with the wishes of the candidates and if neces- 
sary by lot, and his decision in this respect shall be final. If, in any 
particular ward, the number of candidates whose nomination papers are 
found valid exceeds the number of symbols specified in Schedule A, the 
Election -Officer shall, in assigning symbols in the manner hereinbefore 
prescrihed, allocate them also out of the list of additional symbols spevified 
in Schedule B and his decision shall be final. Each candidate or his agent 
shall at the same time be informed of the symbol assigned to such candidate 
and shall be given a specimen thereof. The Election Officer shall then 
prepare a list of valid nominations indicating therein the symbol assigned 
to each candidate. 


(5) Not less than 25 days before the election day the Election Officer shall 
publish at the municipal office a list of the candidates registered under 
clause (a) of sub-rule (4) indicating therein the symbol assigned to each 
candidate. These candidates shall be deemed to he registered as such from 
the date of publication of the list.

By order No, 4989-1. R./IR 11157219197. dated the 19th December 1957, 
دہ‎ amended by order No. 834-1.R./IR/11L-279/57, dated the 7th March 
1958, the Gtovernment of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred 
under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial dispute 
between Mesara. Calcutta Clinical Research Association Ltd., 6 Chowringhee 
Road, Caleutta-13, and ita unit office at 10 Rowdon Street, Calcutta-16, and 
their workmen represented) by Calcutta Clinical Research Association 
Masdoor Union, 1 Jov Bhattacharjee Lane, Caleutta-3, regarding the matters 
specified in the schedule, to the Third Industral Tnbunal constituted under 
section 14 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, by notification No. 808-T.R. / 
18 /3A-2, 57, dated the 1111) Moreh 1957, for adjudication. 


2, After usual summons the parties put in appearance and filed their 
written statements. The plendings were completed on 28th February 1958. 
The parties were thereafier directed to file lists of documents. Then after 
inspections the dispute was heard and award was reserved. 


3. The matters of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference are as follows: 


(1) Dearness allowance. 
(2) Puja Bonus fur 1957. 


872 E CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 29, 1959 [Parr I 


(3) Whether the management was justified in discharging Sm. Sudha 
Dutta? What relief is she entitled to? 


Decision 

Messrs, Calcutta Clinical Research Association Jitd. (hereafter called 
the Company) has its factory at 6 Chowringhee Road and unit office at 
10 Rowdon Street. The Company employs about 63 workers 28) these 
establishments. Calcutta Clinical Research Association Mazdoor Union 
(hereafter called the Union) on behalf of the workmen submitted a charter 
of demands on different dates. Thereupon conciliation proceedings started 
and as no settlement was possible the disputes were referred to thia tribunal 
for adjudication on 19th December 1957. Thereafter there was an amend- 
ment on 7th March 1958 whereby the unit office at 10 Rowdon Street was 
also added. Now let us consider the issues separately. 


Issue 15 The workmen of these two establishments drawing salary up 
to Rs. 150 per month have been getting dearness allowance at the flat rate 
of Rs. 90 per month on the basis of the award, dated 17th March 1950, 
between the parties published in the Calcutta Gazette: Ewtraordinary, dated 
19th April 1950. The Uuion demands dearness allowance at the rate of 
Its. 40 per month for these workmen on the ground of rise in the cost of 
hving index since the award in 1950. The Company opposes the claim on 
the ground that it has no financial capacity to bear any additional burden 
in this respect. Unlike minimum wages, dearness allowance must be 
related to the capacity of the employer to pay. In the present case tho 
balance sheets ৬৭ গান the Company produced from 1950 to 1958 (Ext. E 
series) go to show that the financial position of the Company is anything 
but satisfactory. It appears that during the lust three years the Company 
incurred losses year after year—Rs. 39,670 in the year ended 31st March 
1996 (Ext. 1), Rs. 2,565 in the year ended 3186 March 1957 (Ext. E2) and 
Ks. 17,843 1n the year ended 31st March 1958 (Ext. E38). It further appears 
that the total debit balance up to the year ended 3lst March 1958 comes 
to Rs. 60,847. In the circumstances, although there has been rise in the 
eost of living index since the award in 1950 which would have otherwise 
justified an increment of Rs. 10 as dearness allowance as claimed, the 
tribunal is unable to uphold the claim in view of the financial position of 
the Company as revealed. Claim for increment in dearness allowance is 
accordingly rejected. 


issue 2: The bonus claimed according to both sides is not customary 
bonus but bonus out of profit payable at the time of Durga Puja. The 
fiuancial year of the Company is from April to March. The Union demanded 
bonus out of profit of the vear ended 815+ March 1956 (wide Annexures 1 to 
8), 1.e., the bonus payable on the eve of the Puja of 1956. The claim as 
aforesaid eannot he entertained on the basis of the issue as referred to which 
ls for the year 1957. Be that as it may, it has already been noted, that 
there was no profit either during the year ended 3let March 1956 or during 
(106 vear ended 9158 March 1957. Claim for bonus out of profit can he 
sustained only if there be available surplus after deduction of prior charges. 
In the present case no such question arises as there has been loss in both 
the successive years. The statement (Ext. 3) filed by the Union in support 
of the claim of bonus is useless having not been drawn up according to the 
Full Bench formula. The cliam for honus is accordingly rejected. 


issue 3: The facts, as I find, are as follows:— 


Shrimati Sudha Dutta had joined in the factory of the compauy سپ‎ 
6 Chowringhee Road on 2nd February 1944 (vide Ext. F). She worked 
there for five years and was thereafter transferred to the office of the Company 


pasar I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 29, 1959 573 
eee eee 


10 Rowdon Street in 1949 and was posted there until discharge on 
HOth July 1956 (vide P.W. 2 Shri Gouri Shonkayr, Prosad Roy). There was 
no protest to’the transter (vide P.W. 2). While attached to the office at 
10 Rowdon Street, she was granted maternity leave from 14th August 1952 
till 1156 January 1953. She was again granted leave on that account from 
17th August 1943 to the ۹4181 December 1953 (vide Ext. F and Annexure 0 
to the written statement of the Union). Shrimati Sudha Dutta admitted 
in croms-examination that she took leave from time to time on medical 
grounds. Ext. F also shows this. 


| In these circumstances, Shrimati Sudha Dutta again obtained maternity 
1076 tor three months from 17th January 1956 (vide P.W. 1 and Exts A 
and Al). The discharge certificate granted by the hospital (Ext. 1) shows 
that it was a normal delivery and that she was discharged from the hospital 
on 27th February 1956. On 21st March 1956 Shrimati Sudha Dutta applied 
for extension of leave on the ground of anaemia and general debility after 
child birth বি Exts. A2 and AS) and she got it. On the expiry of the 
leave she did not resume duty and she again applied for extension of leave 
on 2érd May 1956 and got the leave (ride Exts. A4 and A5). On 26th 
June 1996 she again applied for extension of leaye for two months from 
9nd June 1966 to 22nd 40746 1956 (vide Exts. AG and AY). She had 
“hus been on leave continuously on the ground of child birth and ill health 
4or about کتھ‎ months at the tume. The Company on receipt of the last 
application, dated 26th June 1956 (Ext. AG) admittedly wrote to her on 
bth July 1956 as per Annexure 4 to the Union’s written statement. 
‘Shiimati Sudha Dutta was informed by that letter that she was on leave 

r about six months from 17th January 1956 and the Company could not 
seep on setvice an employee like her whose poor health did not permit to 

eaume normal duties after so long a leave. The Company accordingly 
acted her application for extension and she was asked to resume duties 
ithin 7 day» trom the date of the letter, tailing which her employment 
sould cease (ride Ext, B and Annexure 4 to Union's written statement). 
Yu receipt of the saul letter Shrimati Sudha Dutta wrote to the Manager 
f the Company on 17th July 1906 intotming how 1 was not possible to 
sume duties so far on account of ill health and how she came down to 
Yhanbad for a change and how it was not possible to resume duties within 
days as usked for. In that letter she also claimed that the leave asked 
or wus due to her and she was entitled to the said leave within the scope 
f her service conditions and leave rules (Annexure 6 to the Union’s written 
tatement). The Company wrote in reply on 20th July 1956 (Annexure 6 
o Union's written statement). The Company contested the claim of 
1), Sudha Dutta thut leave asked for was due and that she was entitled 
v have it. The Company further pointed out to her how in the past she 
ook leave causing great disloration in carrving out the normal work of 
he Company. She was also told that no leave was due to her. The 
ompany accordingly informed her that it could not alter its previous 
ecision and accordingly discharged her from 20th July 1956 (vide 
mexure 6 to the Union’s written statement), On 27th July 1956 
m. Sudha Dutta acknowledged receipt of the letter terminating her employ- 
lent. In that letter ton she contested the Company's statement that no 
ave was due to her. She informed the Company that she would resume 
* soon as her attending physician advised her to do so (Annexure 7 to the 
nion’s written atatement). Then on 22nd August 1956 she came to the 
fhee at 10 Rowdon Street to resume duty but was not allowed to do so. 
u sth August 1956 she wrote to the Manager to inform her whether she 
ould be allowed to resume duty or not (Annexure & to the Union's written 
latement). On Ist September 1956 the Manager informed her that the 
lanagement was unable {o alter their decision and asked her to collect her 


574 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 29. 1959 [Parr ] 


শপ 


dues (Annexure 9 to Union’s written statement). On 8th Septethber 1956 
the President of the Union wrote to the Labour Commissioner seeking his 
intervention in the matter. 


The question which now arises is whether the discharge is justified. Ag 
the correspondences reveal, this is a case of discharge with notice on the 
ground of continued ill health as oppused to dismissal. Tho standing orders 
regulate the conduct of the parties and their conditions of service. Standing 
orders are framed under the Industrial (Kmployment) Standing Orders Act. 
In the present case the Company has no obligation under the said Act to 
roaintain standing orders and as a matter of tact, the Company had 
admittedly none at the time of discharge on 20th July 1946 (vide 1১. W. 1). 
The question has, therefore, to be judged on general principles. On the 
materials pluced before the Tribunal, it is unable to find that the discharge 
ig unjustified or mala fide. On her own thowing Sm. Sudha Dutta was on 
continued il] health 0061] discharge on 20th July 1956 and did not become 
fit to resuine duty before elapse of a month on 22nd August 1956. The leave 
account of the past period since she joined office on 10th August 1949 
(Ext. F) shows that in the past too she had similarly absented from time 
t» time much in excess of the leave due to her. In the circumstances, the 
action of the management to terminate her employment on 2011) July 0 
on the ground of continued ill health cannot be characterised as mala fide 
and unreasonable. It is a basic principle that the industry should 0 
efficiently managed. So, there must obviously be a limit in granting 
extension of leave. In the present case refusal of the employer to extend 
the leave further, cannot be said to be unreasunable. Though not invoked, 
[ also find no violation of the provisions either of the Bengal Maternity 
Benefit Act or of the Imployees’ State Insurance Act. She got leave more 
than the one admissible under the Maternity Benefit Act. Besides, to 
claim benefit under the said Act, she must have been employed in the 
factory of the employer from whom she claims maternity benefit for a period 
af iidt less than 9 months immediately preceding the day of child birth. 
In the present case Shrimati Sudha Dutta ceased to work in the factory 
Since 1949. As to the Employees’ State Insurance Act, her discharge took 
place after absence for a continuous period of 6 months. So, prema facié, 
there has been no violation of 116 provision of section 73 of the Act. 
Besides to invoke section 73 of the Act, the illness must be duly certified 
in accordance with the regulations. Regulation 54 shows the persons who 
are competent to issue medical certificates. As the medical certificates 
filed by Shrimati Sudha Dutta are not from the persons mentioned : 
regulation 54, section 73 is not also attracted. I, therefore, find nothin 
to interfere. As the case of discharge on the ground of continued ill healt 
has heen excluded from definition of ‘‘retrenchment’’ in section 2000) of the 
Industtial Disputes Act, the workmen cannot also cian retrenchment 
a It, therefore, follows that Shrimati Sudha Dutta is eutitled to no 
relief. 


This is my award.

Short recital of the dispute. 


The Management closed the factory with efféct from 20th September 
1958 vide its notice, dated 20th August 1958, and retrenched all the work- 
men. The dispute arose as to the justifiability of closure and payment of 
retrenchment benefit. The Company intended to pay retrenchment benefit 
to the workmen for the period of service with effect from ita last opening on 
24th February 1964 after the lockout in October 1953 and the workmen 
claimed retrenchment benefit for their period of service prior to that date 
and also thereafter. According to the Company the services of the workmen 
were newly started after the lockout of the factory in October 1953, where- 
as, according to the workmen, there was no break of their service, due ta 
anid lockout and subsequent agreement, dated 19th January 1954, between 
the Company and the workmen. As a result of this dispute the matter was 
referred to the Third Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, vide Government 
of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 4785-I.R./TR /11L-442 /58, 
dated 17th November 1958. 


Both the parties now amicably settle up the dispute and agree to the 
following terms and conditions :— 


(1) The Company withdraws its notice, dated 20th August 1958, regard- 
ing closure and decides to open the factory on Ist January 1909. 


(2) All the workmen, who were in service of the Company prior to 
closure on 20th September 1958 will remain in service without 
any break or prejudice of the service condition. 


(3) The period between 20th September 1958 and 818) December 1958 
will be treated as leave without wages to all the workmen. 


(4) The Company will start work for production of nibs and penholders 
for the present and the work for production of pencils will be 
started on or before Ist May 1959.

(5) The workmen, mentioned under Appendix ‘A’ will join work on 
Ist January 1969, and the others mentioned under Appendix 13) 
will join work on or betore lst May 1959 according to »the 
arrangement of the Company for the purpose. 


(6) The period between Ist January 1959 and 30th April 1959 or any 
part thereof, will be treated as leave without wages to the work-

(whose names are mentioned under Appendix ‘B’) according to

PRESENT: 
Sur G. PALIT, Judge, Fifth Industrial Tribunal, 


Present for the Company: Shri ১, K. Bose, counsel, Assisted by Shri K. Px

by Shri B. K. Bagchi, General Secretary of the Union. 


The originul reference out of which this case has arisen was made under 
(3.0). No, 6441-1.R./D/10L-116/56, dated 20th December 1956. 


AWARD 


It is the contention of the petitioner that he has been dismissed by the 
Company on 25th April 1958 without there being any fault on his part. 
He was given a charge-sheet on 3rd March 1958 and he gave a reply thereto 
on 4th March 1958. The petitioner contends that he had a standing 
instruction of the Finance Officer of the Company, whose car he used to 
drive that the said car No. WBE1532 would be in his residence ond the 
keys of the car should be left at the disposal of his wife. So, when at 
5-80 p.m. Colonel D. N. Sarma, the Security and Estate Officer, asked for 
the said car in the Cash Office, he merely told him just to ring up and 
contact with the wife of the aforesaid Finance Officer so that she might 
deliver the keys to the driver. He never acted in any insolent manner 
showing disregard to the Colonel. So, he has heen wantonly impleaded in. 
the present case, says the petitioner Munshi Sha. 


According to the management, Col. D. N. Sarma received a telephone 
message from Shri A. N. Vorah, the Secretary to the Chief Officer that a 
car was immediately required for taking the Works Manager to the Dum 
Dum airport. When Shri Vorah was informed that no car was available- 
at the moment, he came personally to the office. There he found M 1 
Sha, a driver, in the cash office. On having this information from 
Shri Vorah, Col. Sarma came to the cush office aud asked Munshi Sha to- 
bring his car. Munshi Sha suddenly took up an insulting attitude, and 
replied to the queries of Shrj Sarma in a rough voice snying ‘‘thither the 
car was’. Col. Sarma, the Security and Estate (Officer, repeatedly ordered. 
him to bring out the car, but that only resulted in fresh insults from 
Munshi Sha. Ultimately, however, Munshi Sha did not carry out his 
order. So a charge-sheet was given to him, and there was an enquir 
thereafter in which Munshi Sha was found guilty, and he wus টিউন ক 
Thereafter the Company filed an application under section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act seeking approval of its action in dismissing Munsht 
Sha from the Tribunal. 


Now, turning to the evidence on record, I am satisfied that the versiom 
of the management ia correct, it having been substantiated on material 
particulars. The log book, Ext. 7, shows that the car WHBEI1532 was 


Gee .THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 29, 1969 [Pani I 


سے mak‏ عد = 


not exclusively attached to the Finance Officer of the Company as said by 
Munshi Sha. This car was used by other officers as well. So there can 
e no question of any standing instruction from the Finance Officer that 
é4he ear in question should in no circumstances be taken out from lis 
wesidence without his permission. This Finance Officer, Shri R. S, Sarma, 
thas deposed before me. At the relevant time he was in Delhi. Ife denies 
Guving left any such instruction that the car in question would not be 
callowed to be taken out without his perthission. 


Munshi Sha says that on 8rd March 1958 he was asked by the wife of 
dhe Finance Officer to take her ailing baby to the doctor in Culceutta. Ile 
tooethe baby in his car to Calcutta at 8 a.m. and returned therefrom at 
about টি p.m. That this man is not telling the truth is evident from the 
entries in the log book of that date which reveals that from 8 a.m. to 
10 a.m. on 3rd March 1958 the car No. W.B.E. 1582 was engaged in its 
‘trips to the Air India Office and back to the factory. Ext. 8 shows that 
the car had another trip between 10 a.m. and 1] a.m. Thereafter it was 
again taken out to Calcutta and returned to the factory during the period 
from 11 a.m. to 0 p.m. In the trips from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. and from 
31 am. to 5 p.m. Munshi Sha was the driver. So it appears that Munshi 
Sha does not have strict regard for the truth. 


Munshi Sha is charged with the offence of disobedience to the order of 
Colonel Sarma, the Security and Estate Officer, in refusing to bring out 
ear, as also of unmanuerly and insulting behaviour in course ot the 
Colonel’s talk with Munshi Sha over the matter of the car. In his state- 
iment before me, Munshi Sha tried to conceal the fact that Colonel Sarma 
had told him that the car was very urgently required. But in his deposition 
‘before the Enquiry Committee he admitted that Colonel Sahib had told hita 
that the car was required very urgently and that he should go immediately 
vand get the car out. Munshi Sha wants to say that he politely told 
Col. Sarma that the key of the car in question was with the wife of the 
Finance Officer, and that he should speak to her over telephone so that the 
key might be delivered to the driver Munshi Sha. The plea of politeness 
in his talk with Col. Sarma is displaced not only by the circumstances, but 
also by direct evidence. If he had talked with him politely there could have 
‘deen no occasion for Col. Sarma, a responsible officer of the Company, for 
giving him a charge-sheet on a false and fabricated ground. ৮028 the 
evidence of all the witnesses in this case against whom there is no 
attribution of past grudge or enmity or any sort of ill feeling against 
Munshi Sha, it is abundantly clear that Munshi Sha’s reply to Col. Sarma, 
‘who wus his superior officer, was very insolent, and that he created a row 
on the spot which lowered down the prestige of Col. Sarma in the estimation 
of people present there. In case the key of the car was really with the 
‘wife of the Finance Officer, fhe driver Munshi Sha ought to have gone in 
‘the said lady on receipt of orders from Col. Sarma, and in case the lady 
refused to make-over the key to him, then only he could ask Col. Sarma 
وا‎ to ring up and speak to the lady, meaning, the wife of Finance Officer. 
e fact, as it seems to be, is that the driver Munshi Sha felt tired after 
‘his trip to Calcutta and back, and that he was thinking of going home for 
‘west on receipt of his wages from the cash office. Just at that moment a 
fresh requisition for the said car from Col. Sarma irritated him much, and 
‘he flew mto a rage. But even then, I must say, the driver should have 
pohtely importuned Col. Sarma to spare him having placed before him how 
tired he was. But instead of that, if he indulges in giving replies to the 
superior officer in the manner he did, his conduct amounts to insubordination 
amd borders on insult to the superior offieer. The evidence in the case has 
proved every bit of the actual insult Col. Sarma was put to, and I believe

Murshi Sha wants to say that he did not disobey the order of Col]. Sarina,

Regard being had to al] these facta and circumstances, I disiniss the 
present case under section 338A of the’ Industrial Disputes Act. I hewe 
approved the action of the Company in respect’ of this man Shri Munshi She 
on the petition filed by the Company: under section 33 of the Act seeking
