588 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 29, 1959 [Parr 1 


of 1947), an industrial dispute between Messrs. Asiatic Board Mulls Ltd., 
29-B Beerpara Lane, Calcutta-30, and two of their workmen, ‘Shipi Bahar 
Pondey and Shri Phulohand Shaw, represented by Asiatic Board Milt 
Workers’ Union, 26,8 Dum Dum Road, Calcutta-2, regarding matters 
specified in the second schedule of the Act, to this Court, for adjudication ص۸‎ 


Schedule 


(1) Whether the discharge of Shri Baban Pandey and Shri Phulehand 
Shaw is justified? To what relief are they entitled’ 


AWARD 


This is a case arising out of alleged illegal and unjustified discharge of 
(1) Shri Baban Pandey previously employed as a Durwan and of (2) 
Phulchand Shaw previously employed as a Calendar-man in Messrs. Asiatic 
Board Mills Ltd. (hereinafter described as the Company for the sake of 
brevity). 

The case of the Union in a nutshell is as follows سے‎ 


Shri Pandey went to his native village on leave after the closure of the 
11151] and reported for his duty on Ist November 1955 but he was not allowed 
to join and was told that his services were dispensed with as he was not 
piesent when the mill restarted on 28th September 1955. There was an 
agreement between the Company and the Union embodying the terms and 
conditions pertaining to the reopening of the mill after the temporary 
closure and Shri Pandey was not described as a retrenched worker in this 
agreement. Thus the termination of service of Shri Pandey is without 
justification and thus illegal and mala fide. 


The Union therefore seeks the reinstatement of Shri Pandey with all 
ancilliary benefits. 


The-case-of the Union so far as the other workman Shri Phulchand Shaw 
is concerned is that he had put in 6 years’ service under the Company hut 
he was dismissed arbitrarily on 4th August 1954 without any charge-sheet, 
reason or enquiry whatsoever. His dismissal is thus entirely unjustified 
and arbitrary and the Union secks his reinstatement with الد‎ consequential 
benefits. 

The Company denies the material allegations in the written statement 
of the Union and contends that as Baban Pandey was not present when the 
mill restarted on 28th September 1956 his services stood terminated and the 
Company recruited a new hand in his place and therefore Shri Pandey is 
entitled to no relief. 


The case of Phulchand Shaw is contended to be as follows :—Pulchand 
was @ workman in the finishing section which is inter-linked with the drying 
sectiof. On 4th August 1954 at about 1 p.m. the sky was cloudy and there 
was a heavy shower. Shri HWemendra Kumar Sarkar, the factory assistant 
and supervisor, asked Shri Shaw to help the workers of the drying section 
collect the boards spread over the open field for the purpose of sun drying. 
Shri Shaw refused to carry out the orders of Shri Sarkar and so he was 
called by the Manager in his office to explain his conduct. At this 
Shri Shaw started shouting and using abusive language to the Manager and 
thus his conduct was subversive of all discipline. Thus the Company denies 
that it is a case of victimisation and contends that Shri Shaw is entitled ۸ 


no relief. 
DECISION 


First I take up the case of Shri Baban Pandey. The case is very simple. 
Ii is common ground that the mill was closed temporarily on 23rd Jute 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE. JANUARY 29, 0 589 


০ 


1965. Shri Pandey says that he started for his native village in U.P. on 
2710) May 1955 with the permission of the Proprietor and the Managing 
Direclor also promised to send him information at lis native village as and 
when the mull reopened. His evidence is that he wrote two reply postrards 
one after another and this ia not contradicted, and he got a letter dated 
18th August 1955, Kxt. ہلا‎ from Shri 8. N. Roy wherein the workman was 
intimated that there was no chance of the mill reopening shortly and that 
he was not required to come back. The workman received another letter, 
dated 20th September 1954, Ext. 100, from the General Manager of the mill 
wherein if was said that the mill had not reopened even then and that there 
was nothing to be intimated to him at that moment. Admittedly, the mill 
wag started on 28th September 1955 and he returned from home on Ist 
November 1955, on receipt of information from one Rajdeo. another employee 
of another mill. Thus the fact remains that neither the Managing ن00‎ 
nor the Proprietor of the mill sent any information to this workman about 
the reopening of the mill asking him to come back and rejoin his duties. 
lie was complacently staying at home and relied on the assurance of the 
Managing Director Shri Roy that he would in due course receive information 
from the authorities when the mill would reopen. Shri Roy, Managing 
Director, did not send him any information as promised and so he had no 
means to know if the mill reopened and no blame can possibly be laid at 
hija door for not coming back to the mill on 28th September 1955 when the 
mill restarted The Puja holidays intervened and least suspecting that the 
will reopened he was staying at home and it was only on receipt of 
information from Rajdeo, an employee of another mill, that he returned 
gn Ist November 1955 when he was told by Shri Roy that the mill restarted 
edrlier and that a Nepali Durwan was appointed in his place. Thus this 
prkinan was indeed duped into thinking that the mill did not restart as 
nN got no information of ita restarting and if he had known that the mill! 
restarted earlier he would have certainly come back in jood time to rejoin 
his 101). In this connexion I would refer to the terms of agreement, dated 
27th September 1955, Annexure A, wherein there is & stipulation in 
paragraph 2 thereof showing that the following retrenched workers would 
receive retrenchment henefits under section 26F of the Industrial Disputes 
Act in full and final settlement of their claim :— 

'“')1( Ganesh Sao, (1) Naravani PDashi, (iti) Dbanomani 10881), 
(iv) Abalabala Debi, ۷ Tarak Dashi, (vi) Ram Singh, (vn) Abani 
Chakravorty, (viii) Abinash Chandra De, (ix) Chapala Dashi, 
(x) Peary Telini, (xi) Indu Bhusan Sen Biswas.’’ 


The name of the concerned workman Shri Pandey is conspicuous by its 
absence in the list and so hy virtue of agreement 3 which runs as followa:— 
“Other retrenched workers will be reinstated from the restart of the Mill’? 
this Baban Pandey being a retrenched workman was to be reinstated. So 
T must find that in the circumstances of this case the termination of service 
of Shri Pandey is unjustified, and that he is entitled to reinstatement. 
The Company on the other hand has examined one Shri Anil Kumar 
Dutta, an employee of Eastern Paper Mills, to show that Shri Pandey is 
employed in that mill as Durwan from Ist January 1956. The Company in 
this case played a foul trick upon the workman. The Company, of course, 
has got an absolute right to hire and fire, but subject to certain restrictions 
und fundamental principles as enumerated in 1996 L.L.J., Vol. I, page 5 
(Lipton Limited and their workmen) which runs as follows :— 


that an industrial worker must be placed in such a position that‏ را)' 
the security of his service may not depend upon the caprice or‏ 
arbitrary will of the employer,‏ 


(2) that industrial peace should be maintained, and 


690 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 29. 1959 [Parr 1 


> পলির 


(3) that industry should be efficiently managed.’’ 


“Tn all these types of cases, however, the requirement of 7:10 fides 15 
essential and the termination of service in colourable exercise 
of the power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour 
practice or of caprice, should be prevented............... and that 
arbitrary conduct or unnecessary harshness on the part of the 
employer, judged by the normal standard of a reasonable man, 
may be cogent evidence of victimisation or unfair labour 
practice.’ 


This case illustrates an unfair labour practice which should not ve 
encouraged. The workman is thus entitled to remstatement. 


As regards compensation for the period of his illness, I would think that 
he may be fairly awarded his full wages for the period of his idleness minus 
the amount drawn by him from Eastern Paper Board Mills ‘during his 
employment. This disposes of the case of Shri Baban Pandey. 


Next, I come to Phulchand Shaw. The evidence on record establishes 
that 4th August 1954 was a cloudy day and at about 1 p.m. there was 
admittedly a heavy shower Shri Shaw being a calendar-man was working 
at his pon Se machine when an alarm bell was rung and the practice 
obtaining in the mill is that simultaneously with the ringing of the ٥ص)‎ 
bell all workmen of the mill wherever engaged at the moment would run out 
immediately and collect the boards spread out in the open field for drying 
purpose lest they should be wet and spoilt. The Company’s case is that 
Shri Shaw refused to honour the alarm bell and thus to carry out the 
reasonable orders of Shri Hemendra Kumar Sarkar, supervisor. Shri Shaw's 
version is that he said that he would go out to جات‎ the boards spread 
over the field for sun drying after stopping the calendar machine which 
requires about five minutes to stop it. On the other hand, the Company 
maintains that it takes only a few seconds to stop the calendar machine and 
as such Sliri Shaw should have instantaneously with the ringing of the alarm 
hell stopped the machine and run out the field in order to collect the hoards 
as other workmen did according to the customa obtaining in the mill. To 
add to this, the Company further osserts that Shri Shaw when called ںا‎ 
the room of the Manager, shouted and filthily abused and at this the 
Manager asked the Durwan to drive him out of the gate It is admitted that 
a calendar-man cannot leave his room unless his machine is stopped first, 
and the evidence of Shri Keshab Chandra Sen (O.P.W. 5), another calendar- 
man, is that it takes three to four minutes to stop the calendar machiue. 
So the version of Shri Shaw as to the time taken in stopping the machine is 
eorrect. Q.P.W. 5 Shri Keshab Chandra Sen who was then working as a 
helper at the other calendar machine knew nothing as to what took place 
between Shri Shaw and the Manager on the that particular date. 
0.P.W. 4. Shri Sukhomay Das Gupta who is employed in the finishing 
department also knew nothing as to what happened between the Manager 
ond the workman on that particular date. So the Company has not succeeded 
m establishing beyond doubt that Shri Shaw created a scene by his shouts 
and uttered obscene words, nor is there any convincing proof that the 
Company suffered any loss due to the alleged disobedience of this workman 
tc honour the alarm bell. Thus, it appears that there happened nothin 
particular in the mill on that particular date ao as to justify the dismissa 
of Shri Shaw. Having regard to the principles laid down in Lipton’s case 
as enumerated in 1956 L.L.J., Vol. I, page 328, as already quoted, I find 
that this is a yery fit case in which the dismissal of Shri Shaw should ٥ 
found unjustified and capricious und the interest of the workman should he 
protected. The dismissal of this workman without serving a charge-sheet

on him and in the absence of an enquiry affording him all reasonable 
19011811608 to defend himself is in clear violation of the principles of natural 
justice and there are a plethoru of cases ou this point (1966 L.L.J., Vol. IY,

of Himalayan Paper and Board Mills, to prove that Shri Shaw worked in 
that mill trom 180 December 1954 to 9171 May 1955 and that he again 
worked in the same mill for a month or so. These two are instances of 
temporary employment, so for these periods of temporary re-employment 
under another Company Shri Shaw connot, of course, recover any wages from 
the instant Company and the wages drawn from his temporary employers 
should be deducted سد‎ calculating his due wages from this Company for the 
period of his idleness from the 6 of his discharge (4th August 1954) tall 
the date of his reinstatement in this Company. 


Thus the discharge of these two employees (1) Shri Baban Pandey and 
(2) Shri Phulchand Shaw is found unjustified and illegal and they must be 
reinstated with the continuity of their service unbroken. The Company 
must also pay each of them their full wages for the period of their une:mploy- 
ment minus the wages drawn by them from their employers for the 4 
or periods of their employment under them. The Company is directed to 
reinstate the workmen and pay the aforesaid compensation to them within 
a month of the publication of the award.

of the award.

An industrial dispute regarding the matter specified in the issues,

(5) Unitorm for Darwans, Tindals and Firemen. 


Both parties filed written statements, adduced evidence, oral and 
documentary, and advanced arguments in the case. 


An objection was taken on behalf of the Mills that this reference in 
view of the earlier settlement between the parties touching the matters in 
dispute was had in law, and should be rejected. It was contended that 
this Tribunal has no jurisdiction to adjudicate on the issues mentioned in 
the order of reference. The questions of jurisdiction were gone into on 
the application of the parties in the month of August last, and were dis- 

sed of by an interim award, dated 22nd August 1958, submitted to the 
sb under memo. No. 2418-L.T., of the same date. 


Issue No. 1: ‘Ihe Mazdoor Union has as many as eleven items of dis- 
ules mentioned in its written statement to be adjudicated upon under thie 
issue. The Workers’ Union has one additional item of dispute. That 
relates to introduction of grades and scales for all categories of workmen 
with provisions for annual increment. The Mills contested these demands 


Part I] ‘THR CALCUTIA GAZETTE, JANUARY 29, 0 597 


and contended that they should be rejected on various grounds. Tho issue 
is rew@ricted to the question of Standing Orders. The question of 
decusualisation or abolition of contract labour as well as of attendance 
bonus is outside the issue. Shri তি, (. Sen, on behalf of the Mills, referred 
to Mixt. 0, a letter to the Rice Mills’ Associution by the Assistant Secretary, 
Labour Department, on 9th January 1908, i.e., on the date of reference, 
in support of سط‎ contention that the question relating to scale of pay and 
dearness allowance are not covered by the issue under reference. The 
Mazdoor Union and the Workers’ Union were also informed of the same. 
It is true that the decision of the Government in this matter is not conclu- 
sive on this point, and the Tribunal should decide it independently. 
Ordinarily, scales of pay and dearness allowance are referred as separate 
sues for adjudication by the Tribunal. In fact, the Mazdoor Union did 
not put, in its written statement, any claim for introduction of scales of 
pay for all categories of workmen. 1 am clear, in my mind, that the 
dispute regarding the introduction of grades and scales of pay, with annual 
increment, if there be uny, is not covered by the issue No. 1, but the 
Attendance bonus hus been claimed as a condition of service, and, as such, 
a dispute over its payment is an industrial dispute which properly comes 
under the Jasue No. 1. The objection taken on behalf of the mills partly 
succeeds and partly fails. 


The most important items of dispute under the issue are: (i) 
decusualisation of casual lahour and (11) abolition of contract labour. The 
Workers’ Union demands that all employees who are now working on casual 
basis, should be made permanent after they have put in three months’ 
ا ا‎ service, and that 50 per cent. of wages should be paid to casual 
warkers a3 compensatory allowance for seasonal breaks in service. The 
Mazdoor Union, however. claims that at least one-half of the casual workers 
be made permanent, and the rest should be seasonal permanent with a 
retuining allowance during the off season. The Rice Mills’ Association 
objects to these demands. The objections ure: (i) The abolition ot 
00781018801 labour is outside the issue for the contruct labour is not a party in 
the case, and, therefore, the dispute is not an industrial dispute, and (i1)

The proposal should be rejected forthwith as it is unrealistic and uneconomic. 
It is also because the trading position of the mill» does not permit any

No doubt, these are the two important items of dispute under the 
present issue. The employment of casual labour for an indefinite length 
of period and of Jabour, recruited through the agency of contractors, are 
tender spots in the whole dispute. In the first place, it has to be seen 
whether these are industrial matters which can 0 subject of a valid 
industrial dispute. The employment and non-employment of any person 
is, no doubt, an industrial matter, and, in that way, both these items of 
dispute are industrial disputes. As to the case of decasualisation of casual 
labour, there cannot be any doubt whatsoever that it is an industrial 
dispute. The contract labour, it is stated, is not before this Tribunal. 
They are not separately represented in this case. But then, the important 
point for consideration is whether the condition of service, as “now exists, 
wil improve, when the contract labour is abolished. On this point, Shri 
১.০, Sen points out that the work of casual labour doing chatal work 1s 
done exclusively by female workers, whereas the contract labour 18 
essentially done by the male workers. Shri Banerjee, on behalf of the 
Mavdqor Union, has refuted thia argument. It is in evidence of the 

nion’s witness that there are both male and female labourers doing huller 


598 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 29, 1959 [Parr I 


work, and that with the abolition of the contract labour the conditions of 
service of casual labour will be considerably improved. Further, the 
labour employed in the mills has, on the whole, direct und _ substantial 
interest in the improvement of the conditions of service, of all, including 
the contract labour. On all these grounds, I think it is an industrial 
dispute, which, on a reference to this Tribunal, can be adjudicated upon.

Reliance was placed on behalf of the Rice Mills on the recommendations 
ot the Minimum Wages (Rice Mills) Committee, West Bengal Govern- 


publication 1952, pawe 14. The relevant portion of the report is as‏ سز

“Most of us are in favour of abolishing the contract labour under the 
Sardar system. That the aystem is harsh and unfair for the workers 
under the irresponsible Sardars, who are not always above corruption, can- 
not be denied. But there are practical difficulties. The mill-owners, 
who have to depend to a large extent upon the Civil Supplies Department 
of the Government for supply of paddy and upon the weather conditions 
for the milling, cannot regulate their work. The labour force which 23 
dependent on the supply of paddy and weather conditions, cannot but be 
fluctuating according to daily requirements. The system can be abolished 
only by stabilising employments. The very nature of the industry and 
its present condition make stabilisation of employments impossible, and 
any attempt in this direction is likely to bring in disaster. The system is 
sanctioned by exigencies of the business. We may at best appeal to the 
mill-owneras to have some control over the Sardars so that the workers 
under them receive a fair deal.’’ 


The Union, on the other hand, contended that the said observations

wes harsh and unfair for the workers. But considering the practical 
difficulties prevailing at the time of the report, the Committee could not 
abolish the system of employment through contractors which they thought 
was only possible when employment were more or less stabilised. Regard 
heing had to the very nature of the industry, and its the then condition, 
stabilisation was considered impossible and the system was accordingly

Indispensable is not always desirable. Whatever might have been the

in the same industry the management feels no difficulty at all in recruiting

Accordingly, I have no doubt in my mind that the system of employment 
of contract labour the Rice Mills can be abolished without any serious 
difficulty or Joss to the industry. This would have the immediate effect 
of preventing further exploitation of labour through intermediaries and 
at the same time improve the condition of service of the workers now 
directly working under the management. The abolition of contract labour, 
with immedinte effect at a time when a very large number of Mills involved 
in this dispute are cloned, may create some complications and difficulties 
for the management. It is, therefore, desirable that the abolition should 
be done gradually, i.e., the employment in place of contract labour, when

average monthly labour employed in the 19১০ year should be made

should be made after six months of approved service. Fifty per cent. of 
the contract lahour should be abolished within three months from the date

hat. The process of abolition should be complete within six months from 
the date of the publication of the award.

aforesaid agreement. In the first place, double retirement benefits should 
not be introduced all at once particularly in view of the fact that the Mills, 
for good reasons or had, are not in operation for practically over 2/3 of a 
vear and pleaded financial inability to shoulder heavier burden in this respect, 
1 think, for the present, the gratuity scheme. as contained in the agree- 
mont, dated 18th February 1957, and reproduced in this award, with changes 
indicated below, shall come into force with effect from the date of the 
publication of this award. The only change, made in the said scheme 1s 
that the benefita are availnble to those who have rendered a total period 
of service for 15 years in place of ‘fat least 20 years’ continuous”. J 
answer the issue accordingly. 


15586 No. 4: This relates to workload for different categories of work- 
men. The Mazdoor Union demands revision of the workload for A. ظط‎ C, 
D. ,7ا‎ ঘা, (00. H groups. The suggested workload ia given at page 8 of its 
written statement. The Workers’ Tnion also demands a revision of the 
workload and suggests a 50 per cent. ent in the target fixed by the 
Minimum Wages Committee. The Mills suggest that the workload. দর 
fixed by the Minimum Wages Committee, should continue. The Workers’ 

nion, in its written statement, stated that the said workload is defective 
rom two consideration. It was based on exploitation, and, not on actual 
job_evaluation study, and, secondly, the worklond has in itself room for 
abuse. The quota suggested in the report is humanely impossible ٥ 
perform and, the experience is that it ean never be reached. This has heen 
mit forward as grounds for revision of the existing workload, No case of 
abuse was established in this ease. The evidences of the two female 
Workers give some idea of the work done by casual workers only and that 
is all that has been done in the case to prove that the workload decided 


606 THK CALCUTTA GAZKETTE, JANUARY 29, 1900 [Parr T 
a a De 
upon iu the report of the Minimum Wages Committee is defective, Shri 
Banerjee pointed out that in some cases the Mills havo followed a different 
standard, lower than that fixed in the report. The Association’s evidence 
is that the Mills are strictly following the workload fixed by the Minimum 
Wages Committee. The Minimum Wages Committee fixed the workload 
for different groups of workers, on industrywise basis, and after careful 
study on the apot. In this case, actual job evaluation was not done, or 
even attempted to be done by experts by either party. It is, therefore, 
extremely difficult to undertake the work of a detailed revision of the 
standard workload fixed by the Minimum Wages (‘ommittee, which is in 
operation at present. Any serious attempt to refix the standard for less 
than 10 per cent. of the 11109 Mills within the State is very likely to defeat 
the purpose for which it is sought to be done. The Unions’ suggestion is 
apparently founded on surmise. J] am, therefore, obliged although 
reluctantly, to leave the matter as it ia till such time when a revision js 
either made on agreement between the purties or otherwise done on a more 
scientific hasis. i answer the issue accordingly. 


Issue No. 5: The Unions demand uniform for Durwan, Tindals, and 
Fireman. The Mills’ objection is that this demand is unjustified and 
should be rejected, Not a single workman for whom this benefit is claimed 
has been examined. The demand does not appear to be prima facie 
reasonable one and should not be allowed at present. 1 is, therefore, 
refused. This is my award.

Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by its order 
No, 2890-1. R./ TR / 111-248 /58, dated Caleutta, the 10th June 1958, referred 
to me an industrial dispute hetween Messrs. Sankar Saw Mills and their 
workmen, represented by the Howrah District Saw Mills Maadur Union, for 


udjudication. 
Issue formulated in the order of reference is in the following form: 


Whether the discharge of the following workmen is justified — 
(1) Shri Shew Bachan Ram, 
(11) Shri Appalswamy, 
(018) Shri Kristo Murthy. 


To what relief are they entitled ? 


Notices were issued on hoth the sides. The Union has filed their 
written statement but the notice issued to the company by registered post, 
has been received back undelivered with the postal remark ‘‘refused’’. The 
notice having not heen received hy the company it is held that it baa been 
served properly and the case was taken up ex-parte as the company did not 
appear in spite of the registered notices which they have refused. 


On 3rd January 1959, the case was taken up for ex-parte hearing and 
the Union Secretary Shri Madan Kumat Singh was examined. The three 
concerned employees were also examined. Tt anpears that the company not 
only refused the Court’s summons but they did not appenr even at the 
conciliation proceeding before the Assistant Lahour Commissioner, ۱۰۱ 
and when all attempts for conciliation failed the Assistant Labour Com- 
missioner referred the matter for adjudication and hence this reference was 


mace. 
FINDINGS 


The employer compnny is recalcitrant to a devree and has not vet heen 
fuught the lesson that flouting the Conciliation Proreedings and Court's 
summons will not help them if they want to carry on industry in the enuntry. 
lt appears further from the evidence on record of the Union Secretary aa also

of the workers concerned that rate of wages of Shri Shew Bachan Ram and of 
Shri Appalawamy were Ms. 10-8-0 per week and that of Shri Kristo Murthy 
was tts. 9-8-0 per week. They were permanent workmen and were not on 
the busis of “no work no pay’ although their payment was made weekly. 
[$ appears further that the workers demanded back wages and the company 
promised to give them wages after the ‘Holi’ day, but after the Holi was 
over when they ۸۱ء‎ demanded their wages, the company refused to pay 
them and summarily dismissed these workmen concerned. ‘These workmen 
are the members of Mowrah District Saw Mills Mazdur Union and the Union 
Secretary has filed this case on their behalf. This is not an indivjdual 
dispute but an judustrial dispute of collective nature and | woald consider 
this to be a clear instance of unfair labour practice on the part of the company 
and I would therefore give my award that all these three workmen concerned 
should be reinstated from the date of their discharge, i.e., from 10th March 
1968, and they should get their full back wages until the day of the reinstate-

Officers of the Central Government under the audit control of this office are 
requested to refer to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance (epart- 
ment of Expenditure), 0. M. No. 16-C(22)-EI1(A)/68, dated 11th December 
1958 (copy reproduced below), sanctioning the grant of advance on the eve 
of important festivals subject to the terms and cunditions stipulated therein 
up to the 3lst December 1960 unless amended earlier. 


The procedure suggested in paragraph 4 of this office notification 
No, T.M/579, dated 26th September 1956, as published in page 3728 of the 
Calcutta Gazette, dated 4th October 1956, with regard to the furnishing of 
statement of recoveries of such advances, etc., will continue to apply mutatrs 
mutandis in the cases covered by ihe present orders. ‘The certificate which 
has to be furnished in each bill containing claims on account of the above- 
mentioned advance of pay should, however, be modified as follows :— 


“‘Certified that the terms and conditions laid down in the Government 
of India, Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure), (). M.

beans ot Office Memorandum No. 16-C(22)E.1I(A)/58, dated the 11 
cember 1968, from the Government of India, Ministry of Finance

Subject: Crant of advance to Central Covernment employees on the eve of 
important festivais. 


Weference: Finance Ministry (06) Memorandum No. 16-C(16)-E.I1(A) (97, 
dated the 20th December 1957, and Office Memorandum No. F. 16-C(8)- 
E.II(A) /58, dated the 5th September 1958. 


The undersigned is directed to state that the President is pleased to 
decide that Ministries/Offices of the Government of India may sanction 
advances on the eve of important festivals to their non-gazetted employees 
on the following terms and conditions : — 


(i) The amount of advance will be Rs. 75 or one month’s basic pay 
as defined under Fundamental Rule 9(21)(a)(1)], whichever 8 
eas. 

(ii) The advance will be recovered in not more than four ane monthly 
instalments, the first instalment commencing with ibe next 
month’s pay bill, t.e., the pay bill of the month following that 
in which the advance is drawn. The amount of each instalment 
shall be rounded off to the nearest rupee, any balance being 
recovered in the last instalment. 


(013) The advance may be granted to non-gazetted Central Government 
servants in receipt of basic pay not exceeding Rs. 500 per month 
(including similar categories of ataff in Industrial Establishments 
under the Government of India). The concession is also admie- 
sible to the work-charged staff who are entitled to pension or Con- 
tributory Provident Fund benefits but not to the staff paid from 
contingencies. 

(iv) The advance should not be granted to temporary staff who are not 
likely to continue in service for a period of at least six months 
beyond the month in which the advance is drawn. 


(v) The advance is admissible only to those on duty or on leave on 
average pay or earned leave on full pay at the time the advance 
is drawn. 

(vi) The advance will be admissible only on one occasion in a calendar 
year for members of each community serving in one establishment. 
More than one occasion may, however, be fixed for a community, 
if tho competent authority is satisfied that in his opinion it is 
desirable to do so taking into account the staff composition of 
his establishment. The ‘‘competent authority’’ for the purpose 
of fixing the festival occasions will be the Head of Department / 
Industriel Ftablishment concerned. Such authorities may fix 
the festival occasions after taking into consideration the impor- 
tance attached locally to such festivals and in consultation with 
recognised associations of staff where such exist. 


THE CALOULTA GASERTTE, FEBRUARE 6, 1060 


11099 suboffices of an office loeated at different ‘stations may be tzeated 
as separate establishments for this purpose. No member of an 
establishment shall however be granted more than one suc 
advance in one calendar year. 


(vii) A second festival advance should not be sanctioned till the earlier 
advance sanctioned for the same purpose has not been recovered 
in full. 


(viii) In case a festival falls twice in a calendar year the advance ‘will 
be admissible only on one occasion. 


(ix) The advance shall be drawn and disbursed before the festival in 
connection with which the advance is sanctioned. 


(x) Before the advance is sanctioned to temporary staff, sureties from 
permanent Government servants or any other form of security 
considered udequate by the sanctionmg authority shall 
obtained. The authorities competent to sanction these advances 
may, at their discretion, dispense with this requirement m the 
case of temporary staff/workers in Industrial Establishments who 
have completed 3 years of continuous service and are likely to 
continue in service till the adjustment of the advance. 


2. Wherauthorities competent to sanction these advances will be 2 
‘‘Heads of -(ffices’’ so declared under paragraph 8 of the General Financia 
Rales, Volume I, in respect of non-industrial staff and (ii) ‘Heads of 
Iadustrial Establishments’? in respect of Industrial workers. 


8. These orders supersede any earlier orders providing for similar 
henefits. The present practice in certain establishments of paying the wages 
earned up to date, on eve of important festivals, by an ad hoc reguidtion of 
the wage peiiod, should in future be discontinued. 


4. These advances will, on payment, he debitable to ‘““S—Deposits and 
advances—Part []I—Advances not bearing inierest—Departmental Advance 
—Civil—Ohbjection book advance’’ or other similar suspense head of account 
for the‘ establishment concerned. 


5. These orders will remain in force till 38318۲ । December 1960 wumless 


amended earlier.

Audit and Accounts Department ts concerned, these orders issue after con- 
gultation with the Comptroller and Auditor-General,

No. 908Pub.—29th January 1959.—In exercise of the power conferred 
by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution of India, the Governor is 
pleased to muke the following rules regulating the recruitment to the post 
of Senior Sub-Kditor in the Home (Publicity) Department ot this Govern- 
ment, namely :— 


RULES 


1. These rules may be called the West Bengal Subordinate Services 
(Recruitment of Senior Sub-Kditor) Rules, 1959. 


2. These rules shall apply to the recruitment to the post of Senior 
Sub-Kditor in the Home (Publicity) Department of this Government herein- 
after referred to as the post and shall come into force at once. 


3. Method of recruitment.—The recruitment to the post shall be made 
(a) by promotion of Sub-Kditor or (b) by selection. 


4. Qualifications.—Qualifications for recruitment 10 the post by selec- 
tion shall be as follows :— 


(a) A candidate shall— 
(i) hold a degree of an Indian University; 


(23) have knowledge and experience of producing original manu- 
scripts for publicity hterature and Press features; 


(21) have و هر ا‎ and experience of translating from English ints 
Bengali and wee versa and compiling from articles and sources 
in English; 


(1) have knowledge of make up of magazines and ability to super- 
vise production in the Press; 


(v) have ability to write and edit publicity literature in English 
and Bengali; and matters for releases to the Press; and 


(b) have worked in the editorial or production departments of a 
newspaper or journal, a publicity or advertising firm, a Govern- 
ment Department of Publicity or All India Radio or a business 
establishment in public relations section, for at least three 
years. 


Other qualifications being equal, preference will be given to a candi- 
ate holding diploma in journalism. 


5. Age—A candidate shall be between 30 to 45 years of age on the 
first day of the month in which the post is advertised. 


6. Gharacter.—No person who is not of good character and in all 
respects suitable for appointment to Government service, shal] he appointed 
to the post. 


7. Physical fitness.—A candidate shall have sound health and good 
hysique, and shall be of active habits and free from organic defects or 
bodily infirmity. 
8. Nationality.x—A candidate shal] be 2, citizen of India as defined in 
Part II of the Constitution of India. 


9. Probation.—The probationary period shall be two years in the case 
of outsiders and one year in the case of promotees. 


By order of the Governor, 
9. Kk. CHATTERJEE, 99০১,

3. Method of recruitment.—The recruitment to the post shall be made 
by selection.

1. That every factory shall have a provident fund scheme in force the 
rules of which with respect to the rates of contribution shall not be less 
favourable thun those specified in section 6 of the Employees’ Provident 
Funds Act, 1952, and the employees shall 0150 be in enjoyment of other 
provident fund benefits which on the whole shall not be less favourable to 
the employees than the benefits provided under the Act or any Scheme 
in relation to the employees in any other factory of a similar character 
wnd these rules shall be followed in all respects. 


2. The employer in relation to each factory (hereinafter referred to aa 
the “‘employer’’) shall within three months of the date of publication of 
this notification, amend the constitution of the provident fund maintained 
in respect of the factory in regard to the following matters, namely :— 


(a) the provident fund shall vest in ٭×‎ Board of ‘Trustees and there shall 
be a valid instrument in writing, which adequately safeguards 
the interests of the employees and 81201) instrument shall be 
duly registered under section 5 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882; 


(4) the Board of Trustees shall consist of an equal number of 
representatives of the employees and the employer and all 
questions before the Board shall be decided by u majority of 
votes; 


(c) the employer shall nominate one of his representatives on the 
Board as the Chairman who muy exercise a casting vote if so 
provided under the rules of the fuctory. Where a casting vote 
is exercised or where no casting vote is exercised but the opinion 
of the representatives is equally divided, the matter shall be 
referred to the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner appointed 
under the said Scheme (hereinafter referred to as the Regional 
Cominissioner) within whose jurisdiction the factory to which 
matter relates is situated and whose decision in the matter 
shall be final. 


3. The provident fund rules of any factory shall not be amended 
except with the previous approval of the Regional Commissioner. Where 
any amendment affects the interests of the employees, before giving his 
approval, the Regional Commissioner shall give o reasonable oppurtunity 
to the employees to explain their point of view. 


4. (@) The employer shall maintain accounts of the provident fund in 
such manner and ‘submit such returns to the Regional Commissioner as the 
Central Provident Fund Commissioner may, from time to time, direct. 


(6) The employer shall furnish to the Regional Commissioner such 
accounts relating to the provident fund of the factory as the Central 
Provident Fund Commissioner may prescribe from time to time. He shall 
180 furnish an annual statement of account or a Pass Book, in such form 
as may be approved, to each subscriber who, but for the exemption, would 
have been ہ‎ member of the fund extublished under the Employees’ Provi- 
dent Funds Scheme, 1952. 


(c) The employer shail make all investment of accumulations accruing 
after the date of exemption in securities of the Central Government. The 
reinvestment or conversion of securities on maturity shall also be in the 
securities of the Central Government. The employer shall formulate a 
procedure for promt investment of provident fund moneys and shall get it 
approved from the Regional Commissioner, 


6. The employer shall afford auch facilities for inspection of the 
accounts of the provident fund as the Central Provident Fund Commia- 
sioner may from time to time specify. 


6. All expenses involved in the administration of the Provident Fund 
Scheme including the maintenance of accounts, submission of accounts and 
returns, transfer of accumulations and payment of inspection charges shall 
be borne by the employer. 


7. The employer shall display on the notice board of his factory in 
English, a copy of the approved rules and the translation of salient pointa 
of the rules in the language of the majority of the workers, respectively. 


8. The employer shall within three montha of the date of publication 
of this notification transfer to the Board of Trustees the accumuwations 
standing to the credit of the employees who, but for the exemption, would 
have been members of the Statutory Fund. 


0. When the fund is wound up or exemption of the factory is cancelled, 
accumulation standing to the credit of the employees who, but for the

জানি ا‎ to that fund as soon as possible and, in any case, not later than

Subject: Opening of a new Major Head. 


No, TM /712.—16th January 1969.—Under article 150 of the Constitu- 
tion of India, the President has been pleased to accord sanction to the 
change in nomenclature of the Major Head *‘8hA—Capital Outlay on State 
Schemes of Gdovernment Trading’? in section ‘'JJ—Miscellaneous Capital 
Account outside the Revenue Account” to “85A—Capital Outlay on Schemes 
of Government Trading” and to the deletion of the existing Major Head 
“87—Capital Outlay on Schemes of Government Trading” in section ‘'MM— 
Capital Account of Extraordinary items outside the Revenue 40410011011, 


The above sanction wil] take efiect from the accounts for the year 1959-60) 
from which year the transactions at present classified under the head ‘‘87— 
Capital Outlay on Schemes of Government lading” will be booked under 
the Major Head “8A—Capital Outlay on Schemes of Government Trading’’. 


All Treasury Officers in West Bengal and the Manager, Reserve Bank 
of India, Caleutta, may please note the above orders for information and 
necessary action.

Subject: Preparation of Provident Fund schedules. 


No, TM(Fd.1)/718.—24th January 1959.—H haa been found that the 
Provident Fund schedules received in this office from the various depart- 
mental dishursing officers are often incomplete and inaccurate thereby 
rendering the maintenance of the accounts of the subseribers difficult: and 
making 1 impossible to complete the accounts in oll respects. The result 
is Unnecessary increase in correspondence both on the part of this office and 
that of the departmental officers. 


Instructions have already been issued for avoiding defects in the prepara- 
tion of the schedules. These instructions are repeated, for the guidance of 
the departmental officers, who may ensure the completeness and correctness 
of the schedules attached to payhills: 


(1) The schedules may be prepared in the proper prescribed forms. The 
month to which the schedule relates should be voted prominently 
in the relevant space provided in the scheduler (e.g.) deductions 
made from the paybill for Mareh paid in April, should be noted 
as for April. 


The Index letters to account numbers such as Admn./W.L., C.P.1R./ 
W.B., Tax/W.B. should he quoted. 


The names of the subsenbers should be arranged in the numerical 
serial order of the ueccount numbers assigned to them. The 
drawing offices should as far as possible have schedules ready- 
typed or roneoed, showing the names of the subscribers and their 
account numbers arranged serially. The names of new entrants 
and old subscribers iransferred from other offices, should be 
entered in the typed or roneoed schedules in the end after the 
names of the existing subscribers, But after the expiry of the 
year, these should find a place according to the serial order of 
their account numbers, Special care should be exercised to see 
that correct names and account numbers ate furnished, 


2) The amounts recovered from a subseriber on account of subseription 
and recovery of advance should be noted separately in the 
appropriate columns and in the latter case, the number of the 
instalment recovered should he noted in the ‘‘Remarks” column, 
If interest in recovered, the word “Interest’® should be noted in 
the “Remarks”? column. 


(9) When no recovery is being made in’ the case of any particular 
subscriber, the rensons for non-recovery should be stated clearly 
and briefly against his name in the ‘Remarks’? column, 


4184) when the amount of subscriptions or refund of withdrawals differ 
from those of the previous months, the reasons for such vatiations 
should be specified in the ‘“Remarks” column.

Subject: Expenditure inourred against advances from the 00116178910) 
Fund of India and of West Bengal. 


No. TM/714.—28th January 1959.—Instances have come to notice in 
which expenditure incurred against advances sanctioned out of the 
Contingency Fund were not properly classified by the Drawing Officers. 
Such misclassifications are fraught with the risk of the expenditure relating 
to Contingency Fund being erroneously accounted for as expenditure met 
from the Consolidated Fund. In thia connection, attention is invited to 
this office notification Nov. TM /423, dated 28th May 1953 and TM /593, 
dated 7th February 1957, published in the Calcutta Gazette in which the 
Drawing Officers were requested that while preparing bills relating to 
expenditure met out of the Contingency Fund it should be seen that they 
are invariably labelled as pertaining to the Contingency Fund of India or 
of West Bengal as the case may be. A strict adherence to those instruc- 
tions is solicited so that there may not be any room for misclassification 
and wrong accounting of such expenditure. 


All Treasury and Sub-Treasury Officers in West Bengal are also 
requested to ensure that al] hills pertaining to the Contingency Fund of 
India or of West Benga) as the case may he, presented to the treasury for 
payment, are labelled conspicuously as such by the Drawing Officers in 
each case.

Subject: Instructions regarding bills payable by the Accountant-Coneral, 
West Bengal, within the current financial year. 


No. T.M./715.—3rd February 1959.—In order to ensure payment 
before the close of the financial year, all travelling allowance, contingent, 
grant-in-aid and other bills payable within the year should, as far as 
practicable, be presented at the counter of this office by the 106) March 
1959. The words “‘To be paid on or before the 31st March 1959, should 
be written prominently in red ink on the top of each bill. 11) respect of 
charges actually incurred, or claims accruing on or after the 16th March, 
the bills should be presented with the utmost expedition without losing 
even a single day. Please remember that during the last week of March 
this office is preoccupied with the passing of monthly bills, payable on the 
first working day of April. 


2. Three clear days are required by this Office to complete all processes 
connected with pre-audit. On the fourth working day from the date of 
presentation of a bill, the payee or his messenger should call at the delivery 
counter to demand payment. If for any reason payment cannot be 
obtained on that day, he should call on the next day, or on the second or 
third following day, should it become necessary. Any complaint regarding 
undue delay in payment should be lodged with the gazetted officer in charge 
of the section. No attempt should be made to get into direct touch with 
the sectional staff. 


3. It should be particularly borne in mind that unpassed bills are not 
returned by post; they are required to be received back ut the counter on 
surrender of tokens. 


4. Plense take all possible care to see that the bills presented are free 
from detects and irregularities. There may not be time lett for resubmit- 
ting the bills when once returned unpassed with audit objection. 


5. It will facilitate the payment of bills if the following instructions 
are borne in mind :— 


(a) If the appropriation for the current vear is likely to be or has 
already been exceeded, an additional appropriation should be 
obtained in time to meet the excess and the order sanctioning 
the additional appropriation attached to the bill. 


(b) Tf any charge requiring sanction of a higher authority is claimed 
ina bill, the sanction should be attached to it. As no payment 
can he made on the authority of copies of orders, the sanctioning 
authority sHould be requested to communicate the orders to this 
office in time. 


(c) If no distribution of any appropriation has yet been made, formal 


orders of the competent authority sanctioning the distribution 
should be attached to the bill. 


(d) A bill extract giving particulars of the major, minor and detailed 
heads of account to which the amount of the bill is chargeable 
and the designation of the officer controlling the expenditure 
should invariably be attached to bills. 


6. Between the 16th and 31st March please make it a point to check 
لجا‎ Bill Register every day with a view to receive all payments in good 
ime. 


7. As a special concession to payees, the Cash Payment and Cheque 
Delivery counters of this office will be kept open till 4-30 p.m. on the 31st 
March. N@ payment will be made after that hour. 


8. Establishment Bills for March, 1959, will be paid by this office on 
the Ist April 1959 instead of on the 3lst March 1959. 


P. 0. HALDAR, 
})y. Accountant-General (Admn.).

Sarkar and Shri J. Pal, respectively, represented by the selfsame Union 
nawed Butto Kristo Paul and Co., Ltd. Employees’ Union, 283A Netaji

ot the Act, to this Court for adjudication. 


Schedule in Reference No. 1184-1.R. 


Whether the dismissal of Shri Manmatha Nath Dey Sarkar is justified ? 
To what reliet he is entitled ? 


Schedule in Reference No. 60-1.R. 
Is the dismissal of Shri J. Pal justified? What relief is he entitled to? 


AWARD 


These two references between the same Company and two workmen 
represented by the selfsame Union, are taken up together at the request 
of the Union with the consent of the Company and for the sake ot 
convenience. Two workmen, namely, (1) Shri Manmatha Nath De 
Sarkar and (2) Shri Jashoda Kumar Pal, of Messrs. B. K. Paul & Co., Ltd. 
(hereinafter described as the Company for the sake of brevity) are concerned 
in these two cases. 


So far as Shri Dey Sarkar is concerned, the Union’s case is that the 
Company dismissed him on a charge of theft in respect of a packet of Iodex 
an 30th August 1957 and dismissed the other workman Shri Jashoda Pal 
on a false allegation that he rescued Shri Dey Sarkar while he was betng 
taken to the Proprietor Shri Subol Ch. Paul by Shri Ajit Kumar Daw, the 
Department-in-Charge who is alleged to have caught Dey Sarkar red-handed 
in the very act of lifting the packet of [odex. The Union contends that 
the allegation of theft by Shri Dey Sarkar is altogether false and that the 
Company unjustifiably, illegally and arbitrarily dismissed him. In respect 
of the other workman Shri Pal, the case of the Union is that, he being the 
Secretary td the Union, the Company levelled the false charge against him 
and thus victimised him with a view to stifling all legitimate activities on 
the part of the Union against the Company between whom there are 
already several disputes 


The Company, on the other hand, contends that Shri Dey Sarkar was 
caught red-handed in the act of committing the theft and he was dismissed 
on his own 90110188018 in writing and thus the Company was fully justified 
in dismissing him. So far as Shri Pal is concerned, the Company contends 
that he was duly charge-sheeted and was given an opportunity to explain 
the charge and an enquiry was properly held wherein he was given all 
reasonable facilities to defend himself and the Company rightly found him 
guilty of obstructing Shri Ajit Kumar Daw in producing Shri Dey Sarkar 
before the Proprietor immediately after the theft and thus on a finding of 
guilty of & conduct subversive of all discipline in the Company he was 
rightly dismissed. The Company therefore contends that the Court is not 
eptitled to interfere in the case. 


Decision 
First of all, I take up the case of Shri Manmatha Nath Dey Sarkar. 
The misconduct alleged against him is that he stole a packet of Iodex 
(Ext. X for identification) on 30th August 1957 at about 6 p.m. and that 


Shri Ajit Daw, Department-in-Charge, caught him red-handed. Shri Dey 
Sarkar in Court says that he brought out the packet of 10093 on his 


part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 751 


compounding table for dispensing and that he was massaging it on his knee- 
joint due to pain. It 18 common ground that the Company allows medicine 
17৩4 tothe workmen. The Union therefore contends that there is absolutely 
no reason for his stealing the packet of 10083 which costs a paltry sum of 
about Rs. 2 only. Of course, 11 8, thing can be had for mere asking, there 
19 no reason for stealing it. Be that as it may, in the instant case, the 
Company takey its stand on the admission (Ext,.A), dated 30th August 1957, 
hy the workman concerned. Exhibit A is a clear admission of theft on the 
yart of the workman and he begged to be pardoned and at the sane time 
gave an undertaking that he would not repeat such misconduct in future. 
Qn this admission there is an endorsement by another Shri Harimohon 
Bhattacharjee to the effect that the fact is true. Now the workman during 
the trial contends that this admission was extorted from him under duress 
by the Proprietor Shri Subol Chandra Paul and the Department-in-Charge 
Shri Ajit Kumar Daw as the Proprietor lifted the receiver of the telephone 
and threatened him with arrest by calling in the Police unless he admitted 
jt, aud Ajit Daw threatened to -assault him with shoes. Both Shri Subol 
Kumar Paul and Shri Ajit Daw denied that any pressure was brought to 
hear upon the workman or he was in any way coerced into making an 
admission like this. That the plea of force or pressure being brought to 
bear upon him in the matter of the admission (156, A) is an afterthought 
will be clear from one statement of this workman in Court wherein he stated 
that he did not disclose of the alleged threat held out to him by Shri Subol 
Kumar Paul and Shn Ajit Daw to Shri Jashoda Pal during 3/4 days after 
8011) August 1997. If the admission were really extorted from him we 
would expect that immediately after leaving the spot he would disclose it 
to his other colleagues but he did nothing of the kind. His reticence and 
non-disclosure of the threat, if any, 1s very significant during some days 
following the incident. This workman admittedly put in 46 years’ service 
in the Company without any blemish and there is no reason why the 
Company would frame a false charge against him and dismiss him. The 
Union hkewise argues that after such a Jong period of faultless service it 
is simply incredible that the workman would lift a packet of Iodex worth 
a paltry sum. Let these probabilities apart, the case should be judged with 
regard to evidence on record. Thus unless the workman can prove that the 
mlmission was extorted from him, the Court should accept 16 as a genuine 
006, In this direction the workman stated that once he complained before 
the Proprietor Shri Paul that Shri Ajit Daw attends office late and once 
he granted leave to Shri Jashoda Pal to attend Court in the absence of 
Shri Ajit Daw in connection with another dispute between the Company 
and the Union and this explains why the wrath of Ajit Daw fell upon him 
anil he seized this occasion to take revenge on him. Since the Proprietor 
has denied the statement made by the workman, I am unable to believe it. 
[t is also difficult for me to believe that the Company would for the filmsy 
leasons even assuming them to be true, stoop so low as to bring a false 
charge against the workman. In addition to the admission Ext. A, the 
Company further examined Shri Ajit Daw and Shri Nakur Ghose whose 
evidence clearly proves the commission of the theft by the workman and 
I have no reasons to disbelieve them. I may add that in the circumstances 
of this case, the misconduct proved being of a serious nature and the work- 
man being caught os He the summary dismissal is fully justified. 


In the circumstances, I find that the Company in view of the theft 
committed by the workman in respect of a packet of Iodex however triffling 
its price may be, was fully justified in dismissing him as per letter Ext. 5, 
dated 4th September 1957. No mala fides or unfair labour practice on the 
part of the Company have been proved in this case. In the circumstances 
of this case I uphold the order of dismissal.

Next, I take up the case of Shri Jashoda Pal. The Company has 
produced Ext. 1 and Ext. 1(a) being two charges, dated 4th September 
1957. The charge in Ext. 1 is that he interfered in the matter of Manmathn’s 
being caught red-handed while stealthily removing a packet of Iodey 
belonging to the Company with the evident intention of hushing up the 
matter and that he refused to give out the truth. The second charge in 
Ext. l(a) is that he again absented himself from office without previous 
permission and he was asked to show cause why disciplinary action should 
not be taken against him. Exhibit 2 is the reply to the charge Ext. 1, and 
Ext. 2(a) is the reply to the charge Ext. ৭ In Ext. 2, duted 00) 
September 1957, the workman has categorically denied the charge. His 
statement in brief is that when Shri Ajit Daw was pulling Shri Dev Sarkar 
at about 6-15 p.m. on 30th August 1991 he casually requested Ajit Babu 
not to pull Manmatha as he was not feeling well, and that the packet of 
Iodex was not detected inside the compounding room where he was on duty, 
The workman further denied the allegation that he refused to speak the 
iruth. There is another statement that it is rather eo that to 
fabricate the charge-sheet against Shri Pal the Director Shri 8. Paul tried 
19 coerce Manmatha to confess in the evening on 2nd Septemher 1957 after 
duty hours and in the afternoon on 3rd September 1957 that Manmatha 
would be favourably considered if he gave a statement to the effect that he 
(Pal) persuaded Manmatha to say that sumebody had put the packet of 
Iodex in his pocket. In the concluding paragraph of his reply he has added 
that it is clear from the second charge-sheet of the same date that the 
Company was out to victimise him as he was the Secretary to the Union 
and thereby wanted to cripple legitimate trade union activities in the office. 
In his reply Ext. 2(a), dated 5th September 1957, Shri Jashoda Pal expressed 
surprise at Company’s calling for an explanation from him for his absence 
from office without previous permission without giving the date on which 
he was absent. His further statement is that he was absent from office on 
4th September 1957 due to severe pain in his teeth for which a petition was 
duly sent per post on 4th September 1957 under certificate of posting. The 
Company in this case بر ساسا‎ that a due enquiry was held into this matter 
on 1011) September 1957. Admittedly this workman was given a notice of 
the date of enquiry, but there is nothing to indicate that a proper enquiry 
was held in this case. All that we have before us are two statements, 
dated 10th September 1957 of Ajit (Ext. El) and Nakur Ghose (Ext. 12) 
and another (Ext. E8) showing interrogatories to Jashoda and his replies. 
There is nothing to indicate that the workman was allowed to cross-examine 
these two witnesses, nor are there any proceedings of enquiry. It is suid 
that one Mukti Babu recorded the statement but that gentleman is not 
called in to give his evidence in this case. So these two statements Ext. ا‎ 
and Ext. E2 were not subjected to cross-examination and the denial of the 
right of cross-examination to the workman is tantamount to violation of 
principles of natural justice. The answer to questions 1 and 4 in Ext. 3 is 
a clear genial on the part of the workman that he made any effort to rescue 
Manmatha on 30th August 1957 after the incident. I may add that I had 
the advantage of seeing both Shri Pal and Shri Daw. The latter is a 
physically rebust man and I find it not possible for Shri Pal, a frail and 
an almost old man to push aside Shri Daw. This allegation of Shri Pal’s 
pushing aside Shri Daw while he tried to take Shri Dey Sarkar to ‘he 
Pioprietor does not deserve credence at all. Thus there were no sufficient 
materials before the Company at the enquiry to justify the finding of guilt 
apainst Shri Pal. The finding of guilt is therefore a perverse finding 
which canot be allowed to stand. Besides that, admittedly, the Union ani 
this Company are not on good terms because there were many disputes 


between them and for Company’s failure {o implement some of the awards 


Piast I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 7153 
বস سس سو اجس چس‎ RRR emma سد‎ 
certificates had to be taken out for recovery of the relief under one or 
some of such awards. Thus [ would find in the circumstances of this case 
that there ure valid and cogent reasons for suspecting the bona fides of the 
(ompany in drawing up proceedings against this particular workman who 
is the Secretary to the Union. As Secretary presumably he took a leasing 
part in the Union activities both outside and in Court which have embarrassed 
the Company. It may also be added that the delay in drawing up proceedings 
against Shri Pal is also significant and the reason assigned by Shri Subol 
[aul in this behalf is a mere eyewash. The Company did not also allow 
Shri Pal to be represented by an office-hearer of the Union during enquiry 
as per his request in letter (Ext. 6A), dated 10th September 1957, This 
js tantamount to denial of reasonable facilities to the workman to defend 
himself during enquiry. The decision of the Company in this case, I would 
therefore find, is vitiated with mala fides and its finding is also perverse. 
It is therefore found that the order of dismissal passed in this case is 
unjustified and that the Company is directed to reinstate the workman and 
ay him all his wages from the date of his dismissal till the date of his 
reinstatement treating the continuity of his service as unbroken within a 
month of the publication of the award. 


Thua to sum up, the dismissal of Shri Manmatha Dey Sarkar is found 
justified and he is entitled to no relief. 


As regards Shri Jashoda, his dismissal is found mala fide and unjustified 
and the Company is directed to reinstate him and give him all the reliefs 
set forth above. 


This is my award. This award to govern both the references tried 
together.

AWARD 


This is @ case arising out of termination of service of some workmen 
as per list annexed with the order of reference and of a declaration of lock- 
out from 319 December 1956 by Messrs. Sur Enamel & Stamping Works 
Private, Ltd., 24 Middle Road, Entally (hereinafter described as the 
Company for the sake of brevity). 


The case of the Union, in short, is that the Company is very un- 
aympathetic, uncompromising, unconciliatory and victimising in _ its 
attitude towards its employees. The Union submitted a Character of 
Demands for redressing the genuine and long standing grievances vf 
employees on 7th August 1956. Since then the Company illegally and 
without any just and rensonable cause retrenched 144 efficient workmen 
in two batches. The Assistant Labour Commissioner Shri S. K. Bhatta- 
charjee took up the matter but 00010 not push it to any successful issue. 
In the meantime on 818 December 1956 the Company again illegally and 
without any reasonable cause retrenched 22 permanent workmen of its 
“Fire Extinguisher Department’’. There was no amicable settlement on 
the issue of retrenchment und the Company after the lock-out tried to 
re-open the factory by recruiting new জন দি The Company mala fide 
victimised the workmen in the list and its declaration of lock-out is wholly 
egal and unjustified. 


The Company in short in its written statement denies all the allegations 
made in the written statement of the Union and justifies the dismissal of 
the workmen complaint of and also the lock-out declared.

৯ 


The case was fixed for hearing on 4th June 1099; but in the meantime 
on 061) January 1959, the ‘ete put in a joint petition of -compromise and 
pray that the compromise be recorded. 


The terms of compromise appear to be fair, reasonable and lawful and 
may be given effect to. The dispute is thus disposed of in terms of the 
petition of compromise which do form a part of the award.

the Act, to this Court, for adjudication :— 


Schedule 


1. Whether the discharge of Shri Raj Narayan Singh, Durwan, was 
justified? To what relief is he entitled? 


AWARD 


This is a case arising out of alleged illegal and unjustified discharge of 
one Shri Raj Narayan Singh previously employed as a Durwan in Messrs. 
Ludlow Jute Co., Lid., (hereinafter referred to us the Company for the 
sake of brevity). 


The Union’s case in a nutshell is as follows: — 


The workman was employed in the year 1949 and was confirmed in 
1950. The employees of the Mill formed a Union ‘to ameliorate their 
conditions of service, and this particular workman amongst others took the 
initiative in the formation thereof. This workman was attucked with 
Pulmonary Tuberculosis and was under the treatment of the Ohest 
Specialist appointed by the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation. The 
aforesaid specialist declared him fit to resume duties while he was last 
examined thoroughly. Accordingly on the recommendation of the Insur- 
ance doctor the workman rejoined his duties on 12th March 1957 and conti- 
nued in his duties up to 19th March 1957 when he was asked hy the Labour 
Officer of the Company to appear hefore the Mil) doctor. The Mill doctor, 
however, after a casual examination advised the workman to take further 
rest but the doctor of the Employees’ Stute Insurance Scheme, refused 


Parr 1] THE CALCUTTA 09820157519) HEBRUAKY 12, 1599 760 
ee ee ০০ ৩ دت‎ 


runt him turther leave ou the ground of his illness and reiterated that 
thio سس‎ was fit to resume lis duties. On 16th April 1957 the work- 
man was intimated by a letter of the Persounel Manager that he would be 
allowed {o resume his duties provided the Mill doctor declared him fit. 
The workman, however, was reluctant to submit to any medical examina- 
tion by the Mill doctor as he was already declared fit by the doctor under 
the Insurance Corporation, The workman wus, discharged by a letter, 
dated 28rd April 1957, on the ground of his continued ill health. The 
efforts of the Conciliation Officer to make up this dispute failed, hence the 
reference. 

The Company denies the allegations in the written statement of the 
70101) and contends, inter alia. that this is not aon industrial dispute 
but this point was not pressed during trial, and that sometime in J uly 
1956 this workman was detected suffering from Pulmonary Tuberculosis 
when he took seven days’ leave on the recommendation of the panel doctor 
of theimployees’ State Insurance Corporation and this leave was extended 
by a furtaer period of six weeks with effect trom 30th July 1956 which 
waa sought to be extended by a further period of one month but the 
Company informed him that he should apply for an extension to the doctor 
of the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation. So the Company marked 
him as on authorised leave until 14th November 1956. On 13th November 
1956 the workman came to this Mill when he was medically examined by 
Company’s medical officer, who after thorough examination found hin) 
unfit for work and advised him further complete rest. Thereafter thia 
workman obtained leave from the panel doctor of the Employees’ Stute 
Tnsurance Corporation until 11th March 1957. Thus the total period of 
his leave on grounda of ill health amounted to 33 weeks of which 164 weeks 
wére sick leave granted by the panel doctor. On 12th March 1957 this 
workman produced a certificate of fitness from the panel doctor on the basis 
of which he was allowed to resume his duties on that very date, but the 
Company found that Shri Singh was still ailing and as he was suffering 
from a dangerous disease the Company decided to get him medically 
examined agnin by the Company's medical officer in the interest of the 
vorkman himself as also of the other workmen who would in normal course 
of work come in his contact. The Company’s doctor therefore on examin- 
ing him found that he was not completely cured of his disease and the 
Company did not therefore allow him to resume hia work. The Company 
advised him to obtain further leave from the panel doctor, failing this, to 
apply to the Company direct for further leave which the Company was 
prepared to grant him. The Company, however, marked the workman aa 
om authorised leave. The workman in the meantime neither obtained Jeave 
from the panel doctor, nor did he apply to the Company for leave and 
insisted on resuming his duties. But the Company agreed to allow him to 
resume his duties provided he was checked by the Company’s medical 
officer and found completely cured of the disease. Sri Singh, however, 
did not ultimately turn up for medical examination by the Company’s 
doctor. The Company, therefore, on grounds of his long absence due to 
ill health was compelled to discharge him. The Company affirms that its 
decision to get the workman medically examined before he could be permitted 
fo resume his duties was perfectly justified in view of his infectious disease. 
In short, therefore, the Company contends that the order of his dismissal, 
dated 23rd April 1957, is justified and that he is not entitled to any relief. 


Decision 
There is no dispute that this workman was employed دہ‎ a Durwan in 
the Company in 1949 and made permanent in 1950. The main dispute 


766 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 [Parr I 


centres round the condition of his health at the time of his discharge, ice., 
23rd April 1957. The Company’s learned Advocate referred to a statgment 
on record setting forth therein the chronological events relating to his 
illness which is not disputed by the Union. Admittedly, the workman 161] 
il] in July 1956 of Palmonary Tuberculosis and was under the treatment 
of Dr. Kazi Saheb, doctor of Employees’ State Insurance Corporation, and 
that he was on medical leave for about four months. There is also no 
dispute that on the certificate of the Insurance doctor that he was 
physically fit, he was permitted to rejoin his duties on 12th March 1957 
and continued as such for a week till 18th March 1957. The dispute 
between the parties started after his return to duty and there was difference 
of opinion between the panel doctor and the chest specialist appointed 
under the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation on one hand, and that 
of the Mill doctor Mr. Mitra (0.P.W. 1) on the other. Admittedly, Dr. 
Mitra, Caief Medical Officer, X-rayed him but the workman says that he 
was X-rayed only once and no photo was taken of his chest before his 
examination by Dr. Kazi Saheb (P.W. 3). The Company’s case at this 
particular point is that six days after his rejoining the workman was asked 
to have himself examined by Dr. Mitra, Chief Medical Officer. The Com- 
pany’s further case is that he was X-rayed on three occasions and skiagram 
of his chest was taken on 20th July 1956, 12th November 1956 and loth 
March 1957 (vide Exts. F, ৮] and F2—X-ray photos). The Company in 
view of the skiagram on the udvise of Dr. Mitra, Chief Medical Officer, did 
not allow him to join because there were still extensive infiltrations and 
lesions in both the lungs suggestive of active Tuberculosis and there were 
two cavities in the mght upper zone. In his opinion the workman was unfit 
for his hard duty up to 10th March 1957 and after this he did not examine 
the workman any more as he no longer turned up. 


During the hearing of this case, at a particular stage after examination 
of three witnesses for the Union including Dr. Kezi Kossimuddin, the Court 
was given. to understand by the learned Advocate for the Company that 
the Company had no objection to reinstate the workman if he were found 
physically fit after examination by Chest Specialist Dr. P. K. Sen of 
Calcutta and the case was adjourned. But the Company subsequently 
filed a petition stating that the Company was not agrecable to take him 
back because the workman made several false allegations Impugning the 
bona fides of the Company which therefore did not agree 10 take him back 
simply because he was 0 physically unfit and insisted on having an opinion 
from the Chest Specialist Dr. P. K. Sen on the condition of the workman’s 
health in April 1957 while he was discharged. The opinion of the Chest 
Specialist is that a study of the skiagram of his chest, dated 20th July 
1996, 12th November 1956 and 20th March 1957 (this date should he 
ith March 1957), showed that he suffered from lungs Tuberculosis of 
both sides (determined from strong sugyestive evidences in the skiagram) 
and the disease was active till the date of his 1891 X-ray plate, namely, 
20th March 1957 and that there was also a fair size cavity in the right 
upper zone on that date and he was of opinion that this workman was 
not fit for work till that date 20th March 1957. The Specialist, however, 
observed that his recent condition can only be determined if he submits 
himself again for a thorough check including skiagraphy and sputum test 
and KE. 9.1, test. In view of the attitude of the Company as argued by 
its learned Advocate the Court considered it useless and unnecessary to 
have the Specialist’s opinion as to his present state of health because the 
Company in the meantime had gone back on its own previous statement, 
namely, that the Company was willing to take him back if he was found 


part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 767

ee ست‎ eo 
fi as recorded in Court’s order No. 17, dated 9th June 1908. The learned 
Advocate for the Company insisted on a decision on the point of reference 
وہ‎ to whether the discharge of the workman was justified, in other words, 
whether his state of health on 28rd April 1957 justified his discharge. 
Qn this point, however, the opinion of the Specialist 1s unambiguous and 
decisive that the workman was physically unfit as already said above. 


Yow in view of the Company’s unwillingness to reinstate the workmam 
চিনি because he migat be سز‎ taal fit, the Court would not be justified 
in foisting this workman upon the Company on the basis of the order 
No. 17, dated 9th June 1958. The reference to this Court for adjudication 
runs as follows :— 


‘‘Whether the discharge of Shri Raj Narayan Singh, Durwan, was 
justified? To what relief is he entitled?’ 


So it would neither be legal nor proper for the Court to travel beyond the 
terms of the reference. The Court is to restrict itself to the terms of 
reference and if the Court proceeds to consider and adjudicate 7 
matters not referred to the Court, the action of the Court would be ultra 
vires and the award following thereupon would be void and unenforceable. 
The jurisdiction of the Tribunal to adjudicate on matters and to make am 
award is created by the order of reference made under section 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, and the order of reference limits the power of 
the Tribunal to make tae award (vide 1989 L.L.J., Vol. ,لا‎ page 598 and 
1958 1..L.J., Vol. I, page 572). The Court, therefore, in spite of its 
order No. 17, dated 9th June 1958, considers the evidence on record and 
restricts its decision only on the point of reference with due regard to the 
evidence on record, The opinion of Dr. P. K. Sen, the Specialist is 
decisive on it. At this stage I would advert to the arguments of the 
leamed Advocate for the Union that the Court should rely on the evidence 
of Dr. Kazi Kossimuddin (P.W. 3) and the report of the Chest Specialist 
who declared him fit on 110) March 1957 (vide report Ext. 4). This 
report (Ext. 4) of Dr. Saha does not seem to be acceptable in view of the 
opinion of Dr. P. K. Sen, the Specialist. Dr. Saha’s report Ext. 4(a), 
dated 24th June, 1957, that the workman is symptom free is not relevant 
for the purpose of this case as the Court called upon to decide the 
justifiability of his discharge on 23rd April 1957, I do not think any 
useful purpose would be served by calling in Dr. Saha in view of the 
report of Dr. P. K. Sen, the reputed Tuberculosis Specialist of the City 
which is entitled to greater weight. 


Having regurd to the Specialist’s opinion and the workman’s long 
absence due to his ill-health, the Company could not be expected to wait 
indefinitely for a workman to turn up as that would cause serious disloca~ 
tion in business. Thus following the principle laid down by the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court in the case reported in 1958 14140.» Vol. I, page 260 (Indian 
Iron & Steel Cv., v. their workmen), I think the Company was justified in 
passing the order of discharge as it did in this case according to the provi- 
sion in section 14(c)(v) of the Standing Orders of the Company for absence 
without leave for more than 10 days. 


_As to absence of any charge sheet, or any formal enquiry, I do not 
think any conceivable purpose would have been served if a charge sheet 
were framed und a formal enquiry was held and this same view has been 
pronounced in the above Hon’ble Supreme Court case. The Specialist’s. 
evidence is sufficient to show that he was physically unfit to resume his 
duties on 23rd April 1957. He was absent for about 88 weeks, some portion 
on authorised and some portion on unauthorised leave, and so his dismissal 


"768 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 [Parr 1 


এপ EEE সে সস sae cor alee eee সপ পপ 
is found justified according to the aforesaid Compuny’s standing orders, 
It may be said that the Company had no mala fides 12 discharging him, 
In the circunistunces, I do not find the workman is entitled to any relief 
in strict conformity with law us laid down in section 2(00)(¢) of the Indus- 
drial Disputes Act. But I would, in view of the hardship involved, as o 
special cuse, recommend that the Company would be generous enough to 
grant him retrenchment benefit at the rate of 15 days’ pay for every 
completed year of his service under the Company. This is my award. 


Nictated and corrected by me.

Industrial ispuets Act, 1947, and, as such, it has conrtavened the said 
section. A charge-sheet was given to him on 15th September 1958 and he 
gave a reply thereto on 19th September 1958. An enquiry was held in the 
matter on 20th September 1958. But the Company has not filed any appli- 
eation before the Tribunal for approval of its action against the petitioner. 


I need not go into the facts of the present case as the Company has 
agreed to reinstate Shri Mohanlal Samui, the present petitioner, with effect 
from the 29th December 1958 on his having tendered an apology for his 
past misconduct. The Company agrees to treat this period of absence from 
the date of his dismissal up to the date of his reinstatement 8৭ leave 
without pay. The petitioner agrees to these terms. I accept the terms 
of settlement between the parties as embodied in the joint petition filed 
before fe Tribunal, and pass my award in terms thereof. The case 13 
accordingly disposed of.
