AWARD 


This is a case arising out of alleged illegal and unjustified dismissal of 
one Shri Nirmal Kumar Bhattacharjee previously employed as a Time 


772 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1999 [055 I 


Keeper in Messrs. Sree Ambica Jute Mills Lid., Belur, Howrah (hereinafter 
referred to as the Company for the sake of brevity). 


The case of the Union, in a nutshell, is as follows: ‘The workman con- 
cerned Shri Bhattacharjee was transferred in November, 1956, to take the 
attendance of shifter section of the Spinning Department which had two 
Time Keepers. After a lapse of some time the other Time Keeper being 
absent, Shri Bhattacharjee was asked to carry on the work for the present. 
The Management, however, made no arrangement for bringing un extra 
hand in order to relieve Shri Bhattacharjee of the additional duty on this 
score obviously with the idea of getting the whole work done by one man 
and thereby increasing his workload. Shri Bhattacharjee made several! 
representations directly and through hiy Union (West Bengal Jute Mills 
Clerks Federation) but to no effect. The Company’s written assurance on 
the workman’s application, dated 10th April 1957, to the effect “at present 
we have no extra staff, please carry on ai present’ did not materialise. The 
workman therefore was obliged to inform the Company by his letter, dated 
110 May 1957 that it would not be possible for him to continue the double 
duties and the Management was given 15 days’ time to consider the position, 
but this too had no effect, so the workman stopped doing اس‎ duty and 
started carrying on his own work with eftect from 3rd June 1957. The 
Company, however, legally and unjustifiahly charge-sheeted him with 
suspension by its order, dated 4th June 1957. The workman offered his 
explanation to the charge but the Company ultimately dismissed him hy a 
notice, duted 10th June 1957 with effect from 8th June 1957. The Company 
did not hold any fair and proper enquiry. The Union therefore contends 
that the order of dismissal is illegal, mala fide, unjust and against all! 
principles of natural justice and seeks reinstatement of ‘thia workman 
together with other ancillary henefits, 


The Company in its written statement denies the material allegations 
in the written statement of the Union and contends, inter alia, as follows: 
In November, 1956, this workman was transferred to the Spinning Depart- 
ment as Timé Keeper. The-reason is that in November, 1956, one of the 
Time Keepers Shri Paramananda Varma had resigned his job and the 
other Time Keeper Shri Jagadish Prasad Agarwala expressed his desire 
کا‎ retire. The Company therefore decided to appoint one other Time 
Keeper in the Spinning Department who might get requisite training in 
due course In place of Jagadish Prasad Agarwala when he would retire, In 
March, 1957, Jagadish left the Company’s service and so the workman 
concerned carried on with the job, Truly the workman concerned asked 
for the appointment of an additional Time Keeper but the Management 
asked him to carry on and assured him that if it was not possible for him 
to carry on, wn extra hand would be given to him when available. The 
Management subsequently refrained from giving an additional hand having 
regard to the consideration that the B shift in the same department consist- 
ing of an equal number of emploveer was being managed by one Time 
Keeper all along without any complaint and, secondly, this workman was 
relieved of his clerical duties. The Union took up the cause of the workman 
and complained before the Assistant Tabour Commissioner, Howrah, and 
started a conciliation proceedings, The Assistant Iahour Commissioner 
advised the workman concerned to carry on until the dispute was settled. 
The Management was ultimately taken by surprise by the workman’s notice 
and was thus compelled to take disciplinary action against him. It is 
further contended that the Management held an enquiry with a notice to the 
workman on 7th June 1957 wherein he was given all reasonable facilities 
to defend himself and the Management found him guilty of disobeying its 
lawful and reasonable orders in refusing to carry out the duties allotted

a লিল লা দিলি 
to him and dismissed him by its letter, dated 1011) June 1957. The 
Company thus justifies the order of dismissal and contends that the workman 
is entitled to no relief. 


The Company took another preliminary objection that this is not an 
industrial dispute and therefore the reference is incompetent. 


Kirst of all, I take up the preliminary point. he workman concerned, 
beyond dispute, was a clerk and his cause was taken up by the West Bengal 
Jute Mills Clerks Federation. Accordingly his case was taken up by the 
aforesuid Union, so there is a presumption that when a Union takes up 
the cause of an aggrieved workman-member, 16 ia ro as a representative of, 
and with the support of, its members. It is for the employer to prove that 
the facts are otherwise and that the other workmen in the establishment who 
are also members of the Union are not behind it in its action. The employer- 
Company has not adduced any evidence to rebut the aforesaid presumption. 
I would therefore hold that this is an industrial dispute and not un indi- 
vidual one as contended by the Company. If any authority be needed, 
reference may be made to the ruling reported in 1957 1.14.3... Vol. II, 
page 466 (Hindusthan Times 110.) New Delhi, and Chief Commissioner of 
Delhi and others). Thus this point is found in favour of the Union. 


Next, I come to the merits of the case. It is common ground that this 
workman was employed in the Mills in 1950 as a clerk in the Finishing 
Department and at the material time he was employed as a Time Keeper. 
It 1s also admitted on both hands that there were two Time Keepers, viz., 
Patamananda Varma and Jagadish Prasad Agarwalla in the Spinning 
Debartment all along. This workman was transferred to the Spinning 
زی‎ reg at a time when there were already two Time Keepers but at 
the \time of his joining there, there waa only one, because another Time 
Keeper Jagadish Agarwalla had gone on 168৮6 on the occasion of his sister’s 
marriage, Admittedly, on his return, he and the workman concerned were 
both working ہ٥‎ Time Keepers in the Spinning Department. The trouble, 
however, arose a month or two thereafter when the other Time Keeper was 
absent for a day, but for that day the workman concerned did his work as 
well in addition io his own and ultimately this Time Keeper gave up his 
job and went away elsewhere. As work was running into arrear the workman 
concerned requested R. P. Dubey, Department-in-Charge, to request the 
Secretary to the Company to appoint another Time Keeper in place of 
Jagadish Agarwalla. This Mr. Dubey agreed to do and thus one or two weeks 
passed without any arrangement being made and in the meantine arrears 
naturally mounted high. This is the evidence of the workman concerned. 
Presumably as he found it difficult in managing the job single-handed 
and as payment would commence to be made in new coins he submitted his 
report Ext. 1 to the Secretary and Department-in-Charge, and Mr. Hakim, 
Secretary, made the endorsement Ext. 1(a) as follows: — 


“At present we have no extra staff, please catry on at present.’

This order as evidence stands, however, remained as n dead letter and

in his turn intimated this to the Secretary. I.J.M.A. Shri N. Dey, Labour 
Officer of J.J.M.A., took up the matter with the Secretary to the Company

Mr, Hakim (vide Ext. FE, dated 24th May 1967). To this the Management

“The Management is not in a position to consider the grievances of 
the Time Keeper, The question of workload is nothing but a myth. 
Actually Spinning “‘B’ shift which runs with equal number of

Apprehension of workload due to introduction of new coinage system 
is nothing but a false pretext to avoid his duties.’’ 


Tt is clear from the comments that the Company then intended getting 
the entire job done by this workman single-handed and it resiled from the 
Company’s initial stand as evidenced by the endorsement Ext. l(a). Thus 
the Company shifted ground and this was really nothing short of an unfair 
labour practice on the part of the Company. If it was the case of the 
Company that the workload was not getting to be mnecreased and this was 
really one man’s job and that it would get the entire job managed by one 
man, the Company should have intimated that in clear terms to this 
workman when he first submitted his report Ext. 1, dated 10th April 1957. 
Ry the endorsement Ext. 1(a) it is clear that the Company intended at least 
at that stage to give another Time Keeper and the workman concerned waa 
harbouring the hope that he would get another assistant as soon as available 
as intimatd by the Secretary. The Companv gave that hope to the workman 
initially but ultimately changed front and wanted to have the entire job 
managed by this workman single-handed. Next, I take up the matter of 
enquiry. On behalf of the Union it is contended that there was practically 
no enquiry and nothing but a show. The Company has produced Ext. A 
wherein the charge is as follows :— 

“On and from 3rd June 1957 you stopped your allotted duties partly 
and thereby created an undesirable situation in the department. 
Thia is an act subversive of discipline and a serious neglect of 
work,”’ 


The workman offered his explanation which runs as follows: — 


‘In reply to the charge-sheet drawn against, I beg to state that the 
allegation contained in the charge-sheet is not at all bona fide. 
It should be noted that T was transferred to the department to 
take the attendance of the shifter section from Novemher 1956, 
when there was another Time Keeper for the Spr. Sec, From 
2nd March 1957 the Time Keeper of the Spr. Sec. being absent 
T was compelled to take attendance of both sections. TI was doing 
the work with great hardship and partly some clerical job is 
pending. In the meantime I made repeated request but to no

to arrange for one Time Keeper in place of Jagadish Babu. I 
rot reply thus ‘at present we have no extra staff. Please carry

There 1s overseer’s comments on the back side of the charge-sheet who 
1051 that the conduct of the workman was subversive of discipline 
because he refused to do attendance of the full department though he 
was ordered to do so. Moreover, it is 10 be noted that B shift Time Keeper 
with good number of hands was carrying on his duties smoothly, His 
action on the day was to put the Management in trouble. So he recom- 
mended severe punishment in this case. B. N. Roy Choudhury, Labour 
Officer, ا(‎ appears, made an enquiry on 7th June 1997 at 38 p.m. Labour 
Officer’s comment runs thus:— 


“I made an enquiry into the case on 7th June 1957 at 3 p.m. He 
appeared and made no statement. Only he referred to his Union 
Secretary’s letter 1)/17/5/57 and his letter, dated 3rd June 1957, 
and then left. Mr. R. P. Dubey, Spg. I/c, a witness, submitted 
his statement in writing. The statement is attached herewith. 
The employee joined this Mill on 24th April 1990. He had a 
warning on 318 May 1957 and previous to this he had some 
verbal warnings too. His refusal to take the uttendunce of the 
full department on 3rd June 1957 and his previous warning, dated 
2188 May 1957, prove without any doubt of his ill-motive to put 
the management in trouble. In my opinion, strong action should 
be taken against him in the interest of discipline of the Mill.” 


It 1s clear that there is nothing to indicate in the proceedings of enquiry 
Ext. A that the workman was offered reasonable facilities to cross-examine 
the two witnesses, Thus this is an instance where natural justice was denied 
to the workman and there is further nothing to indicate that this workman 
was offered an opportunity to adduce evidence if he liked in his defence at 
the enquiry, The enquiry, it appears, was purely o uniluteral affair, Shri 
reg ان‎ and Shri Roy Choudhury offered their comments which were obviously 
in favour of the Company whose employees they are and ultimately the 
Secretary M. ও. N, Hakim ordered that after full enquiry into the charge 
framed against him the workman was found guilty and was dismissed with 
effect from 8th June 1957. Now the question is whether the enquiry in 
this case cnn be said to have been 11 and properly conducted and 
whether the decision of the Manayement arrived ut the enquiry should 
stand. The evidence of Shri B. N. Roy Choudhury (0. P. W. 2) has 
exposed the defects at the enquiry and denial of reasonable facilities to 
the workman to defend himself. As is laid down in the famous Buckingham 
and Carnatic Oo. Ltd.’s case, the decision of the Company is liahle to he 
interfered with if,— 


(a) there is want of bona fide, or 


(b) it is a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice or violation 
of the principles of natural justice, or 


(c) there is a basic error of facts, or 
(d) there has been a perverse finding on the material«.” 


In this case, it appears to me that the decision of the Company is liable 
to be interfered with hecause the Company seems to have been actuated 
by unfair labour practice and that the decision also was vitinted by a perverse 
finding and the Company has also committed basic error on facts. In 
doing so, J am not forgetful of the fact that the Labour Officer’of 1.J.M.A. 
Shri Dey who held an enquiry in this case found that the workload of 
the Time Keeper was not too much for one man. The main ground on 
which his finding was based is that in the B shift in the same department 
one Time Keeper has heen working without any difficulty for a long time. 


776 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 | Parr [1 


Shri Dey also stated that he made enquiries of other Mills where also one 
Time Keeper in each shift was found working and that this number 8 
found adequate, If the Company would have proceeded to retrench him 
on the ground of rationalisation of statt, this Court would have nothing to 
interfere as the Company has got every right to rationalise its staft accord- 
ing to its requirements and economise the expenses, The Company cannot 
be allowed to shift ground now and to justify the order of dismissal on 
some ground other than the charge levelled against the worker. In the 
case reported in 1953 (1,۱۰8۷۰, page 149 (Bathgate & Company vs, their 
workmen), it is laid down thut an employer cannot be allowed to justify 
dismissal of workmen on ground other than those he gave in the letter of 
dismissal, 11 the Company would have taken the stand from the very 
beginning that the চা of the workman was not going to be increased 
if he were to manage the job of the Time Keeper in A shift for both shifter 
section and spinning section single-handed, that would have been a different 
matter, This the Company did not do, but what the Company did was to 
hold out a hope to the workman at the beginning and subsequently resiled 
from that stand and intended getting the entire job from him which is at 
variance with the hope held out. Therefore in this case the Management 
was actuated by some ulterior motives and the charge couched in very vague 
term is just a cloak to get rid of a worker and the ostensible enquiry held 
in this case was in violation of the principles of natural justice and that the 
worker was denied reasonable facilities to defend himself at the enquiry 
which he is entitled to have, 


Next T proceed to show that the Company’s finding that the workload 
was not increased 1s not correct. The duties of the workman may be thus 
set forth in details, namely, (1) to keep the attendance of all workers and 
to go round to see which of the workmen out of 490 actually attended and 
which not, (2) to calculate wages of workmen with reference to the number 
ot days attended by them, (8) at the end of the week calculation of wages 
for the week-ended has got to be made on the basin of attendance and pay- 
ment is made on the following Saturday, (4) at the heginning of the shift if 
some workmen were found absent requisition elips are required to he sent 
to the Labour Office which supplies the requisite number of workmen, (5) 
to fill in the Changes’ Report Ext. B and wage tickets commenced to he 
distributed from each Friday nfternoon, (6) caleulations as made in the 
attendance register are forwarded to the Head Time Keener who supplies 
tickets on the basis of the entries in the attendance register, (7) insertion 
of the token number of the workers is made as well as the wages, (8) to make 
entry of wares on the basis of atlendance register in the attendance register 
by Thursday in the next week. Tt mav further he nointed that the number 
of workers 01001010560 in both the spinner nnd shifter sections in A. shift 
where the workman was employed was more than those in the B shift at 
least by 20. In the B shift it ia seriously contended for the Companv that 
there was-enly one workman but the evidence of the workman is that there 
were others to help him which help was not forthcoming to this workman 
concerned, 0 shift was being managed by Biswanath Sharma but there 
were far less number of workmen. T have very carefully considered the 
volume of work required to be done by this workman and really speaking, 
in my opinion the burden of work was too much for one man to carry on the 
eve of introduction of naya paisa. The Company examined one Shri Harihar 
Singh who was emploved as n Time Keener in the ( shift where the 
number of workmen was admittedly less. The Union has drawn the atten- 
tion of the Court to serials 31, 32 and 99 in the attendance register to show 
that there is no emplovee descrihed as Time Keeper in the A shift. The 
learned Advocate for the Company cited a case reported in Taw Reports 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 777 


Appeal Cases 1930 page 271 (Bouzowon and The Ottoman Bank) wherein it 
is laid down as follows ;:— 


‘“‘An order by u master to his servant to remain in a place within the 
area of his employment is a lawful order unless it involves imme- 
diately threatening danger by violence or disease to the person 
of the servant, Observations in Turner ٠. Mason (1945) 14 M. & W. 
112 approved. 


The appellant, u (Christian Turkish subject in the employment of the 
respondent bunk, was ordered by them to be transterred from their 
Stamboul branch to their branch at Mersina, o distant place in 
Turkish Asia Minor. He refused to go on the grounds; (1) That 
Mersina was not within the area of his employment; (2) that the 
order was unreasonable in the view of his ignorance of Turkish, 
and the hostile attitude of the Turkish civil authorities to him. 
He was thereupon dismissed without notice, and brought an action 
for wrongful dismissal : 


Held (1), on the tacty—distinguishing Anderson rs. Moon (1837) 15 
Shaw, 412—that Mersina was within the area of the appellant’s 
employment, and (2) approving Turner ve Mason 14 3]. & W. 112, 
that as he did not suggest that compliance with the order would 
involve him in personal danger, the order was lawful and his 
disobedience to it a faute grave which under the contract justified 
his dismissal.’’ 


But the facts in this case are clearly distinguishable and the ruling cited 
does not apply. in the circumstances of this case it cannot be fairly 
captended that the workman should have continued to work to the point 
of' his death, no matter how perfunctorily or inefficiently the same was 
সু Moreover, there is nothing to show that this workman was ashed 
to bpecifically carry on the job of the Time Keeper in both the shifter and 
spinner sections aud in the absence of any specified order the workman 
cannot be found guilty of disobeying that order. If there be no specified 
order there is no disobedience thereof. In this conexion the following 
observations made in the case of Novelties (Private) Ltd. and their workmen 
reported in 1958 1415. .১ Vol. I, page 148, may be quoted thus:— 


‘A workman working in the accounts section was transferred to stores 
section of the establishment. Prior to such transfer he was pre- 
paring sales tax returns. Subsequent to the transfer he was attend- 
ing to work connected with the stores section only. There was no 
evidence to show that subsequent to the transfer it was part of 
his duties to prepare sales tax returns. In these circumstances, 
refusal by such workman to prepure sales tax returns when called 
upon by the Management could not be considered to amount to 
dereliction of duties deserving the punishment of discharge from 
service. Where the workman denial that this was not part of his 
duties, the order of termination of his services inter alia on this 
ground without holding any enquiry must be held to be improper 
and unjustified.” 


Even if there was say such order ] would go the length of holding that 
this was an unreasonnble order ond the workman could not be found 
guilty if he disobeyed to carry 1৮ out. It 18 very easy either for the Labour 
Officer or for any other man concerned to say that the workload was not too 
much for the workman but examined in all details and viewed in proper 
perspective, all the duties weighed together seemed to be an uphill task 
for one man to discharge honestly and conscientiously. 


778 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 [Parr I 


Thus to sum up, (2) the charge is not specified in the charge-sheet, 
(ii) there was no fair und proper enyuiry held in this case, (111), the 
ortensible charge framed is not the real charge, but it is a cloak to hide 
the real motive of the Company to get the entire work done by one man 
and the Company was thus actuated by an untai: labour practice, (iv) 
there was want of bona fides on the part of the Company and the finding 
of guilty is perverse and so the decision of the Company cannot stand. 


The workman is therefore exonerated from the charge and his dismissal 
is found unjustified. So in the fitnesa of things he is entitled 16 reinstate- 
ment and back wages for the period of his unemployment till his rein- 
statement. 


The Company is therefore directed to reinstate this workman and pay 
him all his wages for the period of his unemployment within a month of 
~ — of the award treating the continuity of his service as 
unbroken.

Issue No. 33 The twenty-one workers, mostly strikers, were laid oft 
when the lock-out was lifted on Ist November 1957. The Union contend,

10110 the rule of last come, first go. That rule, however, is more applicable 
to the cases of retrenchment, as would be apparent from the statutory 
provisions made in section 26002) of the Industrial Dixputes Act. There is 
uo corresponding provisions regarding the lay-off. In this case, no question 
of “last come, first go’’ arises in the case of retrenchment of the binding

compositor, who was appointed temporarily since the middle of November, 
1958, only for some urgent Telegu work. Laying off is a Management 
function. Normally, there should not be any interference with this. 
unless this is done mala fide, or with any ulterion motive. When the volum 
of work has been reduced, as in this instant case, partly, due to the 
fault of the workers, the Munagement 18 justified in adopting this measure 
to suve the industry from financial collapse. The majority of the laid off 
staff did not comply with the provisions of Jaw, in unjustly refusing 00 
attend a roll-call, on flimsy grounds and, therefore, the question of payment 
of lay-off compensation does not arise in their case. Others, who followed 
the provisions of law, should be paid compensation at the statutory rates.

This industrial dispute, over the retrenchment of the seventy-six 
employees, between Messrs. Ispahani Jd. (hereinafter referred to as the 
Company), 91 Ezra Street, Caleuttacl, und their workmen represented by 
Ispahani’s Employees’ Union, Commercial Buildings (2nd_ floor), Block

for adjudication by the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, 
Order No. 4619-1.R./IR/11L-189(A)/57, dated the 4th Decemher 1957. 


Is the retrenchment of the seventy-six employees, as per attached list 
justied? What relief are they entitled? 


Both parties filed written statements, adduced evidence, oral and docu- 
mentary, and advanced arguments in the case. 


AWARD 


The Company has retrenched 19 employees on 27th June 1957, and 57 
employees on 27th September 1957. The Union’s contention is that this 
retrenchment is wholly unjustified, and the only motive behind it is to 
victimise the staff for its legitimute trade union activities. The Company 
supports this retrenchment and denies the Union’s allegation. It contends 
that this retrenchment was made purely for trade reasons. The Company 


784 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1999 [Pari J 


was suflering losses year after year, and it was reducing its staff whenever 
possible. It undertook first reduction of its staff in 1953, which was also 
a ycar of lovs, and iis action was found justified by the Tribunal, adjudicat- 
ing a dispute over it. Since then, the Company was going from bad to 
worse, and by the end of March 1957, its total loss amounted to 
Rs. 75,87,823-3-7. The Shellac Department proved to be a great handicap 
and it was permanently closed down on 3156 March 1956. The Union, of 
course, contested the Company’s case from the very beginning. 


The case of the Union, before this Tribunal, is that this retrenchment, 
made on 27th September 1957, was done in clear violation of a settlement 
in a conciliation proceeding before Shmn N. C. Kundu, A.L.C., on S0th 
July 1957 and, as such, the retrenchment of the 57 employees made on 27th 
September 1957, is wholly illegal. The alleged settlement, which is 
apnexure A to the Company's written statement, is marked as Ext. B. 
There is no settlement or agreement regarding the retrenchment of 19 
employees effected on 27th June 1957. Exhibit B contains the terms of 
agreement entered into between the parties before the Conciliation Uflicer 
in the dispute over the proposed retrenchment of about 50 employees, The 
terms are: 

‘1, The Company agree to keep the proposed retrenchment in abey- 

ance fur the tune being. 


2, In the meantime, representatives of the Company and the Union 

would sit together and find out ways to avert retrenchment or 
alternatively to submit a scheme of retrenchment to avoid closure 
They will submit their findings in the respect to the Labour 
Directorate by 25th August 1967. 


3. If necessary, the dispute will be taken up again by the Labour 
Directorate on receipt of the joint findings of the Company and 
the Union.”’ 


The proposed retrenchment was kept in abeyance for the time being 
The representatives of the parties agreed to find out ways and means to 
avert this retrenchment or in the alternative to prepare a scheme for reduc- 
tion of ataff just to avoid any closure of the Company. They agreed to do 
this by 25th August 1957 when they would submit a report to the Labou 
Directarate on this matter. Shri P. R. Mukherjee, on behalf of the 
Oompany, contends that this is no agreement, far less a settlement, as 
defined in section 2(P) of the Industrial Disputes Act, and as mentioned in 
sections 18(3), 19(1) und (2) of the sail Act. The terms of the so-called 
apreament are not in dispute, heimg put into writing as per Ext. B. It 
appears from the evidence of both sides that no s-heme was prepared eithe: 
to avert this retrenchment or to give effect to 1t on or before 25th August 
1957. In fact, the Company wrote to the Coneiliation Officer on the 26th 
Septenrher 1957, on the eve of this retrenchment in dispute, that due to 
failure on the part of the Wnion representative to co-operate in the inatter, 
they could not evolve a scheme of a retrenchment as required within the 
date fixed. In the meantime, the financial position of the Company did 
not brook any further delay, and the retrenchment in question was put into 
eftect. The terms of the agreement make it abundantly clear that the 
dispute was not settled in its true sense. The alleged agreement, if it can 
be yo called, did not ripen into a settlement, which would bind the parties, 
and would debar the appropriate (fovernment from making a_ reference 
of the said dispute under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act. In the 
first place, the disputed retrenchment was only kept in a stute of suspension 
for the time being, i.e., the proposed retrenchment was not” made 
immediately. [1৭ operation was suspended for the present. Did the parties 


part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 785 


‘uteud that by this agreement the proposed retrenchment would be 
be indefinitely postponed? No such intention, however, appears from the 
textewt the agreement itself, The parties fixed a definite date, by which 
they would further consider the matter of dispute, and settle it by avoiding, 
or, in the alternative, by effecting one on on agreed basis. They agreed 
also to report their findings te the Labour Directorate by 25th August 1981. 
According to both sides, this was not done. No useful purpose will be se: ved 
by trving to ascertain who was ai fault in this matter. The fact is that 
nothing was done in furtherance of a settlement within the date fixed. The 
Company waited for about a month after the fixed date and_ thereafter 
decided to put the proposed retrenchment into effect after submitting a 
report to the Labour Directorate. ‘The question now is whether according 
to the terms of the agreement the Company is precluded from taking action 
ju this matter on 27th September 1957. In the agreement, the intention of 
the parties was to take the dispute out of the hands of the Conciliation 
(fticer and to bring about an amicable settlement by direct negotiation 
hetween them. In doing it, it granted some sort of moratomum to the 
parties, and did nothing more. In my view, Ext. B does not contain the 
tefms of any settlement of the dispute for, in actual fact, the dismite 
remained as it is, and only a standstill arrangement was arrived at to 
facilitate its conciliation. 1, therefore, hold that this is not a settlement, 
as defined in section 2(1’) of the Induetrial Disputes Act, which is binding 
on the parties under section 19(2) of the same Act. It is idle to contend 
now that the alleged settlement would last for six months from its date, 
and two months more after a notice given by the parties terminating the 
same an required hy law. In the atoresaid context, no such contention 
arises. Therefore, the retrenchment of 57 employees made on 27th 
ک۲‎ 1957 was not done in violation of any settlement, dated 100 
July 1967.

of the Management, the Tribunal should not interfere, except when it was

The Union’s next point of attack 18 that in effecting this retrenchment, 
the Management overlooked the question of the seniority of service, and did 
not follow the well-established principle of 4199 come, first go’’. That 
1116 was enunciated in the following words, in the well-known case of the 
Vishttamitra Press decided hy the Labour Appellate Tribunal, and reported 
10 1992, .A.C., page 20 at page 33: ‘Other things being equal, ‘the last 
rome ‘must first go’. If that rule has been departed from, the Management 
must justify the departure......’’.. This has now been embodied in section 
25(4) of the Industrial Disputes Act which says that the employer shall 
ordinarily retrench the workman who was the last person to be employes 
m that category, unless for reasons to be recorded the employer retrenches 
any other workman. 1১,5৬৮, 9, Shri Wali Mahammad, a Driver, could not 
say whether there were anybody junior to him still in service. Other 
witnesses said that they had been retrenched while their juniors were 
continuing in service. Some papers have been filed, on behalf of the 
Company, as well as on behalf of the Union, by which the Union sought to 
establish their claim on this point and the Company wanted to refute it. 
In the long written statement of the Union the names of the alleged junior 
৭71 are not mentioned. Therefore, the Company had no opportunity to 
refer to such cases in ity written statement, though it denied the allegations 
hat the retrenchment was made in violation of the principle “‘last come, 
first (107, In this matter, the papers of the Company, which are apparently 
repared with reference to its booka of accounts, and other records, main- 
tamed in the office, appear to be more reliable than papers prepared on 
information received from persons not examined in the case, on the other 
ide. That being the position I think I should reject the Union’s conten- 
in on this point. The retrenchment is, therefore, justified. 


The next question is one of relief. O.P.W. 1, Shri Arakie, said that 
me of the retrenched staft received compensation from the oftice and some 
id not. In this connection, I would like to place on record that P.W. 7,

tyment of gratuity. It is difficult to find out what he actually meant by

certainly get it, if uot already received. If it meant anything else, he had 
failed ہا‎ establish a claim for that. P.W. 8, Shri S. Jk. Chatterjee, joined 
the service of this Company in 1950. He was not paid any compétiisation 
on the ground that he was a temporary worker. He said that he was not 
temporary. He worked continuously without break since his appointment. 
This evidence has not been contradicted. Exhibit 5, copy of the notire 
terminating his service, described him as a temporary clerk. Even if we 
take him as a temporary olerk, he is entitled to retrenchment compensation 
when, according to evidente, he had been in service for a continuous period 
since 1940. He is entitled to statutory compensation under section . 25) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act. He should be paid such compensution 
within one month from the date of the publication of this award. The 
retrenched emplovees are entitled to statutory Compensation and other reliefs 
mentioned in section 25(F) of the Act. Those who did not receive auch 
compensation, should be paid all reliefs under section 25(F) of the Act 
within one month from the date of the publication of the award. I answer 
the issue accordingly.

2. The reference was received here on 11th June 1958. After service 
of usual notices, the Union did not turn up. The Company entered 
appearance. In the circumstances another notice was issued to the Union 
intimating it that it had taken no step in their case, and that in case it did 
not take action in the matter on receipt of the second notice, the case 
would be liable to be disposed of for non-prosecution. But no 
acknowledgment receipt of the said notice was forthcoming. In view of the 
alleged closure of the factory the Tribunal felt it difficult to serve the notice 
directly by post on the Union. So thereafter a copy of the Tribunal’s 
notice 60 the Union was made over to the Company with the direction to 
cause service of the same on the Union, and to swear an affidavit in respect 
of the said service of notice. Thereafter Shri §. K. Bhanja Choudhuri, 
Labour Adviser to the Howrah Manufacturers’ Association, informed the 
Tribunal that the Company had issued a notice on the Union on 20th 
November 1958. Later on, on 7th January 1959, Shri N. K. Das, 
Assistant Labour Adviser of the aforesaid association, appeared on behalf 
of the Company and filed an affidavit in support of the Company’s service 
of notice on the Union on 20th November 1958 by registered post. Even 
after all this, the Union could not be made to appear before the Tribunal. 


The award was reserved. 


3. The only issue which arose for determination under the order of 
referencé is as follows: — 


Whether the closure of the factory is justified? To what relief the 
workers are entitled in addition to what they have already received 
on closure of the factory? 


AWARD 


4. As it appears from the representation of the Company as also from 
the issue itself in the order of reference, the workers have already received 
some amount consequent on the closure of the factory. Apparently they 
have been satisfied with the said puyment, aud that is why even after 80 
many notices by the Tribunal, neither the workers nor the Union think it

worthwhile to contest the matter. In the circumstances, the only award 
that I can pass is one of ‘‘no dispute.’’ ] pass my uward accordingly.

issue No. 1: It relates to dismissal of Shri Sanat Sarkar from service. 
P.W. 2.) Shri Sarkar, said that he was in service since 19538. He joined 
the Cossipur Factory on 18th April 1957, and worked for seven days, i.e., 
till 19th April 1957. He said that he was refused entry since the next 
day. He has not got the identity card with him. He said that he made 
it over to Durwan on 19th April 1957, and the same was not returned to 
him. He enquired of the same in the Time Office but to no effect. He 
said that he was dismissed most arbitrarily. The Union, in its written 
statement at paragraph 24, gave a different story. It suggested that 
thaugh Shri Sarkar was reporting for duty he was disallowed from doing 
day to day normal work. He wrote to the Management on the 28th April 
and on the 25th May last year ubout this. The Company, in its written 
statement at paragraph 27, denied this allegation and said that Shri Sarkar 
was removed from service for his unauthorised absence since 20th April 
1957. There was proper enquiry after notice which was attended by Shri 
Sarkar. In the copy of his letter alleged to have been sent on 22nd April 


800 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 [Panr I 
a SSS 
1957, Shri Sarkar did not mention auything about his identity card. In 
his second letter, sent more than one month after that date, by registered 
post, he said that his identity card was not returned to him by the Time 
Qffice, where it must be lying. The enquiry proceedings showed that there 
wag no such card lying in the Time Office and there was no evidence on 
the side of Shri Sarkar to show that he ever handed over the time card in 
the way alleged. Further, he did not explain his long silence for over a 
mouth between the alleged refusal of work on 2Uth April 1957 and tho date 
of the registered Jetter to the Management on 25th May 1957. Shn 
Sarkar’s case although reported to the Union was not mentioned in the 
agreement, dated 6th May 1957, between the Management and the Union. 
In all probabilities, this should have been discussed at the time of enquiry 
held on 30th July 1957. Shri Sarkar said to have collected his dues and 
left. The enquiry held on 30th July 1957 was admitied, and after this 
enquiry the Management had taken action for his unauthorised absence 
from work. There is hardly any reason why the Management should 
refuse him work after having permitted him to work in the factory for 
7 days. 11901 any question of victimisation can arise in this matter. 
Absence without permission for over 10 days is a major misdemeanour 
punishable with discharge from service under the Standing Orders. 
Accordingly, this dismissal cannot be said to be, in the circumstances, 
unjustified. Shri Sarkar is not entitled to any relief in this case. 


Issue No, 2: It relates to a demand for abolition of existing piece-rate 
system. The Union, in 21১ written statement ut paragraph 44, stated that 
the Company had introduced piece-rate system for the first time in the 
history of the Company most unilaterally and arbitrarily at a most ‘small 
rate’, to the serious prejudice to the workers, who were not even paid the 
minimum wages. The wages were deducted on the false plea of payment 
under the piece-rate system. The Company, in its written statement at 

aragraph 55, denied the said allegations of the Union and stated that it 
introduced the piece-rate system stage by stage. It was not done 
unilaterally or most arbitrarily. It 1s generous and based on scientific 
analysis of the work performed in the Workshop to help as a great incen- 
tive (0 earn more and, therefore, not prejudicial to the workers. P.W. 1, 
Shri Bhupal Chakraborty, the Assistant Secretary of the Union, said that 
there was no piece-rate system at the Hazra Road Factory. ‘The picce-rate 
system was introduced sometime in May 1957, but not in all departments 
at a time. It now exists in five departments. There was no guarantee of 
minimum rates under the system. The principal objections, according to 
him, are (i) the workers do not get sufficient work throughout the day, 
(ii) no fixed rate for specific job, (111) such rates are not notified to the 
workers, and (iv) piece-raters are getting less than the wages on which 
they are appointed, etc. O.P.W. 2, Shri R. N. Jaju, is the Chief Executive 
of the Factory. He said that this piece-rate system was first introduced 
from the inception of the factory in the Coil Binding Department. 
Gradually it was extended to many departments. These entire piece-rates 
were fixed after careful time and motion study. The rates were notified 
to the workers, Exhibits O, P, Q, R, are the relevant papers on this 
point. Exhibit P will show that in many cases the workers have earned 
more under the piece-rate system between January and August 1957. 
Exhibit Q is the chart showing the actual earnings of P.W. 3, Shri L. N. 
Dey and P.W. 4, Shri F. A. Mallick. It would appear therefrom that 
their evidence, in this case, on this point was not true. P.W. 3, Shri Dey, 
however, admitted that the Management paid him the deficiency in his 
wages under piece-rate. He, of course, said that he did not get more 
wages under the piece-rate system. This statement has been contradicted 


part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 801 
টি 
ہا‎ the evidence of O.P.W. 2, Shri Jaju. P.W. 4, Shri Mallick, said that 
he got less wages under the piece-rate system than under the daily rates. 
He brought this fact to the notice of Foreman and the deficiency was made 
up immediately. His grievences against the piece-rate system are: (i) 
the distribution of work by the Supervisor is such that one is not allowed 
to finish his work in course of a day, (ii) the more favourite workers get 
all tools which are necessary to finish an article whereaa others do not get 
that, and (iii) there is no fixed rate for it. All these have been sufficiently 
disproved by the evidence of the Company. Piece-rates are not only fixed 
on time and motion study by the help of experts but they are duly notified. 
The question is whether anybody is getting less under the piece-rate 
system. A large number of workers are getting more. A few earned less, 
and immediately a complaint was made to the management by a worker, 
his deficiency was made up. Exhibit R shows that. There were short 
ayments and the deficiencies were paid back by the Management. 

urther, the Management pays the workers at a general rate whenever 
there is no full work for them. Qn this evidence, the question of abolition 
of the existing system or fixing the guaranteed minimum does not arise. 
The piece-rate system is beneficial to the Management for it ensures higher 
production. Further, there is less necessity for strict supervision over the 
work. It is beneficial to the worker, as it is an incentive to work and 
provides equal opportunities to everybody to earn more and more wages. 
No ground has been made out, on the side of the Union, for fixing a 
guaranteed minimum of basic wages, under the system, when the Manage- 
ment is agreeable to make up all deficiencies in wages whenever it comes 
to ifs notice and the workers are ensured of payment of general rates when- 
ever they do not get any work under the system. The grievances alleged 
by the witnesses, on the side of the Union, are not against the system but 
against some alleged favoured treatment by the supervisors. The allega- 
tiond have not been established in this case. Further, that it hardly 
considered as a demerit in the system sufficient to warrant its abolition. 
I find the issue against the workmen. 


Issue No. 3: It relates to a demand for abolition of the contract-system 
of work. The Union, in its written statement at paragraph 3, urged for 
abolition of contract-labour system on the grounds that the workers are 
deprived of their legitimate rights under it. The workers now employed 
under the different contractors should be treated as regular workmen of 
the Company, and all the facilities of the ‘statutory’ Act should be extended 
and they should also be paid the rates of wages as paid to the Company's 
workmen. The Company, in its written statement at paragraph 53, denied 
the said allegations of the Union and contended that except for the 
erection work, and the other allied jobs, which were temporary in its 
nature, no labour was employed through contractor. It is, therefore, 
without any substance. 


P.W. 1., Shri Chakraborty, former Treasurer of the Union, and at 
present, the Assistant Secretary of the Union, said that 300 men worked 
under the contractors out of 900 men, now employed in the Cossipur 
Factory. They do these works, viz. (i) Switch Board work, (11) Trans- 
former Tank work and (iii) some amount of painting work. They do the 
sential work of the factory and are not paid any overtime when they 
work beyond the factory hours. He, however, could not say whether the 
Tanks were supplied from outside and parts were assembled inside the 
factory. P.W. 4, Shri Mallick, said that the contract-labourers did not 
pet any bouns at all, no leave and holiday. Their rates were lower than 
the Company’s rates and they worked on regular and essential work of the

Company. U.P.W. 2, Shri Jaju, is the Chief Executive of the Factory. 
He said that there was no Transformer Tank Manufacturing Department 
in the Factory. Tanks and covers were purchased from the market. The 
suppliers fabricated them in their own places. Tanks being bulky 
materials they were made and fitted by the suppliers with their own men. 
There is foundry shop in the premises of the Factory. The Company did

of Contractors, employed in this factory, came and deposed in this case

and examined as such. Accordingly, 1 am _ imelined to hold that the 
employment of the alleged Contractors’ men in regular and essential work 
of the factory is not true. The question of abolition of contract-labour, 
in the circumstances of the case, cannot be decided in abstract particularly, 
in the absence of the Contractors’ men in the dispute. It has also not 
been shown in which way the workmen here are interested in the abolition 
of the so-called contract-labour in the factory. That being the position, 
T am afraid, the dispute has ceased to be an industrial dispute. For all 
these reasons, I decide the issue against the Union. 


Issue No. 4: It relates to a demand for making 40 ¢temporary work- 
men, named in Annexure ‘A’ to the order of reference, permanent. The 
Union, in its written statement at age, Site 42, stated that these men 
were not made permanent in spite of their continuous service for more 
than six months which the Company under the award of Shri G, Palit, 
dated 5th January 1956, was obliged to do unless a workman was found 
unfit as such discharged. Hence, the Union claims that the workmen with 
more than six months’ service in the Company should be made permanent 
and all the privileges of a permanent worker should be extended to them. 
The Company, in its written statement at paragraph 62, stated that the 
award of Shri G. Palit did not apply to the workmen concerned in this 
dispute, and that the award was terminated by the Union by a letter, dated 
9061 June 1957. It, however, contended that the cases of workmen, whose 
names are mentioned in annexure ‘A’ 10 the statement of the Union, would 
be considered in terms of the Standing Orders, and they would be made 
permanent if they were qualified as such. The award of Shri G. Palit was 
terminated by a notice, Ext. 12, by the Union. It does not mean that the 
terms contained in the award had ceased to be of any force in the case, 
because, of its repudiation by a party. 


Now, it appears from the Ext. 6 that 5 out of 40 workmen resigned 
from service and 1 other workmen had been discharged. If the cases of 
above workmen are left out, then the cases of 28 workmen remain to be 
considered in this dispute. Of the seven discharged workmen, six work- 
men were discharged on 16th October 1957, and one was discharged on 7th 
November 1957. According to the Union itself, the dates of appointment, 
in case of seven workmen are not known. Only one of these workmen was 
appointed in December 1955. All others were appointed in 1956. They 
have been described as temporary workmen by both the sides. The Com- 
pany did not, however, think it necessary to prove the exact nature of their 
temporary work, and the terms and conditions of employment in all these 


part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 803 
8 


cused. It is, therefore, idle to contend on a basis of a reported decision in 
11 7.1.) page 209, that the demand is basically incompetent. In the 
aforesaid case, the terms of employment of temporary workmen were proved 
before the Tribunal. In this case, however, it has been stated that these 
pen are continuing im service for over a period of six months. This Com- 
pany hos not got any separate Standing Order of its own but being a 
member of the Engineering Association of India, it has adopted for all 
urposes the certified Standing Orders for manual workmen in the Engineer- 
ing Industry, Ext. K. A temporary workman, under the Standing Orders, 
11601)8 one who has been appointed for a limited period for work of a 
temporary nature. If the Company transefers him to duties of the same 
kind or of a more permanent nature his period of temporary service shall 
be offset against the probutionary period required for a regular worker. 
And a probationer is one who is employed in a regular vacancy and who 
has not completed six months’ consecutive service therein. A permanent 
or regular worker is one who has been entered as such in the Company’s 
muster roll after completing the probationary period of six months, etc. 
This provision, read along with Shri G. Palit’s award, make it abundantly 
clear that a temporary worker is not meant to be temporary for ever. Tf he 
is permitted to continue for over six months in a particular appointment, 
except in a special job for a limited period, the onus of proving which 
is on the Company, he will be treated, to all intents and purposes, ns ۵ 
permanent, or regular workman, and should be paid wages and be offered 
all the privileges of a permanent workman. 1 see no reasonable objection 
to making these 28 workmen permanent provided they have put in six 
months’ service os mentioned in Ext. 6. T decide the issue accordingly.

on stock basis. On the date of the reference of this case, the Company 
had no work of manufacturing electric motors. Being a new enterprise, 
the business is expanding in different departments and, at the same time, .

Then the orders suddenly fell so much so that there came a position to 
decide whether they would collapse and close the factory or somehow under- 
go the agony with some systematic retrenchment to save the industry and 
workmen both. (ood care was taken before the retrenchment was made. 
Exhibits 8 and S(1), two certificates, dated 22nd July 1958, show the 
position of orders received between April and September 1957, and the gouds 
manufactured during the same period. These certificates are from the 
Chartered Accountants, who were specially authorised to prepare them 
with reference to the Company’s books. According to these, orders 
amounted to Rs. 5,38,423.75 nP. and the goods manufactured of the value 
of Rs. 31,50,484.75 nP., i.e., manufactured goods were about six times 
more than the orders received. That there was shortage of orders, 
particularly, for Transformer Tanks was also proved by Ext. X, the 
Engineering Association's letter, dated 11th August 1958 to the Govern- 
ment of India. The position of the industry, ×۸ reflected, in the balance- 
sheet, Exts. W and W(1)—one printed and another typed for the same 
period, i.e., the year ending 3lst October 1957—is that the Company had 
earned profits amounting to Rs. 6,89,795 only for the Hazra Road Factory, 
the Cossipur Factory and the Calcutta Office. Therefore, the balance- 
sheet does not throw any more light on the matter in dispute. Since the 
Factory was run on order basis and not on stock basis, the Management is 
justified in reducing the work of manufacture strictly in accordance with 
158 requirements, Necessarily, at a time, when the orders were falling, 
the Management could not maintain an uneconomic staff, surplus to its 
requirements. The allegations of mala fide and victimisation, common in 
all cases of retrenchment, are not established. On the contrary;-I find 
that, as late as on 25th September 1957, the parties entered into a bonus

shows that the Company had no ulterior motive in this matter. The 
Union had failed to mention, even a single case where the principle of 

last come, first go’’ was not observed. In my view, the retrenchment of 
the workers in dispute is fully justified. The retrenched workers, who have 
not received their legal dues from the Company, will be paid, on their 
reporting to the Company's Factory, all the legal dues, within one month 
from the date of the publication of this award.

is no denying the fact these workers, in fact, majority of them, participated 
in this illegal strike. So, at least one charge against 10 of the workers 
except No. 12, Shri Ranjit Das, is proved. Shri Das was not charge-sheeted 
for participating in any illegal strike, because he was under orders of 
suspension on that. day> As he was under no obligation to come to work 
on that day, his refusal would not, rightly, amount to strike. 


The question is whether there was any picketing and instigating the 
workers to join the strike. The Union’s evidence ia that there wus a 
decision of the workers on the eve of the Puja day to stay away from work 
on 1/ta September 1957 when their request for performing the Puja inside 
the Factory and for a paid holiday on that day was turned down. The 
decision to withhold labour—a concerted action of all—was there, and there 
was no necessity for any one inciting any other to action or dissuading one 
from work during the strike. Obstruction to the Managerial Staft, even if 
established, ia no evidence of incitement or picketing, for that staff was 
no party to the strike. And, to all intents and purposes, the staff move- 
ment formed an altogether different transaction. Obstruction to that 
staff, 1f proved, may be evidence of disorderly behaviour, or violence on 
the part of the strikers. It cannot be any evidence to prove the other 
charges. It is, therefore, very unlikely for anybody to either picket or 
to instigate other workers from joining the illegal strike. In fact, apart 
from the evidence of O.P.W. 1 and 0.P.W. 2, there is no evidence to 
show that any worker was obstructed in proceeding to work. Not only 
that the Union Union made no secret of this decision but informed the 
police as also, the Works Manager about it. The Union’s evidence is that 
the police was present on the spot but, curiously enough, there is no 
evidence on the Company's side to show that the police was informed when 
picketing and instigating were going on, or for the matter of that, the 
Works Manager was assaulted with stones and windows were broken. These 
are acts of violence and when done by a body of men humbering more than 


pat I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 807 


ave would amount to rioting. The Police will not stand by and allow 
71012 to proceed when committed after previous notice. Shri Das, the 
Works Manager, was not injured, at least, no such injury was attended to 
by any Doctor. The Management did not file any complaint with the 
olice although the Works Manager was alleged to have been manhandled 
in that way. This evidence of Shri A. C. Das, O.P.W. 1, appears to be 
against all probabilities and, theretore, cannot be accepted as true. The 
other charges aguinst these ten men are not proved. No charges are 
roved against Shri Ranjit Das for the occurrence taking place on 17th 
September 1997. ‘The case of Shri Gopal Chatterjee stands on × different 
footing. He said that he did not assault the Supervisor, and the Super- 
visor, O.P.W. 4, said that he was hit by Shri Chatterjee. No reason has 
been assigned why Shri Chatterjee would only be charge-sheeted out of 
all persons for assaulting his Supervisor. 1, therefore, cannot disbelieve 
the evidence of Shri Sarma. The charge against Shri Chatterjee is proved. 
Both parties have stated that Shri Chatterjee was dismissed (not only 
suspended) from service, and I find that his dismissal is justified. 


A question arises in connection with the cases of 10 workers whether 
the illegal strike in which they participated on the Viswakarma Puja day 
on 17th September 1957 were justified or not. It is in evidence of Shri 
Das. the Works Manager, that the workmen who were formerly employed 
in the Hazra Road Factory enjoyed Viswakarma Puja day as paid holiday. 
In some years there might not have been a holiday. In 1956, when the 
Cossipur Factory started, the workers were allowed to perform this 
Viswakarma Puja inside the Factory, on a Sunday, which was a paid 
hdliday. In 1958, there was a holiday on the Viswakarma Puja day in 
thé Factory. Shri Das, the Works Manager, said that this was allowed 
apprehending the repetition of the last year’s trouble. That was clearly 
a very wise decision. In 1957, rightly or wrongly, the workers’ request 
to observe un old customary right was refused. Not only that but that 
they were usked to work on that day, on which day the uncontradicted 
evidence is, that the workers did not touch their tools on religious grounds. 
The Union's evidence is that this day is observed 08 a paid holiday in all 
factories. There is no evidence on the Company’s side against it. This 
may or may not be cent per cent. true, but then, the workers do not as a 
rule touch their tools on the said Puja day on religious grounds. This 
religious belief, when not against the public order, morality and health 
should not be interfered with in any way. Our Constitution has ruaranteed 
to all equally the right to observe religious customs and beliefs, when not 
against public order, morality and health. There were two courses open 
to the workers when the Management refused to declare the 1161) September 
1857 as a paid holiday, viz., (i) either to join their duties on 17th September 
1997 disregarding their religious belief in this matter, or (ii) to stay away 
from work even at the risk of being accused of resorting to an “‘illegal’’ 
strike. It is true that a number of festival holidays every year are 
announced by the Management, but then, this was not one declared as 
such in the year 1957. The management’s plea that the holidays were 
settled with the Union previously and then notified in the beginning of 
the yenr, is neither acceptable as true, nor considered sufficient justification 
for their conduct. There was thus clear provocation from the management 
side to the workers to join a strike which though technically illegal, is 
perfectly justified in the circumstances of the case. Under the Standing 
Orders, participation in an illegal strike, is a major misdemeanour, 
punishable with dismissal from service. The management, however, has 
disrretion in this matter of inflicting punishment in lieu of dismissal. 


808 THE. CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 [Parr ] 


The question is whether, in the aforesaid circumstances, the workers, 
technically guilty of participating in an illegal strike, should be punished 
with dismissal from service. To allow the workmen to be dismissed from 
service on this ground is to perpetuate an act of injustice on them, and at 
the same time to allow the management to take advantage of its own wrong. 
In the said circumstances, I am inclined to think that the punishment 
inflicted on these 10 workers is unduly harsh, which alone calls for an 
interference from this Tribunal, particularly, when the management has 
definitely proceeded against some of the office-bearers of the Union, who 
have been struggling hard to establish their claims before it. J think a 
‘‘warning’’ under the Standing Orders is adequate punishment in this 
matter. 

The dismissal of Shri Chatterjee is, however, justified. 


Shri Ranjit Das is not guilty of the charges brought against him. He 
is, therefore, entitled to reinstatement. Ten other workers of Ext. 7 (of 
this issue) are guilty of joining an illegal strike, which is justified in the 
circumstances of the case, being provoked by the management. Therefore, 
they are warned under the Standing Orders. 


In all fairness and reasons, the normal relief of reinstatement cannot 
be denied to them. As to claim for back pay, etc., there is no claim for 
pay for the day of the strike, and there cannot be any. There is no 
evidence worth the name to show that they were out of employment 
throughout the period. The continuity of service should not be allowed 
to be broken, and the men should be treated as on special leave without 
pay for the whole period of unemployment except for a month, for which 
period they shall be paid a month’s wages at the rates last drawn, within 
a fortnight of their rejoining duties, within time allowed, i.e., within one 
week from the date of the publication of the award. I answer the issue 
accordingly. 


Issue No. 6: The Union alleged that deductions from the wages to 1 
workmen were wrongly made by the management on different dates. 
The question is whether these deductions are justified, if not, to what relief 
they are entitled to. The Union, in its written statement at paragraph 6, 
page 20, stated in details the cases of individual deduction with dates. It 
appears therefrom that deductions amounting to Re. 1 to Rs. 9.04 nP. 
and amounting to a total of Rs. 50.88 nP. were deducted from wages of 11 
workmen on three different dates within one month, i.e., on 7th May 1957, 
22nd May 1957 and 7th June 1957. The Company, in its written statement 
at paragraphs 57 and 66, denied the allegations and stated that these short 
payments were repaid as soon as they were brought to notice of the manage- 
ment. P.W. 4, Shri Mallick, is the only worker who deposed on this 
issue. He, however, admitted that he was paid back his dues as soon as 
this was brought to notice of the management. 0.۲.۱۹۷۰ 2, Shri Jaju, also 
said this. An attempt was made to prove that there had been other deduc- 
tions in other cases too subsequent to the date of reference. This is outside 
the issue and ] am not going into merits of that case. The management 
assured us that all cases of short payment were repaid as soon as they are 
brought to its notice. JI decide the issue against the Union. 


issue No. 15: This relates to classification of workers. There is 
nothing particularly mentioned in the written statement regarding this 
issue. But in the charter of demands, the Union claimed several grades 
for different categories of workers, viz., skilled, unskilled, Drivers, 
Durwans, Clerks and Typist. At the same time in the charter of demands 
the Union demanded for appointment of an expert: committee for proper

issue No. 16: It relates io a demand for conveyance allowance at the 
rate of Rs. 20 per head to all transferred from the Hazra Road Factory. 
The demand is contested. It is true that a number of employees who 
worked ut Hazra Road Factory are at present employed in the Cossipur 
Factory. Some of these employees were paid for a limited period some 
allowance to meet the conveyance charges. That was discontinued long 
وی‎ The question is whether these employees should be paid any couvey- 
8005 allowance, for all times to come, and that at the rate of Rs. 20 per 
hea per month. No special case had been made out in support of 
this. demand and ] see no reason why such conveyance allowance should be 
paid to a section of the workers in a Factory in preference to others. 


issue Nos. 7, 9, 12 and 14: The Company’s contention is that these 
issues are barred by the principles of res judicata for, they were decided 11 
two earlier awards of the Industrial Tribunals, presided over by Shri (3. 
Palit and Shri J. N. Maitra, and the awards are dated 2nd February 0 
and 16th April 1958, respectively. In decidiug the preliminary objection, 
faken on behalf of the Company, I had an occasion to deal with this matter 


01 some length in my interim award, submitted to the Government, on the 
80th July 1968. 


The Union’s evidence is that it terminated the award of Shri G. Palit, 
dated 2nd February 1956, by a notice, in writing, addressed to the Assistant 
Secretary, Labour Department, and also to the Director of this Company 
on 2nd June 1957 (vide Ext. 12), Shri §. K. Bose, learned Counsel on 
behalf of the Company, relied on a decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
in the case of Messrs. Burn & Co. Ltd., Calcutta, v. Their employees, 
reported in 1], F.J.R., page 217, and contended that ‘“‘though under 
section 19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, it is open to a party to 
an award to repudiate it by giving two months’ notice, when the matter 
9 brought up again before an Industrial Tribunal as a fresh industrial 
dispute, it is not open to the 12100817110] Tribunal to try it de’novo and 
tome to a fresh decision. To do so will he contrary to well-settled 
principles of law and also contrary to the object of the Act. The matter 
thould be tried afresh only if there he any change in circumstances 
warranting it’’. Shri DD, L. Sen Gupta, learned Advocate for the Union, 
contended that since there was material change in circumstances since the 
date of the lust award, the matter would be well tried afresh. 6 did not 


tw 


810 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 [Pari 1 


dispute the principles of law laid down in the aforesaid decision of fie 
Hon'ble Supreme Court. 

The two points were taken by Shri 8. K. Bose on behalf of the Company, 
viz., (i) there had not been any change, not to spenk of a material oue, 
in the circumstances on which the last award was based, and that (11) the 
financial incompetence of the Company to saoulder any further liability 
on this account. These are economic demands which can only be met out 
of the funds at the Company's disposal. I have already referred to the 
Company’s balance-sheets, Exts. W and W(1), which show a margin of 
profits of about Rs. 6.23 lakhs (roughly). Out of this, a tax amounting 
to Rs. 3.81 lakhs and interest amounting to Rs. 1.48 lakhs should be paid. 
This would just leave a nominal balance of Ra. .94 out of which a dividend 
at the rate of 8 per cent., has to be puid. This does not at all reflect a 
stable financial position of the Company justifying the imposition of any 
big liability on this account, if otherwise justified, 

It is not necessary to refer the two awards, mentioned in the interim 
award, which adjudicated these very issues. It is argued on both sides 
that these issues can be reopened and tried again only if there had been 
any material change in the circumstances since the date of the award. 1 
have once again to refer to the evidence of P.W. 1, Shri Chakraborty, on 
this point. He said, at page 7 of his deposition, that the Union demanded 
increased wages for (i) the Company had grown up in size and earned 
more profits than at the time of the award, (ii) the prices of essential 
commodities had gone up, (iii) the Major Engineering Tribunal had 
increased the rates of wages, and (iv) the Jute and Cotton Textile Indus- 
tries have also allowed increased wages to their workers. In this conner- 
tion, he also referred to a chart, Ext. 11, showing the cost of balanced 
diet, drawn up on the basis of the Famine Enquiry Report, at the 
present market rate. This evidence has not been corroborated by any 
other materials on record. Apparently, there is nothing to show that the 
Company. had-since earned enormous profits. It is, no doubt, true that the 
business is expanding in some directions, and curtailing its activities on 
its uneconomic side. This, by itself, does not establish the stable financial 
position of the Company, or such oa change in circumstances as would 
justify reopening the issues, decided only two years’ ago by 0 competent 
Tribunal. The Company is running its business mainly on secured loans. 
It pays dividend only to attract those loans. The future of the industry is 
not very bright. There is some slackness in respect of orders, which an 
unimpeachable document, Ext. H, will show. It is true that the award 
of the Third Major Engineering Tribunal has since been published. 11 has 
allowed some increase in wages, but this Company was not a party to it. 
Further, these are no circumstances which would justify reopening the 
Issues Ou wages, scales of pay, ete. The cost of living, according to the 
cost of ri Index, published by the authority, has, in the last two years, 
gone up. [That is a material change which would justify reopening of 
the issue of dearness allowance only, and no other issue. The cost of living 
is adjusted only by allowing more denrness allowance, where possible. 
Conditions of service are generally embodied in the Standing Orders. The 
issues of leave and holidays and minimum basic wages, should not, there- 
fore, be reopened at this stage. They are getting 8 days’ festival holidays 
and statutory leave under the Factories Act. They demanded more and 
other kinds of leave. At the some time, it is not disputed that the provi- 
sions of the State Insurance Act are in operation in this Factory. That 
provide sufficient leave and other facilities in addition to above. Apart 
from thin consideration, these issues cannot also be reopened as they are 
barred by the principles of res judicata.

issue No. 10: It relates to a demand for payment of house rent 
allowance at the rate of Rs. 10 per month to workers drawing a basic 
salary up to Rs. 60, Rs. 15 to those drawing basic salary between Rs. 61 
to Rs. 100, Rs. 20 to those drawing Rs. 101 to Rs. 250, and, 10 per cent. 
of the basic salary, as allowance, to those drawing a basic salary Rs. 261 
andiabove. The Company’s contention is that this is not the liability of the 
employers at all and, it denies the claim. Only evidence in support of the 
Unign’s demand is that of P.W. 1, Shri Bhupal Chakraborty, who said 
that the minimum rent for a room, sufficient for occupation of a worker in 
the lgcality, is Ra. 15 per month, and for a family man not less than Rs. 25 
per month. At present, no house rent allowance is paid to any worker. 
Ordinarily, no separate provision for payment of house rent is made. 
Wages are fixed taking into consideration the question of payment for 
house accommodation as well. The Union has not made out any case for 
payment of ৮ separate house rent allowance, and that at the rates claimed 
in the charter of demands. This is, accordingly refused. 


Issue No. 13: It relates to » demand for payment of tiffin § allowance 
at the rate of annas 8 per day, to be paid to workmen of all categories. 
In Ext. 10, the charter of demands, the Union demanded for opening of 
a cheap canteen in the Factory premises, and also for payment of tiffin 
allowance of annas 8 per day. This demand was not conceded on behalf 
of the Company. 


It 1s in evidence of P.W. 1, Shri Bhupal Chakraborty, that there is no 
cheap canteen in the Factory and the worker does not get any tiffin allow- 
ance. In cross-examination, he, however, admits that there is a canteen 
in the Factory, but the goods of this canteen are not cheap. He gets a 
cup of tea at u cost of one anna. This is, according to the Company, 
supplied at cheap rates. By cheap canteen, Shri Chakraborty means, a 
canteen which supplies all articles to workers at cost price. 


There is a canteen in the Factory. 


The question is whether any tiffin allowance should be paid to all 
workers. The Company has started as a new enterprise at the Cossipur 


812 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 12, 1959 [Parr I 


Factory, and this is not proper time to saddle it with new financial 
liability, hitherto unknown. Accordingly, this demand is refused.

Subject: Instructions regarding bills payable by the Accountant-General, 
West Bengal, within the current financial year. 


No. T.M./715.—é8rd February 1959.—In order {0 ensure payment 
before the close of the financial year, all travelling allowance, contingent, 
grant-in-aid and other bills payable within the yeur should, as far os 
practicable, he presented at the counter of this office hy the 16th March 
1959. The words “To be paid on or before the 31st March 19595) should 
be written prominently in red ink on the top of each bill. In respect of 
charges actually incurred, or claima accruing on or after the 16th March, 
the bills should he presented with the utmost expedition without Josing 
even a single day. Please rememher that during the last week of March 
this office 1s preoccupied with the passing of monthly bills, payable on the 
first working day of April. 


2. Three clear days are required by this Office to complete all processes 
connected with pre-audit. On the fourth working day from the date of 
presentation of a bill, the payee or his messenger should call at the delivery 
counter to demand payment. If for any reason payment cannot be 
obtained on that day, he should cal] on the next day, or on the second or 
third following day, should it become necessary. Any complaint regarding 
undue delay in payment should be lodged with the gazetted officer in charge 
of the section. No attempt should be made to get into direct touch with 
the sectional staff. 


3. It should be particularly borne in mind that unpassed bills are not 
returned by post; they are required to he received back at the counter on 
surrender of tokens. 


4. Please take all possible care to see that the bills presented are free 
from defects and irregulurities. There may not be time left for resubmit- 
ting the bills when once returned unpassed with audit objection. 


5. Tt will facilitate the payment of bills if the following instructions 
are borne in mind :— 


(a) If the appropriation for the current year is likely to be or has 
already been exceegéd, an additional appropriation should be 
obtained in time to meet the excess and the order sanctioning 
the additional appropriation attached to the bill. 


(b) 11 any charge requiring sanction of a higher authority is claimed 
in a bill, the sanction should be attached to it. As no payment 
can be made on the authority of copies of orders, the sanctioning 
authority should be requested to communicate the orders to this 
office in time. 


(c) If no distribution of any apprupriation has yet been made, formal 
orders of the competent authority sanctioning the distribution 
should be attached to the bill. 


(d) A bill extract giving particulars of the major, minor and detailed 
heads of account to which the umount of the bill is chargeable 
and the designation of the officer controlling the expenditure 
should invariably be attached to bills. 


6. Hetween the 16th and 8191 March please make it a point to check 
your Hill Register every day with a view to receive all payments in good 
time. 


7. As a special concession io puyees, the Cash Payment and Cheque 
Delivery counters of this office will he kept open till 4-30 p.m. on the 311 
March. No payment will be made after that hour. 


8. Establishment Bills for March, 1959, will be paid by this office on 
the 186 April 1959 instead of on the 3lst March 1959. 
P. C. HALDAR, 
Dy. Accountant-General (Admu.).

The amount available for distribution, as percentage of the paid-up capital, 
works out at 1.85 per cent. compared with 1.3U per cent. in 1966-57 and

2. The State Government, in pursuance of section G of the State 
Financial Corporations Act, 1951, have 62/۳ a minimum dividend ot 
34 pér cent. per annum on the paid-up share capital of the Corporation. It 
is proposed to utilise the ubove umount of Its. 1,85,782.41 nP. towards pay- 
ment of dividend at the rate of 34 per cent. per aunum, free of income tax, 
and request the Government of West Hengal to give subvention for the balance 
of Rs. 1,64,267.59 nP. to make up the deficit. The amount of subvention 
required this year is thus less than the amount of the tax of about 
Rs. 2,10,000, which the Corporation is required to pay on the current year’s 
profits. In other words, had the State Financial Corporations been exempted 
from payment of income-tax, os was ununimously asked for by all State 
Financial Corporations, this Corporation would not have required any sub- 
vention from the Government this year. 


3. New Companies do not normally pay any dividend for the first few 
year but the State Financial Corporations are obliged to pay the guaranteed 
dividend from their very inception. Further, financing companies do not 
benefit from development rebates, depreciation allowances, etc., as other new 
companies ordinarily do. On the other hand, because of the risk inherent 
in industrial financing, it is imperative that Financial Corporations should 
build up strong reserves from the outset. With their limited profit earning 
capacity, it would be no easy matter for the Corporations to do so unless 
their burden of taxation is substantially lightened. The contingent liability 
of this Corporation in respect of subventions received from the Government 
towards payment of the guaranteed dividend, including the subvention 
required this year will amount to Rs. 8,50,421.50 nP.
