6. <A satisfactory progress has been made in the disbursement of loans 
this year, the amount disbursed being Rs. 41,66,000, which is nearly as much 
us was disbursed in the course of the preceding three years, the figure for 
that period being Rs. 43,90,000. The share capital of the Corporation, 
amounting to Rs. 1 crore, hus now been almost fully utilised and the balance 
left does not cover its pending Joan commitments. It became, therefore, 
necessary for the Corporation to increase its resources and this has been done 
with the approval of the Reserve Bank of India and the Government of 
West Bengal by issuing bonds of the face value of Rs. 50 lakhs at 48 per 
ina per annum at a price of Rs, 99 for every Rs. 100 ef the bonds applied 
or. 


7. Tt is somewhat disappointing that the amount of loans applied for 
and the loans sanctioned this vear compare unfavourably with those of the 
previous year. This reflects the prevailing unfavourable investment climate, 
which 1s variously attributed to تنا‎ taxation, uncertain business prospects, 
difficullfy regarding foreign exchange and consequent import restrictions both 
in regan to capital goods and imported raw materials consumed by industries. 
The enhancement of the Corporation’s lending rate from 6 per cent. to 
؟‎ per cent. per annum commensurate with the cost in interest of funds which 
the Corporation has been obliged to raise by borrowing in the market, is 
another factor responsible for the falling off of the better class of upplica- 
tions for Joans. The statistical information available points {to a steady 
decline in Small Saving Collections in recent months, which suggests that 
there is very little margin for saving amongst the general public. Tf savings 
tend to decline rather than to grow, the repercussive effect on industrial 


856 THE CATAUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 19, 1959 | Parr T 


enterprises cannot but be adverse. At the same time there is lack of public 
confidence in industrial enterprises as is evidenced by a continued fall im 
stock exchange values. ‘These are, it is hoped, passing phases; nevertheless 
they affect the working of institutions financing industries. 


. We have stated in paragraph 4 that out of loans aggregating to 
Ris. 1,78,42,000 sanctioned by the Corporation, loans declined by the borrowers 
amounted to Rs. 47,352,500. The amount declined is comparatively high and 
18 mainly accounted for by the refusal of four loans, each for Rs. 94 lakhs, 
aggregating 10 Rs. 38 lakhs. Two of these concerns were jute mills, which 
obfained loans at a lower rate of interest from the National Industrial 
Development Corporation Private Lid.; another was an engineering concern 
which failed to obtain the municipal contract for which the loan was applied 
for and the fourth was a textile mill, which did not disclose the reason for 
not availing themselves of the loan. It may not be out of place to mention 
here that there have been instances of loans sanctioned being declined or 
reduced as well as applications submitted being withdrawn on account of 
failure on the part of the applicants to obtain import licences for the 
capital goods required.

THE R. 0, KAR MEDICAL COLLECE AND HOSPITAL RULES, 1959 
1. These rules may be called the R. G. Kar Medical College and Hospital 


Rules, 1959. 


2. In these rules, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or 


eontext,— 


(1) Ba means the R. G. Kar Medical College and Hospital Act, 


(2) ‘‘Chairman”’ means the Chairman of the Committee and for the 
purposes of rules 6, 7 and 8 includes a member elerted under 
rule 6 to preside over any meeting; 


(3) ‘‘Government’’ means the State Government of West Bengal: 
(4) ‘‘Member’’ means a member of the Committee: 

(5) “meeting’’ means a meeting of the Committee: 

(6) ‘‘Principal’’ means the Principal of the institution: 

(7) ‘Quarter’? means a period of three calendar months; 

(8) ‘‘Secretary’’ means the Secretary of the Committee. 


3. The Secretary shall, on his own motion or on the direction of the 
Chairman, convene meetings of the Committee as often as the business of 
the institution may require, so, however, that at least one such meeting 


shall be held in every quarter. 


4. Save as otherwise hereinafter provided, at least one week's notice of 
every meeting shal] he given to the members and such notice shall include 


the agenda: 


Provided that in the case of an emergent meeting, twenty-four hours’ 


notice shall be sufficient. 


5. Five members shall form a quorum. 


6. The Chairman shall, if present, preside over every meeting. In the 
absence of the Chairman from any meeting, the members present shal] elect 
one from amongst themselves to preside over that meeting. 


7. The proceedings of all meetin 
and shall be authenticated by the C 


৪ shall be recorded by the Secretary 
airman. 


8. (1) Except where the members are unanimous, any matter under 
discussion at any meeting shall be decided by the votes of the majority of 


the members present and voting. 


(2) Every member shal] have one vote. The Chairman shall not vote, 
but shall, in the case of an equality of votes, have a casting vote. 


Ne The votes shall be taken by show of hands or by ballot or by division 
as e 


Chairman may think fit: 


Provided that votes shall be taken— 


(৪) by ballot where any member so demands, or 
(b) by division where votes have already been taken by show of hands 
und any member asks for a division.

LABOUR DEPARTMENT 


ORDER 


No. 480-1.R. /IR/11L-6/57.--10th February 1959.—Whereas under the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 1420-1.R. /D/ 
11L-6/57, dated the 7th April 1958, the industrial dispute between Messrs. 
Rupali Cinema (Private) Ltd., 45/B Ashutosh Mukherjee Road, Bhawan- 


pur, Calcutta, and one of their employees Shri Gour Mohan Ghosh, repre- 
rented by the Bengal Motion Pictures Employees’ Union, 126A Dharam- 


talla Street, Calcutta, regarding the issues mentioned in the said order 
being matters specified in the second and the third schedules to the Induk- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947) was referred for adjudication to 
the Fourth Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas the said Fourth Industrial Tribunal has submitted to the 
State Government its award on the said industrial dispute: 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947)) the Governor is pleased 
hereby to publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 

ANNEXURE 
In the matter of an imdustrial dispute existing between Messrs. Runpali 
Cinema (Private) Ltd., 45/8 Ashutosh Mukherjee Road, Bhawanipur, 
Calcutta, and one of their employees Shri Cour Mohan Chosh, repre- 
sented by the Bengal Motion Pictures Empotyees’ Union, 126A 

Dharemtala Street, Caloutta. (Case No. ৬311-65158.) 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, 
WEST BENGAL 


PRESEXT: 
Suri (4. N. GAN, Judge, Fourth Insdu+trial Tribunal. 


Appearances : 
For the Gaon: Shri Haripada Chatterjee. 
For the Company: Shmn P. R. Mukherjee, M.A., LL.B. 


AWARD 


This industria] dispute, relating to the two issues mentioned below, 
existing between Messrs. Rupali Cinama (Private) Ltd., and one of their 
employees Shri Gour Mohan Ghosh was referred to this Tribunal by the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 1420-7 | 
111.-6/57, dated the 7th April 1958 


Issues 
(1) The date of confirmation of service of Shri Gour Mohan Ghosh. 
(2) The pay scale of Shri Gour Mohan Ghosh. 


Both parties filed written statement, adduced evidence and advanced 
argument in the case. 


934 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 26, 1959 [Parr] 


issue No. 1: Shri Gour Moban Ghosh, Joint Operator-in-Chorge, 
Rupali Cinema, was appointed on probation from 15th June 1956, on con- 
solidated wages of Rs. 150 per month inclusive of dearness allowance. This 
was done by an appointment letter, dated 8th June 1956, 171. 102). This 
period of probation was subsequently extended by letter, dated 6th Novem- 
ber 1946, Ext. 1, up to 3lst December 1956. The Company agreed in 
that letter to make Shri Ghosh permanent with effect from Ist January 
1057. Shri Ghosh is continuing in service on the same consolidated wages 
of Rs. 160 per month. He was not given any separate letter uf confirma- 
tion as promised in Ext. 1. Hence this confusion. Shri P. R. Mukherjee, 
appearing on behalf of the Company, contended, relying on Shri Ghosh’s 
‘own letter, dated 16th February, Ext. A, that Shri Ghosh was already 
confirmed with effect from lst January 1957. Whatever might have been 
the position before, it is now clear that Shri Ghosh was confirmed, in his 
present post, on consolidated wages of Rs. 150 per month with effect fron, 
ist January 1957. I answer the issue accordingly. 


issue No. 2: This relates to his scale of pay. He was not given any 
scale of pay either in his letter of appointment or in any letter subsequent 
thereto. Shri Ghosh aska for ماد“‎ of pay, as embodied in (×۱8, Bengal 
Motion Pictures Association’s agreement, dated 2nd July 1948. The said 
scale of pay applies to all whole-time permanent employees only. It is in 
evidence ٥ Shri Ghosh that there are 5/6 operators, including himself, 
and a part-time operator in the service of this Company. He with his 
senior Shri Manindra Acharyya, gets a monthly pay of Rs. 150 per month 
(all inclusive). Other operators are getting much less than that. No one 
has been allowed any incremental scales. No one received any increment 
up till now. Shri Ghosh does not know whether any of the staff of this 
Company gets the benefit of the agreement Ext 8, or, for the matter of 
that, of any alleged separate agreement with this Company. In fart, a 
dispute over increment of the entire staff including the operators is now 
pending settlement before the Conciliation Officer. Apparently, Shri 
Ghosh is involved in the said dispute. He asked the Company 10 treat 
him on an equal footing with the other employees and give him the same 
increment as given to other employees. He made written representations 
to the proprietor to that effect. He is even now agreenble to accept what- 
ever increments are allowed in the conciliation proceedings to other 
operators. Shri P. R. Mukherjee’s contention is that Shri Ghosh is bound 
by the terms of his agreement embodied in his letter of appointment men- 
tioned above, Shri Ghosh actually asked for his confirmation in terms of 
the said letters. Whether he should be given any incremental scales of 
pay or not is a question which should‘ better be decided upon along with 
the cases of other employees. Shri Ghosh is not entitled to any  incre- 
mental scales of pay at present. His case for increment will receive due 
consideration in the conciliation proceedings along with other employees 
involved in the said dispute. I answer the issue accordingly. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 
M. N. GAN, M. N. GAN, 


Judge. Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
The 28th January 1959. 


By order of the Governor, 
S. C. MUKHERJEE, Asst. Secy.

No. 2749Dis. /1)/11L-125/55, dated 17th June 1955, referred, under 
sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Bharat Glass Works Ltd., Belghuria,

Workers’ Union, 7 Dinanath Chatterji Street, P. O. Belghuria, 
24-Parganas, regarding some matters specified in a schedule to this 
Tribunal for adjudication. The award of this Tribunal in respect of this 
proceeding was made on 16th September 1958, and was published in the 
Caleutta (rosette on 16th October 1958. 


On 18th September 1958, Shri Shankar Kangali, T. No. 18, C/o. Shri 
৭019 Jus Gupta, 18۸ Shrif Lane, Calcutta-16, applied under section 338A 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, complaining against his dismissal on various 
grounds. The petitioner prays for reinstatement with all hack wages,

including allowances, bonus and leave wayes and such other dues asmay 
be deemed fit and proper. The Company opposed the clains on various 


grounds.

Private Ltd., stating that the Managing J)irector felt offended at the 
conduct of Shri Shankar Kangali, who submitted that be had no intention 
to offend the Managing Director, but when he had taken it otherwise, Shri

the joint petition and it appears that the terms thereof are excellent. I 
therefore, accept the joint petition of compromise in Appendix A, and

Appendix A shall form a part of this award.

N.T.C. (National Tobaero Co., I.td.) side, attended the office and formed

The question now is whether this dismissal is justified. 


This resta on the further question whether or not the charges against

It has been urged on behalf of the Company that the scope of enquiry, 
in this reference, is very limited and limited to the decision whether or 
not the management had acted in good faith, whether there is victimisation 
or unfair labour practice, whether the management is guilty of any basic 
error or violation of principles of natural justice and whether, on the 
materials, the management’s findings on the misconduct is completely 
haseless, or perverse. If the Tribunal finds in fabour of the Company, then 
in that ease, it should not interfere with the decision of the management 
in dismissing the employees. In this connertion Shri K. B. Basu, Counsel, 
for the Company, relied on a decision of the Supreme Court in Indian Tron 
& Steel Company and their workmen, reported in 1958, I, L.L.J., p. 6017], 
F.J.R., p. 391, and to a derision of Mr. Justice M. C. Desai of Allahabad

High Court in a case between Radharaman Bajpui und others and Lahour 
Appellate Tribunal and others, reported in 1957, 11, L.LJ., p. 15. and 
contended that this Tribunal, in this reference, is not sitting as a Court of 
appeal trom the decision of the mangement anid, therefore, is not com- 
petent to, in any case, to oubstitute its own judgment tor that of the 
management. Shri Sidharta Sanka: Roy, Counsel tor the Union, in reply 
pointed out that, practically speaking, there is no difterence between the 
decision ot the Labour Appellate Tribunal, in the case of Buckingham 
Carnatic Milla’s case, reported in 1965 L.A.C., p. 491, and the decision اہ‎ 
the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the Indian Iron & Steel Company's 
case, reported in 1958, I, L. L. J., p. 260. He, however, invited 
the Tribunal to interfere with the findings of the Management on 
the ground that there 1s not only want of 09070 7৫64 in the matter but that 
the manugement has been guily of a basic error of tacts und of victimisation 
of the employees concerned. He said that the point at issue is now tully 
covered by the two decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in case hetween 
Lakshmi Devi Sugar Mills Lid. and Ram Swarup and others in 1957, I, 
L.L.d.. p. 17, and in the case of Indian Iron & Steel and their workmen 
reported in 1958, I, L.I..J., p, 260. At the same time he submitted that 
the decision of the Allahabad High Court referred ما‎ above has no applica- 
tion on the facts of the case. In this instant case, the management did 
not take action against the offending clerks under the provisions of the 
Standing Orders, or for the matter of that, any service rules having the 
force of a contract. The management acted in exercise of its inherent 
powers to enforce internal discipline in the office and punish anyone guilty 
of acts of indiscipline amounting to misconduct, In the case of Radharaman 
Bajpai and others, the decision of the Allahabad High Court was to a very 
large extent influenced by the fact that the Labour Appellate Tribunal of 
India, in hearing an appeal from the Industrial Tribunal, had completely 
ignored the terms of contract binding on the parties. The decision in the 
present case does not rest on any contract between the parties. Further, 
the whole question is, in my opinion, now covered by a later derision of the 
Supreme Court and, therefore, the said decision of the Allahabad High 
Court does not appear any to be good law. This Tribunal has jurisdiction, 
in any enquiry of this kind, to scrutinize all the circumstances of the case 
and to allow appropriate relief to the aggrieved party. Their Lordships in 
eng of Lakshmi Devi Sugar Mills J.td., referred to above have observed 
as follows: 


“On such action being taken by the employer, the workmen would be 
entitled to raise an industrial dispute which would have to be 
referred to the appropriate Tribunal for adjudication by the Gov- 
ernment on proper steps being taken in that behalf. When such: 
industrial dispute comes to be adjudicated upon by the appro- 
priate Tribunal, the workmen would be entitled to have all the 
circumstances of the case scrutinized and to the appropriate relic 
at the hands of the Tribunal.”’ (Vide page 25 of the Report.) 


Their Lordships in the case of India Iron & Steel Co. referred to above, 
have observed the following: 


‘‘undoubtedly, the management has power to direct ita"own internal 
administration and discipline, but the power is not unlimited and 
when a dispute arise, Industrial Tribunals have been given the 
ower to see whether the termination of service of a workman is 
Justified and to give ae ce relief. In cases of dismissal on 
misconduct the Tribunal does not, however, art aa a Court of 
appeal and substitute its own judgment for that of the manage- 
ment. 16 will interfere (1) when there is want of good 49111) (2)

{he management has been guilty of a basie error or violation 171

findings completely haseless or perverse.’”’ (Vide pages 269-7() of 
the said Report.) 


It seems that the findings on the relevant points of the Labour Appellate 
Tribunal, in the case 01 Messrs. Buckingham Carnatic Mills Ltd., reported 
at pages 497 and 493, received the approval of their Lordships of the 
Supreme Court,in the two of its decisions discussed above. It will, there- 
fore. be wrong to contend, ar has been done in this case, on behalf of the 
(ompany, that the duty of the Tribunal, in adjudicating this dispute, is 
only to see whether or not the management had conducted the enquiry into 
the charges fully and fairly, by giving full opportunity to the clerks to 
meet the charges and not to interfere with the decision of the management 
even when where the punishment was found to he unjust and unduly 
excessive, being out of proportion to the misconduct committed. 


Another point was taken on behalf of the Company, in paragraph 2 
of its wr.tten statement (at page 8), that since these emplovees were dis- 
missed for misconduct, after a full enquiry into the charges, and after 
obtaining permission of the Conciliation Officer dealing with the dispute, 
this Tribunal will not have any jurisdiction to dirert their reinstatement 
in this case. This point is now covered by a decision of the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court in the case of Lakshmi Devi Sugar Mills Ltd., already dis- 
cussed above. In fact, the Union raised an industrial dispute after the 
dismissal of these employees, and the same was referred to this Tribunal 
for adjudication. The observations of their Lordships in the said case, 
quoted above, furnish a complete answer to the question. This Tribunal 
has jurisdiction to go into the merits of the matter in dispute and decide 
it. It is not precluded from allowing the appropriate reliefs, including 
reinstatement, where necessary.

\apology trom him, udoubtedly went beyond the limits of decency und good 
tonduct, which are expected of them within the office. For this, disciplinary 
dction was rightly taken. But in punishing them the management clearly 
overlooked its own lapses in the matter, as also the admittedly clean and 
satisfactory record of past service of the persons concerned. 60009 after 
another the superior officers under whom these clerks had worked said that 
they had a clean record of service. Shri Sidhartha Sankar Roy, learned 
Counsel on hebalf of the employees, very seriously contested the question of 
punishment, and contended that in the circumstances of the case the extreme 
penalty of dismissal was wholly unjustified. Shri K. B. Bose, the learned 
Counsel for the Company, on the other hand, refuted thia contention by 
saying that in the interest of discipline in office administration such dis- 
orderly conduct should be punished only with dismissal from service. 
have anxiously considered the question of punishment in thia case. The 
clerks ure all fairly senior members of the staff. Shri K. [,. Banerjee, 
Shri M. N. Mukherjee and Shri 8. K. Bose had already served this Company 
for over 20 years. Others had put in 12 to 16 years’ service. They had 
worked to the satisfaction of their superiors, and possessed a clean record 
of service. The question now is, whether on the facts and in the circum- 
stances of this cuse, as also in consideration of long and good past service 
of these clerks, this one and single act of indiscipline should be visited with 
the extreme penalty of dismissal from service. It is, no doubt, essential 
that this matter should not only be considered from the point of view of 
emplover and employees but also in the interest of the industry for bring- 
ing about a harmony in the relationship between the two. In my view, 
the punishment is so unjust that a remedy is called for in the interest of 
Justice. [T have, therefore, decided to interfere with the decision of the 
management in the matter of punishment. The order of dismissal pasred 
٣ the management is, therefore, not justified and, accordingly, set aside. 
The clerks Nos. 1 to 6 on the N. T. ©.'s side are suspended for a period

hes 


— 7. 


af two weeks. The No. 7, Shri Biswas on B. N. E.'s side, is suspended for 
one month only, and the Nos. 8 to 10, viz. Shri Ganguly, Shri 
Bhattacharjee and Shri Banerjee are suspended for a period of two months, 
Normal relief, in all cases of wrongful dismissal, is reinstatement, and the 
Tnion asks for it. In the circumstances of this cnse, this cannot and should 
not be denied to the aggrieved clerks. 


All of them will be reinstated in service, in their former posts, on their 
reporting to duty at the Company's office premises, during the office hours, 
within 7 days from the date of the publication of this award. 


I have anxiously considered the Union's claim for wages for the period 
of unemployment for these dismissed employees. It is in evidence before 
this Tribunal that these clerks are out of employment for this entire per‘od,

to day administration at a considerable cost. Considering the hardships of

one Shri Sudhir Basak, nrevious!y a meulder, to establish that moulders 
repatsthe furnace but it is admitted that the Companv itself bore the cost

issue No. 8: The point tor decision iu this issue is whether the reference 
of the present industrial dispute by the State Government of West Bengal 
is competent. The learned Advocate for the Company presses that as the 
Company are contractors under the Railway Administration, the appropriate 
Government for making the reference under section 2(a) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act is the Centra] Government und uot the State Govermnent. It 
is also stated that at all stages of the dispute, the conciliation proceedings 
between the Company and the Union were conducted before the Regional 
Conciliation Officer of the Government of India and that for that reason, 
the State Government had no reason to hold that any such industrial dispute, 
ay has been referred to the Tribunal, existed, or was apprehended. This 
contention that the appropriate Government for the present reference 
18 the Central Government has been opposed by the learned spokesman for 


the Union. ۱ ۱ 

On a consideration of the matter, آ‎ have no doubt that the objection is 
unworthy of support for the following reasons. Jt was argued by the learned 
Advocate for the Company that as the Company was a contractor under the 
Railway Company, it was carrying on an industry under the authority of 
the Railway Company, and it 1s to be considered that the industry of the 
Company in the present case wa» an industry carried on by or under the 
authority of the Central Government. ‘The Company is a contractor under 
the Railway Board. Section 2(a)(i) of the Act does not provide that for 
an industry carried on under the authority of a Railway Company, the 
appropriate Government was the Central (Jovernment. In relation to a 
disputé of a Railway Company itself, the Central (tovernment is the 
appropriate Government. The section does not provide that the Central 
Government will be the appropriate Government in relation to an industrial 
dispute carried on by or under the authority of a Railway Company. It 
{he contractors are cousidered to be carrying on an tudustry under ٣۶ 
authority of the Railway Company, ther industry is not covered by sec- 
tion 2(a)(i) of the Act. ا‎ do not, however. consider that the Company ap 
a coutractor carries on an industiy by ۴ہ‎ unde> the authority of the ]ءٌ)‎ 7۶۲ 
Company. The next question for consideration is if the contractor carries 
on an industry by or under the authority of the Central Governmeut. The 
decision of the Hon'ble High Court at Caleutta in Bharat Glows Works 
Private Ltd., reported in 1958(1) L.L.J3., 467, shows that no business owned

or cytried on by a private person or a limited company can be a business 
carried on by or undet the authority of the Government. In view of the 
decision of Haris C.J. in the ease of Carlsbad Mineral Water Manufacturing 
(‘v., Ltd., reported in gsi و‎ 1.[,.1., 488, which was approved and accepted 
by the Hon'ble Judge in the Bharat (flass Works case, it appears that the 
business of the present contractor was its own business, which it was

awarded that the termination of service of Shri Balai Sarkar and Shri Ram-

ustified and they are not entitled to reinstatement. The Company shall,

নিন? service. It is awarded that they are not entitled to any other 
relief.

3. The matters of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
16107671106 ure as fullows: 
(1) Pay ৯016৭. 
(2) Dearness Allowance, 
(8) Provident Fund. 
(4) Whether the employees are entitled to get the benefit from the 
resent employer for the past services rendered by them with

Decision 
For proper appreciation of the dispute it is necessary to state certain 
facts lending to the reference as are either admitted or established in 
evidence. Messrs. Lens and Scientific Instrument Company Private Ltd. 
(hereafter called the employer company) was incorporated on 28th January 
1944 (Ext. 2). It has its office and workshop in the premises at 5/2 Old 
Court House Street. The workshop started work with 51 workmen from 
14th March 1944. The employer company has at present 38 workmen of 
different categories in its employ in the said workshop (Ext. A). Besides, 
there are a few contract workers who are suid to be not regular employees 
of the company. In or about April 1956, Jens & Scientific Instrument 
Employees’ Union (hereafter called the union) was formed for improvement 
of service conditions and for collective bargaining. ©n behalf of the work- 
men the union presented a charter of demands of 7th May 1956 for increment 
of wages, dearness allowance and for other benefits (Ext. B). Thereupon 
conciliation proceeding started. The company pleader inability to meet 
any of the demands on the ground of financial inability. On receipt of 
such comment the union wrote to the Conciliation Officer on 24th July 1956 
a 5(a)] stating that it was part and parcel of Messrs. Jamea Murray 
Co. Ltd. and, as such, it was able to meet their demands. To substantiate 
claim that the two concerns were one and the same, the union again wrote 
to the Conciliation Officer on 7th August 1956 (Ext, 5). On 20th May 7 
the union submitted certain data to substantiate its claim that these two 
concerns were one and the same [Ext. 5(b)]. There was, however, no settle- 
ment in course of the conciliation. The employer company, however, agreed 
to raise the total emolument to Rs. 61 per month for those workers who 
were getting less than Rs. 41 as basic wage and it also gave effect to it. 
The Government by its letter, dated 7th September 1957, informed the 
union that the demands submitted by it were examined with reference 
to the financial position of the company and that the financial position of 
the company did not justify further improvement in the service conditions 
of the workers for the Present (Ext. C). The union through its President 
thereafter carried on correspondence with the Government [ Ext. 0ئ‎ 
Ultimately the union submitted a revised charter of demands on 29th 
November 1957 [Ext. 6(c)]. The matter was again taken up for concilia- 
tion end as no settlement was possible the Government referred the dispute 
to this Tribunal for adjudication on 4th January 1968. 


Now let us consider the issues separately. 


issue’No. 1! The union alleges that the workmen of the employer 0010- 
pany are poorly paid and they are deprived of amenities as are giver fo 
workmen of Messrs. James Murray & Co. The company never took into 
vensideration the skill of the workmen and other principlea in fixing the 
wages. There is no grade and scale with annual increments. As efficiency 
und family burden of the workmen increase with lapse of time, some grade 
and pay scales should be introduced. The union accordingly claims grades 
ond scales for all the workmen. According to the union, the workmen of 


Part] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 26, 1959 979 


erg (রা ররর অজি 
০ 


rE | 
جج‎ ৩০ FS TT TEAS 


کت 10د ৯‏ 


all categories shall be divided into two groups—senior and junior. The 
ungon demands pay scales for them as follows:— 


Senior—Rs. 90—5—140—10—250. 
Junior—Rs. 60—4—100—5—150. 


The union claims that the pay scales should he given effect from the date 
of charter of demands and that for fitting in the new pay scales every 
employee should get one increment for every two years of past service. 


The company opposes the claims mainly on the ground of financial in- 
capacity to bear additional burden in this respect. It maintains that being 
ad engineering concern, its workers ure classified into categories of un- 
skilled, semi-skilled and skilled workers and that the basic wages as ure 
paid to the workmen are consistent with those prescribed for engineering 
mdustries under the Omnibus Award in respect of unskilled and  semi- 
skilled workers and differentials are maintained according to categories, 
experience, efficiency and length of service, It is said that increments are 
given to efficient workers from time to time at the discretion of the manage- 
ment. ‘There is no occupational nomenclature in respect of different occu- 
ca 008 either in this industry or any other engineering concerns based on 
sclentific investigation and evaluation and the claim for gradation into 
senior and junior is unknown in the history of engineering concerns. 
Then as the issue does not make mention of grades, framing of grades as 
suggested by the workmen is beyond the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. 
there can be no incremental pay scales fixed for the workers us the company 
has no ability to pay and stability. 


There is no dispute between the parties that the employer company has 
been doing repairs to survey, nautical and ophthalmic instruments and 
vccasionally assembling parts of those instruments from the start of the 
workshop in March, 1944. The said work, it appears, was being carried 
on manually with the help of hand tools by the workmen. From _ the 
ividence it further appears that after introduction of machinery from 1956 
the employer company started to manufacture dumpy Jevel and some other 
items (ride 1).W. 1). There can, therefore, be no doubt that the employer 
company is an engineering concern. Having regard to the nature of the 
work and the instruments to be hundled I agree thut the degree of skill 


involved in the work in the workshop is rather of higher order than is 
ordinarily required. 


The statement (Ext. A) filed by the company shows the existing wages 
and D.A. of the different workmen in the employ of this company. The 
statement shows that skilled workers get wages varying between 
Re, 121.52 .للا‎ and Rs. 156.80 nP. per month of 31 days, while semi-skilled 
workmen get basic wages varying between 60.76 .جس‎ and 119.56 nP. and 
the unskilled workmen get busic wages varying between 41.16 nP. and 
4.08 nP. Besides, they are paid D.A. at the flat rate of Rs. 20 per month. 
Exhibit 6 is on the contrary a statement by the union showing the hourly 
rates টি the total emoluments which are available to the workers in a 
mouth. 

There ix a good deal of difference between the parties regarding classi- 
fication of the workers as to who of the workers would come under which 
vatepory. According to the union, majority of them should مع‎ to the 
Aatevory of skilled and then to the category of semi-skilled and only a few 
te the category of unskilled. While according to the statement (Ext. A) 
of the company, only three come to the category of skilled, 19 to the 
category of semi-skilled and 14 to the category of unskilled. There bein 
no evidence before this Tribunal, as to who performed which duty, it 1s 
obvious that the Tribunal cannot come to any decision in this respect. 
Kesides, on the issue 9৪ it is, the Tmbunal cannot go into the question.

When there has, however, been such difference, I would only desire that 
the company should look into the matter and reclassify the workmen 38060 
different categories so that the workmen may not feel that they are being 
deprived of legitimate dues of their respective categories by treating them 
as of inferior category. 

Regarding claim for incremental pay scales, it has been held by the 
Labour Appellate Tribunals that this. can be introduced only when the 
employer has both financial ability and stability. In the present case these 
requisite conditions are wanting. From the statement as to financial posi- 
tion (Exi, L) it appears that the present company incurred losses up to 1949 
and has been able to recoup the said loss only recently on the trading results 
for the year ending 31st December 1955. The balance-sheets of 1952, 1953, 
1956 and 1957 show that the amount of net profit was not much (vide Ext. H 
series). In the circumstances, it cannot be said that the company has either 
ability or = It is, therefore, obvious that claim for incremental 
pay scales cannot be sustained. 


Regarding wages, the principles of fixation of minimum wages have 
been discussed and settled by the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in 
Buckingham & Carnatic Mills Co., Ltd. 1952, L.A.C, 490. The floor ও] 
of wages of un industrial worker must be such as would enable him to 
maintain 3 consumption units including himself in a state of efficiency with 
provision for education, medical expenses and amenities. This is the 
minimum which the worker must have irrespective of the capacity of the 
industry or of his employer to pay. The minimum wage standards set up the 
irreducible level, the lowest limit or the floor level below which no worker 
should be paid. A fair wage on the contrary is above the minimum, wage 
but below the living wage. A fair wage is a step towards the progressive 
realisation of o living wage and goes through process of approximating the 
living wage. Though the minimum wage as 1s fixed has no regard to the 
capacity of the industry to pay, and is fixed solely on the requirements of 
the worker and his family, the upper limit of wages must however be limited 
by what may he broadly called the capacity of the industry to pay. This 
capacity is not of a particular unit but of the entire industry on industry- 
cum-region basis. 

It will so appear that in the matter of minimum wages including D.A., 
the question of capacity of the employer does not at all come into the 
picture. The employer company has, of course, raised the mimimum of an 
unskilled to Rs. 61 17011001708 D.A. in course of the conciliation proceeding 
in conformity of what then prevailed in the engineering concern under the 
award of the Major Engineering Tribunal of 1950. Since then there has 
been award of the Third Major Engineering Tribunal published in the 
Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary, on Dth November 1958. Under the award 
of the said Tribunal the minimum wage including D.A. of an unskilled 
worker has been fixed at Rs. 71 per month. How the said minimum has 
heen arrived at hus been stated in details in the said award. It is, there- 
fore, useless to reproduce them here. I may only state that I adopt them 
without reservation. The employer company being an engineering concern 
can have no excuse not to pay the said minimum to its workmen. Therefore, 
those of the unskilled workmen in this company whose total emolument 
falls below the said sum of Rs. 71 should be pulled up to the said sam 
either by grant of increment in basic wage or grant of increment in 2۰ 
or by both as the company deems fit and proper. Regarding the minimum 
of a semi-skilled worker, ۲ fix the same at Rs. 76 including D.A. Regarding 
the skilled, their minimum including D.A. should not be less than Ra, 96. 
Those of the semi-skilled and skilled workmen who after reclassification are 
found to have been getting total emolument below the aforesaid sum for 
their respective category should be pulled up to the said minimum.

Hegarding the upper limits, it has lready heen noted that capacity of 
the industry to pay is & relevant consideration in this respect. The balance- 
sheets and profit und loss accounts (Ext. H series) and the statement 
(xt, I) do not disclose that the financial position of the company is satin- 
factory. 16 has already heen noted that there was loss till 1949 and the 
company started to earn profit from 1950 and the amount of loss was recouped 
on the trading results up to the year ending 3lst December 1955. In the 
year 1956 there was net profit of Rs. 4,179 and in 1957 the net profit came 
to Rs. 3,948. Having regard to the financial position os aforesaid, I do 
not ا0‎ any additional burden can be imposed on the company in this 
respect. 


It appears that there are two paid apprentices in this company (vide 
Ext. A). They are now paid total emolument of Rs. 47,76 nP. each. 
They are workmen under section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act. I 
think that their wages should be 2/3rds of the minimum basic salary with 
full D.A. of the category. The company is directed to pay them accordingly. 
The issue is answered accordingly. 


issue No. 2: JD.A. had been formerly at the rate of Rs. 16 per month. 
Subsequently it was increased to Its. 20 per month and this has been now 
current. The union demands that the D.A. of the employees should be 
raised to a flat rate of Rs. 60 per month. . 


The company opposes the claim. The company maintains that دو‎ 
of DA. depends on the capacity of the industry to pay and the financial 
joritioh of the company does not justify further imposition of additional 
fades in this respect. It further pleads that some e2-gratia payments 
ure made almost every year as a gesture of goodwill to supplement the 
earnings of the workmen and to help neutralisation to some extent. 


Under the award of Third Engineering Tribunal the minimum wage 
including D.A. at Rs. 71 for an unskilled worker was fixed comprising basic 
wage of Its. 86 and D.A. of Rs, 36. The basic wage was fixed at the cost 
of living index at 180. D.A. would, therefore, be available on the cost of 
hving index exceeding point 180. The company does not dispute that 
there lias been rise in the cost of living index. The First Omnibus 
Engineering Tribunal found cost of living index at 310 points. The said 
Tribunal disregarded rise up to 180 points at which the prices were then 
expected to stabilise and fixed D.A. on the difference hetween 310 points 
and 180 points. According to the Central Pay Commission, Re. 1 was to 
be given as D.A. for every 5 points rise. On this calculation Rs, 26 would 
have been the measure of D.A. at the time of the award of the First Major 
Engineering Tribunal but it allowed Rs. 25 as D.A. on the basia of the 
(Central Pay Commission’s Report. The Second Omnibus Engineering 
Tribunal found the cost of living index at 340 points in 1950 and on its 
basis fixed 1).A. at Ra. 31. There has been further rise in the cost of living 
index and under the award of the Third Major Engineering Tribunal, D.A. 
was fixed at Rs. 36. This would prima facie support the claim for incre- 
ment in the D.A. if it is not otherwise barred. 


Regarding want of capacity pleaded by the company, I agree that un- 
like basic wage, D.A. must be related to the capacity of the employer to 
pay. But [ am unable to accept company’s case that it has no capacity to 
fay any additional D.A. The financial position as already indicated does 
not appear to be as gloomy as the company seeks to portray. There has 
een progressive improvement in the position of gross profits (wide Ext. H 
08185), The company has also been earning profit for the last 5/6 years, 
though the amount of profit may not be very high. It has also been able 
fo wipe out the past losses. So, giving due consideration to all the relevant 


982 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 26, 1959 [Parr] 


w 
factors as also the wage structure prevalent in the company, I grant an 
increment of Rs, 5 to the existing T).A. so as to raise it to Rs. 25 per month 
which I think to be fair and which I am satisfied the company is able w 
pay with little adjustments here and there. 


In the matter of pulling up the workmen to the minimum of their res. 
pective category, the amount of D.A. should be taken as Rs. 25 as now 
raised, and the balance should be reached by increment in basic wages. 


issue No. 3! The union demands that provident fund should be extend. 
ed to all the employees with equal contributions by the employees and 
employer at the rate of 10 per cent. of the total emoluments comprising 
basic wage and D.A. 


The company opposed the claim. It, however, appears that the com- 
pany has given provident fund facilities to some of its officers including the 
ofticer-in-charge of the workshop D.W. 1. Although the company may 
not be under legal obligation to extend the same facilities to the other 
workmen us the number of employees under its employment is below 50, 
1, however, find no justification for discrimination between employees and 
emplovees. The needs of lower paid employees for such provident fund 
tacilities are obviously greater than those with higher emoluments. I, 
therefore, think tat the company should not grudge extending provident 
fund facilities to all its workmen. The financial burden in this respect, 
it appears, would not be such which the company would not be able to bear. 
The company is accordingly directed to introduce provident fund for the 
workmen in its employ with equal contribution, on the part of the workmen 
and the company, limited to 6} per cent. of the total emoluments in the 
shape of basic wages and J).A. 


The issue is answered accordingly. 


Issue No. 4: The union alleges that some of the workmen in the employ-., 
ment. in the workshop of the employer company had been in employment 
in the workshop of Messrs. James Murray & Co, Ltd. The union demands 
that these employees should be declared to be eligible to get the benefit 
of past service from the present. employer company. The ground alleged 
by the union in this respect in short is that the employer company 1৪ an 
integral part of James Murray & Co., Ltd. The employer company opposed 
the claim. It denies that it is integral part of James Murray & (o. ۱۰ 
and maintains that the two companies are limited liability companies, are 
separate juridical entities, having separate accounts and balance-sheets with 
separate capital investment by their respective shareholders, ench having 
no connection with the other. 


On the materials placed before this Tribunal J am unable to uphold the’ 
claim of the union. The facts as are admitted or established tn ۵6ء‎ 
are as follows: Messrs. Lens & Scientific Instrument Co. Private Ltd. was 
incorporated on 28th January 1944 (Ext. D). Long before this, Messrs. 
James Murray & Co. Ltd. (hereafter called the company) had been 1n- 
corporated. The company had originally been a partnership business owned 
hy 2 or 3 partners and established about 100 years ago. The company was 
carrying on business in imports of survey nautical and ophthalmic instru- 
ments from foreign countries. It had a workshop in the premises at 6/2 
Old Court House Street, Calcutta, for the purpose of assembling them 
and for doing repairs before the said premises were let out to the employer 
company from January, 1944. 


The employer company took lease of the premises at 619 Qld Court 
Jlouse Street from James Murray & Co. Ltd. before its actual incorporation

সপ সস  چجچےّ ہس _ںسس پجججچٹەںەہٴہ ژ‎ সু 


and paid rent for January, 1954. It came into occupation as a monthly 
tenant in January, 1944 (Ext. FE) and then purchased furniture on 
17th February 1944 from Mackenzie Lyall (Ext. F). Thereafter the em- 
ployer company purchased on 14th March 1944 and subsequently some tools 
from James Murray & Co. to run the workshop (Exts. Fl and F2) and 
87680 its workshop on the same premises with 51 workmen on 14th March 
1944 (vide attendance register Ext. Gi). 1 will thus appear that there has 
been no continuity but break in the working of the workshop. Subsequently 
the employer 2007 purchased raw materials from the company on 30th 
May 1944 (Ext. F2). It appears that initially there was no machinery in 
the workshop and that work in the workshop was carried on manually with 
the help of land tools from 14th March 1944 and subsequently machineries 
were introduced from 1956 [de Exts. 5, 5(d) read with D.W. 1]. 


The employer company, it has already been seen, is an engineering con- 
cern. It carries on business of repairs to survey, nautical and ophthalmic 
instruments mainly. It re او‎ the premises where the business is 
carried on as a factory ick, জর the Factories Act. Jt wan initially doing 
repair work and subsequently after introduction of machineries started to 
manufacture some items from 1960 (7126 D.W. 1), 


On the closure of the workshop of James Murray & Co, Itd., the 
employer company, it appears, undertook execution of assembling part af 
the survey, nautical and ophthalmic instruments and/or repair works on 
contract given out hy James Murray & Co. Ltd on payment of amounts as 
settled with the said company. The evidence also reveals that the employer 
company does not do work exclusively for James Murray & Co., but has 
also other customers. 


In this state both the employer company and James Murray & Co. ۰ 
‘admittedly came under the management of N. R. Sarkar & Co., 1+۹ since 
128) July 1946. After assumption of management the employer 7ء‎ 
was developed and it came to instal machineries in its workshop. 


At the {ime when the employer company started work in the workshop 
Mr. Carle was the Manager of the workshop while Mr. Murray was the 
Manager of James Murray & Co. Ltd. Ti is not disputed that Mr. Carle 
was Manager of the workshop of the employer company from 1944 to 1947. 
Then Mr. Smith became Manager of the workshop of the employer company 
from 1947 to 1950 and ultimately one Mr. Evans up to 1955 (wide D.W. 1). 
Only after Mr. Evans left, a common Manager has been functioning for 
hoth the employer company and James Murray & Co. It will, therefore, 
appear that there was no identity even in management of the employer 
company and James Murray & Co. from the start of the employer company 
from 1944 til} 1967. 


There is no record either to show that any of the workmen in the employ 
of the employer company had been working from before 14th March 1044. 
Exhibit TD) shows that out of those now in employment, only 153 were serving 
from the commencement of the workshop from l4th Mareh 1944, Even if 
it be assumed that those 13 workmen had been in service in the workshop 
of James Murray & Co., there is nothing to support their claim for conti- 
nuity of service. Prior to introduction of section 25FI'F there was no 
চক | right to workmen in this respect. The matter was -then entirely 
regulated by contract. The relation of employer and employee between 
these workmen and James Murray & Co. even if it existed would prima 
facte cease on the closure of their workshop. At the time in 1944, Indus- 
trial Disputes Act was not in existence. There was no obligation on the 
part of the old employer to find employment for them, or on the new em- 
ployer to retain them on same terms and conditions. Only if there was 


984 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, FEBRUARY 26, 1969 [Parr] 


se 


۹ 
transfer of assets and liabilities with goodwill us a going concern, the 
transferee company had 90011286102) to continue the workmen on same terma 
and conditions us were available in the transferror company. There was 
no such transfer in the present case. Exhibit I), Memorandum of Articles 
of Association, would go to show that the employer did not come into 
existence as a result of transfer from James Murray. The documents, as 
already referred to alao show that the employer company was started hy 
tuking monthly tenancy of the premises from James Murray & Co., and 
after purchasing furniture, tools and materials. The Board of Directors 
were not also the same initially but only from 12th July 1946, when N. R. 
Sarkar & Co. has heen managing both. The evidence does not also show that 
James Murray was the sole customer of the employer company. The evidence 
rather shows that the employer company executes also orders of outsiders. 
If there had been common Maes since assumption of management of both 
the companies by N. R. Sarkar & Co., this is not unusual. So, giving due 
consideration to the evidence and circumstances, I find that none of the 
emplovees is entitled to get the benefit of continuity of service from the 
present employer for the services prior to 14th March 1944, if any. 


Regarding preliminary objection by the company that the reference on 
this issue is bad as there was no industrial dispute either apprehended or 
in existence at any time, I am however unable to maintain it. It appears 
trom the records of conciliation proceedings that the employer compan 
submitted a chart therein showing length of service of all workmen 0 
culated from 12th July 1946 which the union contested for the workmen. 
It cannot, therefore, & said that no dispute existed or apprehended in 
this respect and that the Government had no jurisdiction to refer the issue. 


This is my award.

ment buildings located in West Bengal the requisite “no demand — certiti- 
cule” has to be obtained from the Manager, Government ot India Katates,

Subject: No Demand Certificate 


Rule 232 of Central Government Compilation of Treasury Rules, 


Vol. ہا‎ provides ےہ‎ 


“The last payment of pay or allowances shall not be made to, or in 
respect of, a Government servant whose pay is drawn on 
Gazetied Government servant's bill form, finally quittiug the 
service of the Government by retirement, resignation, dismissal, 


death or otherwise, or 


placed under suspension, until the 


disbursing ofhcer has satisfied himself, by reference both 00 the 
Accountant-General and bis own records, that there are No 
Demands oustanding against him. In case of other Government 


servants, payment may be 


made without reference to the 


Accountant-General on the responsability of the head of the office 


concerned,”’ 


Lustances have come to notice where final payment to officers quitting 


the service of Government have 


been made without obtaining the 


requisite No Demand Certificate from this office thereby making it rather 
impossible ا١‎ recover outstanding ariears of rent from such officers and 


causing loss of reyenue to Government. 


As Estate Office has ںا‎ recover 


rent, ete., from the officials in occupation of Government buildings, — the 


necessity aud importance of obtaining ‘No 


Demand Certificate” from 


this office is obvious and ean be easily understood. It is therefore 
requested that {o avoid possibilities of loss of revenue {to Government 


arrangements be so made that 50:1 


accounts of officers quitting the 


service of Government by retirement, resignition, diamissal, death, or 
otherwise, are not getiled in the absence of the requisite “No Demand 
Certificate” from this office. This may also be brought to the notwe of 


all concerned,

Decision 


For proper appreciation of the dispute it is necessary to state certain 
Juets leading to the reference as are either admitted or established = in 
evidence. These are as tollows: Messrs. Brooke Bond India Htd. (here- 
after called the company) reuted sheds Nos. 11, 16 and 17 situated in Pahar- 
pur Road from the Port Commissioners of Calcutta. These sheds are 
collectively called Brookelyn. The company has a factory and godown at 
Hide Road at a distance of one turlong from shed No. 12 Brookelyn. Tea 
chests are stored in Brookelyns. 


Shri Ali Hossuin (herenfter called the employer) is a labour contractor 
ot Messrs. Brooke Bond India Ltd. in respect of shed No. 12 Brookelyn for 
leading and unloading the tea chests. At the relevant time Shri Ali 
Hossain employed more than 80 coolies including those mentioned in the list 
under reference for the said purpose. 


falcutta Dock and Port Labour Union (hereafter called the union) on 
behalf of the workmen working in shed No. 13 Brookelyn under the 
contractor Al [Hossain placed a charter of demands on 3rd May 1957 both 
to the company and Shri Ali [ossain demanding direct employment under 
{he company and same tacilities in the matter of wages, overtime, etc., as 
were available to the coolies in direct employment of the company in the 
factory godown at Wide Road (Ext. .(ا‎ The copy of the charter of demands 
was also sent to the Labour Commissioner with ٢ request for intervention. 
Neither the Company vor Ali Hossain replied to the demands. On 11th May 
1907 the union again wrote to the Labour Commissioner (Ext. 3) complaining 
that following submission of charter of demands, Ali Tlossain started 
intimidating and threatening the workers with dismissal und planning to 
recruit fresh hands on terms interior to those existing. The President of 
dhe union also submitted along with the letter a list of workers who were 
members of the union. The list showed 83 workmen to be the members of 
{he union (ade Ext. 3). Thereupon conciliation started, Assistant Labour 
Commissioner Shri 8. N. Roy took up conciliation. On that very date 
(1111) May 1957) he wrote to Ali Hossain asking him to send comments in 
respect of the charter of demands and requesting him to maintain status quo 
pending conciliation of the dispute (Ext. 2). There was no reply to the 
sume. The conciliution officer subsequently wrote successive letters to 
Shri Ali Hoasain requesting him to send competent representative to joint 
conference fixed on different dates | ride Exts, 2(a), 2(b), 2(c)]. The letters 
were addressed to Ali Hossain at Brookelyn, Paharpur Road, Shed No. 12, 
Caleutta [etde Exts, 2(a), 2(b) and 2e)], According to Ali Hossain he 
did not get those letters. 


On 14th May 1957 the union wrote Deputy Commissioner of Port Police 
enclosing copies of the previous correspondences with the Labour Com- 
missioner, the company and the contractor. He was informed that due to 
persecution of the workers by the contractor following submission of charter 
of demands, 8 tense situation prevniled, and he should take adequate steps 
to prevent causing of any trouble by the contractor (Ext. 4). On 27th May 
1077 the union wrote to Ali Ilossain inviting his attention to the fact that 
no reply was received to their charter of demands, dated 3rd May 1957, and 
1011 out of 7 workers locked out only two were given employment and 
reniaiining five were still awaiting employment. Complaint was 0180 made 
therein that it was not fair on his part to lay off the workers. when he was 
recruiting fresh hands. It was further complained that the workmen were 
reduced from the status of monthly paid to weekly paid and that their 
Wages were not being paid regularly but) as and when he liked. The 
President of the Tnion so requested Ali Hossain to revert to the former

system of monthly payment und sent copy of the letter respectively to the 
Labour Commissioner und the company (Ext. 6). On the next date (28th

the last few months. The company was also informed that the contractor 
did not pay the workers on Friday or on Saturday and even on the day of 
writing. The company was accordingly requested to intervene und restore 
bers এ status of the workers and payment of wages to them immediately

Regarding union’s charge of change in service conditions following 
workers joining the union and presentation of charter of demands, ٤ om 
unable to uphold it. I rather believe case of Ali Hossain that the workers 
had all been dhily-rated and never monthly-rated and that they had never 
weekly offs and had no overtime previously. The workers might have been 
monthly paid but not monthly-rated. It is not disputed that the workers 
employed directly by the company in the factory godown are all daily-rated 
workers. Ali Jlossain has been merely a contractor. It is, therefore, all 
the more probable that the workers employed under lim were daily-rated. 
Their wages it appears were Rs. 3 per day. Similarly the workers, I believe 
bad never weekly offs. Some of the workmen in their deposition admitted 
that they were used to be employed on all days of the week and month. 
It uppears that they had thus been getting total remuneration at Rs. 90 or 
Re. 98 according to the number of the days of the month. Jad they been 
monthly-rated the remuneration would not have varied as above. The 
charge of reduction in status after presentation of charter‘of demands 
cannot, therefore, be sustained. It appears that there has heen merely a 
change in the wage period. The evidence shows that the workmen used to

Section 4 of the Payment of Wages Act provides that the employer shall 
fix periods in respect of which wages shall be paid and that no wage 4ة‎ 
should exceed one month. The employer had therefore, right to fix a week 
or a month as the wage period. The system of weekly payment has been 
recognised to be more convenient and appropriate for these classes of daily- 
rated workmen. So the change by Ali Tlossain in the wage period was to 
the advantage of the workmen and not to their prejudice. Similarly the 
evidence shows that ile workmen hud formerly no overtime. The evidence 
of some workmen to the contrary is contradictory and unreliable. P.W. | 
said that overtime was formerly 4 annas and they subsequently demanded

sigher than those of others which varied from Rs, 1-8 00 Rs. 2-8 per day. 
Subsequently when they hecame consciious that their counterparts in the 
direct employ of the company were getting overtime at the rate of 12 annas 
they made demand for same overtime, and ultimately Ali Hossain agreed 
to give overtime at the rate of 4 annas. Thus there is no basis for the 
charge of reduction in the overtime either. 


Regarding terms of employment it ia admitted that the workmen were 
not permanent. As Ali Ilossain has been a Contractor and the workers 
were employed under him, their employment would not necesserily be of 
permanent character but of casual and temporary nature. But Ali Tlossain 
has admittedly heen lahour contractor of the company for ithe last 25 years. 
Evidence further reveals that the work of loading and unloading for whieh 
he got the contract and for which the workers were employed by him was

occasionally additional hands (vide Ext. 17 & Exts. F and 0), Tt further 
appears that all the workers discharged were all employed continuously

eznployment in the way as he did. The workmen can, therefore, legitimately

issue 2: The union demands that the workers in the empoly of نا‎ 
Hossain should be giyen sume rates of wages and other benefits as are

opposes the claim. 


On giving careful consideration to the matter it appears that the demand 
for parity, if conceded, would virtually mean abolition of the contract system 
which the tribunal is not competent to do. It is the exclusive function of 
the management to decide which of the work will be done by contractors aud 
whieh by paid workmen. It is obvious that if the contractor is to exist, 
he cannot afford to give same wages and other facilities as this would leave 
no margin for him. Conceding of the demand would mean his own 
elimination. So if the system is to continue, differences are bound to oceur. 
Adequacy or otherwise of the existing wage nd other benefit has to be 
judged in relation to what prevails in similar institution and not in 
comparison with those of workmen in direct employ of the principal. Lt is 
so obvious thaf the demand cannot be conceded. At the same fime it cannot 
he overlooked that the pnystem of employing contractora is not in the beat 
interest of the employees though the employers derive certain temporary 
advantage from it. ] would, therefore, leave the matter with the 
recommendation to the company to undertake on its own the work of loading 
and unloading and if it is not possible, to introduce an appropriate clause iu 
ute agreement with the cntractor concerned das regards wages ١۱آ‎ other 
vonditions of work to abridge the gaps as ouch as is reasonably possible *or 
the benefit of labour employed by the contractor. The issue is answered 
accordingly.

This is a complaint, under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
by Shri Rama Nath Banerjee against hia employers Messrs. Karamchand 
Thapar & Bros. (Private) Ltd. and two others, the opposite party in this 
ease. [1 is alleged that the eomplainant was appointed a Stenographer 
on 3rd October 1947 and had served the opposite party for the last 11 years 
satisfactorily. THe was on sick leave for 15 days from 6th May 1958 and 
upplied for its extension, with a medical certificate on 2186 May 1958. In 
the meuntime his services were wrongfully terminated because he agitated 
for the stoppage of his increments in the last two years. The opposite party 
contests and contends that the complaint does not lie as there has not been 
any contraxention of the provisions of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. and that the services of the complainant were terminated under 
service rules on account of his frequent absenteeism resulting in his in- 
eHicieney, disqualifying him tor further service. 


Point for decision 


(1) Whether the complaint is maintainable? 
(2) Whether on merits the order of dismissal is justified ? 


part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 6, 1959 109}

FINDINCS 


Point Nos. 1 and 2: It has been urged on behalf of the Company that 
the cotoplaint is: not maintainable for there has not been any violation of 
the provisions of section +3 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The com- 
lainunt, a Stenographer since 1947, adopted the service rules (195৮, A) of 
1115 Company when he was appointed. 11078 dismissal letter and ضا‎ 
evidence will conclusively show that he was found absent for 864 day» in 
eourse of a year due to illness. Shri Hanerjee, of course, did not admit 
that, he was absent for such a long time on account of illness alone, 
ں‎ (۰۱۹۰.۰ ۱ Shr Abraham, Hstabhshment Officer, proved a list, Ext. KE, 
prepared with reference to records, showing the complainant's absence 
during the month of April, 1956 and May, 1958. Tle was warned on 
several oceaxions and was usked 10 improve on his attendance. 1۱۳.۴۷. [1 
Shri Banerjee, admitted that his increment was stopped for frequent 
absence from duty and that he was asked to improve his = attendance. 
Increments were withheld in two successive years, 1956 and 1957. He, 
however, got it im April, 1958, in terms of an agreement between the Union 
and the Management which were incorporated in an award of this Tribunal. 
He was not allowed to crosa the efficiency bar since 1956. Under the 
clause 2407) of the service rules (Kxts, A), an employee is liable to discharge 
on account of his frequent absence from duty for illness. The Manage- 
ment had terminated the complainant's services, not for any misconduct 
connected or unconnected with any dispute pending before this Tribunal 
for adjudication, but for hia frequent absence on account of illness under 
clause 24(1) of the service rules, which operates as contract of service 
between the parties. This contract cannot be avoided on the supposed plea 
of the Union that a dispute for better service rules is now pending for 
udjudication, In fact, Shri Banerjee takes his stand on this ‘‘service rules” 
in support of hus claim for accumulated leave alleged to be due to him at 
the time of discharge. The Company has shown by the complainant’s own 
applications for leave that he was in the habit of falling sick and going on 
191৮ on that pround for a long time. He was warned and cautioned in 
writing. Ile was not allowed to cross the efficiency bar. His increments 
were withheld in two successive years. Shri Banerjee could not make out 
any case of victimisation. Huis services were terminated as the work in 
01106 was suffering for his frequent absence. 1118 repeated 1111)988 and in- 
eficiency in the work cannot he said to be his misconduct. The Company, 
his employer, has the undoubted common law right, under the service 
rules, to terminate his services and that case, in my opinion, does not fall 
under the perview of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. There is 
nothing in section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, as athended now, 
which ean lend support to a contention that the complainant was dismissed 
for nusconduct, and that the approval of this Tribunal is necessary under 
section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act. This is admittedly some- 
thing which is not connected with the dispute. It is not a misconduct at 
all. An approval of an action of the Management is only necessary where 
it proceeds against the workmen, in accordance with the standing order 
applicable to him, for a misconduct, not connected with the dispute, and 
punished him either by dismissal or otherwise, and discharges him with 
payment of wages for a month as reqwred under section 33(2) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. In constructing the provisions of the said section, 
there is no place for invoking equitable doctrines. When the words are 
clear, as here, it is the duty of the Court to give plain meaning to the words 
wed, Iam, therefore, unable to accept the contention urged on behalf of 
the complainant that the termination of service, in the instant case, was 
for ‘‘misconduct not connected with the dispute’. Tu my opinion, there 
has not been any violation of the provisions of section 38 of the Act in 


1092 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 3, 1959 = [Parr y 


Pn en A ST TE SR ER TE A a .سس حوسسسُچھ‎ 
terminating the serviecs of the complainant under the service rules and) 
accordingly, this complaint is not maintainable, 


On merits, the complainant has no case at all. He was falling sick every 
now and then and absented himself from duty on that account. This hag 
impaired his efficiency in work, and the Management could not be blame 
if it could not put up with him and tolerate his absence any longer. Thig 
application, therefore, fails and is dismissed.

AWARD 


This is a complaint under section 388A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by 3 durwans in the employ of the opposite party company. They 
complamed™ that during the pendency of un adjudication proceeding in 
respect of an industrial dispute between the opposite party company and 
their workmen before this Tribunal, the opposite party company altered to 
the prejudice of the workmen the conditions of service as io working 
hours and holidays which were subject-matters of the adjudication proceed. 
ings. It was said that prior to the date of reference their working 
hours were from 8-30 a.m. to 6 p.m. with one hour recess on week days 
and from 8-30 a.m. to 1 p.m. without recess on Saturdays. Besides, they 
were allowed full holiday on the Independence Day on the 15th August. 
The opposite party company during the pendency of the reference altered 
the aforesaid working hours and raised it to 54 hours and employed them 
even on the holiday on the 15th August. The workmen accordingly 
submitted that there had been contravention of section 33 of the Indusrtial 
Disputes Act and prayed for restoration of the previous state. 


The opposite party company resisted the claim. Tt denied that the 
durwans had working hours ns alleged or a full holiday on the 15th 
August as claimed by the petitioners or that the working hours and 
holidays of durwans were subject-matters of the adjudication proceedings. 
If further denied that it altered the working hours to the prejudice of 
the petitioners or that it altered practice ns ما‎ holiday as alleged. The 
Company pleaded that for the purpose of protection of the property, 
the Company had prior to 5th March 1948 one Jomadar and 4 durwans

Decision 

Section 9301) relates to matter connected with the dispute and حا‎ this 
case previous pernussion of the ‘Tribunal 1s necessary. From the record ot 
the original adjudication proceedings it appears that neither tne working 
hours nor leave and holidays which were subject-matter of the said 
adjudicacion proceedings related to the durwans. It is, therefore, obvious 
that section 83(1) is not attracted and no previous permission is necessary 
for effecting alteration. In the present case ار‎ also appears that 01) 
complaint lacks basis, The allegation that durwans had working hours 
trom 8-30 a.m. to 6 p.m. with one hour recess from Monday to Friday 
and from 8-380 a.m. tow p.m. without recess on Saturday has not been 
proved, Juikewise the allegation that) im the past the durwans were 
wlowed to absent wholly on the Independence Day on the 15th August has 
nat been proved, The evidence mad circumstances rather support the 
Cdmpany's version in this respect. P.W.1 Shri Ram Dulari Sharma who 
aluie deposed out of the three petitioners had to admit that one Jamadar 
and four durwans who were empolyed prior to Marah, 1958, had to be 
on duty for 24 hours throughout day and night im rotation. Thais would 
support that they had 24 hours’ duty in rotation on working days and 
holidays as the Company stated. The arrangement as aforesaid it appears 
continued even after commencement of the adjudication proceedings. 
There has been of course a change during pendency of adjudication 
proceedings. But it appears thas was necessitated consequent upen 
appointment of two night guards for night duty absolving the 3 durwans and 
Jamadar from night duty. Under the new arrangement definite duty 
hours for the three durwans and the Jamadar on working days and on 
holidays for day time were fixed (Ext. A). There is sian, کا‎ to show that 
said change waa to the prejudice of the workmen. On the other hand, it 
appears that there was no increase in ‘the workload compared to what they 
had before appointment of night guards, Section 33(2) relates to matters not 
ronnected with the dispute. An employer can resort to it if it has 
sanding orders. The Company has admittedly standing orders. Under 
rection 33(2) an employer is eligible to alter the conditions of service 
applicable to the workmen during pendency of adjudication proceeding 
without permission in accordance with the standing orders. So, if the 
Company had fixed definite hours of work as in roster for day time 
(Ext. A) for ‘the durwans on working days and holidays, it did thereby 
nothing illegal. The standing order enables the Company to take such 
action. The duty hours as fixed in the roster (Ex. A) it also ee do 


not exceed the limita prescribed in the Bengal Shops and Establishments

Act. In the circumstances, I find that there has been مو"‎ contravention 
of section 33. The petition is accordingly rejected. This is my award,

ee a ہے‎ 
সস 


9, I need not reter 10 the facts which have led up to the present dispute 
because the matter is being disposed of on a preliminary issue of law. 


It is contended on behalf of the Company that the application under 
paction 13:34 as tramed, is not muintainable in law because there has been 
no contravention of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as 
)0 in 1956. 


The fact of the cuse is thut the Pedal Section of the Rubber Department 
of the factory having proved to be uneconomic, it was closed down on 27th 
January 1908, and as a result thereof the complainants became = surplus. 
Their services were terminated on the same date. So this is a cuse of 
re(renchment, pure and simple, and the present dispute is not connected 
with the dispute under the aforesaid reference. 


(00611 the present section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
discharge or punishment by way of dismissal must be for misconduct not 
connected with the dispute. ‘‘Retrenchment’’ does nowhere find — place. 
Ii is neither a case of misconduct nor a case of dismissal for misconduct. 
That being so, the question of obtaining permission from the Tribunal prior 
to it or subsequently does not arise. So there is no violation of any of the 
provisions of section 33 of the Act as it stands now. If section 33 has not 
heen contravened, then a case under section 734 cunnot be maintainable. 
Infringement of section 33 is a condition precedent to a case under 
wection 388A. So the present petition under section 1354 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act is rejected ۱× not maintainable legally. I have not gone into 
(he merits of the retrenchment in question. That may be considered im an 
appropriate case brought under a general reference under section 10 of the 
Act. The case is thus disposed of.

5 PRESENT :
