For the Company: Shri S. K. Basu, Counsel, with Shri K. P. Mukherji 
Solicitor of Messrs. Khaitan & Co. 


AWARD 


By order No. 352-I.R. /IR/101T.-29(A) /57, dated the 31st January 1958 
the (Government of West Bengal, in the J.abour Department, referrec 


part I] ‘THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 5, 1959 1106. 


ynder section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Texmaco Limited, Belghoria, 24-Parganas, and 
their workmen represented by 11638011000 Workers’ Union, 49 Nimta Road, 
Belghoria, 24-Parganas, regarding the matter specified in the schedule, to. 
the Third Industrial ‘Tribunal constituted under section 7A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947, by notification No, 808-I.R./IR/3A-2/57, dated the 
1110) March 1957, for adjudication. 


2. After usual summons the parties put in appearance and filed their 
written statements. The pleadings were completed on 10th April 1958. 
The parties were thereafter directed to file lists of documents. Then after 
ydjournments the dispute was heard and award was reserve. 


8. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference is as follows: 


Profit Bonus for 1964. 


''exmaco Workers’ Union (hereafter called the union) on behalf of the 
workmen demands two months’ wages as profit bonus for the year 1954 
over and above what had been paid as customary bonus for that year under 
the award of the Second Industrial Tribunal. 


‘Messrs. Texmaco Limited (hereafter called the company) opposes the 
claim on the ground that it is a belated claim. It is said that there was 
no demand and no conciliation for profit bonus for 1954 before 29th 
January 1957. The claim was first made long after accounts for the year 
1064 had been closed. The present claim thus being belated is not tenable. 
Secondly, it is said that no surplus is left after deduction of prior charges 
according to the Full Bench Formula and thus the claim cannot be sustained 
on merit either. 


Qn giving careful consideration to the evidence on record I agree that 

the elaim is belated and cannot be sustained. Before the present claim 
was made the union had claimed Puja bonus for the self-same year 1954. 
The company was making some payment as bonus before Durga Puja 
annuully. The said bonus was paid at the rates of Rs. 16, Rs. 18 and 
Rs. 20 to workers according to length of service for the year 1953. The 
workers accepted the bonus at that rate for the said year 1953. Then in 
August 1954, before the Puja the workers demanded two months’ wages 
as Puja bonus for the year 1954. The company did not agree to pay bonus 
at that rate but was willing to pay at the rates as in 1953. There was 
discussion about the matter in the Works Committee meeting held on 28th 
September 1954 but no settlement could be arrived at (Iixt. 2). Then the 
dispute regarding the said Puja bonus for 1954 was referred by Government 
to the Second Industrial Tribunal presided over by Shri G. P. Mukherji 
on 14th October 1955. Shri Mukherji gave his award on 16+ March 6 
and this was published in the Calcutta (razette, dated 12th April 1966. 
By the said award Shri Mukherji awarded Puja bonus for the year 1954 at 
the rates us in 1958. During hearing at the said adjudication proceeding 
a question arose whether on the issue referred to ““What should be the 
yuontumn of Puja bonus for the year 1954°’? the matter of profit bonus for 
the anid year could be gone into. The Tribunal found that there was no 
demand for profit bonus for that year ond on the issue referred to the 
vestion could not alao be gone into. Even then the union did not make: 
donnie for profit bonus for the year 1954 before 29th January 1957. 
Demand for profit bonus for the year was first made on 29th January 1957 
(Ext. A), whereupon conciliation started. 


1106 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 6, 1959 [Parr [ 


শা 


The company maintains accounts according to the calendar year from 
January to December. The claim for bonus which has been rested op 
profits earned has accordingly to be determined on the basis of the profits 
carned for the year ended : 18٦ December 1964. The accounts for the saing 
yeur ended lst December 1954 were audited and balance-sheet and profit and 
loss accounts were prepared and submitted on 28th April 1955 (Ext. (), 
Jt also appears that the said audited accounts for the year 1954 wer, 
adopted in the general meeting of the shareholders of the company on 241} 
June 1965. It will so appear that cause of action relating to profit bonus 
for 1954 had accrued even long before the 0919 of reference of Puja bonys 
for the year 1954 on 14th October 1905. 


The union or the workmen, it has already been noted, did not make 
demand tor profit bonus for 1954 prior to 29th January 1957. They 010 
not make such demand even after the award relating to Puja bonus was 
published. The excuse for not making the demand prior to 29th January 
1957 as stated during hearing is that the workmen had no knowledge that 
such claim for bonus out of available surplus could be made. Even if it 
were true, ignorance of the position would be no ground in justification foy 
the laches. According to both sides a dispute also arose between the 
parties regarding profit bonus for the subsequent year 1965. The Secretary 
of the union, P.W. 1, could not say when such demand for profit bonus 
for the year 1955 was made. It is in evidence of the Company’s Finance 
Q)fficer Shri Radbeshyam Sharma ().W. 2) that such demand for profit 
bonus for 1955 was made in the year 1905. The demand might have been 
premature as the account for the year 1955 was yet then to be closed but 
nonetheless this would show that the workmen were aware of their rights 
regarding 2 bonus long before 29th January 1957. It has _ been 
uniformly 1610 by the Labour Appellate Tribunals that if the claim for 
bonus is made long after the year for which the bonus is claimed, has 
ended and the accounts have been closed, the Tribunals cannot entertain 
such a belated claim. The matter was taken up to the Madras High Court 
which 9180 upheld the view [wide 1957(1) 1154. 282]. In the Muir Mills 
Co., Ltd., reported in 1954-55 Indian Factories Journal, Volume VII, page 
483, .the Supreme Court found that ‘‘on the accounts of each year being 
made up and the profits of the industrial concern being ascertained, 11) 
workers during the particular year have their demand for bonus fully 
satisfied out of the surplus profits and the balance of profits is allocated and 
carried over in the accounts. No further claim for payment of bonus out 
of those reserves or undistributed profits can, therefore, survive’. In the 
circumstances, I agree that the present claim for bonus for the year 19174 
is belated and cannot be sustained and must so fail. In this view of the 
matter the question whether there would 1১6 deficit or surplus is not gone 
into. 


This is my award. 

Dictated and corrected by ime. 

J. N. MAITRA, JITENDRA NATH MAITRA, 
Judge. Judge, Third Industrial Tribunal. | 


The 10th February 1959. 


By order of the Governor, 
S. C. MUKHERJEE, Aast. Secy.

Herries Act, 1885 (Bengal Act I of 1885), herem- 
after referred to as the said Act, read with the

L.S.-G., dated the 18৮ December 1904, published

said new public ferry; 


And, in exercise of the power conferred by 
section ud of the suid Act, read with the Govern- 
ment of Bengal notification No. 217L.8.-G., dated 
the 12th January 1905, published at page 183 of 
Part IB of the Calcutta Gazette ot the 18th 
January 1905, I hereby order that the said now 

ublic ferry shall be managed by the District 

oard of Jalpaiguri: 


The Schedule

jurisdiction list No. 94, across the river Mujnai 
in the district of Jalpaiguri. The limitg of the

AWARD 


An interim award, allowing interim relief in the case, was submitted to 
the Government of West Bengal, on the 22nd May 1958. Payment, under 
the said award, was admittedly made to the workmen concerned in this 
dispute. The payments would appear from a petition submitted by the 
Company on 14th July 1958. Admitted vouchers, Ext. B series, would 
conclusively prove this. 


A ticklish question, of some nicety, regarding jurisdiction of this Tribunal 
was taken in paragraph 1 of the Company’s written statement. It is said 
that the original order of reference related to the question of payment of 
gratuity to a number of workers. Subsequently, it was substituted by 
another order under a corrigendum, and a new dispute was referred to for 
adjudication in place of the former. The Government had clearly acted 
without jurisdiction asking the Tribunal to adjudicate upon a fresh dispute. 
It has been urged by Shri N. K. Mukherjee, Advocate on behalf of the 
Company, relying on a decision of the Supreme Oourt in a case between the 
State of Bihar and D. N. Ganguli and others, reported in 1958, II, L.L.J., 
p. 634, that by a subsequent order the Government has superseded the 
original order of reference and thereby cancelling the same. The Govern- 
ment had no powers under the Industrial Dispute Act, read with section 21 
of the General Clauses Act, to do that. Shri S. ظز‎ Singh Roy, Pleader, 
on behalf of the Union, refuted these arguments of the Company by saying 
that the decision, in the aforesaid case, is no authority for holding that the 
Government has no power to amend or add to the order of reference, and 
that the facts of the said case had nothing in common with the facts in the 
present case. “Therefore, that decision has no application to the facts in the 
present case. It appears from the body of the judgment of said case that 
the کت‎ involved there was whether or not the Government can supersede 
a reference pending before a Tribunal consituted for that purpose. In that 
case, while the لی‎ সপ in respect of the earlier two references were 
pending before the Tribunal and had made some progress, the Government 
issued a third notification purporting to supresede the two earlier notifica- 
tions in respect of the two references. In discussing the merits of the case 
and the legal principles involved in it, their Lordships held that the 
appropriate Government had no power to cancel or supersede a reference 
made under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act. At the same time, 
their Lordships made it clear, towards the end of the judgment, that they 
were not considering the power of the Government to amend, or add to a 
reference-made under section 10(1). Their decision was confined to the 
narrow question as to whether an order of reference made by the appropriate 
Government under section 10(1) could be subsequently cancelled or superseded 
by it. The facts of this case are entirely different. The servies of six 
workmen were terminated on the ground of superannuation. They were not 
offered any payment of gratuity, which they demanded in case they were 
refused reinstatement. The original order of reference related to the 
question of payment of gratuitv, although that was only a part of the 
dispute that existed between the parties. On further representation, the 
original order was corrected, by a subsequent order under a corrigendum,

Four workmen of Gurudas Press, all under 50 years of age (vide Ext. 6), 
were retired on superannuation with efteet fiom 25th April 1957. They had 
put in 26 and 27 years and few montha service respectively. Two workmen 
of Bharatvarsha Printing Works who have put in more than 34 years’ and 
29 years’ service respectively, were also retired on superannuation with 
effect from the aforesaid date. Of them, Shri Charan Maity is aged 66 
veara and Shri Ram Hari Bera is aged 41 years. The Union’s case is that 
these workmen were placed on pre-mature retirement although they were 
entitled to continue in service in terms of the Standing Orders of the Press 
Award of 1961. In doing it, the Company exercised unfair labour practice 
on the workmen. The Union, accordingly, asked for their reinstatement, 
end, alternatively, for payment of all dues with pratuity. The Compuany, 
on the other hand, contended that these workmen were superannuated on 
their completion of 26 years of service under the Press Award of 1961. 
Other workmen were also retrenched due to repeated loss in the business. 
They received their dues in full and had left. 


The Press Award of 1951 contains the Standing Orders and other service 
conditions applicable to these workmen. Both the parties rely on this award 
though the Company at one place in its written statement repudiated this 
award on the allegation that it had terminated it by a notice in writing. 
The termination of the award, as alleged, was, however, not proved. Both 
the parties take their stand upon the terms of this award. Notice is Ext. 1 
series. It shows that the Company had discharged these workmen from 
service on the ground of superannuation. In reply to workmen’s represen- 
tation, the Company informed the workmen that their services were termi- 
nated due to superannuation, a decision which was taken purely on economio 
ground, and had nothing to do with any other consideration either from 
the Union’s side or from the side of the Management. The Company 
denies unfair labour practice or victimisation as alleged by the workmen. 
In paragraph 7 of its written statement, the Company stated that 
this discharge was not by way of retrenchment but by way of retirement, 


1180 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 12, 1959 [Part 1 


a 


and pleaded that such discharge was perfectly legal, bona fide and in the 
interest of the industry. Shri Bhutnath Chatterjee, one of the discharged 
workmen of (turudas Press, had deposed before this Tribunal on behalf of 
himself and other discharged workmen. Shri Kumaresh Bhattacherjee, an 
employee of the Company, had deposed on the side of the Company. The 
length of service of the employees is given in Ext. 6) and corroborated by 
the evidence of Shri Chatterjee and Shri Bhattacherjee, and the evidence of 
age us given in Ext. 6, without any objection from the Company's side, are 
undisputed. The Standing Orders applicable for works staff are given at 
page 501 ot the Calcutta Gazette, dated Ist March 1951. Termination of 
employment is mentioned in paragraph 14, page 505 of the same gazette. 
Under paragraph 14(1), all workmen shall retire ordinarily on completion of 
the 55th year of their age. If any workman 1s considered fit even after 
completion of 55th year of his age he may, on his application, be given an 
extension uot exceeding three years, provided no retrenchment is called for 
in the meantime. No workman who is physically fit shall be made to retire. 
Any workman completing 25 years of service shall have the option to retire 
even if he had not completed 55th year of his age. Under paragraph 14(4), 
puge 506, a workman whose superannuation is overdue shall he made to 
retire in the first instance whenever a question of bona fide retrenchment 
arises. 


As already stated above, the Management's case is that the services of 
these workmen were terminated due to superannuation, i.e., by way of 
retirement and not by way of retrenchment. Therefore, the evidence of 
retrenchment, which is very meagie on record, is of no practical assistance 
in this dispute. O.P.W. 1., Shri Bhattacherjee, said that the Company 
is leading towards loss. THe has no direct knowledge of accounts but said 
that they did not receive salaries at a time but they receive it in instal- 
ments. This, according to him, is the evidence of bad financial position of 
the Company. The Company has, no doubt, produced its balance-sheets 
for the four years ending 31st March 1957, and this action was taken by 
the Company within a month of the end of the financial year 1956-57. Both 
the years 1956 and 1957 show losses in Bharatharsha Printing Works and 
Gurudas Press belonging to Messrs. (urudas Chatterjee & Sons. The 
overall loss in these two organisations came up to Rs. 7,736-0-6p. A feehle 
endeavour was made on the side of the Union to show by its own evidence 
that the income from Sailen Press and Bharatbarsha M ugazine was not 
stated in the balance-sheet, although Sailen Press was as good a press 
belonging to Messrs. Gurudas Chatterjee & Sons as the two others are. Shri 
Chatterjee’s evidence appears to be against the Union's pleadings and 
against all probabilities. He said that the composition work was done 11) 
Sailen Press, with the help of new recruits, but they were printed and 
published from Gurudas Press and Bharatbarsha Printing Works with the 


Pio 


part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 12, 1959 118] 


SP a ay 
পপি 


help ot new recruits. This was not the Wnion’s case in its 71191, state- 
ment, and it is not corroborated by any evidence of credit. Some retrench- 
ment of staff was made at the time when the services of these workmen were 
terminated. Some of these men received payment of their dues and had left. 
The business position as disclosed in the balance-sheet in the last two years 
before the discharge of these workmen is not encouraging. But losses in the 
business do not necessarily mean reduction in work for the staff. Since the 
Management is not defending its action on the ground of retrenchment and 
ہر٥‎ there is no evidence except what discussed above to decide the question 
satisfactorily, it is not necessary to go to other questions, viz., whether the 
principle of ‘‘last come, first go’’ was observed in discharging ihese men 
from service due to superannuation. 


Shri Charan Maity of Bharatbarsa Printing Works is aged 66, and had 
put in more than 34 years of service. Shri Maity is above the age of 
retirement fixed under the Press Award, dated Ist March 1951. He has also 
completed more than 25 years of service when a workman has got the option, 
۱ء‎ the freedom of choice to retire even if he had not completed 55th year 
of age. Shri Maity was, therefore, rightly retired from the service due to 
superannuation. He was paid his dues under the interim award. Onl 
question is whether he was entitled to any gratuity under the Press Awar 
Provisions for payment of gratuity were made in the Press Award at page 
00ہ‎ It is clear that gratuity can only be claimed hetween the llth May, 
1948 and the date when the Contributory Provident Fund started. The 
Company had stated in its written statement, at paragraph 9, that it intro- 
duced the Provident Fund since June 1948. This was not denied on the 
Union’s side. Therefore, Sh1i Maity is not entitled to any gratuity under 
the award for the period covered by the Provident Fund. As he waa retired 
from service due to superannuation, he was not entitled to any statutory 
compensation payable in case of retrenchment of surplus staff. 


The cases of other workmen stand on a different footing. Each one of 
them had completed 25 years of service but not completed 65th year of age. 
This position remains unassailed, at the hearing. Shri Mukherjee’s ronten- 
tion 1s that under paragraph 1501) of the Standing (rders under the Press 
Award of 195], at page 500, an employer can retire a workman on اط‎ 
completing 26 years of service though he may not have completed 56th 
year of age. TI am unable to accept his reading of the text of the Standin 
Orders, paragraph 14(1), as correct. The option under the award is wit 
the workman. He has the freedom of choice in this matter. He may retire 
on completing 25 years of service though ordinarily he is entitled to continue 
till the 55th year of age. A workman who retires on his completing the 
26) year of age, has no option in the matter. He may get an extension of 
service not exceeding 3 years provided he is physically fit, and the right to 
grant any extension is with his employer. He cannot, as of right, claim 
an extension of service after completing the 55th year of his age. The 
employer has, however, no right to retire him from service when he has not 
completed 55th year of age simply because he has put in more than 2) years 
of service. The right to give up his service is with the workmen. In this 
particular case, the employer has, however, compelled all these workmen to 
retire from service on the ground that each one of them had completed 
26 years of service. This is against the letter and spirit of the rules of 
retirement embodied in the Standing Orders under the Press Award, 1951. 
In their case, it cannot be said that superannuation was overdue, which 
alone would justify their retirement by way of bona fide retrenchment of 
staff. In my view, the services of these five men were wrongfully terminated 
by way of superannuation. All of them asked for reinstatement. Normal 
relief, in case of wrongful discharge, ir reinstatement, and I find no 


1182 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 12, 1959 [Parr | 


reasonable excuse on the side of the management to deny them this 761161 
1, therefore, find that the termination of services of these four workmen of 
CGurudas Press, and one of Bharatbarsa Printing Works is unjustified, and 
these men are entitled to reinstatement in service. They were paid all their 
dues up to the day of termination of service. 


Now, us to the claim for wages, for the period of unemployment, the 
workmen are not entitled to it. They should remain satisfied with what 
they had already received, i.e., one month’s notice pay from the Manage- 
ment. Further, the Management should not be saddled with any liability 
for payment of wages when the workmen admittedly did not render any 
service to the Management during this period, and when there is no evidence 
on record that they remained idle without any employment whatsoever. 
These workmen should report to the Company’s Head Office, where they 
were last পা fo for রন during office hours, within 7 days from the 
date of the publication of this award. In default, the Company would ৮৬ 
under no obligation, under this award, to reinstate them in service. 


This is my award 
M. N, GAN, 


Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal

AWARD 


The reference wis first made in respect of Messrs. Sahu Jain J.td. of 1] 
Clive Row, Calovtta. This reference was dated 2nd June 1958. By an 
addendum No. 2798-1.R./TR/110-154/57, dated Sth July 1958, four other 
companies were added, viz. :-— 

(i) Messrs. Rohtas Industries J.td., 

(ii) Messrs. Shri Krishna Gyanodaya Sugar Ltd., 
(iii) Messrs. Bharat Collieries Ltd. and 
(iv) Messrs. New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. 


All of them are companies which are managed by Messrs. Sahu Jain 1101. 
as Managing Agents and the offices of all these companies, including that 
of Messrs. Sahu Jain Ltd., are situated at 1] Clive Row, Calcutta-l. The 
companies, in their written statements, pleaded that the reference was bad 
in law, in view of the fact that no dispute for the consideration of the four 
added companies was ever raised by their respective workmen before the 
date of the reference. It is also stated in the written statement of all these 
companies that as Messrs. Sahu Jain is the Managing Agents of the other 
four companies mentioned above, these companies generally follow the same 
wage structure and cther conditions of service as prevalent in Messrs. Sahu 
Jain Limited for their employees who are employed at 11 Clive Row, 
Calcutta-1. In view of these pleadings in the companies’ written state- 
ments, the following additional issue is framed :— 


Issue No. 7 
Is the addition of four companies, viz., (i) Messrs. Rohtas Industries 


T.td., (21) Messrs. Sri Krishna Gyanodaya Sugar Mills Lid., (iii) 
Messrs. Bharat Collieries Ltd. and (iv) Messrs. New Central Jute 
Mills Co. 1511. by the addendum No. 2798-I.R. /TR/11L-154/57, 


dated 5th July 1958, competent ? 


issue No. 7: ‘I'he learned Advocate for the Company argued at the time 
of the hearing of the case that the addition of the four companies by the 
addendum; dated 5th July 1958, has been incompetent in law, because these 
companies were not establishments of a similar nature between themselves 
or to Messrs. Sahu Jain Ltd. Messrs. Rohtas Industries Ltd. dealt with 
cement, papers, chemicals, sugar, etc., Messrs. Sri Krishna Gyanodaya 
Sugar Mills Ltd. dealt with Sugar, Messrs. Bharat Collieries 
Ltd. involved five collieries and Messrs. New Central Jute 
Mills Co. Ltd. was a mill manufacturing jute textiles. These 
details of the companies will be found from Ext. 4, a diary of 1960, 
published by Messrs. Sahu Jain Ltd. It is admitted by both sides that all 
these four companies are managed by Messrs. Sahu Jain Ltd. as Managing

agen Ba WA 


Agents, and it is also admitted by both sides that Messrs. Sri Krishna 
(iyanadova Sugar Mills Ltd. have no employees at 11 Chive Row, Caleutta- 
}, and the Vuion did not press for‘any adjudication in respect of 11018 
Company. This award shall not, therefore, affeet Messrs. Sri Krishna 
(tyanadoya Sugar Mills Ltd., and the name of this Company shall be deemed 
10 have been deleted from the present proceedinys. In respect of the other 
{hrea companies, viz., Messrs. Rohtay Industries Ltd,, Messrs. Bhorat 
Collieries Ltd. and Messrs. New Central Jute Mills (Co. Ltd., i is the 
admitied case of both the sides that they maintain an office at 11 Clive Row, 
Caleutia, and these companies follow the same wage structure and other 
enditions of service in respect of these employees os are prevalent for the 
employees of Messrs. Sahu Jain Ltd. employed in its office at 11 Clive Row, 
Culeutta. There is, theretore, no douht that the establishments of these 
three companies situated at 11 Clive Row, Calcutta, are of a similar nature 
between themselves and also to that of Messrs. Sahu Jain Ltd. situated at 
11 Clive Row, Calcutta. That being so, section 10(5) of the Industrial 
Disputes Art authorises inclusion of the establishments of the three 
vompanies 16 mentioned in the addendum No. 2798-I.R. /IR /113.-1954/ 057, 
dated Sth July 1998, when making the reference of the dispute between

Issue No. 3: The صمتصاا‎ claims for an award directing the (00011202818, 
to pay for overtime work on a working duy at one and 0016 half times the 
ordinary rate of busic salary and for overtime work ou Sundays and 
heliduys at double the ordinary rate of overtime paid on working days. 


The companies state that the question of payment of overtime allowance 
far work done over and ubove the normal period of work is_ fixed, 
According to the existing practice, the workmen are required to complete 
their work entrusted to them in course of the day. Normally the office 
opens for the day's work at 9-30 a.m. and closes at 5 p.m. on the week 08৭ 
and at 1-80 p.m. on Saturdays. But it is understood that if the exigencies 
of business would require, the clerks should stay a few hours wore io 
complete work. The question of payment of overtime does not and cannot 
arise, inasmuch as the condition of the service is to complete the work of 
the Company in the course of the day. If the workers demand fixing of 
dhe rate of the overtime allowance, the Company submits that the normal 
working hours should be fixed, and that should not be less than 48 hours 
per week. If the workers are willing ہا‎ fix 48 hours per week, the 
companies would be ready to consider the payment of overtime for the work 
done beyond 48 hours. 


The normal working hours in the week is 39 hours. The learned 
Advocate for the Company stated that under section 10 of the Bengal 
Shops and Establishments Act, 1940, a worker may be made to work for 
1ا١‎ hours in any day. Section 10, however, does not apply to a commercial 
establishment, but applies only to establishments for public entertainment 
or amusement. Section 7 lays down the hours of work for an establishment. 
The Act does not preseribe any hours of work for a commercial establish- 
ment. Section 13 prescribes wages for overtime work for «a person 
employed in a shop or establishment for public entertainment or amusement. 
There is no provision in the Act for wages for overtime work in a commer- 
cial establishment, which the present employers are. 


It appears from Ext. (‘ that the clerical staff is paid proportionate wage 
on the basis of hours worked on holidays and Sundays. The subordinate 
staff are .paid- proportionate wage on the hasis of hours worked on holidays 
and Sundays and also some payments by way of jalpun on week days and 
সপ when they stuy for some time after the conclusion of the 01008 

ours. . 


Considering all the circumstances, it is awarded as follows: 


Rate of payment for extra work to clerical staff 


They shall work without ullowance for half an hour more after the 
conclusion of the office hours on any day, if the exigencies of service 
requires their presence for such time. If they have to stay for more 11804 
half an hour, they shall get overtime payment at 13 times their wage 
including dearness allowance on the basis of hours worked. Any broken 
period for more than half an hour, shall count as one hour. For work on 
holidaystand Sundays, they shall get overtime payment at the same rate 
as wentioned above. 


Rate of payment for extra work for the subordinate staff 


The subordinate staff shall continue to receive jalpan allowance at 
varying rates, but each of the present rutes shall be increased by 24 nP. 
lor work on Sundays and holidays, they shall get 1} times their wages ou 
the basis of hours worked. Cooks and kitchen bearers shal] get the same 
rate for going to bungalow as they are yetting now.

“Issue No. 4: The Union prays for an award directing the abovenamed 
companies to allow the following leave:- - 


(1) git aac leave—30 days per year with full pay cumulative up to 
ays. 


(ii) Casual leave—14 days per year with full pay non-cumulative, and 
not to exceed 3 days at a time. 


(iii) Sick leave—30 days per year cumulative up to 90 days with full 
pay, after exhaustion of the accumulated leave, further 60 duys 
with half pay, and thereafter without pay for three years. 


The companies state in their written statements that they are already 
granting leave much in excess of what is provided in the Shops and Estab- 
lishments Act. There is no reason to alter the existing facilities provided 
to the workmen. 


Exhibit E shows the leave facilities granted by the companies. It shows 
that privilege leave is allowed at the rate of one month of each completed 
year of service. The learned Advocate for the Union stated this privilege 
leave was cumulative for three years, and he admitted that there was no 
dispute in regard to privilege leave. It appears that the companies allow 
6 days’ casual leave and 6 davs’ sick leave with pay in a 
calendar year. Section 12 of the Shops and Estublishments Act 
provide that a person employed in a commercial — establishment 
shall be entitled after every 12 months’ continuous employment to privilege 
laave with full pay for 14 days, which will be cumulative up to 28 days, to 
sick leave on half pay for 14 days on medical certificate cumulative up to 
20 days and casual leave on full pay for 10 days non-cumulative. It, 
therefore, appears that the companies arevallowing much more privilege 
leave than are provided for by the Bengal Shops and Establishments Act, 
1949. Six days’ sick leave on full pay may be taken to be an equivalent to 
12 days’ sick leave on half pay. Considering the provisions of the Shops 
and Establishments Act and other circumstances on record, it is awarded 
that ‘the companies shall allow 10 days’ casual leave on full pay in a year 
non-cumulative. The companies shall also allow 7 daya’ sick leave oy full 
pay in the year on medical certifieute obtained from a registered medical 
practitioner. 


This isaue is accordingly answered.

1200 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 12, 1959 [Parr 1 


The companies state that they have established a movident fund for i 
workers as a retiral benefit. They opposed this demand of an 20011101111] 
retiral benefit in the form of gratuily over and above provident fund. 


The learned Advocate for the Union pressed the claim for this add). 
{ional retiral benefit on the ground that the companies are very prosperous 
and could afford such an extra retiral benefit in view of thei: financiud 
cupacity. The companies allow provident fund a» mentioned in Eat. ٭[‎ 
Provident fund contribution is 8 1/3 per cent. of the basic wage in Messy 
Sahu Jain Ltd. and Messrs. Rohtas Industries Ltd. and 6} per cent. of the 
total wage in the New Central Jute Mills Ltd. and Bharat Collieries Ltd. 
The learned Advocate for the companies opposed the claim for introduction 
of gratuity as an additional retiral benefit, in view of the fact that the 
finuncial condition of the companies does not justily the introduction of 4 
scheme 01 gratuity for the workmen and it was also pressed before me that 
if any gratuity schemes for the smal] number of office workers at 1] Clive 
Row, Calcutta, were allowed by this Tribunal, there would be similar 
demand for introduction of gratuity for the enormously large number ot 
workers in the factories of these companies, which would be beyond the 
capacity of these industries to pay and will create industrial disputes where 
there was none. It has been fait down by the Hon'ble Labour Appellate 
Tribunal of India in the case of Arthur Butler & Co., reported in 1952 (11) 
1..1.3., 29, ‘‘betore a scheme for gratuity can be sanctioned, the financial 
condition of the Company must he considered in its broad aspect, and that 
its profit-earning capacity, the profits earned in the past, its reserves ani 
the possibility of replenishing the reserves, if occasion arises, and the claims 
of capital to a fair share of the profits in the shape of dividend, having 
regard to the risk of investment, must be considered as material factors, 
and that the general financial’ stability of the concern must be taken into 
consideration before a long-term scheme, like a scheme for gratuity is 
panctioned’’, This view has been approved by the same Tribunal in the 
case of Boots Pure Drug Co., reported in 1956 1..A.C., at page 76. 


The financial position of the companies has been discussed above in 
issue Nos..] and 2. The companies are earning profits, but they are 
carrying heavy loads of secured and unsecured loans. The basic wages 
have been increased by this award. Other amenities by way of overtime 
allowance and leave facilities have also been revised. As it 18) it appeurs 
to me that the financial condition of the companies considered in_ this 
particular aspect is such that a long-term burden in the torm of gratuitv 
over and above the existing provident fund should not be saddled upon the 
companies. That being so, the claim for an additiontal retiral benefit in 
the form of gratuity, as made by the Union, is rejected. 


This issue is accordingly answered.

Tribunal, presided over by me, for adjudication, under section 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947). The said Fifth Industrial 
Tribunal was constituted under Government notification No. 308]Lab., 
dated the 9th June 1951. 


2. The reference was received here on 14th February 1955. After 
usual notices the Union filed written statement on 27th April 1955. The 
Company filed written statement on 6th July 1955. Thereafter the case 
was stayed at the instance of the parties pending decision by the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court in a connected matter. The prayer for interim relief by 
the Union was rejected on 14th August 1957. Ultimately the case waa 
taken up for hearing on 10th December 1958, and it continued till 1813 
December 1958 when the evidence was concluded. The argument was 
heard 7 14th January 1959 and 15th January 1959, and the award was 
reserved. 


8. The only issue which arose for adjudication under the Government 
order of reference is as follows :— 


Whether the discharge of the workers mentioned in the lists ‘A’ 
and ‘R’ attached herewith is justified? To what relief are the 
workers entitled? (The two lists in question have been repro- 
duced in the Appendix to this award.)

Mahammad there was to watch the water level und to see that it whs

(5-8) Iswari (T. No. 51), Larick (T. No. 286), Jagannath Prosad (T. 
No. 2785) and Chora (T. No. 6600): ‘These workmen were all taken into 
police custody from the factory in question. From the jail custody they 
addressed applications to the Company praying for leave till their release. 
But the Company, acting under clause 9 of the Standing Orders, dismissed 
then) on the ground of absence for 14 consecutive days. ‘Phey were dis- 
missed on different dates. The Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in sts 
decisjon in the case of Indian Iron and Steel Company J.id., and another, 
and fheir workmen, reported in the 1.13.14. March, 1908, at page 260 
(relevant page 268) 118 pursuance of another decision of the said (‘ourt in 
the cage of Messrs. Burn & Co., Calcutta, and their employees, reported in 
1997 L.L.3., Vol. 1, page 226, held that in such cases the matter of granting 
leave or its refusal sbould be left to the discretion of the employer. That 
will be in the interest of harmony between Jabour and capital, and alsa in 
the interest of normal flow of production. But if the workmen are arrested 
at the instance of the Company for the purpose of victimisation and in order 
ىا‎ get rid of them on the ostensible pretext of continued absence, the 
novition will be different. It will then be a colourable or mala-fide 
exercise of power under the relevant Standing Order. In view of this 
decision, laa it can be estublished that the Company was guilty of 
mala fides, the dismissal order passed under the Standing Order No. 9 
‘annot be disturbed. But in this case there 1s no evidence to show that it 
wae the Company who had caused arrests of these workmen, and that just 
to get rid of them it applied the aforesaid Standing Order. In the origina] 
ease before this Tribunal relating to the present Companies and their work- 
men out of which the aforesaid decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court was 
given in appeal, it was held by this Tribunal] that leave to the credit of 
sich workmen taken into police custody should first of all be allowed to 
exhaust itself before dismissal when the arrest was to the knowledge of the 
companies concerned. After that, leave might have been refused by the 
employer hecause leave cannot be claimed as a matter of right. But when 
there is « mass arrest of workers, as in this case, the Company, to ensure 
Moduction, must discharge the absent employees and appoint substitutes 
in their places. Though in this case there is no evidence that substitutes 


1206 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 12, 1949 [Parr [1 


dames Ge 


were taken 1n the vacancies caused by their absence, stil] in the absence 
of mala fides on the part of the Company I refrain from disturbing the said 
order of dismissal in respect of this group of four workmen. So their 
dismissal is upheld.

particularly, when he had rendered service during the crisis period of lock- 
out. So there is no bona fides wanting in the present case on the part of 
the Company. If anybody was to be blamed for his discharge, it was ae 
bimself. So I do not disturb the said order of the management discharging 
Juman Mia from its service. 


Dictated and corrected by me 


G. PALIT, G. PALIT, 
Judge. Judge, Fifth Industnal Tribunal 
lhe 9th February 1969.

PRELIMINARY NOTIFICATION OF A PROPOSED SCHEME 


In pursuance of section 29, sub-section (1) of the Electricity (Supply) 
Aci, 1948, it is hereby notified that the West Bengal State Electricity Board 
propose to undertuke the tollowing scheme :— 


1. Name of Scheme.—Bijanberi-Pulbaxar Electrification Scheme. 


2. Brief description of the scheme:— 

(i), Generation of electricity by building up a 370 KVA hydro-eleeiric 
power station on the stream Laringkhola near Bijanbati im the 
district of Darjeeling. A small diversion weir shall be ۹ 
across Laringkhola at an elevation of J.40) ft. so us to divert 
the flow 01 the stream along a 5.800-fi. long, 2-ft. x 2-tt. 
galvanised steel water conductor to a RWC, reservoir oat ۷١ 
elevation of 3,490 ft. The diversion of flow of the stream to the 
water conductor shall be about 4 cusees which is the minnnuin 
diy period discharge of the stream. Fiom the R.C.C. reservon 
water will fow through a 3,40U0-ft. long pipe line and then 
flowing through the power house turbine (elevation : 2.651 ft.) 
will be discharged to ihe Laringkhola near its confluence with 
the river Little Runjit. 

(ii) Construction of a single circuit 6.6 kV transmission line trom the 
proposed power station to Darjeeling and to Pulbasar vu 
Bijanbari. 

(iii) Construction of 400/280 volts distribution lines in Bijanbari and 
Pulbazar areas. 

(iv) Erection of necessary sub-stations at Bijanbari and Pulbuzar. 

(v) Construction of such civil works us are necessary for the exocu- 
tion of the scheme and maintenance of supply of electrical 
energy. 

(vi) Such supplemental, incidental and consequential works us may 
appear necessary and expedient for any of the purposes of the 
scheme und its working. 


8. Area to be served.—Power generated under the proposed scheme 
will be distributed at 400 volis in Bijanbari, Pulbazar and Sukiapokri in the 
district of Darjeeling and the surplus power shall be fed in bulk at 6.6 kV 
into the supply fines of Darjeeling Electric Supply, which needs augmenta- 


tion of supply. There is also a possibility of supplying energy Ju more 


villages in the neighbourhood in future, if eneryzy be available. , 
Population of Bijanhari-Pulbazar—3,000. 


4, Powers for placing of wires, poles, etc,—The RBourd will exercise 
powers of Telegraph authority under provisions of section 42 of the Elec- 
tricity (Supply) Act, 1948. 


5. Estimates.—The estimated capital expenditure of the scheme 1ম 
Rs. 7.51 lakhs. For the scheme taken us n whole, the estimated annual

INTERIM AWARD 


This proceeding is based on an order of reference (No. 4060-I.R./IR}- 
1N1.-112/58, dated 25th September 1958), relating to an industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Krudd Industries Ltd., 22 Ferry Fund Road, Panihati, 
24-Parganas, and their workmen represented by Krudd Industries Staff 
Association, 32/C Sankari Para Road, Calcutta-25, relating to issues 
specified ina schedule to the order of reference. The issues are as 
follows : — 

issues 


(1) Is the denial of employment of Shri M. K. Menon justified? What 
relief hy way of reinstatement and/or compensation ia he 
entitled 7۶ 


(2) Is the retrenchment of the following workmen justified What 
relief by way of reinstatement and/or compensation are they 
entitled to? 


1292 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 19, 1959 [Part | 


سھ ہد 


(1) Shri Goroknath Gond. (7) Shri Sarbanand Ojha. 


(2) Shri Shyamchandra Upadhaya. (8) Shri Ranadhir Bose. 
43) Shri Jadunath Singh. (9) Shri Kamal Bose. 

(4) Shri Kantilal Mehta. (10) Shr P. M. Menon. 

(5) Shri لا‎ 9. Nair. (11) Shri Golokvehari Pulley. 
{6) Shri U. K. Nair. (12) Shri P. K. Baral. 


(13) Shri Murali Mandal. 


Notices were issued on both parties, who filed written statements setting 
forth their respective cases. 


The Assoviation, in its written statement, claimed for restoration of job 
of Shri M. K. Menon with back wages, arrears, leave pay and compensa- 
tion for loss and for defamation and for payment of relief to the extent 
of Rs. 14,843.75 nP., being the total of claims relating to various items for 
Shri M. K. Menon as mentioned in the written statement. 


The Company, in its written statement, opposed the claim of the 
Association on all items and maintained that Shri M. K. Menon was not ؛‎ 
workman. The Company also resisted the claim of reinstatement or grant 
of any relief to Shri M. K. Menon and also the claim of reinstatement of 
the 13 retrenched warkmen. 


On 5th December 1958 the Association filed a petition praying for 
interim relief for Shri M. K. Menon and claimed that the Company should 
pay Shri M. K. Menon a subsistence allowance of Rs. 200 per month with 
effect from Ist June 1958, subject to adjustment. 


The Company filed a written objection on 28th January 1959 and 
opposed the claim for the interim relief as made by the Association on 
behalf of Shri M. K. Menon. It states that interim relief allowing wages 
or allowance should not be granted where there is risk of the money pnid 
on the basis of interim award being not recoverable if the termination uf 
service be upheld in the final award. The Company also referred to :ts 
written statement and stated that no interim relief should be granted. as 
prayed for. 


Shri M. K. Menon himself pressed the application on behalf of the 
Association on the date of hearing. The Company was represented by 
Shri Sambhu Nath Mukherjee, an employee of the Company. Shri M. K. 
Menon referred to the case of Messrs. A. T. Deb Ltd., reported in 1956 
L.A.C., 185, in support of his claim. صا‎ this case, the Hon’ble Labour 
Appellate Tribunal ruled that the grant of subsistence allowance is made 
only to enable the workmen to survive till the justifiability of his suspen- 
sion is considered and decided upon as a matter of interim social justice, 
in view of the poverty of the workman. There is a jurisdiction in the 
Tribuna] to make provision for subsistence on humanitarian grounds and 
the Tribunal cannot be confined to the four corners of the Standing Orders 
in cases 61 such emergency. It further states that interim award will he 
without jurisdiction only if relief granted under it is such as can under no 
circumstances he granted in the final award. It is clear that in this caso 
the Hon’ble Tribunal considered the case of grant of subsistence allowance 
to a workman during the period of his suspension. This decision of the 
Hon’ble ‘Labour Appellate Tribunal was made on 22nd December 1980. 


The decision of the Hon'ble Labour Appellate (Tribunal in the case of 
Jayasree Tea Gardens Ttd., reported in 1957 L.A.C., 199, however, lays 
down that ordinarily where the dispute relates to determination of service 


Pan 1} THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 19, 1959 1293 


of employees an interim award allowing them wages or emoluments should 
not be made especially when there is the risk of the money paid on the 
basis of the interim award being not recoverable, if the termination of the 
service be upheld in the final award, but special cases cannot be overlooked. 
This observation was made by the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in 
the case of Punjab National Bank Ltd., reported in 1952(I) L.L.J., 79], 
and this observation was followed by the Hon’ble Tribunal in the case 
reported in 1967 L.A.C., 199, and the interim award made by the original 
Tribunal, directing the Management to pay the petitioner a lump sum 91 
Rs. 225 and a monthly allowance of Rs. 75 was set aside, on the ground 
that it was unjustified and that there was no special case where any extra- 
ordinary relief by way of interim relief was open. This decision was made 
on 26th April 1956. The Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in another 
case decided on 20th February 1956, reported in 1957 L.A., 45 (the case 
of employers represented by Shertalai Coir Cottage Industries Association, 
Shertalai, Travancore-Cochin State) lays down that in a fit case an Indus- 
trial Tribunal has got power to grant relief by way of interim award, but 
such a power has to be sparingly exercised in really fit cases where the 
unavoidable delay in the proceedings would cause hardship to workmen 
and they have a prima facie case at least for some minimum interim relief 
The Hon'ble High Court of Kerala in the case of Burmah Shell (il Storage 
and Distributing Co., reported in 1957 (II) L.L.J., 51, lays down that av 
interim relief, if any could be granted only if a prima farie case regarding 
the subject-matter of the dispute is made out, 


Considering al] these decisions as detailed above, it is clear that the 
present case is not one of suspension of a workman and the subsistence 
allowance as prayed for by the Association is not one payable during u 
period of suspension of a workman, as was the case reported in 1956 L.A.C., 
page 85. Shri M. K. Menon has been discharged by the Company and he 
wants reinstatement. His reinstatement is opposed by the Company on 
various grounds. No prima facte case also has been made out on behalf 
of Shri M. K. Menon to justify the claim that he is entitled to some 
minimum interim relief. There can be no doubt that if Shri Menon were 
allowed Rs. 200 per month with effect from June 1958 till the date of the 
award, and the termination of service be upheld in the final award, there 
is a risk of the money paid on the basis of the interim award being not 
recoverable from Shri Menon. I do not also find that there is a special 
case where an extraordinary relief by way of an interim relief was open 
That being so, the application of the Association for an interim relief of 
subsistence allowance of Rs. 200 per month for Shri M. Kh. Menon as made 
18 rejected. 


M. C. BANERJI, 


Judge, First Industrial Tribunal.

Second Labour Court.‏ 


Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by its order 
No. 182-1.R./IR/11L-649/58, dated Calcutta, the 17th January 1969, 
referred to me an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. K. C. Dey 
Sons and their workmen represented by Shop Assistants’ Association of 
Bengal, for adjudication. 


Tasue formulated in the order of reference 18 89 follows : 


Whether the dismissal of Shri Hari Sadhan Adhikari is justified. 
To what relief is he entitled ? 


FINDINGS 


Notices were thereupon issued on both the parties to appear on 17th 
Faburuary 1959 and the Union was further asked to submit their statement. 
Qn the day fixed for submitting their written statement the Union sent a 
letter praying for time to submit the same. The workman concerned 
Shri Hari Sadhan Adhikari appeared before me and he was identified by 
Advocate P. Majumder. The workman concerned submitted a petition 
stating that he does not want to proceed with the case and that he has 
no connexion with Shop Assistants’ Association of Bengal nor he has paid 
any subscription for the same, and he prayed that the proceedings be 
dropped in the matter. It appears then that the workman concerned does 
not want to proceed with the case and he has no grievance against 
the employer concerned. In view of the fact that he has disowned his 
connexion with the Union, viz., Shop Assistants’ Association of Bengal, 
his case becomer a case of individual dispute and. as such, does not come 
under the purview of the Industrial Disputes Act as has been held earlier 
in numerous decisions. When the worker is unwilling to pursue the case 


1298 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 19, 1959 [Pant | 
তা সস সস ২২ 


and wants to drop the case, the Union can no longer represent his interest 
and prolong the litigation. The case is therefore allowed to be withdrawn 
and I sheuld give a ‘‘ne-dispute’’ award in the matter, 


Taken at my dictation and cerrected by me.

The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by 
order No. 795-I.R./IR/11L-89/58, dated the 4th March 1958, referred 
under sections 7 and 1() of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), 
an industrial dispute hetween Shree Vishudananda Saraswati Marwari 
Hospital, 118 Amherst Street, Calcutta, and one of their workmen Shri Hari 
Singh Bindra represented by West Bengal Hospital Workers’ Union, 7B 
Ram Rashmoni Road, Caleutta-13, regarding matters specified in the second 
schedule of the Act, to this Court for adjudication. 


Whether the termination of service of Dr. Hari Singh Bindra is justi- 
fied. What reliefs is he entitled to? 


This is a case arising out of an alleged illegal and unjustified termina- 
tion of service of Dr. Hari Singh Bindra by Shree Vishudananda Saraswati 
Marwari Hospital, 118 Amherst Street, Calcutta, hereinafter referred to as 
the hospital for the sake of brevity. 


The Union’s case in short is that Shri Hari Singh Bindra was a_ very 
popular doctor attached to this hospital for a long time. But as he was the 
General Secretary of 85.۲۰۵. Marwari Hospital Staff Association and 
placed the charter of demands regarding privilege leave, casual leave, and 
medical leave, etc., for the employees, the hospital was enraged und unjust- 
ly suspended him and then discharged him without any وہ‎ or ۵۰ 
ing any reason whatsoever and nothing of the kind. Thus the discharge 1s 
thoroughly illegal and unjustified. 


The hospital on the other hand contends that the discharge of Shree 
Hari Singh Bindra is fully justified as the hospital received complaint from 
one Shri Sitaram Begani about deriliction of duties on the part of the 


ParrI] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 19, 1959 1303 


doctor and therefore the Executive Committee of the hospital appointed a 
Sub-Committee consisting of (1) Shri Ramnath Bajoria, (2) Shri Rangalal 
Bagaria and (3) Shri Kedar Nath Poddar which, on proper enquiry, found 
the doctor guilty of the charges and thus discharged him. 


FINDINGS 


The 18th February 1959 was fixed for hearing this reference. The 
doctor workman concerned in this case put in a petition stating that the 
matter has been amicably settled out of Court and accordingly prayed for 
a ‘‘no-dispute award’’. The doctor was heard who stated that the matter 
has been compromised. Accordingly a ‘‘no-dispute award’’ is made in this 
case. The reference is thus disposed of.

Decision 


Messrs. India General Navigation and Railway Company, Lid. (hereatter 
called the company) has Head (ffice at 4 Fairlie Place and a Dockyard 
known as Rajabagan Dockyard in Rajabagan. The company has also a 
dispensary in the said Dockyard for the workmen employed therein, 
According to the i ig the clerical staff in connection with work in the 
dockyard had originally been attached to the Heud Office and doing work 
from there and subsequently in 1947 such clerical staff were transterred 
to the dockyard for facility of work. Besides the said clerical staff there 
aly operatives employed in the dockyard. 


I.G.N.R. Employees’ Wnion (hereafter called Employees’ Union) was 
formed in 1946. This was the only registered and recognised union until 
1954. In March 1955 Dock Engineering Mazdoor Sabha (hereafter culled 
the Mazdoor Sabha) was formed and this was registered on 1011) July 1955. 
It did not, however, initially receive recognition from the company. 
Subsequently there was an agreement between the Mazdoor Sabha and the 
company on 11th March 1958 whereunder the Mazdoor Sabha was recognised 
while recognition from Employees’ Union was withdrawn by the company. 


The operatives in the dockyard have working hours from 8 a.m. to 
5-0) p.m., while the clerks have all along working hours from 10 a.m. 10 
f p.m. with half an hour recegs from Monday to Friday and from 10 a.m. 
10 1 p.m. without recess on Saturday. For bringing in uniformity in the 
working hours between those of the clerks and the operatives for the purpose 
of more smooth work, the company proposed to raise the working hours in 
respect of the clerical staff by requiring them to attend from 8 a.m. in pluce 
of 10 a.m. The company conveyed its proposed change in working hours 
to the employees’ union which was not agreeable to accept it. The Mazdoor 
Sabha also made a representation to the Assistant Tabour Commissioner 
oppgsing suid duty hours of the clerical staff. It then submitted charter of 
demands on 3lst October 1956 to the Assistant Labour Comminsioner (106 
Aunexure to Ext. J). The said charter of demands, dated 3lst October 
1956, was.sent by the Assistant Labour Commissioner to the company on 
ith November 1956 for comments (Ext. J). Then as no settlement was 
possible between the company on one hand and the Mazdoor Sabha and 
Employees’ Union on the other in course of conciliation proceedings, the 
disputes were referred to this tribunal for adjudication. 


Let us now consider the issues separately. 


issue 1: This relates, after amendment of the list, to 99 employees. 
Tt 1s the Mazdoor Sabha which raised the dispute in this respect. In the 
written statement filed before the Tribunal, it limited the claim for 
93 employees including Shri N. K. Mondal as mentioned 10 their 
Annexure A to the written statement. Out of the said 39, case of 
Shri N. K. Mondal was also separately referred to in issue No. 3, where- 
under his case would be considered. So adjudication under thia issue is 
called for only in respect of remaining 38 employees mentioned in 
Anrexure A. 


Before entering into the controversy it is necessary to state certain facts 
about which there is no dispute hetween the parties. These are as follows :~- 


In 1946 the company effected a revision of emoluments in all categories 
of grade then in existence. At that time the grades in existence were the 
special grade, Grade A, Grade B, Grade C, Grade D and Grade E. 


In 1949 hy agreement with the employees’ Union the company abolished 
Grade E for clerical staff proper and all members of then existing clerical

ت تتےےط‎ ً rf 


stafi who were in Grade E were upgraded to Grade D. So far as the 
dispensary staff were concerned consisting of 2 dispensers and 2 dressers, 
separate grades were introduced with the agreement of the employees’ 
Union heing the grades of compounders and dressers. 


In 1958 the company which then had u total of 109 clerka in Grade 1), 
upgraded 107 to Grade .۔۸)‎ Subsequently the remaining two persons in 
(irade 1) were also upgraded into Grade C and since 1996 the company has 
not any clerk in Grade 1), 


The company’s Grade C is Rs, 70—4—134—KH. B.—4—182. The company 
ns a result of agreement with the Employees’ Union has since 1957 adopted 
the principle of upgrading all Grade C employees into Grade B upon their 
completing 10 years of service, by giving them the necessary increment to 
bring their basic pay up to Rs. 110 per month and thereafter giving them 
increments of Rs. 7 annually. The grades after abolition of grades 1 and 1) 
ns above stand as follows :—~

Now regarding the dispute it has already been noted that the Mazdoor 
Saitha raised the dispute on 9181 October 1956 (Ext. J). Complaint was 
mage in general terms that upgrading and promotion were granted by the 
company without regard to seniority, experience and merit, but on the basis 
of union affiliations of the employees. tt was said that those who belonged 
to anplovees’ Union though had not the necessary qualifications were 
upgraded while those who belonged to Mazdoor Sabha though fulfilled the 
aforesaid requirements were denied upgrading (vide xt. J). 


In the written statement filed before this tribunal the Mazdoor Sabha 
dil not cite specific instances but remained content in generalisation as 
before. It alleged that the Employees’ Union was n puppet union which 
the company boosted up in various ways. The members of the clerical staff 
who refused to become members of the said union were refused upgrading 
and/or promotion though by virtue of their education, experience and 
calibre they were entitled to the same. Besides, the company did - not 
hesitate to confer Grade A or even Special Grade to a number of Officers 
aud leading members of the Employees’ Union who were not only junior 
but were far less inferior academically, in experience and efficiency than 
those belonging to Mazdoor Sabha. The workmen mentioned in Annexure A 
to its written statement were those who deserved upgrading having regard 
to their efficiency, experience and length of service. The Mazdoor Sabha 
accordingly prayed that each of those workmen mentioned in Annexure A 
should be upgraded to the respective grades as shown therein against their 
names, 


The company opposed the claim. It denied charge of having taken into 
consideration union affiliations of the workmen in the matter of upgrading 
or promotion and pleaded that the matter was decided solely upon a 
consideration of the abilities of the individual employee. If further denied 
that any one of the Ijst to the order of reference or Annexure A to the 


1308 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 19, 1959 [Parr ] 


written statement of Mazdoor Sabha deserved any further upgrading than 
those they had received and pleaded that the transfer of clerks or any 
employee from. one grade to another was 0 management function and was 
solely for the company to decide upon a consideration of the abilities of the 
individual. It was said that the company was in fact exceedingly liberal 
in upgrading clerks and granting them increments and seniority within the 
vrades as the previous history of the matter would show. The relative 
position of the employees im the different grades compared to the total 
complement would appear from Annexure A to its written stutement. 
Besides, the company maintained that the dispute us raised in the issue was 
Lot capable of forming the subject matter of industrial dispute within the 
meaning of Industrial Disputes Act and the reference in so far as it 
apy ertained to this issue was invalid, void and of no effect and the tribunal 
had no jurisdiction to adjudicate it. 


During hearing the 7 filed its statement (Ext. A) showing the 
position of each of the 89 workmen as mentioned in Annexure A to the 
written statement of the Muzdoor Sabha with date of appointment, basic 
pa:? and grade—past and present from 1945 to 1958. The Mazdoor Sabha 
has not challenged the aa statement (Ext. A) as incorrect in any respect. 
Annexure A to company’s written statement shows number of employees in 
ech of the grades in the years 1954, 1955, 1956, 1957 and 8۰ 


Promotion as such, I agree, is not an industria] dispute. It is only where 
there are certain rules in this respect, non-observance of them may lead to 
an industrial dispute. It is now well-settled that the matter of promotion 
to a higher grade is entirely management function and that the tribunal 
will not interfere unless there 1s mala fide in the matter or unless there has 
been non-vbservance of any rule in this respect. The management are the 
eole judges of ‘conduct and aptitude of the employees for promotion, unless 
uctuated by malice or by motives of victimisation or unfair labour practice. 
It is not for an outside authority like the tribunal to go into the relative 
merits of the individuals upgraded and those not upgraded with them. In 
the present case the Mazdoor Sabha has nothing sntisfactory to show that 
the company passed over the case of the workmen under reference from a 
motive to victimise or from an indirect motive of unfair labour practice 
nor has it alleged or proved breach of any rule in this respect. There 
would be so no basis for interference by the tribunal. 


Promotion to a higher grade cannot be claimed as a matter of right. It 
has to be deserved by application to duty, good conduct and by aptitude and 
qualifications for discharging the duties of the higher post. The statement 
(Ext. A) shows that all of the 38 employees for whom upgrading has been 
claimed during hearing got different promotions in the past. The state- 
ment further reveals that they were promoted to their existing grades not 
long ago and that none has reached maximun of their existing grade. 
These do not prima facie go in support of their claim for upgrading. 
Promotion to a higher pi can only be made when there are requirements 
and vacames. It is for the management to fix the number of posts in the 
several grades. So, all individuals of equal merit and service cannot be 
upgraded simultaneously if there are no posts available in the higher grade. 


The evidence on the side of the company, on the contrary shows that 
in the matter of promotion to higher grade nomination is first made by the 
heads of different sections and then these go to departmental Managers and 
these are ultimately considered hy a Board consisting of the General Manager 
of the workshop, Departmental Managers and Senior Labour and Welfare 
Officer. The procedure as aforesaid, prima facie, goes to ensure fair play. 
Annexure A to the written statement of the company shows that promotions

to different grades were not restricted but were progressively fair. The 
(feneral Manager of the workshop J).W. 1 Mr. Earnest Gordon Fortes 
deposed that 11 any complaint was received in this respect, the matter 
received his personal attention. He denied that in giving acting ‘appoint- 
ment to one Aswini Paul in 1958 they were in any way actuated by the fact 
that he was the Vice-President of the Employees’ (Union. According to the 
company it reviews the case of each individual member of the clerical staff 
at the beginning of each year taking into consideration all factors such as, 
discipline, attendance, merit and execution as well as any individual or 
collective representations on the subject. The action taken by the company 
from 1946 till 1956 in the matter of improving the grades and upgrading the 
employees as already referred to would belie the سا سار‎ of the Mazdoo 
Sabha that the union afhliation had been the criterion in the matter of 
uppiading. D).W. 1, of course, admitted that Sections-in-charge were 
generally in Grade A but it does not follow from it that all Sections-in- 
¢haige should be in (71006 A, when there is no evidence to show that all have 
to perform same duties. Merely because they are similarly designated it 
does not necessarily follow that their duties are identical and they have 
same amount of responsilility and trust. The evidence of D.W. 1 is that a 
Section-in-charge is not necessarily given (1805 A. This would show that 
the duties of all Sections-in-charge are not similar or their responsibilities

Masiloor Sabha for upgrading of any of the workmen under reference cannot 
be sustamed and 19 rejected. 


The issue is answered accordingly. 


issue 2: The issue an it stands, avecording to ull concerned, does not 
raise the real dispute between the parties, The clerical staff have admittedly 
wotking hours from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. with half an hour recess from Monday 
to Friday and from 10 a.m. to ] p.m. without recess on Saturday. It is 
agréed on all bands that the company proposed to raise the working hours 
of the clerical staff of the dockyard from 8 a.m. in place of 10 a.m., while 
hoth Employees’ Union and Mazdoor Sabha were opposed to it. So the real 
dispute is whether the clerical staff are liable to work from 8 a.m. and not, 
whether they should he compensated for extra working hours from 8 a.m. 
The issue, os it is, is therefore not in order, und no adjudication is 
accordingly called for. 


issue 3: The dispute in this respect has heen raised by Mazdoor Sabha.

In the year 1949 on or about 14th July the company concluded its 
discussions with the Employees’ Union relating to upgrading and increment 
of clerical staff, as a result whereof the said (7106 K was abolished and all 
clerical ‘staff proper in Grade EK were upgraded into Grade ]), At the said 
time, however, the cases of the two dressers and the two dispensers were 
expreasly reserved for further discussion and agreement. 


Accordingly on 15th July 1949 the company’s Chief Engineer sent to 
the Dockyard Manager at Kajabagun under a covering letter the finally 
agreed rates for regrading of E Grade clerks at the Dockyard expressly 
mentioning that the casos of dressers remained outstanding as well as the 
dispensers and Canteen Manager (Annexure € to the written statement). 
Thereafter further discussions were held between the company and the 
Kimployees’ Union and agreed scales were arrived at for compounders 
(01819908918) und dressers, the prade for dressers being Is. 60—2—90 
(Annexure D to the written statement). 


In the meanwhile letters were being sent to all the clerks previously in 
Grade E who had heen upgraded into Grade D and along with such letters 
a letter, dated 19/26th July 1949, was by mistake sent to Shri N. K. Mondal 
confirming him in his previous Grade EK with one year’s গস A 1) that 
grade. As already stated Grade E was being abolished and the letter was 
plainly an administrative mistake caused by the matter being dealt with in 
n routine manner in accordance with the practice of the previous years 
when persons who were not upgraded received letters confirming them in 
their existing grades. 


Such letter was never acted upon either hy the company or by said 
N. K. Mondal and he continued to draw the pay of the dressers’ grade 
newly fixed, namely, Rs. 60-—2—90 with one year’s seniority therein by 
siarting at Rs. 62. The said terms and emoluments of the said dressers’ 
grade were better than those of Grade E mentioned in the said letter. 


Shri Mondal nade numerous applications for leave, ete., which he signed 
08 $ Dresser and -has without, objection received letters addressing him as a 
Dresser aid has never at any time been treated as a clerk nor claimed to be 
so treated until the present claim was made in the adjudication proceedings 
or shortly before. 


Shri Mondal has also at all times observed the working hours of 
Dressers and not the working hours hitherto observed by the clerks. 
Shiri Mondal has enjoyed the benefit of the Dressers’ grade which was 
superior to Grade 19 mentioned in the letter, dated 19th /26th July 1949, and 
is estopped from contending that he ought to be treated as a clerk on the 
basis of the said letter. 


In support of the case Mazdoor Sabha examined Shri Mondal (P.W. 1) 
besides proving the letter, dated 19th/26th July 1949 (Kixt. 1), the copy 
of his letter, dated 8th October 1956, to the General Manager (Ext. 2) and 
the reply “dated 6th November 1956, of the General Manager *Ext. 2(a)]. 


The company, on the other hand, examined the General Manager 
(D.W. 1), the Labour Welfare Officer (D.W. 2) and Medical Officer 
(I).W. 3) besides proving documents (Exts. B, C to C2, D to D2, KF to K6, 
,لا‎ G, H to H11, I and J). 


On giving careful consideration to the evidence and circumstances 
I accept the case of the company. The letter of appointment, Ext. F, 
shows that Shri N. K. Mondal was appointed as a Dresser in the Dockyard 
dispensary on and from 14th January 1946 on a salary of Rs. 25 per month
