plus usual allowance as then existed. In the latter part of 1946 company 
effected a revision of emoluments of all categories of workmen. According 
to company Shri 28101505115 salary was then raised to Rs. 40 and in October 
1948 his salary was again raised to Rs. 9 per month with effect from Ist 
Fanuary 1948. The Dressers had admittedly no Grade or Pay Seale of their 
own. The Grade EK which was for the clerks was from Rs. 55—24—7(). 
Shri Mondal whose salary was raised to Rs. 56 per month from Ist January 
1948 was thus allowed to draw salary in accordance with Grade E of the 
clerical staff. 


On 15th July 1949 FE Grade was abolished and all the clerks in 10 Grade 
were upgraded to Grade D (vide Ext. B) which had pay scale of 
Re, 60—2—90. Whuile forwarding the agreed rates of the employees who 
were being upgraded from Grade E to Grade D, the Chief Engineer 
specifically made mention that the cases of 2 Dressers, 2 Dispensers and 
Canteen Manager would remain outstanding and would be settled very 
short] pm Ext. B). In the list of the clerks who were then heing 
কি from E Grade into Grade D, the name of Shri N. K. Mondal did 
not appear. Qn the contrary, it was specifically mentioned that the two 
Dresners 1). K. Adhikari and N. K. Mondal who were at the time drawing 
salary of E Grade would be bracketted with 7۳00ھ‎ and separately 
graded as Dressers. This would show that N. K. Mondal was not till then 
appointed or in any way treated us a clerk but remained Dresser as he had 
originally heen appointed. 


On 8th August 1949 the company wrote to the President of the Employees’ 
Union embodying the agreed conclusions regarding the outstanding points 
(Ext. 1). In the said letter for the first time separate prade for the 
Dressers wis laid down, the grade being Rs. 60—2—90 exactly in line with 
the existing D Grade of clerks which was Rs. 60—2—90 (vide Ext. H). 
Span company’s letter, dated 19/26th July 1949, addressed to Shri N. K. 
Mondal (Ext. 1) which is the foundation of the claim, the company’s letter, 
dated 8th August 1949, laying down, among others, grade for the dressers, 
made the said grade operative with retrospective effect from Ist January 
1949 and Shri N. K. Mondal’s salary was fixed at Rs. 62. Shri N 
Mondal admitted im cross-examination that separate Dresser’s Grade with 
Rs. 60—2—90 was introduced in August 1949 and his salary was fixed at 
Its, 62 and he got the said salary with retrospective effect from lst January 
1949. This would give go by to the letter Ext. 1 upon which he based his 
01711) and would show that he knowingly continued as a Dresser and accepted 
the grade us introduced tor Dressers in August 1949. The letter Ext. 1 
upon which claim has been laid did not provide for any retrospective 
operation. The fact that Shri N. K. Mondal udmittedly received salary with 
retrospective effect from Ist January 1949 leaves no room for doubt that it 
was on the basis of the new Dressers’ Grade as introduced by the letter, 
dated 8th Auguat 1949 (Ext. I). Grade D of the clerks, it may be noted, had 
heen in existence from 1946, while grade for compounders was introduced 
for the first time on 8th August 1949 although hoth Grade D of the clerks 
and compounders’ grade so subsequently introduced had same pay scale of 
Rs. 60—2—90. Though the clerks proper on FE Grade were upgraded into 
Grade 1) of Rs. 60—2—90 for the clerks on 15th July 1949, they were not 
given any retrospective operation and their pay on promotion to Grade D 
was however in no case helow Ry. 70 (vide Annexure to Ext. B). The 
difference in salary at the start for Shri N. K. Mondal and of those upgraded 
from EK Grade to D Grade would also negative the claim of Shri N. K. 
Mondal that he was promoted as a clerk in 1949, 


Shri N. .کا‎ Mondal admittedly functioned and has been functioning as a 
Dresser since hia apointment on 14th October 1946. He described himself 


1912 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCI] 19, 1959 [Pant I 


throughout as a Dresser in his dealings with the company even after the 
date of the letter Mat. 1 (515 Exts. )' and 1) series). The company also in 
its official dealing with him in making temporary transfer described him 
throughout as a Dresser (Ext. E series) even after the date of the letter 
Kat. 1. The story of Shri N. K. Mondal im his deposition trying to explain 
it away is unconvincing and unreliable. The conduct as above would 
support company’s case that the letter Ext. 1 was never acted upon either 
by Shri Mondal or by the company. 


Now regarding the company’s letter, dated 19th/26th July 1949, 
addressed to Shri N. K. Mondal (Ext. 1) which is the foundation of the 
claim, it appears that the most important portions containing his basic 
salary mentioned in it at the time as also the scale of Grade K were 
purposely blurred, the former portion as it apparently ran counter to the 
present case. Be that as it may, the terms therein do not also support thie 
0৪৭৫ Of Shri N. K. Mondal. The letter recites excluding the portion so 
blurred as follows: 


“Further to your appointment, dated 14th January 1946, we have much 
pleasure in confirming you in your employment as clerk on a basic 
salary of per mensem in Grade KE with one 
year’s seniority in that grade.”’ 


His appointment on 14th January 1946, it has already been noted, was 
as a Dresser. So there was no scope for confirming him as a clerk. The 
letter was, therefore, in the nature of routine as the company contended. 
The practice pleaded in this respect by the company has been borne out 
by Ext. H series. It appears that similar letters bearing date 19th/26th 
July 1949 were issued to different clerks confirming them in their respective 
ধু in which they were at the time. Be that as it may, the letier Ext. 1 

ees not in any case support the case as pleaded in the written statement of 
the company betore this tribunal that Shri N. K. Mondal was promoted 
as clerk in 1949 hy that letter. There was no such appuintment as clerk by 
that letter (Ext. 1). The Mazdoor Sabha, it appears, having become 
conscious that the recitals in Ext. 1 did not speak of appointment but of 
confirmation introduced the story in the charter of demands presented on 
26th October 1956 that Shri N. K. Mondal was promoted as a clerk luter on 
in 1946 evidently to fit in with the recitals. For in the charter of demands 
it was stated: “Shri N. K. Mondal was appointed at first as a Dresser in 
the Dockyard dispensary. Later on in 1946 he was promoted as a clerk’’. 
This was apparently to give conform to the words ‘‘confirming you in your 
emplovment as clerk” in the letter, Ext. 1. It was however lost sight of 
that the appointment, dated 14th October 1946, referred to in Ext. 1 was us 
dresser and not as clerk. In the subsequent written statement filed before 
this tribunal the said case of appointment as clerk in 1946 was also lost 
sight of and it was alleged that Shri N. K. Mondal was ag eo as clerk 
in 1949 by that letter, Ext. 1. The letter (Ext. 1), it has already been 
noted, did not do so. Had that letter, Ext. 1, been received 
contemporaneously through a messenger in 1949 as deposed to by P.W. 1, 
this would not create any right whatsoever. The letter was apparently a 
mistake. There would be no meaning to confirm one in Grade E on 
19th /26th July 1949 when the said Grade E was abolished by the letter, 
dated 15th July 1949. 


Now as to when the letter, Ext. 1, was received, claim of Shri N. K. 
Mondal during hearing that he received it through messenger in 1949 1s 
unreliable. His inaction prior to 8th October 1956 does not support such 


Pant 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCIL 19, 1959 1313 


claim. Jt was on the contrary stated in the charter of demands, dated 
26th October 1956 (Annexure to Ext. J), as follows: — 


‘Shree N, A. Mandal was appointed ot firat as a Dresser in the Dockyard 
dispensary. Later on in 1946 he was promoted as a clerk. But 
the Company kept his promotion letter suppressed for all these 
years. About a month ago Shree Mondal found that letter in which 
the Managing Agents of the Company directed the Rajabagun 
authority to treat Shree Mandal as a clerk fix his pay accordingly. 
Shree Mandal approached the Gencral Manager with that letter of 
the Managing Agents and demanded promotion. He also gave a 
written representation to him and a copy of that letter in which 
his case has been stated in detail hus কপ sent you for your 
information. We hope you will please take up the case and do 
justice to the gentleman.”’ 


So the letter (Ext. 1) according to the charter of demands was received some 
time in latter part of September 1956 and not before. This is also in 
conformity with the written demand which was made for the first time by 
Shri N. K. Mondal on 8th October 1956 (Ext. 2). On that day Shri N. K. 
Mondal wrote to the company for the first time as the letter, Ext. 2, itself 
recited making claim on the basis of the letter, Ext. 1, with copy to the 
Labour Commissioner and Mazdvor Sabha. On 6th November 1956 company 
replied that the matter was receiving attention [Ext. 2(a)]. It was a 
mamuls reply and would not convey anything beyond what it stated. The 
recitals in the letter, Ext. 2, that there had been earlier verbal demands, 
are not reliable. The witnesses on the side of the company gave denial that 
there was claim previously. After that letter on 8th October 1956 (Ext. 2), 
the Mazdoor Sabha, it has already been seen, placed charter of demands 
inclyding claim of Shri N. K. Mondal to the Assistant Labour Commissioner 
or 26th October 1956 (Ext. J). The Assistant Labour Commissioner on 
receipt of the said charter of demands forwarded the copy of the charter of 
demands to the company on 7th November 1956 for comments (Ext. J). 
These would clearly negative the claim of Shri N. K. Mondal. 


So, on the materials placed before this tribunal, I find that Shri N. K. 
Mondal had never been appointed a clerk nor had he been treated as such. 
Merely because on occasions few and far between he made some entries as 
required of a clerk in the registers in the absence of regular clerk on leave 
in addition to his duties as a Dresser, this would not make him ao clerk. 
He remained a Dresser and continued as such. The claim of Shri N. ۰ 
Mondal must accordingly fail. The issue is answered accordingly. 


This is my award.

AVERAGE EARNINGS 
Decision. 


For computation of average production bonus, the year will he divided 
intc two parts, January-June first period and July-December second period. 
The average of the first period will be applied to the second period and the 
average of second period will be applied in the next first period of the 
subsequent year. 


The average production bonus earning wil] be calculated by dividing 
the total production bonus earned during the six months excluding the 


1318 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 19, 1959 (Parr I 
বি ০০০০০০১১১০১ ১১০১ 


amount of compensation puid by the total number of days present excluding 
the days on which compensation was paid or idle due to clause 7 of the 
agreement. 


The worker will be paid compensation on monthly basis calculated at 
the average rate multiplied by the days present, less the days he was idle 
due to reasons in clause 7 of the agreement. 


It is also agreed that in case a worker does not earn the average produc- 
tion bonus per month calculated on the basis of actual production bonus 
earned days, then his case will be considered for compensation.

For Messrs. Kamala Press (Sertal No. 12): None. 


For the rest of the Presses: Shri M. N. Ghosh, Secretary of the 
Burdwan District Printers’ Association. 


The issues that were framed for the decision of this case are the same 
aa those mentioned in the order of reference and are as follows:—~ 


Issues 
(1) Classification of workmen. 
(2) Pay scale. 
(3) Dearness allowance. 
(4) Meal allowance. 
(6) Half holiday on Saturday. 
(6) Puja or annual bonus. 
(7) Leave and holidays. 
(8) Gratuity. 
(9) Service conditions. 
AWARD 


Messrs. Damodar Press, in its written statement, states that there was no 
industrial dispute existing between the employer of the said Press and 
any workman at any time and that the present reference so far as it relates 
to Damodar Press 19 illegal and void. Messrs. Kamala Press and their 
employees also filed a joint statement stating that they had no industrial 
dispute between themselves and they need not appear in the case. The 
question that arises is whether the reference in respect of Kamala Press 
and Damodar Press is competent. Issue No. 10 is, therefore, framed on 


this question. 


issue No. 10: Is the present reference in respect of Mesars. Damodar 
Press aud Messrs. Kamala Press competent? 


The employers and employees of Messrs. Kamala Press filed o joint 
statement on 9186 July 1968, stating that there was no industrial dispute 
between the employers and the employees. Messrs. Damodar Press, in its 
written statement, stated that there was no industrial dispute between the 
employers of that Press and their employees. The question is whether the 


Pare زا‎ THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, 80411600197 1959 1321 


en aun. = oe SC .دہ‎ eee ہے ہو . ےی‎ ee See! eee ے کے‎ ০০] 
০১ অরিন. এল হিল ہوا‎ SS ee Se eS —_ جو‎ চাল SS Sse 


reference of the issucs Nus. 1 to 9 on the order of reference is competent 
in rerpect of these two Presses. Section 10(5) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act lays down that where a dispute concerning any establishment or 
establishments has been or is to be referred to a Tribunal, and the appro- 
priate Government is of opinion that the dispute is of such a nature that any 
other establishment or a similar nature is likely to be interested in or 
affected by such dispute, the appropriate Government may at the time of 
woking the reference include in that reference such establishment, group 
or class of establishments whether or not at the time of such inclusion any 
dispute exists or 1s apprehended in that establishment, group or class of 
establishments. This clause clearly shows that the inclusion of Kamala 
Press and Damodar Press in the present order of reference although there 
iy no dispute between the employers and employees in those establishments, 
is competent on the part of the appropriate Government. The Tribunal 
is, therefore, obliged to adjudicate on the dispute as referred to it by the 
appropriate Government under section 10 of the Act. 


This issue is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 1:—Classification of workmen: The Union states that there is 
nu proper classification of workmen. Generally there are three categories 
of workmen, viz., Compositor, Machineman and Binder, but all of them are 
required to do the job of others. The Union claims that occupational 
pomenclature of the workmen should be determined, and the workmen 
should be classified mainly in two groups—senior and junior. Workers 
serving consecutively for more than 5 years should be treated as senior 
nit workers and those working for less than 5 years as junior grade 
workers. 


The Burdwan District Printers’ Association, representing twelve 
Presses as mentioned hereinbefore, states in its written statement that the 
deninnds preferred by the Opposite Party Union, are not tenable. 


Evidence was adduced by both sides. P.W. 1 Shri Shib Nath Mohanto, 
a workman of Sarbamangala Printing Works, deposed for the Union. 
Q.P.W. 1 Shri Subhas Chandra Chatterji, Manager of Bharati Press, 
deposed for the Presses. 


On a careful consideration of the matter, it is awarded that the workmen 
in the Presses shall be classified into three categories as follows :— 


(1) Compositer, 
(2) Machineman, and 
(3) Binder. 


It will be open tu the Presses to use the same person for a combination of 
duties, but in that case, the worker shall be entitled to get the wage for 
the most highly paid job in the combination. The classificatjon of workers 
of the same category into senior and junior grades is not allowed as being 
unnecessary in the circumstances of the case. 


This issue is accordingly auswered. 


Issues Nos. 2 and 3.—Pay Scales and dearness allowance: The Union 
claims that the monthly basic pay of the senior grade workers should be 
raised to Rs. 100 and that of the junior grade workers to Rs. 70. The 
initial pay in no case shall be less than Rs. 60 per month. The annual 
increment for the junior grade should be at Rs. 3 and that for the senior 
grade should be Rs. 5. Promotion from junior grade to senior grade 
would be automatic. The Union filed a statement 10. Annexure A to its 


1322 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 19, 1959 [Part I 


written statement showing the total number of Compositers, Machinemen 
and Binders, their salaries and the total duty hours in all the Presses 
mentioned in the order of reference. It appears that the number of work- 
met in the Presses vary from 1 to 8. There are two Presses with only one 
worker and three with only three workers. The establishments involved 
in this reference are, therefore, of very small size. The evidence of P.W. 
1 shows that the lowest pay of a workman in the Sarbamangala [Printing 
Press, where he works, is Rs. 36 per month, and in the Burdwan Press, 
it is Rs. 30 per month. The witness states by gueas that there are about 
9> men in the 14 Presses who are paid the minimum wage of Rs. 30 per 
month. They are to work overtime at single rate and are paid 4 annas as 
jalpan for 7 hours’ overtime work and 2 annas for 34 hours’ overtime work. 
One Press paye 7 annus as tiffin allowance in place of 4 annus, in addition 
tu overtime wage at single rate. In cross-examination, it was suggested 
to the witness by the learned spokesman for the Association that the learners 
it the Presses get a monthly wage of Rs. 30 and other workers are paid 
the minimum wage of Rs. 40 per month. 0.7۶.۲۷۰۰ 1 Shri Subhas Chandra 
(10781069111) states that the minimum pay in his Press is Rs. 40 per month and 
that is paid to a Compositor. O.P.W. 1 further states that Bharati Press, 
Naba Bharat Press and Burdwan Press are the best profit-earning Presses of 
Burdwan, and the maximum annual profit of these Presses would be 
Rs 4,000 a year. It was stated by the learned spokesman for the Associa- 
tion that the other Presses mentioned in the order of reference earned very 
meagre income to the tune of Rs. 1,000 or so in the year. The statements 
as to annual income, as mentioned in Annexure A to the Union’s written 
statement, shows that the Presses have a net income varying between 
Ras. 4,000 and Rs. 18,000 in the year. No audited account for the Presses 
were filed in proceedings. P.W. 1 states in evidence that the statement 
as to profit in Annexure A has been given by him on reference to the 
quantum of work put in by the workmeu. 


Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I do not consider 
that the 14 Presses of Burdwan that are involved in this proceeding are in 
a very prosperous condition. 


The Union also claims dearness allowance at Rs. 82 per month. Till 
now the wages paid by the Presses at .Burdwan were consolidated. I 
consider that consolidated wages should also be fixed by this Tribunal and 
there is no necessity for separating the dearness allowance from the 


basie pay. 


Considering the financial condition of the Presses, it appears to me that 
৪. major alteration of the wage structure would he inappropriate for the 
present case and may hit the Presses in question too hard, which may 
আসা cause unemployment. (31512) my best consideration, I award 
ar follows :— 


Rupees 50 shall be the minimum wage of a Compositor and a Machine- 
man and Ro. 45 shall be the minimum wage for Book-binders. All work- 
men shall be given an increment of Ra. 5 per month, subject to the condi- 
tion that a Machineman and oa Compositor shall get the minimum total 
wage of Rs. 60 per month and a Book-binder the minimum total wage 
of Rs. 45 per month. No separate dearness allowance will be paid to any 
worker, and the wage as mentioned above shall be considered ta be consoli- 
dated wage inclusive of dearness allowance. For a learner, the consolidated 
wage shall be Rs. 35 per month. A worker shall be kept as a learner for 
a maximum period of one year and not more.

Period of work shall be ¢ hours a day and 42 hours im the week, as at

paid at 11 dimes the normal single rate. 


These two issues are accordingly answered. 


Issue No, 4.—Meal allowance: The Wnion claims that if the workmen 
are required to work tor 4 hours after the scheduled 7 hours’ work, they 
should be paid a meal allowanee ot the rate of Re. 1 per day, besides the 
overtime wages, The Association opposed this claim. 


11 appears that worker gets annas 4 as jalpan for 7 hours’ overtime work 
and annas 2 for 34 hours’ overtime work, over and above the overtime 


my 


wages, while one Press pays annas 7 as jalpan., 


On a consideration of the matter, it is awarded that all the Presses 
should pay annas 7 as jalpan for more than 5 hours’ overtime work and 
annas 3 as jalpan for more than 3 hours’ overtime work. This will be in 
addition to the overtime allowance. 


This issue is accordingly answered. 


issue No. 5. Half holiday on Saturday: The Union claims that all the 
Presses should grant half holiday on Saturdays. In view of the hours of 
work as mentioned in Issues Nos. 1 and 2, the workers in the Presses should 
have 7 hours’ work on Saturdays as on other working days. The claim 
for half holiday on Saturday is, therefore, rejected. 


Issue No. 6.-—Puja or annual bonus: The Union claims that the work- 
men should be given one month’s pay as Puja bonus every vear immediately 
before the Pujas and in addition to the Puja bonus, two months’ wages 
shoald be paid to the workmen এল annual bonus for the year 1957-58. 
Thee is no evidence to justify this claim. The claim for one month’s 
Puja bonus as a condition of service is unworthy of support and is rejected. 
There is nothing on record to show that the workmen are entitled to two 
= wages as annual bonus for the year 1957-08. This claim is 
rejected. 


This issue is accordingly answered. 


issue No. 7.—Leave and holidays: The Wnion claims the following 
categories of leave and holidays:— 


(x) Privilege leave ... 80 days with full pay in a year, 
cumulative for 3 years. 

(hb) Cusual leave wv» 14 days with full pay in a year. 

(c) Medical leave ,.. 12 days with full pay in a year. 


The Union also claims that the workmen should be allowed all the 
holidays that are available to the offices of the Government of West Bengal. 
The Presses state that the workmen in the Presses are allowed 93 days’ 
holiday in the year und it is not possible for the Presses to grant any 
further holiday. Exhibit A is a list of holidays. This shows that various 
periods of holidays are granted throughout the year, totalling 33 days in 
the year. he Union claims for privilege leave, ৫8808] leave and medical 
leave and also for u few days’ festival holidays in preference to the 8 
days’ listed holidays us available at present. 


1324 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 19, 1959 [Parr] 


Qn a consideration of the matter, the following leave and holidays are 
allowed :— 
(1) Casual leave .. oO days in the yaor with full pay. 
(2) Sick leave ... LO days in the year on half pay on 
production of a certificate from a 
registered medical practitioner. 


(3) Privilege leave ... 14 days in a year cumulative for 3 
years. 
(4) Festival holidays **০ 12 days on full pay in the year to be 


fixed by the Presses in consulta- 
tion with the Union. 


This issue is accordingly answered. 


issue No. 8.—Cratuity: The Union claims that the workmen should he 
paid gratuity at the rate of one month’s wages for every completed yeur 
of service at the time of retirement, or otherwise termination of service. 
The claim was opposed by the Associution on grounds of financial 
incapacity. 

On a consideration of the matter, I do not find that the Presses are 
financially able to undertake the burden of paying gratuity to the workmen 
as claimed. 

This claim is rejected. This issue is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 9.—Service conditions: The Union claims that rules relating 
to security of service and termination of service should be framed and that 
the Union wil] deal with this matter in detail at the time of the hearing. 


On hearing both the parties, the following rules for security of service 
are framed :— 

(1) At the time of appointment, every employee shall be given an 
appointment letter. 

(2) No one should be dismissed for a misconduct without a proper 
enquiry by the authority concerned. Every employee against 
whom an enquiry is held should be furnished with the charges 
that are brought against him. He shall also be given an 
opportunity of defending himself at the enquiry. In such 
defence, he may take the help of another employee, who may 
be a member of the Union. 

(3) Any workman who wants to avail of a period of leave should 
submit an application to the Management praying for such 
leave. If for uny reason beyond his control, he is unable to 
apply for leave before availing of the leave, he must submit the 
application fur such leave within two days of the commence- 
ment of the period of such leave. 

(4) Any workman who will remain absent without leave from his job 
for 10 days at a stretch, shall lose his lien on his appointment, 
and shall be liable to be discharged. 


This issue is accordingly answered.

Rules regulating grant of rewards and punishments to collecting Sarkars

Commissioners, be fined to the extent of half-month’s pay if the total collec-

arrear and current. 


2. <A Collecting Surkar is neither to he fined nor to he rewarded if the 
{otal collection made by him durmg the yeur amounts to 85-90 per cent. of 
the total demand, arrear and current. 


3. Kach Collecting Sarkar shall be rewarded half-month’s pay if the 
total collection made by him during the year exceeds 90 per cent. but does 
not exceed 96 per cent, of the total demand, arrear and current, and & 
month’s pay if it is over 90 per cont.

hy the Municipal Commissioners, disputed demands, if any, and the amount 
of rates 19810 by the rate-puyers themselves into the Municipal Office, shall 
be excluded from the total demand, arrear and current.

ANNEXURE 


in the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs Karoo 
Restaurant, New Market, Calcutta.13, and their employees represented 
by Karco Workers’ Union, 4C Kalighat Road, Calcutta. (Case 
No. ۷۱۱۱ 6/58.) 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT: 
Suri 81. N. GAN, Judge, Fourth Industrial Trilunal, 
For the Umon: Shri Suprabhat Mukherjee, Advocate. 
Far the Company: Shri K. K. Moitra, Advocate. 


This industrial dispute between Messrs Karco Restaurant (hereinafter 
referred to us the company). New Market, Caleutta-13, and their employees 
represented by Karco Workers’ Union, 407 Kalighat Road, Calcutta, in 
respect of the following issues was refered to this Tribunal for adjudication, 
hy the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No, 90-I.R./ 
TR /117,-438/67, dated the 7th January 1958. 


issues 
(1) Bonus for 1956-57, 
(2) Is the dismissal of Shri Sudhir Dey (Boy No. 11) justified? What 
relief is he entitled to? 


Beth parties filed written statements, adduced evidence, oral and 
documentary, and advanced arguments in the case. 


AWARD 


Issue No. 2. Shri Sudhir Dey (Boy No. 11) was dismissed from service 
دہ‎ u charge of misconduct by a letter, dated 2910) November 1957. Shri 
Dey denied the charges, and the Union, of which he was a member, toak 
up his cause and negotiated for a settlement. The Union's case is that 


1372 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 26, 1959 [Parr I 
2:25 


his dismissal was arbitrary and an act of victimisation and unfair labour 
٣٥٠٠٠۷٠۶ and, accordingly, Shri Dey is entitled to reiustatement. The 
company contests, Its case is that Shri Dey was a temporary hand, and 
his work was unsatisfactory for which he was warned on several occasions. 
Gu a complaint of tampering with the attendance register, by drawing 
bogus pictures on it, Shri Dey was churge-sheeted on llth November 1957, 
to which he submitted a written explanation. Meanwhile, the page with 
the objectionale drawing on it was torn from the nattendence regiater. 
Afler an elaborate enquiry on 22nd November 1957, which Shri Dey 
atleuded, he was dismissed by a letter, dated 25th November 1957. 1১, W. 1 
te Shri Sudhir Ch. Dey. He deposed in support of hia case. ©. .۶ط‎ W. ہا‎ 
Shri Nirode Chowdhury and 0. P. 9৬. 2., Shri Nirode Sen, proved that 
there was an enquiry into the charges made against Shri Dey, and that 
Shri Dey was ا‎ Ps of it. Exhibit 1 is the charge-sheet, and Exhibit I(a) 
is the reply. Exhibit 2 is the letter of dismissal. Exhibit C is the 
attendance register. Exhibit FE is the enquiry proceedings. I have 
consiflered the evidence. There is no evidence to show that Shri Dey was 
victimised for his Union activities. O. P. W. 1, Shri Chowdhury, held an 
elaborate enquiry in the presence of Shri Dey, and allowed him sufficient 
91190111101 of stating hia case and of adducing his evidence and to cross- 
examine the witnesses on the Management side. Shri Dey after having 
refused to avail of that opportunity cannot now turn round and say that 
the principles of natural justice were denied to him in this case. I am 
aatisfied from the evidence that there was no denial of natural justice to 
Shri Dey, and that his dismissal from service was not actuated by any 
ulterior motive. The dismissal of Shri Dey, in the circumstances of this 
case, appears justified. He is not entitled to any relief in this case, 


issue No. 1: It relates to a claim for bonus at the rate of one month’s 
wages, including allowances, for the year 1956-457. The compony contests 
this claim and contends that it earned a very small profit in the year in 
uestion, -and suffered losses in the two previous years. The next profit 
oes not justify any pryment of bonus, The company has no avuilable 
surplus under the Full Bench Formula af the Labour Appellate Tribunal in 
the case of Rombay Mill Owners’ Association, P. W. 2, Shri Saroj 
Chatterjee, on behalf of the Wnion and 0. P. W. 3, Shri Arun Kumar Dey, 
on behalf of the Company deposed on this issue. The audited balance- 
sheet and profit and loas accounts, a consolidated one, for the three yeara 
ending March, 1954, 1956 and 1957 have been marked Exhibit K, and the 
calculation of the available surplua under the Full Bench formula filed جا‎ 
the company ia Exhibit K(1). The profit and loss account for the year 
under reference shows a net profit of Rs, 975-5-3 only. The Tnion contends 
that the balance-sheets and the profit and loss accounts were drawn up only 
to defeat the workmen’s claim for bonus and do not represent the correct 
financial position of the company. It is in evidence of Shri Arun Dev, 
Acceuntant, that the proprietor of this Company (it is a proprietorship 
concern) invested Ra, 13,000 only as capital in the year 1950 when he 
started this business. It was in the last year that there won some expansion 
of the business. This capital was not shown in the company’s acrounta, 
and on the advice of the income-tax authorities it was shown in the vear 
under reference and the corrosponding capital expenditure under thde 
heading ‘‘Furniture’’ of Rs, 14,5887 waa 8180 shown in that year as a 
part of the assets of the business. The TWnion contests that this was highly 
irregular and was done to defeat the present claim after refusal to submit 
proper accounts to the Commercial Accountant of the Labour Directorate 
wn the conciliation proceedings. The dispute over honus was ৭1111 in the 
conciliation proceedings hefore the Conciliation Officer on 19th-September

examined by the Commercial Accountant of the suid Directorate when final

issue No. 8: This issue is not pressed for adjudication as the workman

As to the remaining seven issues, the 01000990518 contention is that the

by section 19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act. Py sie Sy the reference

change of cirrumafances was either pleaded or proved in support of this 
case for fresh demand. The company contests that the issues are barred 
hy the principles of res-gudicata. Shri P, R. Mukherjee, appearing on 
behalf of the company, relied on a decision of Punjab High Court, in the 
Punjab Distilling Industries, Ltd. and Industrial Tribunal, Punjab and 
others, reported in 1858, .ا ,ا‎ J. II, p. 109, and contended that if the 
disputes referred for adjudication were subject-matter of the prior award 
in force hetween the parties, them the reference of the same dispute would 
be illegal, He also relied on a decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 
Burn & Co. Ltd. and their emplovees reported in 1947, I. 1, J. I, p. 226, 
and pointed out that since the Union had not endeavoured to plead or 
prove any change in circumstanees since the Jast award, the findings of 
that award operated as res-judicata in the present case. Shri Suprabhat 
Muhherjee for the Union refuted the arguments by saying that the charter 
of demands, Ext. 1, submitted ١ the Management on the 20th May 1957, 
amounted to a notice, in writing, terminating the previous award, and 
since this reference was made more than two months from that date, the 
previous award must be taken to be of no legal effect. In my opinion. 
this contention ia fallacinus, and cannot he accepted. The charter of 
demands contains a liat of «laims made on behalf of the employees upon the 
Management for improved conditions of service and higher wages, ete. 

Ha can never be trented ۸× notice contemplated in section 19(6) of the 
Tndustrial Disputes Act. Such notice should be in writing and must 
clearly indicate the mteution of the party to terminate the award, T am 
afraid, T am to hold that this reference relating to issues covered by the 
previous award of 1950 between the parties is illegal and invalid. Accord. 
ingly, this Tribunal is not competent to adjudicate upon those issues.

The issues contained in the award of 1950 were published in the Calcutta 
Gazette, dated 22nd November 1050. Section 19 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act was amended by Act 48 of 1950 on the 20th May 1950. The amended 
~ection came into operation when the said award was still in force, The 
applicability of section 19(6) to that award cannot be challenged, That 
award contained 11 issues including seales of pay, gratuity, provident fund, 
leave und holidays and restoration of Khoraki. Though slightly differently 
worded in places the issues of annual increment, retiring benefits, leave 
and holidays and free meal appear to be the same as in the award of 1950.

circumstances on which the previous nward was based since the date of 
that award. Therefore, in any case, the reopening of the issue does not 
arise. The parties must remain satisfied under that award. 


Overtime (Issue No, 3): Overtime was claimed at double the rate of 
ordinary wages. DP, W. 2, Shri Baijnath, a mistry in the service of this

Medical facilities (Issue No. 5): ©. 1). W. 1, Mr. Martin, said that 
the company offered medical facilities to employees who were seriously ill. 
He voncluded his deposition here by saying that if really the employees 
were 1]], he would certainly offer medical farilities to them. In Ext. 1, 
the Union asked for medical facilities, e.g., cost of medicine. The company 
agrees, The company will grant medical facilities to its emplovees falling 
sick, including cost of medicine, 


Rest (issue No. 4): The demand is for half-an-hour rest for the 
workers during the duty hours from 6-30 a.m. to 2 p.m. There iw no 
evidence before this Tribunal to show that the workers have to do work 
continuously without any break for more than six hours at a stretch. I 
cannot assume that all the workers work under heavy pressure and do not 
get any time for rest. I believe that the Management would not grudge the 
workers short rest if they do not get it at present,

৪৭ the Management was justified in dismissing Shri Niranjan 
.سس0‎ 
To what relief is he entitled? 
AWARD 


This 1s a case arising out of alleged illegal and unjustified dismissal of 
one Shri Niranjun Saha, previously employed in Messrs. Gokulrhand 
Gajadhar, 38 Cotton Street, Caleutta-7. hereinafter described as the com- 
pany for the sake of brevity. 


Pant ] | THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 26, 1959 1381 
৮ "পপ 


109 case of the Union 1s that the aforesaid workman served this com- 
pony for the last 17) 5৬77৮ and bad an unblemished recoid of service. The 
age of the workman 18 66 and as such the Management terminated the 
service with effect from 20th June 1957 without any previous notice or notice 
pay or gratuity or retirement benefit. The Company, therefore, ignored 
all principles of natural justice and disminsed iim most illegally. The 
Union therefore seeks his reinstatement with compensation, 


The Company, on the other hand, justifies the termination of service vf 
this workman as he is aged about 70 years und he is physically unable to 
do any work. The workman was absent on and from 3146 May 1967 and it 
was ascertained on enquiry that he was ill and could not work. The Union 
took up his cause and 11 was decided at 2 conference at the Labour Direc- 
torate that the workmun would be reinstated. The workman, however, 
accordingly came to the company but did not join his work and gave out 
that he would be satisfied if he was paid Rs. 100 as retrenchment compen- 
sation as he could not work due to ill health. Accordingly, Shri Saha 
received an amount of Ra. 100 and accordingly a receipt was granted by him 
and thin relinquished his further claim to remstatement. The company 
therefore contends that there is an end of the Union’s case. 


Admittedly there was a memorandum of settlement through the Con- 
ethation Officer, The memorandum of settlement is marked Ext. 3 and 
dated 17th August 1957, The terms of agreement are as follows: ‘It is 
agreed that the Management shall reimetate Shri Niranjan Saha in hia 
service, He shall be paid 14 days’ wages for the period he remained out of 
employment”, If the terms of agreement were given effect to by the com- 
pany there would have been an end of the matter. Now it is to be investi- 
gated why the terms of agreement were not given effect to and who is 
responsible for it. In this ease I have had the advantage of closely observ- 
ing the workmau concerned who seemed to me to be nearing 70 and 
appeared to have had sparms of asthma while giving his deposition in Court. 
I therefore find that there is truth in the allegation of the company that the 
workman could not rejoin due to ill health in pursuance of the agreement. 
The company obviously, as it appears to me, took advantage of the illness 
and physica] mability of the workman to resume work and tried to get rid 
of him by making some payment. It is the version of the company that 
Rs. 100 was paid on the basis of receipt Ext. A, dated 30th August 1957. 
The workman, on the other hand, denies to have received Rs. 100 as 
acknowledged in the receipt. The workman accordingly made a complaint 
Ext. 4, dated 30th Bhadra 1365 (0161) September 1958). The evidence on 
the mde of the company also as regards payment is materially discrepant. 
Shri Madhusudan Pal, 0.P.W. 1, says that Rs. 80 was paid m ten rupee 
notes while the receipt was taken from the workman. O.P.W. 2, Shri 
Bholanath Tapadar, on the other hand, says that he saw the payment of 
Re. 100 under the receipt. So the evidence regarding payment of Rs. 100 
under the receipt is wholly unreliable and there is no consistent story in 
regard to payment. The sumtotal of the evidence however convinced the 
Court that the workman due to continued 11] health agreed to relinquish his 
claim if he were paid Ra. 100 and this is consistent with the receipt he 
admittedly granted for Rs. 100. 


Reinstatement is out of the question as he cannot physically work and 
the workman does not seem {to presa for it os he says that he would be 
driven out by the company again if he is reinstafed. As the workman him- 
self. T am convinced, agreed to accept Re. 100 and give up his other claims 


1382 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 26, 1959 [Parr | 
ern a a me a ee en سے ےت تج‎ a eC ارہ سد سے سس سے سے‎ ale 
ugainst the company, the sum of Rs. 100 may be paid by the company to 
the workman as agreed to by him. The termination ot service of the work- 
man is therefore found justified due to continued ill health and as such he is 
not entitled to retrenchment benefit under the Act (tide 1964 L.1.J., Vol. 
IT, page 637, Imperial Tobacco Co, of India & Ikthiraj’s) und the company 
Is directed to pay Rs. 100 to the workman as previously agreed to by him 
within a month of the publication of this award. 


This is my award.

4, Short recital of the dtspute: 

The issue ‘“‘whether the enforced idleness of the workers for five days in 
a week as per notice of the Management, dated the 16th November 1957, 
wus justified’’ was referred to the Second Labour Court for adjudication 
under G.O, No, 2546-1.R./1R/10L-123/57, dated the 18th June 1968. 
The parties held a series of bipartite negotiations and with the good offices 
of the Engineering Association of India of which the company abovenamed 
15 a member, a settlement has now been reached. 


1384 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 26, 1959 [Parr I 


The terms of the settlement are as under: — 


(1) It is agreed that all the present workers, who have been laid off 
for 6 days in a week on and trom the 18th November 1957, will 
be paid compensation at the rate of 18 per cent. of the lay-off 
days’ wages, after deducting the days on which the workers 
were absent, or on sick leave ur on stututory leave or on any 
other leave and the days for which lay-off compensation had 
already been paid in full. The Management agree to start 
work immediately but in view of the non-availability of raw 
materials and other trade reasons, the present workmen will be 
provided with the work sectionwise «as per the following 
schedule: 


(i) Machine Shop, Stores and godown—Frow 10th February 1959. 
(ii) Press Shop—From 20th February 1959. 

(iii) Assembly and Soldering—Fiom 2ud March 1959. 

(iv) Painting section—From 5th March 1959. 

(v) Final fittng—From 7th March 1959. 


(2) Having regard to the request made by the Union the Management 
agree that the lay-off compensation paid to the workmen us per 
this Agreement will not be set off against the compensution 
payable for any retrenchment within the period of 12 months 
from the date of this Agreement. 


(3) It is agreed by the workers that they will have no objection to 
undertake any alternative work that may be provided by the 
Management in the event of their deciding to curtail production 
on lanterns. 


(4) It is further agreed that the parties will file a joint petition before 
the learned Labour Court for passing an award in terms of the 
settlement. 

(5) The Union agree to maintain industrial peace and not to raise any 
demand involving financial liability on the company for a 
period of one year.

AWARD 


This is an application under section 338A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act against Messrs. Dutson Engineering Corporation Private Ltd., herein- 
after described as the company for the sake of brevity. 


The applicant states that he is a permanent employee of the company 
and the company suspended him from 815 March 1958 without any ground. 
‘The company did not pay him any wages. The applicant therefore-prays 
for a direction that the company do reinstate him and pay him wages in 
full for the period of idleness. 


1386 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 28, 1959 = [Varr J 
১০০০০০১১020 ১১১১2০১১১১2 سس‎ 


The company put in a written statement contending, anter alia, that 
on 29th March 1958 the applicant workman assaulted his colleague Shri 
Rabindra Nath Kundu aud on prelimmary investigation he was placed 
under suspension as a measure of security and on due enquiry he was 
found guilty of the charge framed against him. 


The company further contends ‘that the workman is not conneocled with 
the dispute pending agaist 8 others workmen, nor is the subject-matter 
of that dispute in any way connected with the one forming the subject- 
matter of this application. 


Twenty-third February 1959 waa the date fixed for hearing of the 
application. On this date the applicant is absent nor was any step taken 
on his behalf. So it is presumed that no dispute is pending at the present 
moment. Besides that, it is represented to me by Shri’ Panchanan Bhatta- 
charyya, President of the Union of the workmen of the company, that 
the applicant has since got a job elsewhere and will not proceed with the 
case. Thus a “no-dispute’ award is passed in this case. 


This is my award.

AWARD 


This is an application by Shri Dulal Chandra Das under section ۸ 
of the Industrial Disputes Act against Messrs. Dutson Engineering Cor- 
poration Private J.td., hereinafter described as the company for the sake 
of brevity. 

The applicant states that he is a permanent employee of the company 
which suspended him without any ground or reason whatsoever with effect 
from 3lat March 1958 and that he was later on informed on 9th July 1958 
that he was dismissed retrospectively. 


The applicant prays for a direction on the company to reinstate him 
with full wages for the entire period of his idleness. 


The company in its written statement denies applicant’s allegations 
and alleges that the applicant picked up a quarrel with his colleague 
Shri Rabindrau Nath Kundu and abused him and struck Lim with a rod 
causing injury. On preliminary investigation the company suspended him 
and later on the applicant was found guilty of the charge framed against 
him and gave him un opportunity to offer upology of which he did not avail 
himself. It is further contended that the inatant dispute has got no 
connectiun with the main dispute pending. 


Twenty-third February 1959 was fixed for hearing this application. On 
this date the workman did not appear, nor take any steps. Presumably 
there is no dispute pending at the moment. Moreover, it is represented by 
Shri Panchanan Bhattacharjee, the President of the Union of the workmen 
of the company, that the applicant has since got a job elsewhere and will 
nol proceed with the dispute. 


So a “‘no-dispute’’ award is made in this case. 
This is my award.

The order of reference relates to 34 workmen who are claimed by the 
Union’ to be doing clerical work. These 34 workmen are mentioned in a 
list attached to the order of reference. According to the Union, the work- 
men Nos. 1 to 20 in the list are doing clerical jobs and have been designated 
as clerks, but the other 14 workmen, being from Nos. 21 to 34, are doing 
clerical work, but have been designated as Helpers. It is the Union's case 
that workmen Nos. 1 to 20 کہ‎ the list are nat being given the clerical grades 
fixed by the First Omnibus Cotton Textile Tribunal, but are paid much leas 
basic pay and their basic calaries were not fixed according to the award of 
the Tribunal in 1948, when the award of the Tribunal was published and 
enforced on the company. The union further states that workmen Noa. 21 
to 34 are being paid as manual workers, although they are duing clerical 
jobs. In the written statement, the Union stated that, inasmuch as, the 
Company had revised the basic wages of 7 workmen, being Nos. 5 to 11 
of the“list, no relief was claimed by the Unien on their behalf im this 
proceeding. At the time of the hearing, the Union adduced no evidence on 
behalf of workmen Nos. 1 to 4 and 12 to 20, although in the written 
statement, it detailed claims for fixation of their basic salary accordmg to 
the First Omnibus Cotton Textile Award, and also made a claim for 
recnyery of loss in wages incurred by them till the date of the filing of 
the written statement on account of the company’s failure and negligence 
an fixing their basic salaries in accordance with the terms of the First 
Cotton Textile Tribunal Award. I learnt at the time of the hearing that 
the basic salaries of these workmen, being Nos. 1 to 4 and Nos. 12 to 20, 
have heen adequately fixed and the Union bad no claims to make fr them 
in the present proceeding. It is, therefore, clear that in the present pro- 
ceeding, no relief is pressed on behalf of the workmen Nos. 1 to 20, as their 


۸ 1] THE CATCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 26, 1959 1307 


claims have been satisfied amicably by the company partly before the filmg 
of the written statement by the Union, and purtly betore the commencement 
of the hearing of the case, 


The Tribunal is now concerned with the case of 14 workmen, being 
those from Nos, 21 to 34. It is also admitted by both the parties that out 
of these 14 workmen, No, 23 Shri Nirmal Chatterji, No. 28 Shri Panchu 
Gopal Ruy, Nu. ۹80 Shri Gora Chand Saha and No. 32 Shri Bidhu Bhusan 
De had left the service of the company. No relief is, therefore, claamed 
oy the Union on their behalf 


The company, In its written statement, opposed the claim of the Union. 
It states as follows: 


The First Cotton Textile Tribunal Award was passed in 1948, with a 
period of operation of one year fiom the date of enforcement of the ××. 
The award expired after one vear and the henefits flowing thereform were 
recoverable by a civil suit or under the Payment of Wages Act and not by a 
fresh order of reference. The Government of West Bengal, by an order of 
reference, dated 12th September 1956, referred certain industria] disputes to 
this Tribunal between the Cotton Textile Industry of West Bengal as 
employera, in which this employer and their workmen were included. The 
grades of clerical staff and scales of wages to be fixed for them and the 
method of fitting in the said scales were the subject-matter of adjudication 
before the suid Tribunal. In view thereof, the present reference whether 
the employees should be fitted in the scales of wages prescribed by the 
First Cotton Textile Tribunal] Award for the clerical ajaff is not maintain- 
able. The reference is, therefore, not valid in law and is inoperative. The 
Firat Cotton Textile Tribunal Award of 1948 did not provide therein that the 
workmen mentioned in the list attached to the present order of reference 
were members of the clerical ataff. The employees mentioned in the 
atiached list had no rights conferred by the said award to be reckoned 
as clerks or to he entitled to the 83169 meant for clerks. In view thereof, 
no question of applicability of the scales of wages awarded tor cJ-.ical staff, 
or payment of any difference between the awarded rates and the present 
rates of wages does arise. Employees mentioned in the attached list to 
the order of reference from Nox. 1 to 34 are all workmen doing manual work 
and all the workers who were in service in 1948, have been paid wages as 
prescribed hy the First Cotton Textile Award, and on the expiry of the 
award after one year their wages were not reduced. The applicability of 
the award or implementation of the same in cases of employees who were 
employed after the expiry of the award is not contemplated under the law 
and their claim under the award is not maintainable. The workers 
mentioned in the list are 01] manual workers and helong to the categories of 
unskilled or semi-skilled labour. It ts denied that they discharged any 
clerical duties or that they were recruited as members of the clerical staff. 
The workmen Nos, 31 and 32 are employees in the category of Telper 
Bearer in the Medical Department. The employer denies the liability for 
inclusion of the employees in the grade of clerical staff, or tor application 
of the scales of wages meant for clerical staff to the said employees, or for 
payment of any difference between the rates of wages in the scales meant 
for clerical staff and the rates at which they are paid, and submits that the 
rights flowing from the award were alive only for one year in respect of hose 
who were in employment prior te the award or subsequent thereto within 
the period of operation রী have been extinguished on expiry thereof,

Issue No. 2: The plea of the company that the benefits conferred by 
the First Cotton Textile Tribunal Award, which was made in 1948, could 
not be availed of by the workmen after the expiry of the period of operation 
of that award was opposed by the learned Advocate tor the Union. It 
appears that the First Cotton Textile Tribunal Award was published on 2181 
August 1948, and was made effective for one vear from Ist August 1948. 
It was argued by the learned Advocate for the company that the period of 
operation of the First Cotton Textile Award expired on 9171 July 1949, 
and the benefits conferred by that award could not be availed of by the 
workmen after that date. This claim is not supported by the decision of 
the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Messrs. Burn & Co. 1410.) reported 
in 1966 T,.A.C., 799. The Hon'ble Court decided that an adjudication did 
not lose its force when ا1‎ was repudiated under section 19(6) of the Act 
and approved of the decision of the Hon'ble Iabour Appellate Tribunal in 
the case of the Army & Navy Stores Ltd., Bombay, and their workmen, 
1991 (11) L.L.J., 31, and Ford Motor Car Co. of India [td. and their 
workmen, 1951 (IT) L.L.J., 231. In the cuses of the Hon’ble Labour 
Appellate Tribunal mentioned above, it was decided that awards made in 
January 1948 and May 1948, were to continue to be effective even beyond 
the period of their operation, unless there was o change of circumstances 
on which they were based. The same is the opinion of the Hon'ble High 
Court at Bombay as enunciated in the case of Mangaldas Naraindas, reported 
in 1947 (11) L.L.J., 2596, where it is stuted that the termination of the 
award has not the effect of extinguishing the rights flowing therefrom. It 
is stated that the effect of termination of the award is only to prevent 
enforcement of the application under the award in the manner prescribed, 
but the rights and obligations which flow from the awards ure not wiped 
out. The same is the opinion of the Hon'ble Kerala [Ligh Court as expressed 
in the case of Kumarswamy, reported in 1958 (01) L.4..d., 72. It is, 
therefore, clear that the termination of the First (Cotton Textile Award by 
eftux of time did not wipe out the rights flowing therefrom. It appears 
that another (imnibus reference between the Cotton Textile Industry in 
West Bengal and their workmen, in which the present company and their 
workmen are parties, was pending before the First Industrial Tribunal on 
the date of the present reference and an award in the second Omnibus 
reference hay heen already published on 10th June 1958. [1 is argued by 
the learned Advocate for the Company that as the First Cotton Textile 
Tribunal Award has been superseded hy the Second Cotton Textile Tribunal 
Award published on 10th June 1958, there oan be no reference for fixation 
of the wages of any workmen of the company into the scales fixed by the 
first award, as the parties are bound by the second award ut the present time. 
This question need not be answered, in view of the facts enumerated above, 
viz., that the company has already amicably settled the case of the clerical 
staff Nos. 1 to 20, who were alleged by the Union to have been designated 
as clerks, hut were not given the wage scules awarded by the First Cotton 
Textile Tribunal Award. The issue hus since been amended by thé appro- 
priate Government and it has been added as to whether the employees 
should be fitted into any other scale of wages considered suitable by the

Tribuaal. This amendment was avsailed by ihe learned Advocate for the 
Company on the ground that 1 was ultra rirea of the Government to do so, 
in view of the decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the ease of State 
of Bihar vs. D. N. Ganguli and others, usually known as the Bata Shoe Co. 
Case, reported in 1958 (11) L.L.J., 634. This decision of the Hon’ble Court 
has no application in the present case. The decision only enunciates the 
doctrine that under section 21 of the General Cluuses Act, the appropriate 
(Giovernment has no powers to rescind or cuncel an order of reference. In 
the present case, the amendment of the issue of the order of reference has 
not the effect of rescinding or cancelling the order of reference. This 
amendment is mate under section 21 of the (Gieneral Clauses Act. The 
decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court clearly states that in the present 
case, the Hon'ble Court was not considering the powers of the Government 
(0 amend or add to a reference made under section 1001) of the Act. The 
Government bas the clear jurisdiction under section 21 of the (General 
Clauses Act to add to or amend a reference inade by it under section 10(1) 
of the Act. That being so, the Tribunal is entitled to consider the fitting 
in of the wage of the employees under reference into any scales, whether 
of the First Cotton Textile Tribunal Award, or any other scales including 
that awarded by the Second Omnibus Cotton Textile Tribunal. 


জল) 


Under section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code the Civil Court is entitled 
to take notice of subsequent events, although it is not bound to do so and 
may decide the case on the facts existing on the date of the institution of 
the suit (vide A.I.R. 1951, Assam, 103). In the same way, in exercise of 
its inherent powers to do justice between the parties, the Tribunal can 
decide the case on the facts existing on the date of the reference. The 
Second Cotton Textile Award was made several months after the date of 
the reference. 


In the present case, however, the only question that arises for decision 
will be whether the workers Nos. 21 to 34, who are alleged to be doing 
clerical duties, really do such duties and if they should be fitted into any 
scale of wages as awarded by the First Textile Tribunal or any other scales, 
as considered proper by the Tribunal. I do not consider that there is any 
incompetency in the order of reference, or that the company has succeeded 
in showing that the order of reference is not maintainable in law in any 
way. This issue in accordingly anawered.

MINISTRY OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
NOTIFICATION 
New Delhi, the 7th October 1958 
G.S.R. 945.—In exercise of the powers conferred 0 section 8 of the 


Cinematograph Act, 1952 (87 of 1952), the Central Government hereby 
makes the following rules, namely :— 


THE CINEMATOGRAPH (CENSORSHIP) RULES, 1958 


1. Short title and commencement.—(1) These rules may be called the 
Cinematograph (Censorship) Rules, 8۰. 


(2) They shall come into force on the 14th day of October, 1958. 


2. Definitions.—In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires,— 
(i) ‘Act’ means the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (87 of 1952); 


(ii) ‘Advisory Panel’ means the Advisory Panel of the Board consti- 
tuted under rule 8; 

(iii) ‘Applicant’ means a person applying for a film to be certified for 
public exhibition; 

(iv) ‘Assistant Regional Officer’ means an Assistant Regional Officer 
— under rule 10 and includes the Secretary to the 
Chairman; 

(v) ‘Board’ means the Board of Film Censors constituted under section 
3 of the Act; 
(vi) ‘Bombay film’ means any film other than a Culcutta or Madras 
m; 

(vii) ‘Calcutta film’ means a film imported from abroad into, or produced 
in, the States of West Bengal, Bihar, Orissa or Assam or the 
Union territory of Manipur or Tripura or the Andaman and 
Nicobar Islanda; 

(viii) ‘Chairman’ means the Chairman of the Board;

(ix) ‘Madras film’ means a film imported from abroad into, or projuced 
in, the States of Madras, Andhra Pradesh, Mysore or Kerifla or 
the State of Pondicherry or the Union territory of Laccadive, 
Minicoy and Amindivi Islands; 

(x) ‘Regional Officer’ means the Regional Officer appointed under rule 
সপ an Additional Regionul Officer appointed under 
that rule; 


(xi) ‘Schedule’ means the Schedule to these rules. 


3. Constitution of the Board.—The Board of Film Censors constituted 
under section 3 of the Act shall be known os the Central Board of Film 
Censors, and shall consist of a Chairman and six other members ںا‎ be 
appointed by the Central Government. 


4. Terms of Offioe.—(1) A member of the Board shall hold 90106 
during the pleasure of the Central Government. 


(2) Subject to the provisions of sub-rule (1), every such member shal! 
hold office for a term of three years: 


Provided that any person holding office as 0 member of the Board 
immediately before the commencement of these rules shall hold such office 
only for the remainder of the term for which he was appointed, 


(3) A retiring member or a member whose term of office has expired 
by efflux of time shall be eligible for re-appointment. 


5h. Gasual vacancy.—A casual vacancy caused in the Board by resigna- 
tion, death or removal of a member, or otherwise, shall be filled by the 
appointment of another member who shall hold office for the remainder of 
the term of the member in whose place he is appointed. 


6. Weadquarters.—Uuless otherwise directed by the Central Govern- 
ment, the headquarters of the Board shall be at Bombay. 


7. Temporary absence of Chairman.—Notwithstanding anything con- 
tained in these rules, during the absence of the Chairman from the city of 
Bombay or whenever the Chairman is temporarily unable to exercise his 
powers or perform his duties under these rules owing to illness or any other 
কঃ the Central Government may appoint another person to be the 
Chairman : 


Provided that where no such appointment is made, the Regional Officer 
at Bombay shall, in addition to his other duties, exercise the powers and 
perform the duties of the Chairman, and shall have the right to participate 
in meetings of the Board, but shall not be entitled to preside at any such 
meetings. 


8. Constitution of Advisory Panels.—(1) The Central Government 
shall constitute an Advisory panel at euch of the towns of Bombay, Calcutta 
and Madras and at such other places as the Central Government may con- 
sider necessary. 


(2) An Advisory Panel constituted under sub-rule (1) shall consist of 
such number of members as the Central Government may, after consultation 
with the Board, determine. 


(3) The Central Government may, after consultation withthe Board,

(2) Every member of the Board other than the Chairman and every non-

14. Meetings of the Board.—(1) The Board shal] ordinarily meet once 
a quarter for the transaction of business, hut the Chairman may at any 
time call an extraordinary meeting if he considers it necessary to do. 


(2) Meetings of the Board shall be held at such places as the Chairman 
in his discretion may fix for the purpose. 


15. Co-opted Members.—The Chairman may co-opt any one or more 
of the Regional Officers as a member or as members of the Board for the 
purpose of attending a particular meeting of the Board, and such officer 
or officers shall then be entitled to participate in the deliberations of the 
Board at that meeting but shal] not be entitled to vote. 


16. Notice of meeting.—(1) At least seven clear days’ notice of all 
meetings_of the Board shall be given to each member, but an urgent meet- 
ing may be called by the Chairman at three clear days’ notice. 


(2) The notice shall state the busineas to be transacted at the meeting 
and no business other than that stated shall be transacted at such meeting 
except with the consent of the Chairman or on his motion. 


17. Business ordinarily to be transacted at meetings.—The business of 
the Board shall ordinarily be transacted at a meeting duly called in acco:d- 
ance with the provisions of these rules: 


Provided that the Chuirman may, if he thinks fit, circulate any urgent 
matter among the members for their opinion. 


18. Quorum.—At every meeting of the Board three members if the 
Chairman be present and five members if he be absent, shall form a quorum. 


19. President of the meeting.— Meetings of the Board shall be presided 
over by the Chairman or, in his absence by a member elected by the members 
present from among themselves. 


20. Question to be decided by majority of votes.—Every question 
before the Board shal] be decided by a majority of votes and in the case of 
equality of votes, the Chairman or the member elected to preside under rule 
19, as the case may be, shall have a second or casting vote. 


21. Board etc. may function notwithstanding vacancies.—The Board 
or any Advisory Panel may exercise its functions notwithstanding any 
vacancy therein, and no act or proceeding of the Board or the Advisory 
Panel shall be called in question on the ground merely of the existence of 
any vacancy in the Board or the Advisory Panel, as the case may be.

26. Issue of certificate subject to removal of portions of film.—(1) 
Where the applicant 1s informed by a Regional Officer or the Chairman that 
a film will not be certified for unrestricted publie exhibition or for public 
exhibition restricted to adults, as the case may be, unless 2 specified portion 
or portions thereof be removed from the film the Regional Officer may, with 
the approval of the Chairman, issue a certificate certifying the film for 
unrestricted public exhibition or for public exhibition restricted to adults, 
as the case may be, if he is satisfied on a declaration made in writing by the 
applicant that the portion or portions objected to have been deleted from 
the film and from all copies thereof in the applicant’s possession and 
surrendered to him. The portion or portions of the film and of all copies 
thereof so surrendered shall be preserved for a period of three months and 
thereafter dsteroyed : 


Provided that single excisions exceeding seventy-five feet in Jength shall 
be preserved for a period of six months before they are destroyed. 


Explanation.—For the purpose of satisfying himself that the portion or 
portions objected to have been deleted, the Regional Officer or the Chairman 
may, atthe expense of the applicant, himself examine the film, or cause it to 
be examined by one or more members of the Advisory Panel at such time and 
place as he may determine. 


(2) A certificute issued under sub-rule (1) shall be endorsed with a 
specification of the pertion or portions required to be removed and a state- 
ment of the exact length of each part or parts removed, and shall bear ৪ 
clearly visible triangle drawn at the left hand bottom corner of the certificate. 


(3) Where any film has been granted a certificate under this rule subject

portion or portions In any such copy.

83. Re-examination of certified films.—(1) In the case of a film which 
has been certified for public exhibition, if a representation is received from 
any member of the Bourd or any of its Advisory Panels, the representation 
shall be considered by the Board as soon as convement. Any representation 
received from a member of the public or from any association or group of 
individuals shall be examined by the Chairman und, if he considers 11 
desirable, shall be laid before the Board for consideration. 


(2) Where the Board considers that the film should be re-examined or 
where the Central Government directa the Board to arrange for the re- 
examination of a certified film, the Chairman shall appoint o Reviewing 
Committee to re-examine the film, consisting of the Chairman and_ two 
members of the Board nominated by the Chairman: 


Provided that where two members of the Board ore not readily available 
to serve on the Committee, the Chairman may, in place of one such member, 
nominate a member of an Advisory Panel to the Committee. 


(3) The place, date and time of such re-examination shall be determined 
by the Chairman. 


(4) The Chairman shall forward the opinion of the Committee to thie 
Central Government who may pass such orders thereon as it deems fit. 


(5) The original applicant for the examination of the film or the person 
to whom the rights of ownership or distribution in the film have passed 
shall, on receiving written notice from or on publication of the notice in 
the Official Gazette, by the Chairman or the Central Government, as the 
case may be, arrange to deliver a copy of the certified film to the Regional 
Officer concerned within such time as may be specified in such notice for 
examination by the Reviewing Committee under sub-rule (2) or by the 
Central Government to enable it to arrive at a decision under sub-rule (4) 
or sections 0 and 6 of the Act. 


(6) No order under sub-rule (4) or under section 5 or section 6 of the 
Act shall be made to the prejudice of the applicant unless he has had an 
opportunity of representing his case.

MINISTRY OF IRRICATION AND POWER 
New Delhi, the 18th October 1958/ Asvina 26th, 1880(Saka) 
RESOLUTION 


No. 1)W.V.616(6) /58-II.—The Government of India have accepted the 
recommendations contained in Volume I of the report of the High Level 
Committee on Floods regarding the functions of the four River Commissions 
(Floods) set up under the Government of India, Ministry of Irrigation and 
Power, Resolution No. DW.V.14(9)/54, dated the 30th September 1964, 
Resolution No. DW.V.14(9)/54-(1), dated the 3lat January 1955, and 
Resolution No. DW.V.14(42)/55, dated the 30th November 1966, as amended 
from time to time and have accordingly decided that the functions of the 
snid Commissions shall hereafter be as follows :— 


(1) To examine and rétommend for approval to the Central Flood 
Contro] Board, outline master plans for flood control works of 
the river basin concerned as prepared by the States; 


(2) to advise the State Governments on technical problems pertaining 
to flood control whenever referred to them; and 


(3) to advice the Central Flood Control Board im respect of 
flood problems on which there is difference of technical opinion 
between two or more States, or between the Central Water and 
Power Commission end the State uuthorities. 


T. SIVASANKAR, Secy.

MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 
NO'LIFICATION 
New Delhi, the 5th November 1958 


2403,—I1n exercise of the powers conferred by section 17 of the‏ مم ۔ 
Standards of Weights and Measures Act, 1956 (89 of 1956), the Central‏ 
(iovernment hereby makes the following rules namely :—‏ 


1. These rules may be called the Standards of Weights and Measures 
Rules, 1958. 


2. In these rules,— 

(a) “Act’? means the Stundaids of Weights and Measures Act, 1956 (89 
of 1956); 

(b) “Director” means the J)irector, National Physical Laboratory, 
Delhi, and includes any person authorised by him ص×ا‎ this 
behalf ; 

(c) “iuternatjonal proto-types’’ means the proto-types declared to be 
the international proto-types of the metre and kilogram by the 
Conterence Generale des poids et Mesures held at Paris in 1889; 


(d) ‘Mint’? means the Mint of the Central Government either in 
Bombay or in Calcutta. 

(e) “national proto-typea”? means the proto-types of ihe metre and the 
kilogram kept in pursuance of pub-section (2) of section 3 and 
sub-section (2) of section 4 of the Act; 

(f) “‘reference standards” means the sets of standard weights specified 
in the First Schedule and supplied by the Central Government 
to State Governments in pursuance of sub-section (2) of section 
15 of the Act; 

(8) “Schedule’’ means a Schedule appended to these rules; 

(h) ‘standard weight or measure” means any unit of mass or measure 
referred to in sub-section (1) of section 18 of the Act and 
includes any integral multiple or decimal fraction of such unit 
notified in this behalf by the Central Government. 


3. (1) The national proto-type of the metre shull consist of a platinum- 
iridium bar certified in terms of the international proto-type of the metre 
by the International Buraeu of Weights and Measures. 


(2) The national proto-type of the kilogram shall consist of a platinum- 
Iridium cylinder certified rm terms of the international proto-type of the 
Kilogram by the international Bureau of Weights und Measures. 


(3) The national proto-types shall be kept in the custody of the National 
Physical Laboratory, Deihi, and the Driector shall cause them to he verified 
and certified hefore they ure deposited in the National Physical Laboratory 
and at intervals of not more than ten years thereafter. 


(4) (1) Reference standards shall be prepared at the Mint and verified 
and certified in terms of the National proto-types by the Director before 
they are supplied to State Governments and at intervals of not more than 
five years thereafter. 


(2) A set of reference stundards verified and certified by the Director 
phall be supplied free to each State Government; and, in respect of each 
subsequent verification, the State Government shall pay transport charges 
an] such verification charges as may be fixed by the Central (tovernment. 


5. Where a weight or measure purporting to be a standard weight or 
Ineasure is manufactured for being used or used, in any transaction for trade 
or commerce (hereinatter in these rules referred to as commercial weight or 
measure), the limits of error which may he tolerated in commercial weights 
and measures shall, at the time of their verification und inapection, he as 
specified in the Second Schedule.

P. N. Mooxtrzke J: These three appeals are directed against the 
declaration granted by an Election Tribunal, that a certain purliamentary 
eleotion is void. The respective appellants ure Shri Brojo Gopal Das, and 
Shri Nirmal (handra Das, two of the persons who were substituted under 
section 116 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, in place of the 
original contesting respondent betore the Tribunal, namely, Shri Biren Roy, 
who was the successful candidate at the above election, upon the lattera’ 
retirement from contest, and the said Biren Roy himself is the appellant 
in the third or the other appeul. 


The proceedings had had a chequered career before the Tribunal and 
they were lively and interesting and the questions that arose tor considera- 
tion had also their own peculiar difficulties aud interest. 


The election in question was the lust General Election of the Calcutta 
South West Parliamentary Constituency, held in March 1957, in which 
Shri Biren Roy was elected from the said constituency to the Lok Sabha 
or the House of the People. There were three cundidates (one) Biren Roy, 
(two) Asim Krishnn Dutta, and (three) Rajani Mukerjee. They, 
respectively, polled 94,944, 82,444) and 11,297 votes at the polling which 
took place on two dates, namely, the 4th and the 14th March 1957 and 
Roy was declared elected on March 20, 1957, when the results of the voting 
were announced. 


On May 3, 1957, the first two respondents of the present uppeal, namely, 
Kalipada Banerjee and Anil Kumar Sadhukhan who ‘at all material times 
were citizens of India and residents of Calcutta” within the above cousti- 
tuency and ‘‘were electors of the same und entitled to vote” at the above 
election, applied before the Election Commission, New Delsi, for » 
decluration that the above election, সি of Shri Roy was void on certain 
grounds, of which the relevant ones will be duly noticed and referred to 
in the course of this judgment. The application (petition) in which 
originally all the three candidates, the successful Roy as well as the two 
défeated candidates Dutta and Mukerjee, were made parties as respondents, 
was revistered as Election Petition No. 439 of 1957 and after the necessary 
preliminaries, if was forwarded by the Chief Election Commissioner and 
sent for Trial to Shri Bijoyesh Mukerjee, Additional District Judge, 
v4-Pargunas, who had meanwhile been constituted ithe Tribunal for the 
purpose under section 86 of the Representation of the People Act, 1961. 
That was in dune, 1957, and the first date of uppeurance of the parties 
before the Tribunal was fixed 8৭ July 18, 1957. On or before that date, 
the first {wo respondents, Roy and, Dutt, duly dppeared before the Tribunal

The controversy in the present cuse, as we have seen above, centren

ment of India or the Central Government for installation of automatic vote 
recording equipments in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha which con-

be elected to the Lok Sabha under section 100(1)(a) of the said Act. That 
was the substance of the allegation on which Roy’s election was challenged 
and on which the parties diftered and upon which the fate of the instant 
election petition depended. The Tribunal, therefore, did the right thing 
in clearing up the matter betore the resumed heazing by declaring that the 
relevant issue that is, the first part of issue No, 3, would be discussed under

we shall return to that aspect later on.

do so sertatim.
