With the above preliminary observations we proceed to consider — the 
question of Roy’s alleged statutory disqualification on the merits. That 
involves inainty construction of section 7(d) of the Representation of the 
People Act, 1951, and its application to the facts of this case. The question 
of construction in its turn mainly depends upon the meaning to be given 
to the words ‘‘share or interest’? used in the section. rina facie the words 
are wide and having regard to the purpose of the section and the mischief 
11 is intended--nand seeks—to prevent we would have been glad to take the 
words in the widest import. For our present purpose, however, it will not 
he necessary to go so fur as, even on the restricted meaning, which at least 
the words should bear on the decided authorities, this appeal upon the facts 
before us, should fail and Roy should be held to ا١‎ sufficiently disqualified 
wthin the mischief of the relevant sections or sections or statutory provisions 
so 3৭ to lose his present seat in the House of the People and this electiou 
petition should succeed. 


Provisions like section 7(d) have been a familiar feuture of election laws 
from very early times. They ure based on a sound, solemn and salutory 
piineiple which democracies or democratic conatitutions can الا‎ afford to 
apare or ignore. Their purpose is to guarantee the purity of the legislature 
and of the administrative machinery as well and it has heen variously put 
by various eminent judges and noted authorities but always with an ء٥‎ 
{0 the grantee of purity of the legislature and administration and to keep 
the source or the fountain head of Jaw and the stream of administration 
unsullied and free from corruption. The basic standpoint is ‘‘to prevent 
ennflict between interest and daty which would otherwise inevitably arise” 
[per Lindlay LJ. in Nortton va. Wilson (1889) 22. Q.B.D. 744 at p. 748] 
and to prevent the member concerned from being exposed to temptation or 
even the semblance of temptation [per Lord Graham M.R. in the same case 
Nortton va. Willson (1889) 22. (Q).B.D. 744 at p. 747] and that has never 
been questioned. It has also been authoritatively laid down that 4 
اکسج‎ interest is as much as interest as an open interest, and the court 
in such matters will always look at the substance and not at the colourable 
exterior” [per Mc.Cardic J in Evereth va. Griffiths (1924) 1.K.B. 941 at 
p. 947]. It has been ruled further that ‘‘no device to conceal the real nature 
of the transaction would prevail”? [per Lord Loveturn L.€. in North va. 
Taylor (1906) A.C. 878 at p. 380]. In that context, the word ‘‘interest’’ 
in section 7(d) may well receive a wide connotation and may well include 
even more than material interest but, for reasons which it is not necessary 
to examine now, decisions have restricted 11 to pecuniary or at the most 
material interest and that, as we shall presently see, being suftticient for 
our present purpose, any further discussion on the point of construction is 
Unnecessary.

That, in the two relevant contracts, constituted by the relative tenders

above conclusion, We are just incidentally referring to the said letter us 
even without that, the conclusion in view of our foregoing discussion would 
be the same. In that view, it is not strictly necessary to consider the 
question of privilege raised in connection with the said letter (Ext. 3) vut 
as the said question has been fully argued before us, we proceed to express 
briefly our views on the same. Privilege has been claimed by the head of 
the department which had produced the letter on subpoena from the 
Tribunal. The claim has been made by a purported affidavit which, however, 


8 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 19, 1909 


[Parr IA 


“ec ০ রাত SE 


ia not properly sworn. That defect, however, may be ignored as it has 
been by the Tribunal. The answer depends on three sections of the 
Evidence Act, namely, sections 123, 124 and 162 to quote all the relevant 
provisions on the point. So far as the present case is concerned, the 
decision would really turn on the answer to the question as to who is the 
proper authority for deciding whether a particular document relates tv 
ufluirs or matters of State so as to justify or establish a claim of privilege. 
The question of privilege has been considered by the Privy Council 
(৮৫৫০ Henry Gour Robinson vs. The State of South Australia 35 ۰ 
1121) and also by the House of Lords (vide Duncan and another vs. Cammell 
Laixa & Co., Ltd., 1942 A.C. 624) and by this court too in 13 
Talukdar vs. ید‎ ig 47 O.W.N. 928. As the law on the point has 
been codified in this country in the sections, quoted above, we would prefer 
to go by the terms of the said sections and, on the construction of the said 
terms, we respectfully agree with this court's view, as expressed in the 
cited authority (47 C.W.N. 928). We do not deem it necessary to refer 
to the other decisions on the point, e.g., Bhaiya Saheb Dajibabhan Kumbi 
rs. Pandit Ramnath Rampratap A.I.R. 1988 Nag. 358, Khawja Nazir 
Ahmad vs. Emperor A.I.R. 1944 Lah. 484 and Governor-General in 
Council vs. H. Peer Mohd. Khoda Bux and others A.I.R. 1950 E.P. 6 
and as to the case of Irwin vs. Reid reported in 1.L.R. 48 Cal. 304 which 
uppears to support the contrary opinion it is enough to say that even on 
principle on which correctly speaking it purports to proceed it is inconsistent 
with the Privy Council’s exposition of the same in Lobinson’s case 
(85 C.W.N. 1121) which is better suited to conditions in this country than 
the other exposition us given by the House of Lords (vide Duncan and 
another vs. Cammell Laird and Co., Ltd., 1942 A.C. 624). Asa matter of 
tact also Irwin’s case has been held to require modification (vide 47 C.W.N. 
al p. 934). In the above view of the law, we agree with the Tribunal جا‎ 
overruling the claim of privilege in respect of Ext. 3 in the light of the 
events which happened before the Tribunal and which have been recorded 
by it in its order No, J4 dispensing with the necessity of other evidence 
under section 162 of the Indian Evidence Act. 


We have so long studiously avoided placing any reliance on the evidefice 
of either P.W. 9 or P.W. 10 who seek to make out that Roy was the 
proprietor of the Indo German Trade Centre as in our opinion these 
witnesses do not appear to be wholly disinterested—at any rate they do nut 
seem to be quite safe or dependable witnesses. It may be argued, however, 
that at least the evidence of these two witnesses, where it is supported or 
corroborated by circumstances or other evidence, may well be accepted and 
that their statements to the above effect receive such support or corroboration 
from the exhibits to which reference has been made by us, and even the 
release or disclaimer (Ext. G) which apparently suggests the contrary muy 
be explained away by referente to and in the light of Ext. 27 and the 
attending circumstances and that Ext. 3(10) was a necessary corollary to 
Ext. 4 and does not really affect or alter that position. That may well be 
a plausible argument, particularly when Roy and Mukherjee who could and 
should have been examined by the appellunts to contradict the said state- 
ments and explain the true position if it was otherwise, were not examined 
and did not take the oaths on the witness box. We do not, however, deem 
it necessary to examine it or express any opinion on this extreme argument 
of the petitioners-respondents as on our finding already made, that Roy 
had at least a material interest in the aforesaid concern—and so in its afore- 
said two contracts even though he may not be its proprietor, section 
100(1)(a) read with section 7(d) and section 67A after Representation of 
the People Act, 1951 and Art. 102(1)(a) of the Constitution would invalidate 
his present election and the instant election petition would succeed on the 
xround of his said disqualification under the statute. 


One word before we conclude the above part of the case. We have 
freely confess drawn adverse inference against the appellants for non- 
#xamination of Roy and Mukherjee and for non-production of some 
dlocuments (which might and ought to have heen produced hy them) and 
for the abyence of any attempt on their part in that behalf. This was <0 
by us notwithstanding the fact that the Tribunal chose not to do ao, being 
of the opinion that it was unnecessary. We think however that what we 
have done is amply حم‎ in the circumstances of this 06886 by the authority 
of the Privy Council (vide Murugesam Pillai vs. Manickavasaka Pandarn and 
others 44. 1.4. 98 of 103 Gurbakash Singh vs. Gurdial Singh and another 32. 
C.W.N. 119 at p. 124 and Mussammat al Kuawar rs. Chiranji Lal 37 
LA. 1 at pp. 4-5). We may add further that the case of Bilas Kunwar vs. 
Desraj Ranjit Singh 42 I.A. 202 at pp. 206-207 does not also stand in our 
way as the relevant circumstances there were entirely different and the 
relative observations were made in a wholly different context. 


A small point was also argued before us on bebalt of the appellants 
touching the maintainability of the instant election petition on the 
allegation that it was not presented by a duly authorised person as required 
by the statute. The petitioners by Shri Ashim Krishna Iutta. The statute 
requires authority in writing for such presentation [vide section 81(2)(ii) 
of the Representation of the People Act, 1951] and there ia no such direct 
authority on the present record. Accordingly the point is taken that the 
petition was not duly presented. The petition, however, beara an endorse- 
ment of the Secretary, Election Commission, as to due authority of

Shri Dutt and due ند جا‎ and in the absence of an issue on the point 
tu which the Appellants never objested in time and for which they are os 
much responsible as anybody also in view of what is recorded in Tribunal’s 
order No. 14 and which presumably explains the lack or paucity and 
absence of direct evidence on the point particularly the full records of the 
Election Committee we think the presumption, arising from the above 
official endorsement, should be held sufficient to repel the appellants’ ৪01৮6 
argument, 

Lastly, we would refer to the present respondents’ preliminary objection 
tuken to 10055 appeal on the ground thut he ভন retired from the contest 
and having intimated to the Tribunal that he would not oppose the election 
petition, had no focus standi to file or maintain the above appeal. We do 
not think however that that objection is at all material or need be considered 
in view of the other two appeals which seek the sume relief and to which 
no such objection can be taken aud as further the appeals on our findings 
made above would fail on the merits. 


In the result then we overrule the appellants’ contentions and dismiss 
these appeals and uphold the Tribunal’s order, declaring the instant election 
of Shri Biren Roy to be void under the law. 


As to costs, however, we would take a different view from the Tribunal. 
As it is fairly clear from the records before us that the petitioners in this 
election petition have been set up by the defeated candidate Shri Ashim 
Krishna Dutt and as a large mass of unreliable oral evidence has been 
introduced in the case by the petitioners, we do not allow them any costs 
either here or in the Tribunal below notwithstanding the circumstances 
pointed out by the Tribunal in support of its award tor costs in their (the 
petitioners’) favour and we set aside the Tribunal’s said order for costs, 
directing that each party would bear his or their own costs throughout and, 
subject, as ubove, the appeals are dismissed.

NOTICE 
Calcutta, the 22nd December 1958. 


The Examination of candidates for Mukhtarship 
in mofussil courts subordinate to the High 
Court at Calcutta. 


The Examination of candidates for Mukhtarshi 
will be held on the 25th and 26th of February 1959, 
in the top floor of the Darbhanga Building of the 
University of Calcutta. 


One Paper will be set each day for Mukhtarshi 
Examination from 12 noon to 8 p.m., on the 25% 
and 26th of February 1959. 


In no circumstances, any candidate be admitted 
to the Examination after these hours. 


The candidates will be required to produce at 
the Examination Hall, the Extracts from the 
Register of Persons which will be furnished to 
them by the District Judge, on a foo 
through whom their original petitions have been 
sent to the Committee of Legal Education, High 
Court at Calcutta. 


No candidate will be allowed to enter into the 
Examination Hall with any memoranda or loose 


paper of any description (with exception of the 
sald Extract). 


All writing materials will be provided with the 
exception of pens which the candidates must 
bring with them. 


JAJNESWAR MAJUMDAR, 


Secretary, Committee of Legal 
Education, High Court, Calcutta.

BENGAL ENCINEERING COLLECE 


P.O. Botanic Carden, Howrah 


The Bengal Engineering College will open next session on July 6, 1959. 
The College, which is completely residential, prepares students for the 
B.E. Degree Examination of the Calcutta University in Civil, Mechanical, 
Electrical, Metallurgical, Mining and Tele-Communication Engineering, 
and for the Degree in Architecture (B. Arch.). Admission will be granted 
cn the resulta of an Admission Test consisting of a written examination for 
ull candidates, to be held on April 27 and 28, 1959 (and also on April 29 
for Architecture candidates), a Viva Voce and an Aptitude Test, and a 
medical examination, commencing on May 18, 1959. Applications must be 
mide in the prescribed form. The prospectus and the application form 
may be obtained from the College Office either personally or by sending an 
17512717766 Self-addressed envelope of foolscape size. A number of scholar- 
ships and stipends wil] be awarded to meritorious students on the results 
of the Admission Test. Applications will be entertained from candidates 
who have either previously passed the I.Sc. Examination or have appeared 
iu that examination this year with Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics. 
The selection of the latter category of candidates will, however, be subject 
to their passing the examination this year. Candidates must not be over 
20) years of age on January 1, 1959, but the age limit may be relaxed up to 
22 vears with the prior approval of Government in the case of deserving 
applicants belonging to the educationally backward classes and communities. 
A total of fifteen candidates may be admitted from the States in which 
there are no engineering colleges. These candidates wil] not be nominated 
ہہ‎ in previous years, but will have to apply to the Principal and appear for 
examination and interview in the ordinary way. Separate centres may be 
opened in the States, where there are no engineering colleges provided 
there is sufficient number of candidates for these centres, but such candi- 
dates who are successful at the written test will be required to appear for 

Viva Tuce aml Aptitude Test and medical examination at the R.E. College. 
Application form which will be available from the College Office from 
March 9, 1959 onwards, must reach the College Office by April 18, 1959. 


A. C. ROY, 
Crincipal, Bengal Engineering College.

BENCAL ENGINEERING COLLECE 
P.O. Botanic Garden, Howrah 


The Bengal Engineering College will open next session on July 6, 1959. 
The College, which is completely residential, prepares students for the 
13 19. Degree Examination of the Calcutta University in Civil, Mechanical, 
Electrical, Metallurgical, Mining and Tele-Communication Engineering, 
and for the Degree in Architecture (B. Arch.), Admission will be granted 
ou the results of an Admission Test consisting of u written examination for 
ull candidates, to be held on April 27 and 28, 1959 (and also on April 29 
for Architecture candidates), a 1 556 Voce and an Aptitude Test, and a 
medical examination, commencing on May 18, 1959. Applications must be 
made in the prescribed form. The prospectus and the application form 
may be obtained from the College Office either personally or by sending an 
(Tnstamped Self-addressed envelope of 16901809158 size. A number of scholar- 
ships and stipends will he awarded to meritorious students on the results 
of the Admission Test. Applications will be entertained from candidates 
who have either previously passed the 4০১০, Examination or have appeured 
in that examination this year with Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics. 
The selection of the latter category of candidates will, however, be subject 
৮) thei: passing the examination this year. Candidates must not be over 
20 years of age on January 1, 1959, but the age limit may be relaxed up to 
22 years with the prior approval of Government in the case of deserving 
upplicants belonging to the educationally backward classes and communities, 
A total of fifteen candidates may he admitted from the States in which 
there are no engineering colleges. These candidates will not be nominated 
ax in previous years, but will have to apply to the Principal and appear for 
examination and interview in the ordinary way. Sepurate centres may he 
opened in the States, where there are no engineering colleges provided 
there is 80171686786 number of candidates for these centres, but such candi- 
dates who are succeasful at the written teat will be required to appear for 
12552 Voce and Aptitude Test and medical examination at the F.E. College. 
Application form which will be available from the College Office from 
March 9, 1959 onwards, must reach the College Office by April 13, 1959.

The Bengal Engineoring College will open next session on July 6, 1959. 
The College, which is-completely residential, prepares studenta for the 
B.E. Degree Examination of the Calcutta University in Civil, Mechanical,

and for the Degree in Architecture (B. Arch.), Admission will be granted 
en the results of an Admission Test consisting of و‎ written examination {or 
ull candidates, to be held on April 27 and 28, 1959 (und also on Apri] 29 
for Architecture candidates), & Kiva Voce and an Aptitude Test, and a 
medical examination, commencing on May 18, 1959. Applications must be 
made in the prescribed form. The prospectus und the application form 
may be obtained from the College (Office either personully or by sending an 
("nstumped Self-addressed envelope of fvolsvape size. A number of scholar- 
ships und stipends will be awarded to meritorious students on the results 
of the Adinission Test. Applications will be entertuined from candidates 
who have either previously passed the I.Sc. Examination or have appeared 
in that examination this year with Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics. 
The selection of the latter category of candidates will, however, be subject 
ta their passing the examination this year. Candidates must not be over 
۱ا“‎ years of age on January 1, 1959, but the aye limit سر‎ be relaxed up to 
22 years with the prior approval of Government in the case of deserving 
appheants belonging to the educationally backward claswes and communities. 
A (10141 of fifteen candidutes muy be admitted from the Stutes in which

an 1n previous yeurs, but will have to apply to the Principal and appear for

there is sufficient number of cundidates for these centres, but such cundi- 
dates who are successful ut the written test will be required to uppeur for

PART IB—Educational Notices 


BENCAL ENCINEERING COLLECE 


P.O. Botanic Carden, Howrah 


The Bengal Engineering College will open next session on July 6, 1959. 
The College, which is completely residential, prepares students for the 
B.E. Degree Examination of the Calcutta University in Civil, Mechanical, 
Electrical, Metallurgical, Mining and Tele-Communication , Engineering, 
and for the Degree in Architecture (B. Arch.). Admission will be granted 
on the results of an Admission Test consisting of a written examination for 
ull candidates, to be held on April 27 and 28, 1959 (and also on April 29 
for Architecture candidates), a Viva Voce and an Aptitude Test, and a 
medical examination, commencing on May 18, 1959. Applications must be 
made in the prescribed form. The prospectus and the application form 
may be obtained from the College Office either personally or by sending an 
Unstamped Self-addressed envelope of foolscape sise. A number of scholar- 
ships and stipends will be awarded to meritorious students on the results 
of the Admission Test. Applications will be entertained from candidates 
who have either previously passed the I.Sc. Examination or have appeared 
iu that examination this year with Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics. 
The selection of the latter category of candidates will, however, be subject 
tu their passing the examination this year. Candidates must not be over 
20 years of age on January 1, 1959, but the age limit may be relaxed up to 
22 years with the prior approval of Government in the case of deserving 
applicants belonging to the educationally backward classes and communities. 
A total of fifteen candidates may be admitted from the States in which 
there are no engineering او پا‎ These candidates will not be nominated 
an in previous years, but will have to apply to the Principal and appear for 
examination and interview in the ordinary way. Separate centres may be 
opened in the States, where there are no engineering colleges provided 
there is sufficient number of candidates for these centres, but such candi- 
dates who are successful at the written test will be required to appear for 
Viva Voce and Aptitude Test and medical examination at the B.E. College. 
Application form which will be available from the College Office from 
March 9, 1959 onwards, must reach the College Office by April 18, 1959. 


A. 0. ROY, 
Principal, Bengal Engineering College.

BENCAL ENGINEERING COLLECE 
۳.٢. Betanic Carden, Howrah 


The Bengal Engineering College will open next session on July 6, 1959. 
The College, which is completely residential, prepures students for the 
B.E. Degree Examination of the Calcutta University in Civil, Mechanical, 
Electrical, Metallurgical, Mining and Tele-Communication Engineering, 
and for the Degree in Architecturo (B. Arch.). Admission will be granted 
cn the results of an Admission Test consisting of a written examination fur 
ull candidates, to be held on April 27 and 28, 1959 (and also on April 29 
for Architecture candidates), a Viva Voce and an Aptitude Test, and u 
medical examination, commencing on May 18, 1959. Applications must be 
made in the prescribed form. The prospectus and the application form 
دا‎ be obtained from the College Office either personally or by sending an 
Unstamped Self-addrested envelope of foolecape size. A number of scholar- 
ships and stipends will be awarded to meritorious students on the results 

-.of the Admission Test. Applications will be entertained from candidates 
who have either previously passed the I.Sc. Examination or have appeared 
iu that examination this year with Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics. 
The selection of the latter category of candidates will, however, be subject 
tu their passing the examination this year. Candidates must not be over 
20 years of age on January 1, 1969, but the age limit may be relaxed up to 
22 ‘yeors with the prior approval of Government in the case of deserving 
applicants belonging to the educationally backward classes and communities. 
A total of fifteen candidetes may be admitted from the States in which 
there are no engineering colleges. These candidates will not be nominated 
an in previous years, but will have to apply to the Principal and appear for 
examination and interview in the ordinary way. Separate centres may he 
opened in the States, where there are no engineering colleges provided 

cre is sufficient number of candidates for these centres, but such candi- 
dates who ere successful at the written test will be required to appear for 
Viva Voce and Aptitude Test and medjcal examination at the 13০19. College. 
Application form which will be available from the College Office from 
March 9, 1959 onwards, must reach the College Office by April 13, 1959. 


= eget A.C. ROY, 
Principal, Bengal Engineering College.

BENCAL ENCINEERING COLLEGE 
P.O. Botanic Garden, Howrah 


The Bengal Engineering College will open next session on July 6, 1969. 
The College, which is completely residential, prepares students for the 
B.E. Degree Examination of the Calcutta University in Civil, Mechanical, 
Electrical, Metallurgical, Mining and Tele-Communication Engineering, 
and for the Degree in Architecture (B. Arch.). Admission will be granted 
cn the results of an Admission Test consisting of a written examination for 
ull candidates, to be held on April 27 and 28, 1959 (and also on April 29 
for Architecture candidates), a Viva Voce and an Aptitude Tost, and a 
medical examination, commencing on May 18, 1959. Applications must be 
made in the prescribed form. ‘The prospectus and the application form 
may be obtained from the College Office either personally or by sending an 
Unstamped Self-addrested envelope of foolscape sise. A number of scholar- 
ships and stipends will be awarded to meritorious students on the results 
of the Admission Test. Applications will be entertained from candidates 
who have either previously passed the I.Sc. Examination or have appeared 
iu that examination this year with Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics. 
The selection of the latter category of candidates will, however, be subject 
to their passing the examination this year. Candidates must not be over 
20 years of age on January 1, 1959, but the age limit may be relaxed up to 
22 years with the prior approval of Government in the case of deserving 
applicants belonging to the educationally backward classes and communities. 
A total of fifteen candidates may be admitted from the States in which 
there are no engineering colleges. ‘These candidates will not be nominated 
an in previous years, but will have to apply to the Principal and appear for 
examination and interview in the ordinary way. Separate centres may be 
opened in the States, where there are no engineering colleges provided 
there is sufficient number of candidates for these centres, but such candi- 
dates who are successful at the written test will be required to appear for 
Viva Voce and Aptitude Test aud medical examination at the B.E. College. 
Application form which will be available from the College Office from 
March 9, 1959 onwards, must reach the College Office by April 18, 1969. 


۱ A. C. ROY, 
Principal, Bengal Engineering College.

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION, WEST BENGAL 


General instructions to candidates applying in response to 
advertisements issued by the Commission for recrult- 
ment to posts by ‘‘Selection’’. 


(1) Instructions regarding submission of application.— 
Applications are to be made on the prescribed form which 
will be available from the office the Public Service 
Commission, West Bengal, Anderson House (ground 
floor), Alipore, Caleutta-27, personally or on sending «a 
large self-addressed envelope with stamps sufficient to 
cover the postage affixed to it. Candidates who are unable 
to obtain copies of the prescribed form may apply on any 
similar typed (not handwritten) form showing exactly the 
‘wording and spacing of the same form published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette” of the lst September 1855 provided 
the blanks are filled up in tho candidates’ own handwriting. 


(2) Particulars and oertificeates required.—Candidates 
should furnish evidence of their age, qualifications and 
previous experience together with certificates written not 
more than one year prior to the date of their applications, 
ee بی سا‎ persons, testifying . their private 
character. 


(3) Fee.—Candidates must encluse with their applica- 
tions a fee of Rs. 5 (for each category of posts) in the 
form of a receipted chalan from a Government Treasury 
or the Reserve Bank of India under the head “XXXVI— 
‘Miscellaneous—Receipts of the Public Service Commission 
Weat Bengal’’. Money orders, cheques, etc., in lieu of 

Treasury chalans are not accepted. Postal orders 
liowever, may he accepted from candidates. They should 
and made س0‎ to “The Secretary, Public 
Sarvice Commission, West Bengal". No application will 
be considered unless accompanied with the requisite 
application fee. 


Candidates in Government service should make aure 
before depositing fee that their mepieesings will 
forwarded by their superior officers. In no case will the 
fee paid with the application be refunded. 


The Commission may remit fee in case of genuinely 
indigent and bona fide displaced persons from Pakistan. 


Nete.—‘‘(i) A displaced person claiming ago concession 
must furnish with his application satisfactory evidence 
that he is a bona fide displaced person from Pakistan, 
@.g-, refugee registration card or a_ certificate from a 
85660 offiver or a Member of Parliament or State 

gislature, in original. 


ii) A member of the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled 
Tribe claiming age concession must farnish with _ bis 
application a certificate in original from a gazetted officer 
or a Member of Parliament or State Legislature belonging 
to the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, specifying the 
particular caste or tribe to which he claims to belong. 


(iii) ھ‎ displaced ہد‎ seeking remission of the 
application fee must furnish besides the evidence required 
under Note (i) above a certificate (in original) from a 
District Officer or a gasctted officer or a Member of 
Parliament or State Legislature to show that he is not in 
&@ position to pay the prescribed fee.’’ 


(4) Address.—Candidates should give their present 
address and should communicate at once any subsequent 
change of address. 


(5) Ganvassing.—Any attompt on the part of candidates 
to enlist support of their applications through persons of 
influence or officiala of Government will disqualify them 
for appointment. Spontaneoux recommendations fron 
bersons tnterasted in the candidates or otherwise known 
to them will be disregarded. , 

(6) Applications from candidates who are in permanent 
or temporary employment under any Government, a local 
or Statutory e.g., Damodar Valley Corporation), in 
India will he rejected unless they are submitted through 
the appointing authority of their posts or service. 


Cundidates serving under Government or a ৮0001 or 
statutory 10005 should submit an advance copy in the

attached to the advance copy and not to the original.

General instructions to candidates applying in response to 
advertisements issued by the Commission for reorult- 
ment to posts by ‘‘Selestion’’. 


(1) Instructions regarding submission of appilcation.— 
Applications are to be made on the prescri form which 
will be available from the office of the Public Service 

mission, West Bengal. Anderson House (ground 
floor), Alipore, Calcutta-27, personally or on sending a 
large self-addressed envelope with stamps sufficient to 
cover the postage affixed to it. Candidates who are unable 
to obtain Le ere of the prescribed form may apply on any 
similar ty (not handwritten) form showing exactly the 
wording and spacing of the same form published in the 

‘Calcutta Gazette” of the lst September 1955 rovided 
the blanks are filled up in the candidates’ own ha; writing. 


[Parr I] 


(2) Particulars and oertifioates required.—Candidates 
should furnish evidence of their age, qualifications and 
previous experience together with certificates written not 
more than one year prior to the date of their applications, 
from responsible persons, testifying to their private 
character. 


(3) Fee.—Candidates must enclose with their applica- 
tions a fee of Rs. 5 er each category of posts) in the 
form of a receipted chalan from a Government Treasury 
or the Reserve Bank of India under the head “XXXVI— 
Miscellaneous—Receipts of the Public Service Commission 
West Bengal’. Money orders, cheques, eto., in lien ٥ 
treasury chalans are not accepted. Postal orders 
however, may he accepted from candidates. They should 
be crossed and made 77 to “The Secretary, Public 
Service Commission, West Bengal’. No application will 
be considered unless accompanied with e requisite 
application fee. 


Candidates in Government service should make sure 
before depositing fee that their applications will be 
forwarded by their superior officers. In no case will the 
fee paid with the application be refunded. 


The Commission may remit fee in case of genuinely 
indigent and bona fide displaced persons from Pakistan. 


Note.—‘‘(i) A displaced person اس"‎ ago 000 
must furnish with his application satisfactory evidence 
that he is a bona fide displaced person from Pakistan, 
e.g., refugee registration card or a certificate from u 
azetted officer or a Member of Parliament or State 
egislature, in original. 


(ii) A member of the Scheduled Caste or Schedule: 
Tribe claiming age concession must furnish with his 
application a certificate in original from a gazetted officer 
or 2 Member of Parliament or State Legislature belonging 
to the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, specifying the 
particular caste or tribe to which he claims to belong. 


(iii) A displaced person secking remission of the 
application fee must furnish besides the evidence required 
under Note (i) above a certificate (in original) from a 
District Officer or a gazetted officer or a Member of 
Parliament or State Legislature to show that he is not in 
a position to pay the prescribed fee.’’ 


(4) Address.—Candidates should give their  prosent 
address and should communicate at once any subsequent 
change of address. 


(5) Canvassing.—Any attempt on the part of candidates 
to enlist’ support of their applications through persons of 
influence or officiala of Government will disqualify them 
for appointment. Spontaneous recommendations fron 
versons interested in the candidates or otherwise known 
to them will be disregarded. 


(6) Applications from candidates who are in permanent 
or temporary employment_under any Government, a 10081 
or Statutory Body (e.g., Damodar Valley Corporation), in 
India will rejected unless they are submitted througb 
the appointing authority of their posts or service. 


Candidates serving under Government or a local or 
etatutory body should submit an advance copy in the 
নি form. The application fees should in such cases 

attached to the advance copy and not to the original. 
The candidature of such applicants may not however be 
considered if the original applications do not reach the 
Commission’s office within a fortnight from the closing 
date. Unless od haa in original or advance copies 
with application fees are received within the closing date, 
late applications may be rejected.

Age concession for all the posts 


The age limit for all the posta is relaxable by five years 
for Scheduled Castes/Tribes and up to 45 years for 
displaced persons from Pakistan. 


The age limit is also relaxable for a non-Mushm Gov- 
ernment servant in undivided Bengal who had originally 
opted to serve in East Bengal and was working under the 
Government of Fast Bengal after partition hut has since 
formally resigned his service under that Government and 
hax come over to India as refugee. 


A candidate who before the 15th Auguat 1947 was 
detained, imprisoned, interned or externed on account of 
hin activities in connection with the country’s struggle for 
independence, not being convicted of an offence indicating 
moral turpitude, shall be entitled to a concession in respect 
of the age limit. The concession granted will be equal to 
the exact period of detention, imprisonment, internment or 
externment suffered up to a maximum of four years.

ARTICLE III 
Section 1. financing Operations 
The Corporation may make investments of its funds in 
productive private enterprises in the territories of its 
members. The existence of a government or other public 
interest in such an enterprise shall not necessarily preclude 


the Corporation from making an investment therein.

member’s territories pursuant to Section 1 of this Article 
shall not he free solely by reason of any provision of this 
Agreement, trom generally applicable foreign exchange 
restrictions, regulations and controls in force in the terri- 
tories of that member. 


ARTICLE VI 


Status, IMMUNITIES AND PRIVILEGES 
Section [. Purposes of Arttole 


To enable the Corporation to fulfill the functions with 
which it is entrusted, the status, immunities and privileges 
set forth in this Article shall be accorded to the Oorporation 
in the territories of each member. 


SECTION 2. Status of the Corporation 
The Corporation shall possess full juridical personality 
and, in particular, the capacity: 
(i) to contract; 
(ii) to acquire and dispose of immovable and mevable 
property ; 
(iii) to institute legal proceedings.

Section 3. Position of the Corporation with reyard to 
udicial l’rocess 


Actions may he brought against the Corporation only in 
w court of competent jurisdiction in the territories of a 
member in which the Corporation has an office, has appointed 
an agent fur the purpose of accepting service or notice of 
process, or has issued or guaranteed securities. No actions 
shall, however, be brought by members or persons acting 
for or driving claims from members. The property and 
uasets of the Corporation shall, wheresoever located and by 
whomsoever held, be immune from ull forms of seizure, 
attachment or execution before the delivery of finul judg- 
went against the Corporation. 


Section 4. lmmumty of Assets from Seizure 


Property and assets of the Corporation, wherever located 
and by whomsvever held, shall be immune from _ search, 
requisition, confiscation, expropriation or any other form of 
seigure by executive or Jegislative action. 


Stction 5. /mmunity of Afchives 
The archives of the Corporation shall be inviolable. 


SEction 6. Freedom of Assets from Restrictions 


To the extent necessary to carry out the operations pro- 
vided for in this Agreement and subject to the provisions of 
Article III, Section 5, and the other provisions of this Agree- 
ment, all property and assets of the Corporation shall be 
free from reatriotions, regulations, controls and moratoria of 
any nature. 


SEcTion 7. Privilege for Communications 


The official communications of the Corporation shall be 
accorded by each member the same treatment that it accords 
to the official] communications of other members.

Employees

1991). () Where this Act or any other law requires

ACT NO. LIX OF 1958 
THE DELHI RENT CONTROL ACT, 1958 


[918 December, 1958] 


An Act to provide for the control of rents and evictions and 
of rates of hotels and lodging houses, and for the 
ease of vacant premises to Government, in certain areas 
an the Union territory of Dethi 


Br it enacted by Parliament in the Ninth Year of the

1. (1) This Act may be called the Delhi Rent Control 
Act, 1958. 


(2) It extends to the areas included within the limits of 
the New Delhi Municipal Committee and the Delhi Canton- 
ment Board and to such urban areas within the limits of 
the Municipal Corporation of Delhi os are specified in the 
First Schedule:

oad gg from the operation of this Act or any provision

appoint.

by notification in the Official Guzette, declare that the 
ancient and historical monument or archwological site and 
remains, as the case may be, has ceased to be of national 
importance for the purposes of this Act. 


36. Any clerical mistake, patent error or error arising 
from accidental slip or omission in the description of any 
ancient monument or archeological site and remains 
declared to be of national importance by or under this Act 
may, at any time, be corrected by the Centra] Government 
by notification in the Official Gazette. 


No suit for compensation and no criminal proceed-

act done or in good faith intended to be done in the 
exercise of any power conferred by this Act.

38. (1) The Central Government may, by notification 
in the Official Gazette and subject to the condition of 
previous publication, make rules for carrying out the 
purposes of this Act. 


(2) In particular, and without prejudice to the generality 
of the foregoing power, such rules may provide for all or 
any of the following matters, namely :— 


(a) the prohibition or regulation by licensing or other- 
wise of mining, quarrying, excavating, blasting 
or any operation of a like nature near a 
protected monument or the construction of 
buildings on land adjoiming such monument and 
the removal of unauthorised buildings; 


(b) the grant of licences and permissions to make 
excavations for archeological purposes in 
protected areas, the authorities by whom, and 
the restrictions and conditions subject to which, 
such licences may be granted, the taking of 
securities from licensees and the fees that may 
be charged for such licences; 


(c) the right of access of the public to a protected 
monument and the fee, if any, to be charged 
therefor; 


(৫) the form and contents of the report of an archro-— 
logical officer or a licensee under clause (৫) of 
sub-section (7) of section 23;

(f) the form and manner of preferring appeals under

preferred ; 


(g) the manner of service of any order or notice under

(ti) in the case of a rule made with reference to 
clause (c) of sub-section (2), with fine which may 
extend to five hundred rupees. 


(4) All rules made under this section shall be laid for 
not less than thirty days before each House of Parliament 
as soon as possible after they are made, and shall be 
subject to such modifications as Parliament may make during 
the session in which they are so laid or the session

COVERNMENT OF INDIA 


Ministry of Law 


The following Act of Parliament received the assent of 
the President on the 16th September, 1958, and is hereby 
published for general information :— 


Act No. XXX of 1958 
THE SUGAR EXPORT PROMOTION ACT, 1958 
[16th September, 1968.] 


An Act to provide for the export of sugar in the publec 
interest and for the levy and collection wm certam 
circumstances of an additional duty of exctse on sugar 
produced in India. 


Br it enacted by Parliament in the Ninth Year of the 
Republic of India as follawa:— 


1. (1) This Act may be called the Sugar Export Promo- Short title 
tion Act, 1958. and extent, 


(2) It extends to the whole of India. 


2. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— Definitions, 


(a) “export” means taking out of India by sea, land or 
alr; 


(b) “export agency’’ meaus any such agency as may be 
specified in this behalf under section 3, and 
when no such agency has been so specified, the 
Central Government; 


(©) “export quota’ means the export quota referred to 
in rection 5; 


(d) “factory’’ means any premises (including the 


precincts thereof) wherein sugar is being produced 
by the vacuum pan process;

3. (1) For the purposes of this Act, the Central Govern- 
ment may, by notification in the (fficial (tazette, specify as

4, (1) The Central Government may, by notification in

(০) the necessity for exporting sugar with a view to 
earning foreign exchange in the public interest. 
(2) The power conferred by sub-section (1) shall be so 
exercised as do ensure that the quantity fixed under that 
sub-section for any year does not exceed in the aggregate 
twenty per cent. of the quantity of sugar produced in India 


in the season ending with the month of October falling within 
that year.

Committees presented to Parliament; and Bills published before

RAJYA SABHA 


The following Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha 
on the 29th August, 1958:— 


Bitt No, IIT or 1958 
A Bill to amend the Companies Act, 1956. 


Bz it enacted by Parliament in the Ninth Year of the 
Republic of India as follows:— 


1. This Act may be called the Companies (Amendment) Short title. 
Act, 1958. 


[of 1956. 2. In section 293 of the Companies Act, 1956, in sub- Amend- 
section (1), after clause (e), the following proviso shall be ment of 
inserted, namely :— 203 
‘*Provided that no contribution shall be made to the 
fund of any political party or to the election 
fund of any candidate for the purpose of elec- 
tion to Parliament, or a State Legislature, or a 
Territorial Council.” 


STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


A number of big business houses have been liberally contributing to the 
funda of political parties. In their recent judgments, the Bom y and 
Calcutta High Courts have drawn particular attention to the undesirability 
of such practice. It is, therefore, considered necessary that clause (e) of 
sub-section (1) of section 293 of the Companies Act, 1956, which enables 
companies to contribute to charitable and other funds should be suitably 
amended to prevent such contributions 06175 wade to political parties. The 
Bill seeks to achieve this object. 

BHUPESH GUPTA.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


The rate of compensation a» given in the Schedule [ of the Workmen's 
Compensation Act, 1923, computed in 1924 was based on the then financial 
circumstances of the country. About 35 years have passed since then and 
the financial circumstances including cost of. living index have changed, 
bui this chart has not been revised. Moreover some items of compensation 
also require deletion. There is no justification in the retention of the 
differences in the rates of compensation for the loss of hand just above 
1100 elbow and for the loss of a hand just helow the elbow. 


Hence this Bill.

STATEMENT OF ORJECTS AND REASONS 


The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923, which cume into force on 
the Ist July, 1924, has been emended several times, the major amend- 
ricnts being as followa:— 


Act V of 1929 anter aha enlarged the categories of workmen, removed 
the restrictions on compensation in the building trades and altered the 
provisions relating to the distribution of compensation. In 1933, the Act 
Wat revised ‘extensively on the lines recommended by the Royal Commission 
ou Labour in India in 1931; the main amendments carried out were, a 
considerable enlargement in the number of workmen covered by the Act, 
increase in the scales of compensation and reduction of the ‘“‘waiting 
‘period’’, By the amending Act I of 1946, the wage limit of workers 
covered by the Act was increased from Rs. 300 to Rs. 400. 


2. The working of the Act has shown that it requires to be further 
amended in certain respects. Some of the important amendments the Bill 
‘pecks 10 make relate to:— 

(a) removing the distinction between an adult and a minor for the 
purposes of workmen’s compensation; 

109) reducing the waiting period of seven days to five days for being 
entitled to compensation and, in cases where the period of dis- 
ablement is twenty-eight days or more, providing for payment 
of compensation from the date of disablement; 

(c) providing for penalty for failure to pay compensation, when due; 


(d) enlarging the scope of Schedules I, I] and III. 


3. The reasons for the amendments are, wherever necessary, given in 
tthe notes on clauses attached to this Bill. 


G. L. NANDA. 


NEW DELHI; 
The 16th September, 1958. 


Aotes on clauses 


Clause 2.—This clause removes the distinction between an adult and a 
minor fyr the purpose of workmen’s compensation. At present the Act 
prescribes different rates of compensation for adults and minors for death 
and permanent disablement on the ground that a minor will have, as 
: general rule, no dependants. There is not much justification for this 
distinction and it is reasonable that there should be uniform rates of com- 
pensation for workmen in similar wage-groups. 


Though for purposes of payment of compensation the distinction 
between an adult and a minor is being removed, for other purposes a 
“minor’ wil] have the normal meaning, namely, a person who has _ not 
attained the age of 18 years. 


Reference to a foreign Act in clause (2) has been omitted, “being

FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM 


The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1925, covers a large number of 
persons in (Central (iovernment undertahings such as the railways, posts 
and telegraphs, construction works, ete. Some of the amendments proposed 
in the Bill will have the effect of increasing the liability of the employers 
(including the Central Government) tor payment of compensation. Clause 
5 of ‘the Bill seeks to provide a penalty for failure to pay compensation 
when due with the result that the employer will have to pay increased 
umounts in cases where payment of compensation has been delayed for more 
than a month. Clause 17 contemplates replacement of Schedule I by a 
more comprehensive Schedule which will increase the percentage of dis- 
ablement and will correspondingly increase the rates of compensation for 
the various types of injuries. the amendments proposed to Schedule II 
to ihe Act will make the Act applicable ٤10 an increased number of persons 
in factories, mines, ports, construction works and also to persons employed 
in manufacture, efc., of aircraft, in farming by tractors, in construction, 
working, repair or maintenance of tube-wells, efc. Schedule III to the 
Act, which contains a list of occupational diseases, is proposed to be 
amended and enlarged with the result that compensation will be payable 
in respect of the new diseases being included in that Schedule. The above 
‘roporals will thus involve increased expenditure from the Consolidated 

und of India in so far as they concern the Central Government under- 
takings. As compensation becomes payable only in the event of an employ- 
ment injury resulting in disablement or death, it is not possible to estimate 
the amount of increased expenditure.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


As ao result of the experience gained in the working of the Cinemato- 
graph Art, 1942, for the last six years, it is considered necessary to make 
certain changes in its provisions for clarification, without making any 
substantial change in the working of the present Act. 


Section 3 of the Cinematograph Act, 1952, empowers the (Central 
Government to constitute a Board of Film Censors consisting of such 
number of persons as may be prescribed for the purpose of examining ana 
certifying films as suitable for public exhibition. The films are examined 
by the regional officers with the nid of the advisory panels consisting 
of non-officials. The composition of the Board, the constitution of 
the advisory panels and the procedure for examination of films by tle 
regional officers with the aid of the advisory panels are at present laid 
down in the Rules. The Bill makes express provisions in this behalf in 
the principal Act. It also incorporates the principles for guidance in 
certifying films, based on the provisions of article 19(2) of the Constitu- 
tion. In addition, the Bill makes provision for certain matters of a 
procedural and routine character. 


New 10۶,۰: B. V. KESKAR. 
The 8th December, 1958. 


FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM 


The Bill seeks to include express provisions in the principal Act, 
respecting the composition of the Board of Film Censors and the constitu- 
tion of advisory panels to enable the Board to perform ita functions of 
sanctioning films for public exhibition. As at present the Chairman will 
continue to be a wholetime official and the members will be non-officials, 
working part-time in an honorary capacity. They will be paid travelling 


30 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 12, 1959 [Parr VI 


allowance only for aitending meetings in convertion with the work of 
Board. The advisory panels have been constituted at present at Bombay, 
Calcutta and Madras under the Rules framed under the Act. Their 
membership is also honorary, but conveyance allowance nat the rate of 
Rs. 10 per diem is paid to them for attending film shows or meetings 
convened by regional officers in connection with the examination of films. 
The annual expenditure on the salary of the Chairman, the travelling 
allowance of the members of the Board and conveyance allowance of the 
members of the advisory panels is estimated at Rs. 90,000. The expendi- 
ture on these items is already being incurred through appropriations made 
by Parliament, and no additional expenditure is anticipated 


MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATE) LEGISLATION 


Clause 4 of the Bill provides for the determination by the Central 
Government of the salary and allowances payable to the Chairman and 
the fees or allowances to the other members of the Board of Film Censors 
und to the members of the advisory panels. It 8190 provides for determina- 
tion of other terma and conditions of service of the members of the Board 
and the advisory panels. It empowers the Central Government to pre- 
scribe the manner in which applications shall be made to the Board for 
certification of films. The rule making power already conferred by section 
8 of the Act is sufficiently comprahensive to enable all such matters being 
regulated by Rules. All that the amending Bill seeks to do is to refer to 
these topics in the body of the Act in appropriate places. The rule making 
power 18.01 a normal character.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


The Bill is largely based on the recommendations of the Advisory 
Board appointed by the Government of India in 1953 to suggest amend- 
ments to the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 (hereinafter referred to as the 
Act). In making these recommendations, the Board had, besides consult- 
ing the State Governments, given careful consideration to the views of the 
private sector of the electricity supply industry. 


2. The main objects of the Bill are:— 
(a) to enlarge the scope of facilities availuble to consumers of 
electricity ; 
(b) to extend the same facilities to consumers served by a overn- 
ment Electricity Department, as are enjoyed by consumers of 
private licensees und State Electricity Boards; 


(0) to exercise stricter control over licensees; 


(d) to take powers to regulate the distribution, supply, consumption 
and use of energy in certain circumstances; mi 


(e) to provide for the inspection of electric works and installations of 
the Central Government. 


J. With a view to making it easier for even scattered consumers to 
obtain the supply of electricity, the minimum number of persons entitled to 
vet the mains extended to their premises at the licensee’s cost is being 
reduced trom six to two. Under the existing provisions of the Act, the 
gross revenue to be guaranteed by a consumer before receiving the supply 
of electricity is not definite and varies from undertaking to undertaking. 
Such gross revenue is now being specified as 15 per cent. of the cost of 
dS tribution mains (excluding the equipment in the sub-station) required 
for compliance with the requisition for supply of electricity. This figure 
1৭ based on the average revenue actually guaranteed by a large majority of 
consumers of electricity in the country. 


4. Persons served by licensees or State Electricity Boards, are entitled 
to certain statutory rights and privileges in respect of extension of the 


§2 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 12,1959) = [Parr VI 
লিলা উস 
distribution mains, requisitioning the supply of energy and meters, supply 
61 energy tor public lighting and treedom to use the energy im a perseribed 
mannet. Although the Government Electricity Departments generally 
extend similar tacilities to their consumers, 00 statutory obligation is 
imposed upon them in this behalf. It is accordingly proposed to give the 
sane rights to consumers of a Government Electricity Department os me 

enjoyed by those receiving supply from a State Electricity Board. 


». Control over licensees is being tightened by empowering the State 
(rovernment to forfeit the security deposit of a licensee on account of his 
failure to complete within the period specified in the licence, compulsory 
works referred to in the Schedule to the Act Inspectors appointed to investi- 
gate the causes ot an electrical accident are being vested with powers of 4 
civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for the purpose of 
compelling attendance of witnesses and production of documents, ete. 


G. Difficulty is often experienced on account of a licensee neglectin 
to supply energy promptly to essential services. It is, therefore, propose 
to empower State Governments to direct a licensee to supply and to 
continue to maintain the supply of energy, to essential services within his 
aren of supply. Any dispute with respect to the price or other terms and 
conditions governing such supply shall be nettled by arbitration. With 
a view to maintaining the sana and equitable distribution of energy, the 
State Governments are also being empowered to regulate the distribution, 
supply, consumption or use of energy. 


7. Tu view of the increasing share of the Central Government in the 
field of generation and utilisation of electricity, it has been found necessary, 
for ensuring the safety of life and property, to subject their installations 
in all fields, to inspection and tests, similar to those prescribed in the case 
of the installations in mines and railways. It is, therefore, proposed to 
authorise the Central Giovernment, to appoint inspectors with powers 
exercisable by electrical inspectors for mines and i, under the exiat- 
ing provisions of the Act, in respect of all other electric installations under 
the control of the Centra] Government.

Notes on clauses 
Clause 2.—This clause makes certain formal amendments. 


Clause 3.—This clause makes a few clarificatory amendments in certain 
existing definitions and adds a few new definitions. 


Clause 4.—This clause provides that a State Government while granting 
a licence under the Act sball consult the State Electricity Board. 11 
further provides that where an aerodrome is included in the area of supply, 
the State Government shall not grant a licence without ascertaining that 
the Central Government has no objection to the grant of such licence. 
The clause further brings the provisions of section 3 in line with those of 
paragraph I of the Sixth Schedule to the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. 


Clause 5.—This clause provides that where a State Government propose-~ 
to revoke a licence, it shall consult the State Electricity Board. Au 
additional ground for revocation of a licence would be non-compliauce by 
the licensee with any directions issued under new section 22A, The 
clause further provides for giving an opportunity to the licensee of being 
heard before his licence is cancelled.

of revocation of a licence, purchase of an undertaking, the conditions on

CORPORATION OF CALCUTTA 


NOTICE 
Calcutta, the 20th December 1968. 


It is hereby notified for general information that the Corporation of 
Calcutta in exercise of the powers vested in it under section 356 of the Calcutta 
Municipal Act, 1961, read with section 363 of the said Act, has, by ite 
resolution, dated the 2156 November 1958, prescribed a 40-foot alignment 
in continuation of Asoke Road to meet Alipore Road affecting a portion of 
premises No. 14, Asoke Road as shown in the plan in blue dotted lines in 
ward No. 72(Old 24). 


A copy of the plan prepared in this behalf may be seen in the office of 
the Chief Valuer and Surveyor of the Corporation on any working day 
between 11 u.m. and 2 p.m. on psyment of usual fees. 


P. C. MAJUMDAR,

SUPPLEMENT—Official Papers 
Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional Reports on the condition of weather, crops, etc., for the week ending the 17th December 1958. 


Summary.—During the week under report there was no rainfall in any subdivision. The condition of weather was unfavourable 
in five subdivisions. In most of the subdivisions harvesting of Aman paddy continued. The prospect of standing crop was not satia- 
factory in one subdivision, and other places, it was fair on the whole. 

Fodder was insufficient in six subdivisions and cattle epidemic was reported from one subdivision, There was scarcity of seeds in 
five subdivisions. 

The daily wages of a labourer varied frou rupee one to rupees two and fifty nP.

Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional Reports on the condition of Weather, Grops, etc., for the week ending the 24th December, 1058. 


Summary - omg the woek under report there was no rainfall in any subdivision. The conditions of weather were nut favourable 
in four subdivisions. In most of the subdivisions harvesting of aman paddy continued. The prospect of standing crops was not satis- 
factory in one subdivision and iu other places, it was, on the whole fair. 

Fodder wap insuffigent in four subdivisions and cattle epidemic wan reported from one subdivision. There was scarcity of Rabi 
needs in three subdivisions. 

The daily wages of a labourer varied from rupee one to rupees two and fifty nP.

Subdivisional Reports on the condition of Weather, Crops, etc., for the week ending the 7th January, 1959. 


Summary.—During the week under report there waa no rainfall in any subdivision. The conditions of weather were unfavourable 
n five subdivisions. arvesting and threshing of Aman paddy and harvesting of Sugarcane continued. In aome subdivisions har- 
rating of Aman paddy has been completed. The prospect of atunding crops was, on the whole, fair. 

Fodder was insufficient in four subdivisions and cattle epidemic was reported from one subdivision. There was scareity of seeds 
n two subdivisions. 

The daily wages of » labourer varied from rupee one and twelve nP. to rupees two and fifty nP.

Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional Reports on the condition of Weather, Crops, etc., fer the week ending the 14th January, 1959. 


Summary. —During the week under report there was no rainfall in any eubtlivision. The conditions of weather were unfavourable 
in four subdivisions. Harvesting and threshing of Aman paddy and harvesting of Sugarcane continued. In some subdivisions har- 
vesting of Aman paddy has been vompleted. The proapeuvt ‘of standing crops was, on the whole, fair. 

Foddor was insufficient in four subdivisions and cattle epidemic was reported from three subdivisions. Thero was scarcity of 
seeds in two subdivisions. 

The daily wages of a labourer varied from rupee one and twelve ,کت‎ to rupees two and twenty-five mP.

CORPORATION OF CALCUTTA 


NOTICE 


Calcutta, the 2nd February 1959 


It is hereby notified for general information that the Corporation of 
Calcutta in exercise of the powers vested in it under section 356 of the 
Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, has by its resolution, dated the 19th Septem- 
ber 1968, prescribed the alignment of 1)0108 Charan Doctor Road (portion 
running east to west from Tower Circular Road only) to a width 30) ft. in 
modification of the Corporation resolution, dated the Ith July 1956, 
Ward No. 50. 


A copy of plan prepared in this behalf may be seen in the olfice of the 


Chief Valuer and Surveyor of the Corporation on any working day between 
11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Gn payment of usual fees. 


P, C. MAJUMDAR, 
Chief Executive Officer, 


Printed and published hy the Superintendent, Government Pritting, West Bengal, 
at the West Bengal Government Press, Alipore.

CORPORATION OF CALCUTTA 


Byo-elections held on 8th February 1959 to olect Councillors of the 
Corporation of Calcutta for the Constituencies Nos. 70 and 75. 


NOTICE 
Central Municipal Office, the 9th February 1959. 


[0 compliance with the provisions of sub-section (6) of section 59 of 
the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951 (West Bengal Act XXXIII of 1951), it 
is hereby notified that Shri Barindra Kumar Chattopadhyay and Shri Balai 
Bhusan Paul have been declared duly elected as Councillors of the Corpo- 
ration of Calcutta for the Constituencies Nos. 70 and 75, respectively. 


P. C. MAJUMDAR,

SUPPLEMENT—Official Papers 


Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional Reports on the condition of Weather, Crops, etc., for the week ending the 4th February, 1969. 


Summary.—During the week under report there waa rainfall in twenty-four subdivisions. The conditions of weather were 
unfavourable in eight subdivisions. Harvesting of mustard, potato and sugarcane and land preparation for Kharif crops continued. 
The prospect of standing crops was not satisfactory in two subdivisions and in other places, it was, on the whole, fair. 

Fodder waa insufficient in tive subdivisions and cattle epidemic was reported from three subdivisions. There was scarcity of 
89635 in three subdivisions. 


The daily wages of a labourer varied from eighty-seven nP. to rupess two.

Calcutta, the 4th February 1959.

Caleutta Municipal Act, 1951, has by its resolution, dated the 16th January 
1969, proscribed a 12-ft. alignment connecting 16 ft. and 20 ft. public rouds 
oft Fern Road and 12 ft. public road off Kankulia Road followimg a partly 


filled up puble drain in Ward No, 61.

Third and Final Forecast of Spring Oilseed Crops 
of West Bengal for 1957-58 


(Note.—The figures of Linseed and Rape and 
Mustard for both this year and last year 
except. for those of Darjeeling district 
shown in this forecast are based on the 
results of sample survey and crop-cutting 
experiments conducted by the _ State 
Stutistical Bureau, West Bengal. The 
figures of (ther Uilseeds for buth this year 
and 188৮ year and of Linseed and Rape and 
Mustard in respect of Darjeeling istrict 
for this yeur und last year are based on the 
reports received from the staff ot this 
Directorate of Agriculture.) 


Season.—The weather conditions have ou the 
whole been fair for the growth of the crop in dis- 
tricts other than Nadia, Murshidabad, Midnapore, 
Malda, West Dinajpur and Purulia. 


Area and yield.—The total areca under Spring 
Gilseed crops (except Sesamum for which separate 
forecusts are published) is estimated at 0 
acres this year compared to 301,000 acres of 1081 
year. The total outturn of different Spring 
Oilseeds for the State as a whole is estimated at 
30,800 tons this year compared to 33,200 tons cof 
last yoar. The average outturn per acre 
of different Spring Oilseeds for the State us a 
whole has been estimated at 3.64 maunds this year 
compared to 3.00 maunds of last yeur. The above 
estimates relate to West Bengal excluding 
territories transferred from Bihar. For West 
Bengal including territories transferred from 
Bihar, the acreage, production and yield per evre 
of different Spring Ooilseed crops for 1957-58 have 
roughly been estimated at 254,300 acres, 34,100 
tons and 3.65 maunds, respectively, 


Linseed.—43,900 acres have been estimated to 
be under Linseed this year compared to 118,400 
acres of last year. The total outturn of the crop

DIRECTORATE OF ACRICULTURE, WEST 
BENCAL 


Calcutta, the 18th October 1958 


Second Forecast of Sugarcane Crop of West 
Bengal for 1958-59 


(Note.—The estimates of area and yield of Sugar- 
cane for last year have been taken from last 
year's final forecast which was based on the 
results of sample survey conducted by the 
State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal, except 
for the district of Darjeeling. The estimates 
of Darjeeling district for last year and all the 
estimates for this year have been based on the 
reports of the Agricultural staff.) 


Season.—The weather conditions have not 
generally been favourable for the cultivation and 
rowth of the crop in all the districts exceptin 
urshidabadl and Jalpaiguri. Reports of attac 


of inseot pest and stem-borer have been received 
from the districts of Nadia and Purulia. 


Area and yield.—The total urea planted with the 
crop 1s estimated at 63,600 acres this year as 
against 61,800 acres and 58,300 acres reported 
respectively in the corresponding and in the final 
forecasts of [ast year. 


The average outturn per acre of Sugarcane 
crop for the State as a whole is estimated at 
915.41 maunds this year as against 499.19 maunds 
and 394.75 maunds reported respectively in the 
corresponding and in the final forecasts of last 
year. 


The total outturn of the crop for the State as a 
whole is estimated at 1,014,900 tons this year as 
against 940,800 tons and 846,600 tons reported 
respectively in the corresponding and in the final 
forecasts of Jast year.

40 feat in Ward No. 66.

the Chief Valuer and Surveyor of the Corporation on any working day

CORPORATION OF CALCUTTA 
NOTICE 


Dated Calcutta, the 16th March 1959 


It is hereby notified for general information 
that the Corporation of Calcutta in exercise of the 
powers vested in it under section 7966 of the 
Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, has by its resolu- 
tion, dated the 14th January 1959, prescribed the 
alignment for widening the narrow portion of 
Dehi Serampore Lane (now Ballygunge Place 
Kast) at its junction with Bondel Road to a width 
of 20 feet in Ward No. 61. 


A copy of the plan ور‎ in this behalf may 
be seen in the office of the Chief Valuer and Sur- 
veyor of the Corporation on any working day 
— 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on payment of usua! 
ees. 


P. C. MAJUMDAR. 
Chief Executive Officer

1. Short title, extent and commencement.«-(1) This Order may 46 
called the West Bengal Rice and Paddy Price Control Ordar, 1959. 


(2) It extends to the whole of the State of West Bengal. 
(9) It shall come into force on the lst January 1959. 


2. Definitions.—In this Order,— 
(a) ‘Calcutta Industrial Area’’ means the 87608 specified iBchedule I; 


(b) ‘‘coarse’? means any variety of rice or paddy other ‘Tian the

(h) ‘‘Schedule’? means a Schedule annexed to this Order. 


3. The prices at which rice and paddy may he sold or purchased— 


(1) The price chargeable by a producer, a. wholesaler or a rotailer in 
any area specified in column 1 of Schedule. III for rice“or paddy 
of superfine (non-aromatic), fine, medium or coarse variety shall 
not exceed the rate specified for such producer, wholesaler or 
retailer for that variety of rice or paddy in the appropriate entry

Provided that—

PART I- 1099 and Notifications by the Governor of West Bengal,

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
DEPARTMENT OF FOOD, RELIEF AND SUPPLIES 
Food and Supplies Branch 
11۸ Free School Street, Calcutta-16 


ORDER 


No. 27F.S.—2nd January 1959.—In exercise of the power coriferred b 
section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 1955), read wit 
the Government of India, Ministry of Food and Agriculture, order 
No. G.S.R. 1088, dated the 15th November 1958, published at pages 511-12 
of Part II, Section 3(i) of the Gazette of India, Extraordinary of the 15th 
November 1958, the Governor, with the concurrence of the Central Govern- 
ment, is pleased to make the following order, namely :— 


Order 


1. Short Title, Extent and Commoncement.—(1) This Order may be 
called the West Bengal Wheat or Wheat Products (Restrictions on Rail- 
Bookings) Order, 1959. 

(2) It extends to the whole of the State of West Bengal. 


(3) It shall come into force on the date of its publication in the Oficial 
Gazette. 


21 


22 THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., JAN. 2, 1959 [Part I 


2. Doefinitions.—In this order, unless there is anything repugnant in 
the subject or coptext,— 


(a) ‘‘bypk’’ means to accept for despatch by rail; 


(b) ‘‘transport’’ includes taking into the premises of a railway station 
for the purpose of despatch by rail; 


(c) ‘“Wheat’’ includes broken wheat, and ‘““Wheat Products’”’ includes 
Maida, Suji, Rawa, wholemeal Atta and resultant Atta but does 
not include bran. 


3. ReStrictions on Transport and Booking by Rail.—(1) No person shall 
transport or attempt to transport or abet the transport of wheat or wheat 
products into any railway station specified in the Schedule to this Order 
except under und in accordance with a permit issued by the State Govern- 
ment or by any officer authorised by the State Government in this behalf. 


(2) No person shall present or offer for booking wheat or wheat products 
into any railway station specified in the Schedule to this Order from any 
other railway station lying within the State of West Bengal except under 
and in accordance with a permit issued by the State Government or by 
any officer authorised by the State Government in this behalf and no person 
shall book wheat or wheat products presented or offered for booking in 
contravention of the provisions of this clause: 


Provided that nothing contained herein shall apply to transport or 
booking of wheat or wheat products— 


(i) on Government account, 
(11) under and in accordance with Military Credit Notes, and 


. (111) not exceeding five seers in weight by a bona fide traveller as part 
of his or her luggage. 


4. Effect of the Order.—The provisions of this Order shall be in addition 
to and not in derogation of the Calcutta Wheat (Movement Control) Order, 
1956 and West Bengal Wheat (Export Control) Order, 1968. 


5. Powers of Entry, Search, Seizure, etc.—(1) Any Police Officer not 
below the rank of an Assistant Sub-lnspector and any other person authorised 
in this behalf by the State Government may, with a view to securing com- 
pliance with this Order or to satisfying himself that this Order has been 
complied with— 


(1) Stop and search, or authorise any person to stop and search, any 
person, boat, motor or any vehicle or receptacle used or intended 
to be used for the transport of wheat or wheat products; 


(11) enter and search and authorise any person to enter and search 
- any place; 


(111) seize or authorise the seizure of any wheat or wheat product in 
respect of which he suspects that any provision of this Order 
hus been, 1s being or is about to be contravened, along with the 
packages, coverings or receptacles in which such wheat or wheat 
product is found or the animals, vehicles, vessels, boats or other 
conveyance used in carrying such wheat or wheat product and 
thereafter take or authorise the taking of all measures necessary 
for securing the production of the packages, coverings, receptacles, 
animals, vehicles, vessels, boats or other conveyances ৪০ seized, 
in a court and for their safe custody pending such production. 


(2) The provisions of sections 102 and 103 of the Code of Criminal 


Procedure, 1898 (5 of 1898), relating to search and seizure shall, so far as 
may be, apply to searches and seizures under this clause.

when present, 81181] preside over all meetings of the Council.

the absence of the Chairman, the Secretary to the State Giovern-

No. ہ1801‎ 26th January, 1969.——The following Act of the West Bengal Legislature, 
having been assented to by the President, is hereby published for general information :— 


West Bengal Act XXIV of 1958 
THE WEST BENCAL ANTI-PROFITEERING ACT, 1958. 


[Passed hy the West Bengal Legislature.] 


[Assent of the President waa first publuhed in the Calcutta Gazette, 
Extraordinary, of the 26th January, 1959.) 


An Act to prevent profiteering in certain articles in daily use. 


WHERE«s it is expedient in the public interest to prevent 
profiteering in certain articles in daily use; 


It is hereby enacted in the Ninth Year of the Republic 
of India, by the Legislature of West Bengal, as follows: — 


Short title 1, (1) This Act may be called the West Bengal Anti- 
andextent. profiteering Act, 1958. 
(2) 1t extends to the whole of West Bengal. 


Defini- 2. In this Act, unless there is anything repugnant in 
ons, the subject or context,— 


(a) “dealer” means any person carrying on the business 
ot selling any scheduled article, and includes a 
producer, importer, wholesaler or retailer; 


(b) 42010066211 means any person who brings any 
scheduled article into the State of West Bengal 
from any place outside the State for the purpose 
of sale in the State; 


(6) ‘tproducer”’ means a person engaged in the produc- 
tion, manufacture or processing of any scheduled 
article; 


(d) ‘profiteering’, with its grammatical variations and 
cognate expressions, means the sale by a dealer 
of any scheduled article at a price or rate higher 
than that fixed under section ৪3 


(s) “retailer '' means a person who sells any scheduled 
article to a consumer not beizg a dealer;

(f) ‘‘scheduled article’? means an article specified in 
the First Schedule; and 

(g) ‘‘wholesaler’’ means a dealer who sells any acheduled 
article to any other dealer, and includes a broker, 
cominission agent or any other agent having 
authority to sell any scheduled article belonging 
to his principal. 


3. (1) The State Government may, by order notified in 
the Oficial Gazette, fix im respect of any scheduled article 
the maximum price or rate which may be charged by a 
dealer or the minimum price which 18 to be paid by a 
purchaser. 


(2) Any order made under sub-section (4) may fix the 
maximum prices or rates or the minimum price to be paid 
by the purchaser for the same description of scheduled 
articles differently in different localities or for different 
classes of dealers. 


4. Any dealer who profiteers in any scheduled article 
shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment which may 
extend to two years or with fine or with both, and any 
scheduled article in respect of which the offence has been 
committed -0 such part thereof as to the court may seem fit 
shall be forfeited to the Government. 


5 (7) Any dealer who, witnout reasonable excuse,— 
(a) refuses to sell any scheduled article, or 


(b) refuses to sell any scheduled article at the price or 
rate fixed in respect thereof under section 3, 


shal] be punishable with rigorous imprisonment which may 


> extend to two years or with fine or with both. 


Ezplanation.—The possibility or expectation of obtaining 
a higher price for a scheduled article at a later date shall not 
be deemed_to be a reasonable excuse for the purposes of this 
section. 


(2) Any purchaser who purchases any scheduled article 
at any price less than the minimum price fixed therefor 
under section 3 shall be punishable with rigorous imprison- 
লা which may extend to two years or with fine or with 

oth. 


6. (4) Every dealer shal) on requisition by an officer 
duly authorised in this behalf by the State Government by 
order notified in the Oficial Gazette, submit to him in the 
form specified in the Second Schedule by such date and relat- 
ing to such period as may be mentioned in the requisition, 
returns of stocks of any scheduled article acquired, held or 
sold by him. 


2) Every dealer, unless exempted by an order made in 
thie behalf, shall— ৮ 


keep in the form specified in the Third Schedule a‏ ری 
true account of any scheduled article acquired,‏ 
held or sold by him after the commencement of‏ 
this Act;‏ 

(6) display in his place of business in a prominent manner 
مہ‎ as to be open to public view, a list of those 
scheduled articles intended for sale the prices or 
rates of which have been fixed under section 3 in 
respect of such dealer, with the prices or rates, 
80 fixed in respect thereof; 


(6) furnish to any officer referred to in sub-section (2), or 
any police officer referred to in sub-section (2) of 
section 9, any information in respect of the acquisi- 
tion or sale by him of any scheduled article 
mentioned in clause (b); 


(d) make available to any officer mentioned in clause (c) 
for his inspection such uccounts, registers, 
vouchers or other documents relating to the 
import, production, purchase or sale of any 
scheduled article mentioned in clause (1)) or matters 
connected therewith as may be required by him.
