25. (2) The protective homes shall not be used os a

and the principle of secularism shall be maintained strictly. 


(2) Religious and moral instructions to the inmates of

music. 


(3) The Superintendent shall endeavour to secure the

deputed to impart religious ond moral instruction to the 
inmates of their own faith at least once a week.

ability of the books chosen.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 


DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH 
Public Health 


NOTIFICATION 


No. P.H./306/2R-3/59.—27th January 1959.—Whereas the Governor 
is satisfied that the municipal aren of Siliguri in the district of Darjeeling 
18 threatened with un outbreak of smallpox; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by section 2 of the 
Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (III of 1897), the Governor is pleased to 
prescribe the following temporary regulations for the prevention and control 
of smallpox, and for the medical inspection, isolation, observation and 
surveillance of persons suffering from or suspected of being infected with 
smallpox in the said municipal area for a period of six months :— ۱ 


Temporary Regulations for the Prevention and Control of Smalipox 


1, In these reguiations, unless there is unything repugnyunt in the 
subject or context :— 


(a) ‘‘Health Officer’? neans the Health Officer of the municipality; 
115 


116 THE CAL. GAZ, WXTRY., JAN, 28, 1959 [Pant | 
LN A TT yd 
(b) “Sanitary Inspector’? means a Sanitary Inspector appointed by 
the municipality ; 
(c) “Smallpox”? means any disease accompanied by an eruption of 
vesicles or pustules; 


(d) “Patient” means a person suffering from or suspected to be suffer- 
ing from smallpox; 

(e) “Medical practitioner’ means any person practising the medical 
profession. 


Notioes 


2. If in any case the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector considers 
that the issue of a notice under these regulations 18 likely to lead to such an 
amount of delay as might facilitate the spread of amallpox, he may forth- 
with take such steps as he may think fit for carrying out the work and shall 
thereafter, as soon as possible, issue a notice on the person concerned stating 
the reason why such work has been carried out. 


3. If any measure which the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector 
has, by a notice issued under these regulations, required to be carried out, 
be not carried out to 1019 satisfaction within the time stated in the notice 
the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector shall be entitled to carry out 
the measure. 


Cost and compensation 


4. (1) All expenses incurred in carrying out any work in pursuance of 
un order issued under these regulations shall be paid by the municipalit 
except in any case where the order directs a person to carry out any ane 4 
mm relation to property in his possession, in which case the expenses shall 
be paid by such person: 

Provided that where the conditions, which led the Health Officer or a 
Sanitary Inspector to pass such an order, are not attributable to any act 
or default of the person in possession of the نب‎ the municipality 


may pay to such person the whole or a part of the expenses incurred by 
him in carrying out the order. 


(2) The municipality may recover all expenses incurred by the Health 
Officer or a Sanitary Inspector in carrying out the measure under regule- 
tion 8 from the person or persons to whom the notice was originally issued. 


5. The municipality shall pay adequate compensation to any person 
who has sustained substantial loss or damage by reason of anything done 
under these regulations: 


Provided that no person shall recetve any compensation for anything 
done or suffered under these regulations, if he has failed to carry out an 
order issued under these regulations within the time specified in the order 
and to the satisfaction of the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector. 


Location 0۹ disease 


6. When a case of smallpox occurs in a house, the nearest male rela- 
tive in attendance upon the patient, or in the absence of any such relative

The Employees’ Association started agitation for improvement of the

issue 1: This relates to revision of scales of pay of different categories

After the Tribunal award in 1949 fixing up sealea and prades of 
different categories of employees of this company, there has been 


Parr 11 THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., TAN, 29, 1959. 129 
ہے جووصح×سسبتب‎ পা চি ৩ Ee eee 


enormous change in the economical condition and/or structure of 
the country. Several declarations by State and Central Govern- 
ments to mprove the status of the middle-class people would 
justify the union's claim for an improved scale of pay, There 
now exists three grades ‘A’, ‘B’ and ‘C* and 3 special grades 
which are considered too many in the existing changed circum- 
stances. Many of the firms of similar standing have given better 
zrades and scales af pay introduced either by agreement or by 
subsequent awards. Moreover the present grades and scales of 
pay are not adequate enough for providing better amenities 01 
life for workers. The Employees’ Association accordingly lay 
stress on the introduction of one grade or at the most two grades 
for the clerical staff as without this there will be much difficulty 
to stand against creation of division amongst the workers, 
Moreover, the nature of details performed by the clerks are almost 
the same, In consideration of this the Bank Award and the

case of Messrs. Burn & Co., Ltd., Towrah fron Works and their employees, 
it has been held by the Hon'ble Sapreme Court of India that رج‎ 
section ,لا‎ ©. 1), 015 is in terms inapplicable to adjudication proceedings, 
the principle underlying if, expressed in the masnun 55181161616 rot 19111917041 
ut sit finis litium’’, is founded on sound public policy and is of universal 
application. (Vide Broom’s Legal Maxims, Tenth Kdition, page 218) It 
has further been found: ‘There are good reasons why this principle should 
be apphenble to decisions of Industrial Tribunals also. Legislation regu- 
latwny fhe relation between Capital and Tabour has two objecria in view, 
It seeks to ensure to the workmen who have not the capacity ٥٦0 treat with 
capital on equal terms, fair returns for their labour, Tt also seeks to prevent 
disputes between employer and employees, so that production might not be 
adversely affected and the larger interest of the sociely might not. suffer. 
Now. if we are to hold that an adjudication loses its foree when it is 
repudiated under section 19(6) and that the whole controversy is at large, 
then the result would he that far from reconciling themselves to the award 
and settling down to work it, either party will treat it as a mere stage in 
the prosecution of a prolonged struggle, and far from bringing industrial 
peace, the awarda would turn out to be but truces giving the parties breath- 
ing time before resuming hostile action with renewed vigour, On the other 
hand, if we are to regard them as intended to have long term operation 
and at the same time hold that they are liable to be modited by change in 
the circumstances on which they were based, both the purposes of the 
legislature would be served. That is the view taken by the Tribunals them- 
selves in The Army & Navy Stores Ltd. vs. Their workmen 197] (2) J. .ما‎ J 
231 and Ford Motor Co, of India Lad. ve. Their workmen 1951(2) 15715 J 
231 and we are of opinion that they lay down the correct principle, and 
a there were no grounds for the Appellate Tribunal for not following 
them’, 


In view of this decision, claim for revision of the grades and scales of 
pay can only be sustained if there has been change in the circumstances on 
which the were based. The allegations which the Employees’ Union made 
in this respect in the written statement are none which can hehecepted as 
such change in the circumstances, A change in the economical condition ot

Then as to claim of employees’ association for revision during argument 
on the ground that the Mercantile Tribunal did not go deep into the matter, 
fixed these grades without any scientific basis whatsoever and merely 
confirmed the grades and scales of pay fixed by the company on an ad hoe 
basis, IT am unable to uphold the contention. The Bengal Chamber of 
Commerce is an association of mercantile firms whose duty was to guide the 
constituent members with its recommendations on matters touching upon 
smooth working in the industrial establishments. The Bengal 
Chamber of Commerce prepared a scheme of wage structure for different 
categories of workmen which included among other things grading the 
different jobs, fixing the minimum and the maximum of each grade, the 
scales of increment and a libere] scheme of dearness allowance, This was 
recommended th constituent members and most of them including the 
present company adopted the same, In this state the case of Bengal 
Chamber of Commerce was first taken up by the Mercantile Tribunal among 
the contested cases for adjudication. There the tribunal carefully went 
into the question and after taking into consideration the recommendations 
of the committee appointed by the Bengal Chamber of Commerce, Report 
of the Central Pay Commission and other awards made at the time came to 
the conclusion that the grades and scales of pay both of the clerical and 
suhordinate staff were proper and adequate. As the Enquiry Committee of 
Bengal Chamber of Commerce overlooked to provide for the house rent in 
its recommendations on the basis of the figures compiled from the weekly 
periodical “Capital’’, the tribunal made good the said omission by fixing 
the minimum basic salary of a clerk at Rs. 70 by adding to the minimum 
basic salary of Ra, 60, as recommended hy the Bengal Chamber of Commerce, 
Rs. 10 on account of house allowance. This necessitated a uniform incre- 
ment of Rs. 10 at all stages of the severa] grades recommended by the 
Bengal Chamber of Commerce including the minimum and maximum. The 
tribunal stated full reasona in the award relating to the Bengal Chamber 
of Commerce. The said case was intended to be the mode] and the Mercan- 
tile Tribunal expressed in the awards of some of the firms that ita intention 
was, having regard to the then existing service conditions including wage 
structure and dearness allowance, to conform substantially to the award for 
the Bengal Chamber of Commerce. This is why in the award of the present 
company which wns subsequently made, the said tribunal did not record 
reasons separately. It cannot, therefore, he said that the award of 1949 
relating to this company war made on ad hoc hasis Now ar to the minimum 
basic wage of a clerk which is Rs. 70 per month the matter has been con- 
sidered in appeal in the case of James Finlay & (o, and it has been found 
that it is not comparatively low when 10060. on the industry-cum-region 


basis (ride 1957 L. A. C. at pages 166 to 171),

issue 2: Clerical staff including Stenographers and Bengali Sircars are 
aid dearness allowance according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
Rats linked with middle-class cost of living index. Such dearness allowance 
was also prevalent for the subordinate staff. The total emoluments of none 
of the subordinate staff was below Rs. 60 while in some cases the minimum 
basic was below Rs. 30. So by the award the Mercantile Tribunal directed 
that the minimum basic should be raised to Rs. 30 by deducting the corres- 
onding amount from the dearness allowance. Subsequent to the award the 
earness allowance of the subordinate staff was linked with working class 
cost of living index from 18th September 1960. Deduction of Rs. 5 from 
the dearness allowance to increase the basic pay to Rs. 30 continued. At the 
time of linking the dearners allowance with working class cost of living 
index the Bengal Chamber of Commerce intimated about such change to the 
Federation of Merrantile Employees’ Union (Ext, 1). There had been no 
protest to the proposed change and dearness allowance of the subordinate 
staff was linked from then onwards with the working class index. The scale 
of such dearness allowance is to be found in Annexure to Ext. 1. Not only 
this company adopted the change but also other constituents of the Bengal 
Chamber of Commerce. The change was also contested by adjudication 
proceedings in different concerns but without success, This tribunal had 
also to consider the matter in the case of Messrs. Duncan Brothers and 
their workmen. The tribunal also upheld this change. Since then there 
has been discontinuance of deduction of Rs, 5 from the dearness allowance 
in the present company. The present rate of dearness allowance for the 
subordinate staff is Rs. 61 per momh. The company pays the whole 
amount of Rs. 61 without deducting Rs, 5 as permitted under the award of 
1949, The Emplovees’ Union has no grievance regarding dearness allowance 
of the clerical staff. It demands that the dearness allowance the subordinate 
staff should be linked with the middle-class cost of living index T find 
nothing to uphold this claim. Difference between middle-class cost of 
living index and working-class cost of living index lay on the stress which 
18 age on the different items of necessities which are, however, common 
in both the categories. This is very natural. The subordinate staff cannot, 
therefore, have any grievance and the claim for dearness allowance linked 
with middle-class cost of living index is accordingly rejected.

declaratory relief,

settled that both forms of retiring | ক পরী কি Fund and Gratuity

benefits to the employees of the clerical and subordinate staff. After 

aving done so, it will be in the fitness of things that the company now 
extends full operation of the scheme of gratuity without making deduction 
مہ‎ that the employees may get full benefit out of the same on retirement. 
The demand of the workmen is عسطا‎ considered reasonahle and it appear 
that the company has also financial capacity to hear the burden. The 
demand for discontiuance of deduction of company’s share of contribution 
to the provident fund from the gratuity is accordingly granted.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
LAW (JUDICIAL) DEPARTMENT 


RESOLUTION No. 653J. 


Calcutta, the 28th January 1959. 


Government have received with deep regret the news of the untimely 
death of Shri Phatik Chandra Ray Chaudhuri, lately Chief Judge, Court 
of Small Causes, Calcutta, on Monday, the 19th January 1969. 


Shri Ray Chaudhuri joined the Bengal Civil Service (Judicial) in 1935. 
He served in various districts in Bengal and Assam and after 1947 in West 
Bengal, from the 23rd April 1935 to the 22nd December 1955 at first as 
Munsif and later as Subordinate Judge and Assistant Sessions Judge. He 
was promoted to officiate in the West oct سو‎ Higher Judicial Service from 
the 23rd December 1955 and was appointed as District and Sessions Judge, 
Birbhum. In June 1968, he was appointed as Additional District and 
Sessions Judge, 24-Parganas. In September 1958, he was appointed as Chief 
Judge, Court of Small Causes, Calcutta. He was confirmed as District and 
Sessions Judge in the cadre of the West Bengal Higher Judicial Service 
from the 11th May 1956. He was suddenly taken الا‎ and wus on leave from 
the 12th January 1959 until his demise on the 19th January 1959. 


Throughout his service Shri Ray Chaudhuri upheld the highest tradi- 
tions of integrity and devotion to duty of the judicial service. His sense 
of fairness and his pleasant personality earned for him the esteem and 
affection of all those who came in contact with him. 


The Government of West Bengal desire to record their profound regret 
at the untimely loss of an experienced officer and wish to convey to his family 
the sincere expression of their sympathy. 

By order of the Governor, 
K. K. HAJARA, 
Secy. to the Govt. of West Bengal.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


Under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, and certain other 
tux laws of the State and also the Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 
1913, action is required to be taken for matters connected with the purposes 
of those Acts including the issue of registration certificates and initiation 
of proceedings for the realisation of taxes and recovery of arrears of taxes 
in the name of a person or persons. 


. Due to practical didicullies, however, 11 is not always possible for 
the Commercial Taxes Directorate to avoid issuing registration certificates 
and initiating assessment proceedings in the trade name of a business 
rather than in the name of its proprietor. Certificates for the recovery of 
the arrears of taxes are also sometimes filed in such trade names. The 
object of the present Bill is to safeguard revenue by rendering all such 
actions and proceedings free from objection.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
HOME DEPARTMENT 
Constitution and Elections 


NOTIFICATION 


No. 261A.R.—5th February 1959.—In exercise of the power conferred 
by clause (2) of article 166 of the Constitution of India and in supersession 
of all previous rules made in this behalf, the Governor is pleased to make 
the following rule :— 


Rule under clause (2) of Article 166 of the Constitution of India 


Orders and other instruments made and executed in the name of the 
Governor shall be authenticated by the signature of a Secretary, 
a Joint Secretary, a ee Secretary, an Under Secretary or an 
Assistant Secretary to the Government of West Bengal, or of an 
Officer of the Government of West Bengal specially empowered in 
this behalf by the Governor. 


Ezplanation.—In this rule the reference to a Secretary, a Joint 
Secretary, a Deputy Secretary, an Under Secretary and an Assistant 
Secretary shall include, respectively, references to an Additional Secretary, 
an Additional Joint Secretary, an Additional Deputy Secretary, an 
Additional Under Secretary and an Additional Assistant Secretary. 


By order of the Governor, 
S. N. RAY, 
Chief Secy. to the Govt. of West Bengal.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


In accordance with the provisions of the Dentists Act, 1948, which came 
in force on the 29th March, 1948, applications fur first registration were 
received up to 31:1 March, 1060, the appointed date under section J2 of the 
Act and the first registration of dentists was completed in 1950. 


The dentists who were in the State of West Bengal during the time of 
first registration had the opportunity of registering their names with the 
West Bengal Dental Council according to their respective qualifications. 
The dentists of Cooch Behar and Ohandernagore which were merged with 
the State of West Bengal on the 1৭1 January, 1950 and 2nd October, 1954, 
৮1 and in which areas the Dentists Act, 1948, was not in force 
before such merger, could not avail of the privilege of registering their 
names with the said Council in the first register. Although the persons 
having recognised dental qualifications mentioned in the Schedule to the 
Act are eligible for registration, the dentists of the said areas who had been 
im practire a» principal means of livelihood for not less than five years 
Lefore the appointed date, that is, the 3lst March, 1950, cannot have the 
privilege of registration like those who were in the State of West Bengal 
before merger of the said areas with the State of West Bengal, as the date 
has already been over. 


In order to ameliorate the hardship gf the dentists practising in Cooch 
Behur and Chandernagore an amendment to the Act was considered essential 
and the Government of India were moved for the same. The Government of 
India observed, inter alia, that this wad a Jedal matter and the State Legis 
Jature might be prompted to amend the Act. This Bill, which has the con- 
currence of the Government of India, has been framed with this object 0 


view.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The Wild Life in West Pengal is in a sad state of depletion and many 
interesting apecies are fast becoming extinct. The tempo of expanded 
human activity in modern times tends to eliminate wild life. The imbalance 
which results from such destruction has far-reaching adverse consequences 
on the material welfare of man; the diminution of the rich variety of wild 
life will be detzimental to the cause of science; und the indulgence in, or 
the adoption of an apathetic attitude towards senseless slaughter has a 
stultifying effect on the human apirit. 

This realisation has led many countries in recent times to tighten their 
game laws and to enact more ৪৮ legiglation in order to extend 
the scope of the protection of wild life and wild life habitats. It 1s 
also these considerations that gave rise to the establishment, in our country, 
of the Central Board for Wild life and the State Boards for Wild Life. 
Informed public opinion, the Central Board and our State Board for Wild 
Life have all been insistent on the early introduction of effective legisla- 
tion to prevent further depletion of our wild life heritage. The present 
Bill has been drafted in compliance with this growing demand. 

The Wild Birds and Animals Protection Act, 1912 is sketchy; it has 
been ineffective as offences ugainst the Act are non-cognizable. The pro- 
posed legislation makes such offences cognivable. It also purports to 
restrict snuring and trupping; to regulate the trade in trophies and pet 
animals; to make provision tor the constitution of wild life habitats even 
outside the Reserved and Protected Forests into sanctuaries; to impose 
deterrent penalties for crimes against wild life; and to provide for the 
0-4 of officers and Honorary Game Wardens to implement the 
new law. 

With the above objects in view 16 has been proposed to enact the West 
Bengal Wild Life Preservation Bill, 1959. 


H. C. NASKAR,

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 


DEPARTMENT OF LOCAL SELF- 
COVERNMENT AND PANCHAYATS 


RESOLUTION 


No. 1226/M.1M-19/59.—18th February 1959.— 
The attention of Government has been drawn to 
the serious situation which has arisen in the 
Raiganj Municipality in the district of West 
ای مد‎ as a result of the resignations tendered 
by all the nine Commissioners of the said muni- 
cipality. It appears that seven Commissioners of 
the municipality, including the Chairman and the 
Vice-Chairman, submitted their letters of resigna- 
tion which were considered and accepted at a 
meeting of the Commissioners held on the 5th 
February 1959. The remaining two Commis- 
sioners also sent their letters of resignation to the 
District Magistrate of West Dinajpur after the 
date of the aforesaid meeting. Although their 
resignations have not been formally accepted by 
the Commissioners at a meeting as required under 
sub-section (4) of section 60 of the Bengal 
Municipal Act, 1932, these two Commissioners 
cannot carry on the administration of the munici- 
pality until the vacancies caused 0 the 
resignations of seven Commissioners are filled up 
as their number is insufficient to form the neces- 
gary quorum prescribed in section 82 of the Act. 
A situation has thus been created in the munici- 
pality in which there is no one to carry on its 
administration which has virtually reached a state 


of deadlock. 
275 


276 THE CALCUTWA GAZETTE, KATRAURDINAKY, [Pant] 
FEBRUARY 13, 1959 


চি 

Aiter 3৮025215101 consideration of the matter, 
Government have come to the conclusion that the 
Commissioners of the Raiganj Municipality have. 
by their conduct as aforesaid, clearly shown their 
incompetency to perform the duties imposed on 
them by or under the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932, 
and that the present state of affairs cannot under 
any circumstances be allowed to continue without 
serious detriment to the interests of the residents 
of the municipality. 

In the exercise of the power conferred by 
section 553 of the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 
بد اس‎ Act XV of 19382), the Governor is, 
therefore, pleased to declare the Commissioners of 
the Raiganj Municipality to be incompetent and 
to supersede them for the period from the date of 
publication of this resolution in the Calcutta 
Gazette to the $list March 1960. 


ORDERED that this resolution be published in 
the Calcutta Gazette. 


By order of the Covernor, 
A. NIYOGI, 
Jt. Secy. to the Govt. of West Bengal.

surveillance of persons suffering from, or suspected of being infected with 
small-pox in. the said districts for a period of six months:—

State Government:

in writing, into any premises or building used for humun habitation at any 
time between sunrise and sunset for the purpose of carrying out any 
measure or making any enquiries authorised by these regulations. 


37. The crew of any inland steam vessel or bout which plies in any 
canal or river and other persons on board such vessel or boat shall he 
subject to these regulations. 


38. (1) All vaccinations under these regulations shall be performed 
gratuitously provided they be done (a) at such public vaccination stations 68 
may be opened or (b) by house-to-house visits in the case of such females 
as are by the custom of the country unable to attend at publie- vaccination 
stations and are too poor to pay fees.

VIII of 

at STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


The Sikh Gurdwaras both historic and others are situated 
aud squattered in almost all States und parts of Lndia and 
are held in great esteem and reverence by the entire ১110) 
Community. For lack of uniform legislation they are 
managed and governed by different sets of rules and 
regulations mostly influenced by local customa und usages. 
There ,is no unformity in the performance of Sikh rites and 
ceremonies in the Sikh Gurdwaras. 


The Bill seeks to secure better administration of the Sikh 
(furdwaras which may he duly notified by the Government, 
by having more effective and efficient supervision and 
superintendence of the Board over the Committers of 
Management of (furdwaras spread over various territories of 
4ndia. The Bill also seeks to bring uniformity in the 
performance of all religious rites in all the Sikh Gurdwara: 

١ 


Hence thia Bill. | 
16th June, 1958. A. S. 3101,

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED 
LEGISLATION 


Clause 66 authorises the Board to make hye-laws 
cousisteut with this law us to the procedure, functioning and 
fees to be levied under clause 77. 

Clause 7) authorises the Committee of Notified Sikh 
Gurdwarn to make regulations consistent with this law as to 
the procedure of all proceedings. 

Clause 87 of the Bill deals with the rule making power 
of the Central Government consistent with this law. The 
matters in respect of which rules may be made are set out 
in that clause. 

The rule making powers sought to be conferred are of a 
normal character.

By order No, 4794-1.R./ ik ভা dated the 9th December 1957, 
the Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred under 
section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Indian Hume Pipe Company Lid., P.O. Barakuar, district 
Burdwan, and their workmen represented by the Barukar Hume Pipe 
Workers’ Union, P.O. Barnkar, district Burdwan, regarding the matters 
specified in the schedule, to the Third Industrial Tribunal, constituted under 
rection 7A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, by notification No. 804- 
I.R./TR/cA-2/57, dated the 11th March 1957, for adjudication. 


2. After usual summons the parties put in appearance and filed their 
written statements. The pleadings were completed on 10th February 1958. 
The parties were thereafter directed to file lists of documents. Then after 
adjournments the dispute was heard and award was reserved. 


$. The matiers of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference ure as follows:— 

(1) Categorisation of workmen and fixation of scales of pay. 

(2) Increment in basic wager. 

(3) Housing and housing allowance. 

(4) Festival holidays. 

(9) Lf closure during 19th August 1957 to 27th August 1907 was 
- Justified, what relief the workmen are entitled to? 

(6) If discharge of Shri Beuu Binode Dingal was justified: what relief, 

if any, is he entitled to? 


(1) Whether suspension for 4 days of Shri Ananda Bihar was justified;

On the materials placed before the Tribunal, it is rather difficult to come 
to any definite conclusion in the matter of designation and classification. 
No evidence has been given apart from assertions in the pleadings. This 
is too technical a job which, in my opinion, should he done by experts in 
this line. The Central Puy Commission felt the same difficulty and 
made the following recommendations :— 


“The assignment of a particular worker to one category or another 
must largely be u matter of opinion based on standards recognised 
in industry. It seems to us that it will be convenient if each 
important industria] establishment will constitute a Board, say, 
of three of its officers, to determine the class in which every worker 
in that establishment is to be based. The classification will, -of 
course, be reviewed from time to time.’’ 


The question of classification is essentially 1 matter for the Company, 
based upon standards recognised in any particular industry. Although 
the materials are not sufficient to come to any definite conclusion in the 
mutter, it cannot at the same time be ignored that there are real causes for 
the workmen to herome sore over the matter on account of absence of 
designation and classification. When according to the Company there 
have been designations and classifications in its Coimbatore Factory, there 
1s no reason why it would not do ad in this factory. The Company should, 
therefore, take immediate steps to designate the workmen and classify 
them according to the catogury of skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled having 
regard to the nature of work done by each. It is both in the interest of 
the employer and employees that this should be done at the earliest possible 
opportunity. After this is done if the Union thinks that justice has not 
been done in respect of any particular employee, such specific case may 
then be taken up for redress. 


Regarding claim of incremental pay scales, the principles are to be 
found in the case of Britannia Building reported in 1954 7,.A.C. 11. 
In¢rementa] pay scales can be allowed only when the employer has both 
financial ability and stability. In the present case though the Company 
has not pleaded want of financial ability, it, however, appears that its 
stability is uncertain as claimed by the Company having regard to the 
nature of the production it undertakes in its factory at Barakar, As one 
caunot be certain about the stability of its factory at Rarakar, I agree that 
incremental pay scales cannot be introduced here. 


Regarding basic wages I, however, find no justification not to concede 
the minimum of Re. 1 per day as claimed for each of the daily-rated 
workmen (ride Ext. 3). It is to he considered whether the said sum should 
be regarded as the absolute minimum of a worker of the lowest category. 
In the matter of minimum an industry has to pay the same irrespective 
of the question of capacity to pay. The principles of fixation of wages 


Pant I] THE CAL. GAZ, EATRY., FEB. 19, 1959 315 
ওরস সা স্পস্ট —_ ই... ১ স্পিন সি... 
have been discussed and settled by the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal 
11) Buckingham and Carnatick Mills 00.) Ltd. vs. Workers of the Company. 
11 has been found that the floor level of wages of au industrial worker 
must be such as would enuble him 10 maintain three consumption units 
including himself in a state of efficiency with provision for education, 
medical expenses and amenities. This is the minimum which the worker 
must have irrespective of the capacity of the industry or of his employer 
to pay. In that particular case Their Lordships fixed the minimum wages 
nt 138. 28 per month considering the available muterials bearing on the 
matter. On similar considerations the amount of minimum basic’ wage 
was fixed at Rs. 30 per month or Rs. 1-2-6p per day for the engineering 
industry. In the case of jute industry the total minimum emolument was 
fixed at Rs. 58.50nP. per month under First Award of 1948. It rose to 
Rs. 68.4001. os a result of the Second Award of 1951 and it was enhanced 
to Rs. 67.17 nP. as ৮, result of Third Award of 1955. In the case of 
engineering industry it was Rs. 54 under the First Award of 1948 and 
Rs. 61 os a result of the Second Award of 1950. Under the last award of 
Engineering Tribunal in 1958 the basic wage for an unskilled worker has 
been raised to Rs. 35 and dearness allowance to Rs. 36 yielding a total of 
Rs. 71. Even if the industry at Barakar would come under the classtfica- 
tion of Ceramic Industry or Glass Industry and not under Engineering 
Industry, I would find no justification on the part of the Company not to 
give the minimum basic wage of Re. | per day as claimed. The said 
minimum basic wage of Re. 1 per day taken with dearness allowance of 
Rs. 1-6 per day would yield a total of Rs. 61-12 for 26 working days in o 
month and this must be considered io be the absolute minimum of a worker 
of lowest category. The awards relating to their own factories at Coirmba- 
tore and Delai نل‎ that nowhere the Company pays basic wages below 
Rs. 30. The basic wage has, of course, to be determined on the basis of 
industry-cum-region. There is, however, nothing to show that a lesser 
minimum is current on induatry-cum-region basis. I, therefore, allow the 
claim of the Union for a minimum basic wage of Re. 1 per day. The 
statement Ext. H filed by the Company giving existing wages show that 
out of 20 employees named therein, 19 get hasiec wages below Re. ] per 
day. Their daily wages in some cases go as low as annas 8 per day (vide 
Ext. 10). The minimum of annas 10 aa shown in the Company’s state- 
ment (Ext. H) is apparently as a result of subsequent enhancement given 
to those who had basic wage of annas 8. Je that as it may, the existing 
basic wage below Re. 1 taken with the existing dearness allowance of 
Rs. 1-6 cannot be considered to be adequate minimum. The claim of the 
Union for a minimum basic wage of Re. 1 per day should, therefore, 
prevail. The Company is accordingly directed to pull up the workmen 
who get basic wage helow Re. 1 per day to the said minimum of Re. 1. 
For those who get basic wage above Re. 1 per day, T find that the Company 
is under obligation to grant them biennial increment of annas two per 
day. So I do not allow separate increment to them. It is, however, hoped 
that the Company would continue the beinnial increment of annas two per 
day as stipulated in the agreement, dated 26th November 1956. Regarding 
the watchman Shri Janak Bahadur who ia on monthly basis, it appears 
that his basic wage is Rs. 48 per month. I consider it to be fair compared 
to the basic wages of two other watchmen (Jit Bahadur and Bir Bahadur) 
which would be only Re. 1 per day. The issue ia decided accordingly.

with housing or should be granted house rent allowance of Rs. 10 per

ক 007 or house rent allowance. The demand is accordingly 
rejected.

The question now is whether dismissal of Shri Benu Binod Dingal and 
suspension of Shri Ananda Behura is justified. On giving careful considera- 
tion to the matter 1 may forthwita note that I am unable to accept either 
dismissal of Benu Binod Dingal or suspension of Ananda Behara an 
justified. The Company has admittedly standing orders (vide paragraph 8 
of their written statement). The stauding orders would, therefore, regulate 
the conduct of the parties and their service conditions. The Company has 
not produced the standing orders in support of management's actions against 
the workmen. There is nothing to show that under terms of their employ- 
ment these workmen were liable to work anywhere and everywhere according 
to the direction of the management. They were admittedly ordinary 
workers of unskilled or semi-skilled category and cannot, therefore, prima 
facie be asked 10 operate the main power engine of the factory whieh 
according to Company is the work of a worker of skilled category. So the 
order in this respect by the Manager cannot he accepted as either reasonable 
or lawful. If the direction be not lawful or reasonable, it is obvious there 
would be no disobedience or insubordination. The mere fact that these two 
workmen in the past worked the engine—Benu Binod Dingal for 1} years 
ond Ananda Behara for a day on one occasion—would not authorise the 
management to direct them to run the engine against their will, and with- 
oul payment of legitimate wages. Benu Binod Dingal did nothing wrong 
in ‘Imposing terms before agreeing to work the engine having regard to the 
treatment he had received in the past. Likewise Ananda Behara was within 
his right to refuse to work the engine as he was an ordinary worker of 
unskilled category, and not liable to work the engine under terms of employ- 
ment, The whole question in this respect, therefore, resolves into whether 
the workmen had any obligation in terms of their employment to work the 
engine. The Company has nothing to show that they had such obligation. 
Even the standing orders, it has already been noted, has not heen produced. 
This is presumably because they show otherwise. The manner in which the 
matter has been dealt with by the Manager from the very beginning suggests 
want of hona fides on the part of the management. It ‘appears that the 
Manager was not so much keen as -how to work the engine but how to force 
the workmen to run the engine without paying legitimate wages although 
it was not their 101). Before one is held guilty of disohedience, it is to be 
shown that the orders which the workmen are purported to have disoheyed 
are reasonable and lawful. In the present case I am unable to hold ao. 
The charge of disobedience cannot, therefore, be accepted to have heen made

and pay scales rather than one common scale for al] of the clerical ৭1181,

except at the sacrifice of incentive to work and efficiency. At the same

Regarding their minimum basic wage, 1t iy not disputed that 1).A. is 
paid for the cost of living index exceeding point 180. The basic wage 
should, therefore, be fixed with 180 point as cost of living index. The 
principles of fixation of minimum wages have been discussed and settled by 
the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in the case of Buckingham & 
Carnatic Mills Co. Ltd. (reported in 1952 L.A.C. 490) and Caltex (India) 
Ltd. (reported in 1952 L.A.C. 402). It has been found thal the floor level 
of wages of an industrial worker must be such as would enable him to main- 
tain 3 consumption units including himself in a state of efliciency with pro- 
vision for education, medical expenses and amenities. This is the minimum 
which the worker must have irrespective of the capactiy of the industry or 
of his employer to pay. Four factors laid down by the Fair Wages Com- 
mittee Report were considercd. 10 the case of Buckingham & Carnatic 
Company minimum was fixed for 3 consumption units on a cost of living 
index at 100. While in the case of Caltex (India) Litd., the basic mintmum 
salary of a clerk was fixed at Rs. 80 on the basis of cost of living index at 
180, but on a lower estimate of 24 consumption units at the start. The case 
of Caltex (India) Ltd. cannot however bear comparison with the present 
Company as the former ia ص:‎ 011 Company with considerable resources carry- 
my monopoly trade. Besides, in the said case at every stage of calculation 
the figures were rounded. In the case of Karam Chand Thappar & FProthers 
Ltd. decided hy the same Tribunal the minimum of a clerk was fixed at 
Rs. 70 on the cost of living index at 180 with 24 consumplion units at the 
start. The figures arrived at in this case were the oxact figures found on 
calculation. The Mercantile Tribunal of West Bengal also fixed the mini- 
mum of a clerk at Rs. 70 for 3 consumption units but on the living index 
at 100. The minimum fixed in the award of Mercantile Tribunal which is 
in conformity with the one in the case of Karam Chand Thappar is more 
appropriate to the clerical 619 in the present Company. I, therefore, think 
that Rs. 70 is the adequaté minimum for a clerk in this Company. Similarly, 
I consider Rs. 100 to be adequate minimum basic salary for a Stenographer 
in this concern. Having regard to Union’s claim, the Company’s offer as in 
Ext. H and other factors, I lay down the following grades and pay scales 
for the clerks and Stenographers :—

certificate from a registered doctor. Considering the needs of the time I 
raise the quantum of sick leave to 10 days with full pay and 7 days on half 
pay ina year. The sick leave on full pay will accumulate up to 20 days. 
The issue is decided accordingly. 


issue No. 4: Under the award of 1950 working hours as then existed 
were upheld, The workmen in the Company can be divided broadly under 
two categories—those employed in the showroom and those employed 12) the 
workshop. For those employed in the showroom, the hours as prescribed in 
the Shops and Establishments Aci would govern them, while for those who 
are employed in the workshop, the Indian Factories Act will govern them. 
There is nothing to show on the side of the Union thai the existing work- 
ing hours are in excess of those prescribed in these Acts. There is also 
nothing to show that since the award there has been change in the working 
hours of any category of workmen. The demand of the Umon that the 
working hours of the clerks should be from 9-30 a.m. io 5-30 p.m. with one 
hour recess in place of the existing from 9-30 a.m. to 6 p.m. with one hour 
recess, cannot so be allowed. Merely because such working hours prevail 
for the clerks in the Dalhousie Square area would be no sufficient ground to 
introduce it in this Company when the existing hours are less than the 
maximum limit fixed under those Acts. The claim for reduction of work- 
ing hours is accordingly rejected.

wis, therefore, righi in dismissing him in view of the terms of reappoint- 
meet and service rules already referred to and having regard to his past 
conduct. 


As the charge against him was indicated by the Company in their letter 
of suspension ond as the workman has no satisfactory explanation to the 
said charges, I find nothing to interfere. Merely because he was not 
formally proceeded against, (his would be no ground for interference. 
There is no allegation or proof that the action of the Company was mala 
fide or from a motive of victimisution, The circumstances show that the 
fompany 86160 bona fide throughout. It, therefore, follows that the work- 
man is entitled to no relief, 


This is my award.

3. The only issue arising for decision as per the order of reference 
stands as follows: سے‎ 
Are the workmen at the factory as well us al the Head Office entitled 
aa 10 bonus for the years 1994 and 1954 and, if ,ہہ‎ what should be the 
quantum of bonus for those years? 


AWARD 


According to the Union lhe Company is an old and well-reputed concern, 
and is steadily expanding its business. It manufactures railway fencings, 
steel fabrications, etc., as also does take undertakings of contract for agri- 
cultural and industrial buildings. It also does import business of barbed 
wires, nettings, ete. The Union claims four months’ basic pay as ‘bonus for 
the year 1954 and also a similar quantum for 1955. This claim is said to be 
exclusive of the customary Puja bonus of one month. - 

The Company contends that it is a branch of A. & J. Main & Co. Ltd, 
a firm of structura] engineers incorporated in Great Britain. Tt is an engi: | 
neering concern, pure and simple. 14 designs, fabricates and erects steel 


Part 1] THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., FEB. 19, 4959 37 


structittes. 18 has no import business. 16 employs 52 persons in the Head 
Office and 200 workmen in its Howrah factory. During the year 1954 there 
-was op illegal strike by the workmen for several weeks resulting in loss in 
trade. But the Company still granted bonus of one month’s salary 
ex-gratta, only ما‎ maintain amicable relation with the workmen, and to 
keep up increased production. It also granted one month’s salary as bonus 
for 1955 though, it contends, there was no available surplus according to 
the formula set forth by the Labour Appellate Tribunal of India in the case 
of Bombay Mill Owners’ Association versus Rastriya Mill Mazdoor Sangha, 
[It stubbornly denies the existence of any Puja bonus or customary bonus in 
the Company as a condition of service. Lastly, it contends that the claim 
of bonus for 1954 and 1955 is a belated one and, as such, liable to be 
rejected. 


Coming to the issue itself, I find on evidence that the balance-sheet as 
per the supplementary profit and loss account for 1954 shows a loss to the 
extent of 10. 90,000 and odd. It is now well-established law, and it has 
also been held by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the Muir Mills case that 
no bonus would be available for the year in which the Company has 
sustained a loss. “No profit, no bonus 1s the guiding principle’. Parti- 
cularly, the workmen here are not entitled to a rm any bonus in the face 
of loss resulting from any strike or 5810৮ down” resorted to by them. I need 
not go into the detailed calculation on the lines of the formula set forth for 
bonus in the aforesaid case in respect of the yeur 1954, because loss is fatal 
to such claim. 


Regarding the claim of bonus for the year 1955, | have taken charts of 
yeomputation both from the Company und the Unions based on the lines set 
forth in the aforesaid Labour Appellate Tribunal’s formula. Before I go 
{nto the actual calculation I dispose of the preliminary objections raised রে 
the Company to defeat the claim of bonus for the year 1955. The 00101097718 
188 objection is that the claim is a belated one. It was held in the Muir 
Mills case by the Hon’ble Supreme Court that 0 belated claim for bonus, 
viz., when the accounts have already been settled and the amounts distri- 
buted, cannot be sustained. This position in law has not been controverted 
by the representatives of workmen before me. They, however, contend that 
the claim on fact is not a belated one. Exhibit C filed by the Company 
shows that the accounts for the year ending 3let December 1955 were closed 
on the 24th August 1956. I find from the Ext. 1 that the Workmen’s Union 
already made a demand for annual bonus im respect of the year 1955 on the 
28th September 1956. So the claim scems to have been made only a month 
after the accounts had been closed of the year 1955, as admitted by the Com- 
any in the Ext. C. If I take into account some time which is bound to 
apse between the points of time of the closure of accounts and its coming 
to the knowledge of the workmen, I must hold that the claim for bonus in 
respect of 1955 is not at all a belated one. ‘[his disposes of the preliminary 
objection in respect of bonus claimed by the workmen. 


The other objection about bonus 18 that 1 was never a customary or 
Puja bonus, and that it was not a condition of service. The Union on whom 
the onus Jay in this respect, has not placed any evidence before me to come 
to the conclusion that there was any bonus which was either customary or 
which was treated as a condition of service. To answer the requirements in 
such 1) ease it is necessary to show thai such payment of bonus is continu- 
ous, and that it must trace back its origin to a distant date. It must also 
he shown that such bonus was paid despite losses. But such evidence is 
wanting here. So J find that there is no honus here in this Company which 
= be claimed either as Puja bonus or customary bonus or as a condition 
01 service.

AWARD

inafter described as the Company for the sake of brevity). 


The facts in this case, as stated by the Union, in brief, are as follows :— 


The Company is a successor to the Joint Route Committee for 1009 
No. 51, Route No. 54 and Route No. 56 after the aforesaid Joint Service 
Committee ceased to exist on or about 15th August 1957,

the said Route Vommittee and a neur relation of Shri Sachindra Nath 
Bhowmic, the Secretary of the said Route Committee, came to the place 
of duty of Shri Ganguly and tried to interfere m an irregular manner 
against which Shri Ganguly protested. Shri Ganguly availed himself of 
2 days’ leave on 24th October 1997 und 25th October 1957 and on 26th Octo-

sheets’ from Shri Ganguly’s hand and unjustly and abruptly terminated his 
yervice. Shri Ganguly was not charge-sheeted, nor was any enquiry held.

The Company, in its written statement, denies the material allegations 
in the written statement of the Wmion, and contends that it was a case of 
voluntarily leaving services for reasons best known to the workman. He 
left the job without submitting any explanation while enquiry was pending.

amicably and the terms of settlement are that Shri Ganguly will not press

in two instalments first instalment by February 1959 and the second and 
lust instalment in April 1959. Both parties therefore pray for an award in

The terms of the petition of compromise appear to be fair, reasonable 
and lawful and may he given effect to. 


The dispute is therefore disposed of in terms of the petition of com- 
promise which do form a part of the award.

fuctors—(1) the capacity of the industry to pay and (2) the cost of living 
index justifying variation of its amount. Ordinarily neutralisation between 
60 to 90 per cent. are allowed in the case of manual workers. At present, 
all except one out of 7 total of 12 gets dearness allowance at the flat rute of 
{en annas a day or Rs. 16-4 a month. Ten workmen, out of them one is 
skilled, are getting more than Rs. 68 per month. T see no justification 
whatsoever why Nimai Chandra Ghose and Nilmoni Menta he paid, though 
doing the work of a regular worker, wages not exceeding Re. 52 and 
18৭. 45-12, respectively. There is also no justification why Nilmoni should 
not be paid any dearness allowance at all. 


Considering the fact that there has been admittedly a rise in the cost 
of living index in the last three or fowr years by more than 20 points and 
also the fact that the Company hus the financial capacity 10 pay for an 
increase in the dearness allowance sufficient to neutralise this rise up to a 
certain point, I allow dearness allowance at the flat rate of thirteen annas 
per day in place of ten, i.e., a total increase of Rs. 4-14 for a month of 
20 duys, to al] workmen, including Nilmoni Mehta. Nimai Chandra 
(those should also get an increment of eight annas per day over his existing 
rate of wages (Re. 1-6 per day). That would enable him to earn a mintmum 
busic rate of wages. 


As to the demand for allowing four grades with imeremental scales of 
pay, I am afraid, 1 cannot do that. Considering the nature of the business 
and iis present financial position, I should not 01706110806, for the first time 
in its history, any incremental scales of pay with grades. Further, classi- 
fication of workmen according to grades demanded, is ×× fairly difficult 
job, which has become, more so, due to absolute absence of proper materials 
on record on this point. Classification of workers, aceording to skill is ne 
longer considered desirable, for skill has now been transferred from the may 
to the machine. A man's work is now better assessed by his manipulating 
wwer to operate a machine. In classifying workers into grades, the 
est of service, physical and mental strain, effort, ete., of the workers 
are also to be taken into consideration. Therefore, the classification of 
workmen, into four grades as supggesied on behalf of the Union, cannot be 
undertaken in this dispute for want of proper materials. I accordingly, 
do not nake any endeavour to do it. The increment in wages and ۱1۱٥٥٥٥ 
allowance under this award should take effect from February 1959. I 
answer the issue accordingly,

AWARD 


The Company No. 1, Messrs. B. 11. Agrahati, states that it is a con- 
tractor appointed by the Railway Board of the Government of India for 
handling railway goods at Howrah goods shed and it employs about 450 
workmen. These workmen, commonly designated as coolies: are employed 
by the Cmpany as contractors on tenders for loading and unolading of goods 
from railway wagous to stations and vice versa. These contracts usually 
last for 3 years, but are liable to be terminated on three months’ notice by 
the Railway at their pleasure. This Company states that the dispute had 
heen preferred by the Wnion before the Regional Conciliation ()fficer of the 
(fovernment of India, and was at no stage raised before the State Govern- 
ment. The appropriate Government for the purpose of this reference was 
the Central (iovernment and not the State Crovernment of West Bengal. 
The Company No. 6, being Messrs. S. (. Kundu, and the Company No.3, 
heing Messrs. H. C. Dey & G. K. Agarwal, also raised the same objection, 
viz., that the appropriate Government competent to make the reference 
14 the Central Government and not the State Government of West Bengal. 
Tn the cireumstances, an additional issue has to be decided by the Tribunal 
and the following issue is, therefore, framed for decision :—~ 


Issue No, 4.—Is the present reference of the dispute by the West 
Bengal Government competent? 


Part 1] THE CAL, GAZ, EXTRY., FER. 19, 1959 303 


= wc << «meee: ےج‎ 
ہے‎ রগ — = ees ees ee 


The issues ure taken up for decision here below. 


issue No. 4: The point tor decision in this issue is) whether the 
reference of the present industrial dispute by the State Government of 
West Bengal is competent. The learned Advocates tor the Companies 
press that as the Companies, which are contractors under the Railway 
Administration, the appropriate Government tor making the reference 
under section 2(n) of the Industrial Disputes Act is the Central Government 
and not the State Government. 16 is also stated that at all stages of the 
‘tlispute, the conciliation proceedings between the Companies and the Union 
were conducted before the Regional Conciliation Officer of the Government 
of Indias that for that reason, the State Government had no reason to 
hold that any such industrial dispute, as has been referred to the Tribunal, 
exists, or was apprehended. This contention that the appropriate Govern- 
ment for the present reference is the Central Gfovernment has been opposed 
by the learned Advocate for the Union. 


On a consideration of the matter, T have no doubt that the objection is 
unworthy of support for the following reasons. It was argued by the 
learned Advocates tor the Companies that as the Companies were contractors 
under the Railway Company, they were carrying on an industry under the 
authority of the Railway Company, and it is to be considered that the 
industry of the Companies in the present cave was an industry carried on 
by or ander the authority of the Central Government. The Companies are 
contractors under the Ruilway Bonrd. Section 2(a)(i) of the Act does not 
provide that for an industry carried on under the authority of a Railway 
Company, the appropriate Company was the Central (tovernment. In 
relation to a dispute of a Railway Company itself, the Central Government 
is the appropriate (10611120161, The section does net provide that the 
Central Government will be the appropriate Government in relation to an 
industrial dispute carried on by or under the authority of a Railway 
Company. If the contractors are considered to be carrving on an industry 
under the authority of the Railway Company, their industry is uot covered 
by section 2(a)(1) of the Act. I do not, however, consider that the Com- 
panies as contractors carry on an industry by or under the authority of the 
Railway Company. The next question for ‘consideration is if the con- 
tractors carry on an industry by or under the authority of the Central 
(fovernment. The decision of the Hon'ble High Court at Caleutta in 
Bharat Glass Works Private Ltd., reported in 1958(T) ...ا‎ 467, shows 
that no business owned or carried on by a private person or a limited 
company can be a business carried on by or under the authority of the 
(105৫0101601, In view of the decision of Harris C. J. in the case of 
Carlsbad Mineral Water Manufacturing 00,171, reported in 1982(1) 
.ا ,ا‎ dos 488, which was approved and accepted by the Hon'ble Judge in 
the Bharat Glass Works cave, it appears that the business of the present 
coutractors was their own business, which they were conducting for their 
own personal profit and benefit and the contractors in the present case can 
in no sense be described ×× being persons authorised to carry on a business 
of the Government or the Railway Company. That being so, the appro- 
priate Government for the present dispute wonder section 2(a) of the Tndus- 
1191 Disputes Act is the West Bengal State Government and not the 
Central Crovernment. 


It appears that the conciliation proceedings were held before — the 
Regional Conciliation Officer of the Central Government. The West Bengal 
State Government made the reference to the Tribunal for reasons best known 
to them and the act of the Government in coming to the conclusion as to 
the existence or apprehension of an industrial dispute is administrative and 
its correctness cannot be questioned in a court of law. An administrative

order if not vitiated by mala ساد‎ is immune from being impugned in a 
court of law | ride case of Cashewnut Manufacturers’ Association, reported 
in 1953(I) L.1..J., I, 568, 1950 9. C. 222 and 1968(1) L.LJ., 174, Supreme: 
Court|. 11) these circumstances, 1t is awarded that the reference of the 
present industrial dispute by the State of West Bengal to this Tribunal is 
competent and the Tribunal is competent and even hound to adjudicate on 
it. This issue is accordingly answered.

issue No. 2: The Union claims the fullowing holidays:— 

(1) 1 day paid weekly holiday, 

(2) 15 days paid casual leave, 

(3) 16 days paid privilege leave, 

(4) 15 days paid sick leave, 

(5) 15 days festival holidays, and 


(6) 45 days paid holidays in lieu of casual leave, privilege leave and 
sick 16850, 


০5০8৮ SS era 


The Companies state in their written statements that in view of the 
fluctuating character of labourera engaged by the Companies, the demand 
for leave and holidays is not maintainable. 


On a careful consideration of the matter, it appears to me that the claim 
for casual leave, sick leave, privilege leave und festival holidays, with pay 
is inappropriate in the present case, as the workmen are not en loyed on ৪ 
permanent basis under the contractors and their service is always of ٤ 
casual nature. Jt appears that many of the workers are continuing to 
work under a succession of contractors. The contractors are usually engaged 
for the work for a period of 3 years only. 1 is claimed that many of the 
workers are doing the job for more than 16 or 20 years. Even then, it 28 
not possible to allow the amenities of casual leave, privilege leave, festival 
holidays and sick leave with pay to these workers, as they are not employed 
on ৪ permanent basis and are free to go or be absent at their choice. It is, 
however, awarded that each worker shall get one day as unpaid holiday in 
the week. The wage has been fixed on the 8 of 26 days’ work in the 
month. it is awarded that all workers shall get one day as unpaid holiday 
in a week, or in other words, one day’s unpaid holiday for 6 days’ work in 
{he week, All workers shall get two months’ privilege leave without .pay in 
the year to enable them to go home away from Howrah. No other leave or 
holiday is allowed to the workmen in the circumstances of the case. 


This issue is accordingly answered. 

Issue No. 3: The Union states that the normal working hours shall be 
8 hours and for all work in excess thereof, as well as for work on holidays, 
the workmen ghall be paid double rates of wages. 

The Companies Nos. 1 and 2 state that there is no punctuality of arrival 
of trains and therefore no overtime allowance should be given. 


Qn a careful consideration of the matter, it is awarded as_ follows: 
The normal duty hours of a worker shall be 8 hours in a day and 48 hours 
in the week. When a worker works for more than 9 hours in any day, or 
for more than 48 hours in any week, he shall, in respect of overtime work, 
be entitled to wages at the rate of twice his ordinary rate of wages. 

This issue is acrordingly answered.

No. 114Ex.—18th February 1959.—In exercise of the powers conferred 
by section 5 of the Opium Act, 1878 (1 of 1878), the Governor is pleased 
to make the following amendments in the West Bengal Upium (Restriction) 
Rules, 1952, published with notification No. 7U2F.T., dated the 28th

ordinary, dated the 19; April 1952, us subsequently amended, namely سے‎

‘ ‘ration card’ means a permit granted under these rules authoris- 
ing the holder thereof to purchase excise opium for personal 
consumption on medicinal grounds every week ending with 
Sunday from the licensed shop fixed for registration of the 
holder of the permit in a quantity specified in the permit 
as the weekly quota’”’;

1956 (102 of 1956), or under any other law for the registration

part of India whether in Government employ or otherwise;”’

rests on the quantity of metal produced in the Cell House (vide Ext. 0), 
Now, if this agreement Ext. ( still operates, no bonus can be had on any 
quantity of extra paste produced in the Paste Plant for the simple reason

granting bonus. So that is fatal to the Union’s claim. But the [00101

by the Company. The Company on 10th September 1957 wrote to the

Thus there is a deficit of 53 lakhs, and there is no available surplus. 


In the calculation given by the Union no Rehabilitation cost has been 
provided for. It is suid to have heen included in the depreciation. But 
this I cannot accept because Rehabilitation cost is never synonymous with 
depreciation awarded annually. 


Regarding income-tax, the Union has given deduction of rebate as 
bonus. But this is not as per the Labour Appellate Tribunal’s formula. 
Rehate on bonus is indeterminate. Income-tax notionally has been given 
in the formula on the balance after deduction of normal depreciation. The 
Company has deducted income-tax as per their return on the net profit of 
Rs. 2 lakhs and 30 thousand. That may be correct according to the 
assessment made by the incume-tax authorities, But in the formula of 
bonus a notional amount has been allowed and that on the balance as it 
stands after the deduction of depreciation in the formula. So I do not 
accept the Company’s version about the income-tax. 


Regarding the return on working capital at 4 per cent., the Union has 
made no submission. The Company has given how the working capital 
has been found out. I am at one with the said calculation. The Company 
has shown written down value of fixed assets on 31st December 1956 as 
Rs. 20,48,000 and odd. It has deducted subscribed capital of Rs. 128 lakhs. 
The balance of Ks. 7 lakhs and 98 thousand was found out of the reserves. 
So it must be taken that this amount of reserve was actually utilised as 
working capital. 

Regarding the other branch of the liquid working capital, the Company 
has udded together current assets, loans, advances and cash 870 bank 
htlances amounting to Rs. 1 crore and 50 lakhs. Current habilities 07 per 
the balwnce-sheet amounted to Rs. [ crore and 12 Jakhs. So the working 
capital stood at Rs. 37 lakhs and 87 thousand. This was met partly by 
bank overdraft of Rs. 22 lakhs and 71 thousand. So Rs. 15 lakhs and 15 
thousand which stood as the balance was met by drawing upon the reserve. 
Su the total working capital stands at Rs. 7 lakhs and 98 thousand, and 
Rs. 15 lakhs and 15 thousand, 1.e., together Ra. 23 lakhs and 18 thousand. 


Now, even if 2 per cent. is given on the working capital the total balance 
would not be upset except to the tune of Its. 46 thousand. 


There is no dispuie regarding the return of dividend on the subscribed 
capital. 

Regarding the Rehabilitation charge, the Company has worked out in 
the tollowing manner: 

The total original cost value on 31st December 1956 as = the halance- 
sheet stood at 108. 39 Jakhs and odd. From that Rs. 2 lakhs have been 
deducted as additions made during the year. The balance Rs. 37 lakhs was 
myltiplied ط‎ 2.7. Then the breakdown value at 5 per cent. and the total 
depreciation were deducted. The balance stood at Rs, 74 lakhs and odd. 
This was divided by 15, that being the normal life and efficiency of 
macheneries. So the annual replacement value would be Rs. 5 lakhs. 


Regarding the fixtures of workshop buildings and offices, the original 
cost value stood at Rs. 20 lakhs and odd. It was multiplied by 2.25 and 
depreciation was deducted. The balance was Rs. 3] lakhs and odd. It 
was divided by 30. So the annual replacement cost came to Rs. 1 lakh 
and odd on this head. So the annual total replacement cost stood at 
Rs. 6 lakhs ond odd. This is the calculation on the lines as given in the 
Appellate Tribunal’s tormula. I accept the Company’s computation on this 
head as correct.

Whether the 15 days’ basic wages given as an advance would be 
recovered and, if so, how, would depend upon the agreement arrived at

So 1 give no direction in the matter,

between Messrs. Brifish Painty (India) Léd., Shaliuar, Howrah, and their 
fechnical and clerical staff represented by British Paints (India) Ltd. 
Employees’ Umion, 283A Netaji Subhas Road (top floor), Caleutta, regarding 
{he matter specified in the schedule, to the Third {ndustrial Tribunal, 
constituted under section 7A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, by 
notification No. 808-1.R./TR/3A-2/57, dated the 11th March 1957, for

2. After usual summons the parties put in appearance and filed their 

‘itten statements. The pleadings were completed on 6th September 1958. 
Bre parties were thereafter directed to file lists of documnts. Then the 
dispute was heard and award was reserved, 


8. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
roference is as follows :— 


Leave and holidays for the technical and clerical staff. 


Decision 

Issue 1! Messrs. British Paints (India) Ltd. (hereinafter called the 
Company) is one of the reputed paint manufacturers in India. The present 
claim has been laid on behalf of the technical and clerical staff attached 
to the factory of the Company at Howrah. The members of the technical 
and clerical staff of the factory get 10 days’ festival holidays with pay and 
14 days’ privilege leave with pay m a year cumulative up to 28 days 
hesides “declared holidays” (a special feature of this Company and said 
te number about 6 days 1) a year) and 10 days’ casual deave with pay. 


The Union demands leave and holidays as follows :— 


Festival holidays—All the holidays as per Neyotiable Instruments Act 
excepting 3011) June, 9186 December and Easter holidays, 


Privilege Jeave—One month with full pay in a year. 


in the number of existing festival holidays ia rejected. Likewise claim of 
the Union during argument for inclusion of the number of ‘‘declared 
holidays’’ in this category cannot be conceded as this would bring the total 
Tiumber of festival holidays to abnormally a high figure at 16 days which 
is not desirable in the interest of smooth running of the factory and 
industrial peace. 


Regarding gages leave, the Union alleged that technical and clerical 
staff of most of the offices carrying on similar trade enjoyed privilege leave 
of not less than 28 days with full pay in a year. In support the Union files 
statement (Ext. 3). Out of the five companies mentioned therein it is 
admitted that No. 1 Messrs. Shalimar Works Private Iitd. is not a paint 
manufacturing concern but an engineering concern. None from the four 
other concerns has been brought to show that really 28 days 
privilege leave are granted in those concerns. The statement does 


Parr I] THE CAL. GAZ, EXTRY., FEBRUARY 26, 1959 459 


not 10180 show whether the said 28 duys’ privilege leave are all 
pad leaves. The Assistant Secretary of the Union (P.W. 1) admitted 
thal he has no knowledge whether the privilege leave shown in Ext. 3 are 
paid holidays. There is also no evidence tn show what other kinds of leave 
are granted in these concerns to the clerical staff. If really these four 
concerns grant 28 days’ privilege leave with pay, the existing quantum of 
14 days’ privilege leave in a year as জল for these categories of 
workmen in the factory of this Company can he said to be inadequate. At 
the same time it cannot be overlonked that in this Company there js a 
practice of granting “declared holidays’? which ia a special feature of this 
Company alone. [t is not disputed that such type of holidays does not 
exist anywhere else (vide PW. 1). The number of “declared holidays”, 
it appears, is variable and is so liable to be a source of dispute. ہا‎ there- 
fore, 899 that there would he no justifiention ٥١ continue the ‘declared 
holidays’? separately. It appears that number of auch holidays in a year 
is اس‎ about 6 days. The Company can rightly claim that the number. 
of such holidays is to be taken into account in determining the quantun 
of the privilege leave. The Company is agreenble to grant 7 days more 
privilege leave in lieu of ‘‘declared holidays’’ of about 6 days per annum 
ক ۔((1)8‎ I consider the proposal to be fair and accordingly accept it. 

his would raise the quantum of privilege leave to 21 days with full pay 
ina year, Although the total would not come up to what is said to prevail 
in four other concerns as mentioned in Ext. 3, this would certainly be an 
improvement over what actually prevails for the clerical staff attached to 
the Head Office of the Company in this respect. As further rise would 
muke a great disparity and necessarily bring discontentment amongst the 
clerical staff uttached to the Head Office, I think it will not be in the 
interest of industrial peace to go further in the matter. It appears that 
under awards of both Firat a Second Major Engineering Tribunals 
سان‎ leave for 21 days with pay in a year had been granted for the 
clerical and supervisory staff attached to the factory. So giving due 
consideration to all aspects of the matter 1 fix the number of privilege leave 
with full pay in a year at 21 days cumulative up to 42 duys as fair and 
adequate. The leave as aforesaid is granted in supersession -of the leave 
as is now granted by the Company under the nomenclature ‘‘declared 
holidnys’’. The privilege leave ۵ہ‎ fixed above will be operative from lst 
January 1959. 


This is my award.

2. The reference was received here on 23rd July 1957. After usual 
notices to the parties the Union filed written statement on 3rd November 1957. 
The Company filed written objection on 25th November 1957. After several 
adjournments ihe case was taken up for hearing on 27th January 1959. 
The evidence including the argument was concluded on that date. The 
award was reserved. 


3. The issues which arise for determination under the order of reference 
stand as follows :— 


(1) Whether the management was justified in dismissing Shri Arun 
Kumar Sarkar and Shri K. N. Chaklader and what relief ure 
they entitled to? 


(2) Seale of pay. 
(3) Nearness allowance. 
(4) Leave and holidays. 


Part 1] THE CAL. GAZ, EXTRY., FEBRUARY 26, 1969 461 


AWARD 


4. According to the Union the concern employs about 175 workmen and 
ie equipped with most up-to-dale machineries. It manufactures wooden 
serews Of different types, screw machines, SAP blades of standard sizes, ete. 
The Union was formed in January 1957 just to claim the legitimate economic 
demands. But the Company was perturbed by the formation of the Union 
and dismissed two permanent workmen who were Assistant Secrcturies of 
the Union and who took active part in organising the workmen, There 
was a conciliation proceeding which yieldad no tangible results. Henee the 
present reference, 


According to the Company it is not at all prosperous but has been 
sustaining systematic losses for the last five years. It raises two legal 
objections, viz. (1) that the Tribunal is not competent to go into the issues 
Nous. 2, 3 and 4 which were not before the Conciliation Officer, (2) that the 
issue No. 1 is pre-mature because the Company has not yet dismissed the 
two workmen mentioned. It has only placed them under suspension. But 
as the case was pending before the Conciliation Officer it applied for 
permission to dismiss the said workmen. The said permission 18 not yet 
forthcoming. I¢ is further siated that since January 1959 the Company has 
introduced the minimum scales of pay for different workmen as enjoined 
by the Third Major Engineering Tribunal of 1958, 


Next I turn to the issues. 


issue No. 18 It could not be disputed hy the Union that Shri Arun 
Kumar Sarkar and Shri K. N. Chaklader have not yet been dismissed by 
the Company. The Company decided to dismiss them and for that reason 
hag put in an application before the Conciliation Officer for permission to 
dismiss. The Conciliation Officer has not either granted the permission or 
rejected the application. These two men, are at present under suspension. 
So it is clear that the issue دہ‎ framed by the Government is misconceived, 
The Tribunal has been called upon to decide the question whether the 
management was justified in dismissing the two workmen and to specify the 
consequential relief. But it is clear that they have not been dismissed. 
So the propriety of the order of dismissal which is yet to come cannot be 
gone into a the Tribunal. Noither can the Tribunal decide what should 
be the consequential relief following their dismissal which is still in the 
future. So I hold that the issue is pre-mature and [ am unable to decide 
1 on the facts elicited. 1 have not heen called upon to go into the 
question of the propriety or otherwise of the order of suspension. That was 
evidently a security mensure. At all events, it has not been referred to this 
Tribunal for adjudication. So it does not ٥۰ 


Issue Nos. 2 and 3: These two issues are taken up together because 
the Company grants only a lump-sum as wages. That includes dearness 
allowauce also. Such practice is not very unusual though it is always 
desirable to split up the two and specify the aalary and the dearness 
allowance separately, In the case of retrenchment as in the case of bonus, 
the salary and not the dearness allowance is granted. So in such circum- 
stances the salary is required to be determined. But since this is the 
practice to grant consolidated wages [ do not like to disturb in the present 
case. 1 only see how far the two together is adequate or not. The 
Company has given a list marked Ext. A in which the minimum pay of 
unskilled, semi-skilled and skilled workmen have been mentioned. Under 
the Third Major Engineering Tribunal the minimum salary of unskilled 
Workmen is Rs. 36 per month. The minimum dearness allowance up to 


462 THE CAL, GAZ, EXTRY., FERRUARY 26, 1959 [Part | 
SS Se ge i ae 


Rs. 60 is Rs. 36. ‘The two together make up Ks. 711 per month which the 
Company is granting since January 1968, 


For the semi-skilled category of workmen, the minimum salary is Rs. 40 
per month and the minimum dearness allowance up tu Rs. 50 is Rs. 30. 
So the two together will make Rg. 76, 1:94 what the Compuny is granting 
since January 1909 as per 192৮, A. 


For the skilled category the minimum galary is Rs. 75, the minimum 
dearness allowance from Kis. 61 to Rs. 100 will be 188. 47. So the two 
tugether will make Rs. 122 per month, 1.¢., what the Company has been 
granting since January 1999 aa per Ext. A. So I get that tho present 
Company has conformed to the minimum salary and dearness allowance 
an provided under the award of the Third Major Hnygineering Tribunal of 
1968. | find from Ext. A that other workmen in these different cateyories 
have been getting more than this minimum salary. That must be taken 
to have been adjusted to the respective merit of the said workmen. No 
salary in particular calls for any specific interference from this Tribunal 
in the present case. 


Regarding the introduction of grade.I do not think that the Tribunal 
would be justified in placing this heavy economic burden on 0 Company 
which is already struggling hard against extinction, This unit is bard 
put to it to keep up its existence as I find that it has been suffering 
systematic losses ever since ils inception spreading over the last five years. 
In such circumstances if the grade and scales as outlined by tho Third 
Major Engineering Tribunal are introduced, that will only precipitate the 
crisis and spell disuster to this already tottering concern. 1 quote from the 
award of the Third Major Engineering Tribunal to which 1 was a party at 
page No. 5441, Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary, dated the 5th November 
1958: ‘‘Before this award is concluded, it remains to be answered whether 
the marginal units who are already hard hit by trading reasons will be 
subjected to this new burden of increused basic pay and dearness allowance 
‘and this incremental scale. My first answer will be that 1 am averse to 
make any differential treatment in respect of any trading unit which is 
ہ‎ party to this industry-wise Tribunal and that for the following among 
other reasons: (1) disparity in wage will be the result. ‘That may give 
rise to discontent already noticed; (2) prices of commodities manufactured, 
being linked up with wage, will be different; (3) low wages in one will 
push up sales in one at the cost of another and that there will be an 
unhealthy competition among the employers. But all these considerations 
cease to be important when the very existence of the trading unit is at 
stake. That is why the ‘capacity to pay’ is so essential in granting 
dearness allowance and also fair wage. So I am _ bound to make a 
differential treatment concerning companies which cannot bear a heavy 
financial burden’. These remarks which were made by the Major 
- Engineering Tribunal with reference to the marginal units in the industry- 
wise award, apply mutatis and mutandis to the facts of the present case. 
So regard being had to the systematic losses sustained by this Company 
1 turn down the claim for grades and scales. So 1 do not allow any 0 
und uphold the salary introduced from January 1959 as meeting the ends 
of justice. 


Issue No. : Leave and holidays: The Union haa claimed for the 
clerical section 12 days’ festival holidays, 10 days’ casual leave, 21 days’ 
privilege leave and 15 days’ sick leave on full pay. For the workers, it is 
claimed 12 days’ festival holidays, 15 days’ statutory leave and (8 days’ 
casual leave all on full pay. Tf ۱ turn to the award of the First Major

10 duys’ on half pay. 

Here 1 get from the Manager that the Company grants J0 days’ festival 
holidays and 3 days’ National holidays, viz., the LKepublic Day, the 
Independence Day and the Biswakurma Puja day. So on the score of 
holidays the workmen us well as clerks are getting more than what they

was provided for. But now after the amendment of the Factories Act, 
the statutory leuve has been increased to 18 days in a year or more, Over 
and ubave there are 10 festival holidays. There are also 3 National holidays. 
So altogether the workers get 31 days’ holidays in a year. I ain unable to 
grant them other leave in such changed setting. So the claim for casual 
= or other leave as made by the workers is rejected. So I award as
