Before I part with the records of the case, I dispose of the objection on 
the score of alleged want of jurisdiction in the absence of no issue befure

essential’ that a matter must be mooted or raised before the Conciliation 
Officer before it can be referred to a Tribunal. Government is competent

nspector. 


7% (1) Every medical practitioner called in to attend upon any case 
of small-pox shall forthwith give notice of the case by a special messenger 
to ‘the nearest Sanitary Luspector or lo the Health Officer by post and the 
cost of such messenger in each case shall be defrayed by the State Govern- 
ment. 


(2) The doctor-in-charge of a hospital or a dispensary within the district 
shall forthwith give notice of any case of small-pox brought to such hospital 
or dispensary for treatment to the nearest Sanitary Inspector by a special 
messenger and to the Health Officer by post, and the cost in each case shall 
be defrayed by the State Government. 


8. Presidents of union boards in union board areas and thana officers 
in non-union bourd arcas shall supply to the Tlealth Officer such periodical 
oo 7 cases of small-pox as he may from time to time call upon them

9. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may examine any persou 
who is, or suspected to be, suffering from small-pox or who in his opinion, 
may he infected with or likely to spread small-pox, 


Isolation of patients 


10. When the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector considers that the 
isolation of any patient is a precaution necessary for the protection of the 
neighbouring population, he shall order the patient to observe isolation and 
may order the nearest relative in attendance on the patient, or the occupier 
of the house in which the patient is staying, to arrange for the isolation 
of the patient in such a manner and for such a time as may be approved by 
the Health Officer. 


11. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may order that any 
person, who has been in contact with oa person found to be suffering from 
small-pox, shall be segregated for a period not exceeding a fortnight in a 
manner and in a place to be approved by the Health Officer. 


12. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may order that any 
person who has been im contact with s person found to be suffering from 
রা od ag be vaccinated or re-vaccinated within a time to be specified 
in the order.

Tnapector. ۱ 

14. When a patient has been removed from & house for isolation under 


regulation 10, the State Government shall provide for him free of charge 
& suitable place, with necessary attendants, diet, ete.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH 
Public Health 


NOTIFICATION 


No. P.H./945/2R-40/68.—9th March 1959.—Whereas the Governor is 
satisfied that Chandermmagore, as defined in clause (2) of section 2 of the 
Chandernagore Municipal Act, 1956, in the district of Hooghly, is 
threatened with an outbreak of smallpox; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred hy section 2 of the 
Mpidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (111 of 1897), the Governor is pleased to 
prescribe the following temporary regulations for the prevention and 
contol of smallpox, and for the medical inspection, isolation, observation 
und surveillance of persons suffering from or suspected of being infected 
with smallpox in Chandernagore as defined in clause (2) of section 2 of the 
Chandernagore Municipal Act, 1955, for a period of three months. 


Temporary Regulations for the Prevention and Control of Smallpox 

1. (1) These regulations shall apply to Chandernagore as described in 
cluuse (2) of section 2 of the Chandernagore Municipal Act, 1955 (West 
Nengal Act XVIII of 1955) (hereinafter referred to as Chandernagore), 


(2) They shall come into force at once. 


515 


516 THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., MARCH 10, 1959 = [Parr I 


2. In these regulations, unless there is anything repugnant in the 
subject or context :— 


(a) ‘Tlealth Officer’? means the Health Officer of the Corporation and 
includes the Subdivisional Health Officer, Chandernagore, 
appointed hy the State Government ; 


(b) “medical practitioner’” means any person practising the medical 
profession ; 


(c) “patient’’ means a person suffering from or suspected to be suffering 
from smallpox; 


(d) “Sanitary [nspector’’ means u Sanitary Inspector appointed by the 
Corporation; 

(e) ‘smallpox’? means any disease accompanied by an eruption of 
vesicles or pustules; 


(1) “the Corporation” means the Municipal Corporation of Chander- 
nagore constituted under the Chandernagore Municipal Aet, 1954 


(West Bengal Act 5111 of 1956). 


Notices 


3. If in any case the Wealth Officer or a Sanitary Inspector considers 
that the issue of a notice under these regulations is likely to lead to such 
an amount of delay as might facilitate the spread of smallpox, be may 
forthwith take such steps as he may think fit for carrying out the work and 
shall thereafter, as soon as possible, issue a notice on the person concerned, 
stating the reason why such work has been carried out. 


4. If any measure which the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector ا‎ 
has, by a notice issued under these regulations, required to be carried out, 
be not carried out to his satisfaction within the {ime stated in the notice 
the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector shall be entitled to carry out the 
measure. 


Cost and compensation 


O, (1) All expenses incurred in carrying out any work in pursuance of 
an order issued under these regulations shall be paid by the Corporation 
except in any qase where the order directs a pergon tu carry out any work 
in relation to property in his possession, in which case the expenses shall 
he paid by such person: 


Provided that where the conditions, which led the Health Officer or a 
Sanitary [Inspector to pass such an order, are not attributable to any act 
or defanlt of the person in egg of the property, the Corporation may 
سر‎ to such persou the whole or a part of the expenses incurred by him is 
carrying out the order. 


(2) The Corporation may recover all expensese incurred by the Health 
Officer or 0 Sanitary Inspector in carrying out the measure under regulation 4 
from the person or persons to whom the notice was originally issued. 


6. The Corporation shall pay adequate compensation to any person who 


bas sustained substantial loss or damage by reason of anything done under 
these regulations: 


Provided that no person shall receive any compensation for anything 
done or suffered under these regulations, if 7 has failed to carry out an 
order issued under these regulations within the time specified in the order 
and to the satisfaction of the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector.

isolation of patients

Inspector.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The object of the Bill is to provide for the appropriation out of the 
Consolidated Fund of West Bengal of الم‎ moneys required to meet— 
(a) the grants made by the Assembly; and 
(6) the expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of West Bengal 
but not exceeding, in any case, the amount shown in the finan- 
cial statement previously laid before the House 


for the service of the year 1959-60). 


2. Under the Constitution of India no money can be withdrawn from 
88 Fund of West Bengal except under appropriation made 
y law.

INTERIM AWARD‏ ا 


Un 12th August 1958 the workera of the Company went on a strike. 
Nogotiations for a settlement were poing on for some time. While talks 
of settlement were in progress, a proposal was made that as the workers 
hud not drawn their pay for a pretty long time, the Company would make an 
advance payment 81 the rate of Ra. 75 per month to the Ministerial staff 
and at the rate of Rs. 55 per month to other workers, such advance would 
be realised by monthly deductions from the wage. of the workers from 
January, 1959, in 11 equal instalments. 


Before the Tribunal. the workmen at first prayed for stay of payment 
of the instalments pending the final adjudication of the present reference. 
The offer was not ultimately accepted hy the Company. 


Failing in the above attempt, the workmen filed this petition on 4th 
February 1959 praying for an interim award or order of decision by granting 
an Increase of Rs. 10 per month in wages with effect from October, 1988, 
or for a direction upon the Company to stop all deductions of wagea on 
account of advances taken by the workers. 


It was asserted that the effect of issue No. (I) was that in the final 
adjudication, a sum in excess of Rs. 3 per month might he awarded an basic 
wages, and in addition increased emoluments in the shape of dearness 
allowance, house rent allowance, improved grades or acales of pay might 
also be awarded. It was also asserted that the workers had made a prima 
facie case for the award of the above emoluments aa also for other retiral 
benefits set forth in item No, (II). It was also stated that in those days 
of soaring prices, it would be very hard on the workmen if the monthly 
deductions are made during pendency of the adjudication proceedings. 
The workmen accordingly prayed for stay of the monthly deduction or in 
سوہ‎ for an interim award for Rs. 10 per month from October, 


The Company filed a petition of objection alleging, inter alia, that the 
Trjbunal had no jurisdiction to stop the deduction, which was unconditional, 
and that there are no cogent reasons for making an interim award, that 
there will be no hardship if the monthly deductions are made from the 
wages of the workers. 


The first part of the prayer is taken up first. It appears that while the 
proposals for making an advance payment were being discussed the Joint 
Central Committee of the Tramways men suggested that the a 
whether the advance would be repayable or not, should be decided by an 
independent authority. In reply, the Company by its letter,-dated 22nd 
September 1958, paragraph 5, point No. 2, clearly stated that the repay- 
ment was unconditional. 


It is argued by the workmen that their prayer can be adjudicated upon 
by the Tribunal as the matter was incidental to the industrial dispute 
which has been referred to it, In Stroud’s Judicial Dictionary it has been 
said that a matter is incidental to another matter if the former necessarily 
depends on the latter. This interpretation has been accepted by the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal] in the case of The Punjab National Bank Ltd. 
vs. Their workmen (1952) 1.A.C., page 73. In this view, the deduction 
being unconditional cannot he said to be incidental to the dispute referred. 


The Tribunal has thus no jurisdiction to give a direction to the Company 
7 stop all deductions in realisation of the emoluments in respect of the 
advance, 


576 THI CAL. GAZ., EXTRY.. MARCH 21, 1950 [Parr T 


The question remains whether the alternative prayer for 00৬ interim 
relief by way of an award should be granted or uot. At the time of heuring, 
the amount of interim relief claimed was limited to Rs. 4 per ,زا ×مد:‎ ۷ 
was argued that there can be no doubt that the final award hy way of 
basic wages and increased emoluments would exceed Rs. 5 per month, 


Kvidence has been led on the question whether the agreement to pay 
Rs. 6 as minimum increase in basic wages was unconditienul or not. The 
condition uttaching to the increase, as alleged by the Company but which 
ihe workmen dispute, are that the strike should he called off and that the 
funds of the Company should permit the increase. The fact is that the 
strike was culled off immediately afterwards. 


As regards the other condition, the evidence is conflicting. But there 
is evidence that the introduction of decimal scoinage is expected to bring 
in an additional revenue of 18 lakhs of rupees. It is said by the Company 
that the expectation has not been fully realised and that it will not be so 
realised so ie us the system of double coinuge remains. Such time is 
not far off. 

In these circumstances there is a prima facie case that) the minimum 
addition to the wages of the workmen would not tall below Rs, 5 per month. 


A» regards hardship, if seems to me that in these days, the workmen 
will be hard put to it if there is a monthly deduction of Rs. > or more till 
December, 1959. It bas been pointed out by the workmen that the State 
of West Bengal has granted increased dearness allowance to a section of 
their employees and that several awards of Industrial ‘Tribunals have 0 
recent times conferred udditional monthly benefits on the workmen. It is 
also suid that a Central Pay Commission is cousidering the claims of the 
employees for the award of monthly benefit. On behalf of the Company 
it has heen pointed out that workmen in many other concerns draw Jess 
wages. 11 must be remembered that the workmen did uot draw their 
salary fer the strike period which runs into about six weeks, 


No question of mala fide on the part of the workmen arises, From the 
fact that the first prayer of the workmen was nusconceived and failed, it 
does not follow the workers’ action in pressing a good claim should he 
considered ns mala fide. 


1 may add that the power of the Tribunal to pass an interim award was 
not challenged. [1 will not be difficult to adjust the claims of the parties 
if the final award does not implement the interim award of Rs. > per month. 


My interim award is that the workmen will be entitled to a sum of 
Rs. 5 per month in addition to their present wages. 


Such award will take effect from the Ist February 1994. 
This is my interim award.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, filed by Shri Hrishikesh Sarkar, an employee, against his employer, 
the Howrah Municipality, in connection with 0.0. No. 431-1.R./1R - 
14L-7 57, dated 6th February 1958. (Case No. 160'58 under section 
33A.) 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAT, 


PRESENT! 
Sunt M,N, GAN, Judge, Foarth Tnlustrial Terbanal, 


For the Unions Shm PLS. Basu, Advocate. 


| 
For the Mumeipality: Shri 1. Banerjee, Secretary 0100119৮100 
۸۰ 


This is a complaint by Shri Hrishthesh Sarkar, an employee of Howrah 
‘Municipality, against his employer, in which he alleged that oe was dis- 
missed from service, by a letter, dated 21st July 1958, without the approval 
of this Tribunal before which an industrial dispute between the parties 
was pending for adjudication. He was not paid one month’s wages as 
provided in section 35(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act. Tle served the 
Municipality as a Collecting Sarkar for the Just 15 years. He was 
suddenly charge-sheeted on 28th January 1958 to which he submitted an 
explanation on 10th February 1998. Thereafter, without any enguiry, the 
ppposite party on some extraneous consideration dismissed him from 
service. He had preferred an appeal before the Chairman, Howrah 
Municipality, on 5th August 1958. The Opposite Party contested this 
ease alleging that Shri Sarkar, the complainant, was guilty of grave mis- 
conduct and negligence for which he was dismissed on 2156 July 1968. 
The dismissal was fully justified, which wus not on extraneous considera- 
tion, and there was no violation of the principles of natural justice. The 
complainant was dismissed after proper charge-sheet and enquiry for 
temporary defalcation, non-affixation of Revenue Stump, where necessary, 
aod misappropriation of stamp money. 


During argument, Shri J. Banerjee, appearing on behalf of the Howrah 
Municipality, contended that the complaint was not maintainable for (1) 
the complainant was not a workman under the Industrial Disputes Act, 
and as such, the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act do not apply, 
(ii) there has not been any violation of the provisions of section 38 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act for, the complainant was dismissed for an offence 
and not for a misconduct for which on approval of the authority 1s 


Parr 1] THE CAT. GAZ. EXTRY,, MARCH 26, 1959 597 


necegyiry and (ili) payment of monthly wages and taking approval are 
conditions subsequent and not precedent. 


Points for decision 


(1) Whether this complaint is maintainable? 
(2) Whether on merits the dismissal of the complainant is justified P 
(4) To what relief, if any, the complainant is entitled ? 


AWARD 


Points Nos. 1 to 3: Shri Banerjee contends that there is no evidence 
on the side of the complainant to show that he is a workman within the 
meaning of section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act although the com- 
plamant’s allegations as to the nature of the duties, made in paragraph 
4(b) of his complaint, were denied by the Opposite Party in paragraph 11 
01 11১ written statement. Shri P, S. Basu, Advocate for the complainant, 
refutes this contention by pointing out that the pleadings require a 
eategorial and specific denial of the adversary’s allegations in the pleadings 
in order to be effective in any judicial proceedings and that an omnibus 
denial, like tue one, made in paragraph 11 of the Opposite Party’s written 
statement is no denial at all. Theretore, the complainant is not obliged to 
adduce evidence to prove that his duties were clerical in nature, and as 
auch, he was a workman. Further, this question affects the jurisdiction 
ot the Tyibunal and is a mixed question of facts and law. Shri Banerjee 
ha» taken this objection, during argument, and did not put any question 
to the complainant, when be was being examined and cross-examined in 
the witness-box in this case. The duties alleged in his petition of com- 
plaint and not denied categorically by the Opposite Party, do not, in my 
opinion, requite particular proof in this case. The pan went to trial 
on the assumption that Shri Sarkar was a workman who was dismissed for 
grave misconduct, during the pendency of adjudication proceedings before 
this Tribunal. A municipal employee may be a workman, It Has been 
so held hy the Supreme Court in a case of 1). N. Banerjee us. P. R. 
Mukherjee, reported in 1959, L.L.J. I, p. 195. Since there is no specific 
denial of the allegation as to the nature of the duties of complainant, 
which allegations definitely show that he was mainly performing clerical 
duties, the Tribunal is entitled to hold and do bold that Shri Sarkar, the 
complainant, is a workman under section 208) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. That being so, the provisions of the said section apply to this case. 


The question now is whether there has been any contravention of the 
provisions of section 30 of the Industrial Disputes Act by the employer, 
entitling the employee concerned to file this complaint under _provi- 
sions of section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act. The complainant 
contends that an adjudication proceeding was pending before this Tribunal 
ata time when he was dismissed 101 an alleged misconduct when (i) payment 
of a month’sa wages and (ii) an application for approval of the action by 
the employer, as required under proviso of section 38(2) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, were not made. An industrial dispute, in which the com- 
10181218101 was concerned, in respect of several issues, waa adjudicated by 
this Tribunal by an award, dated 6th June 1958, This was directed to be 
published in the Calcutta Gazette, on 26th June 1958, and wus published 
in the Culeutta Gazette, Ertraordinary, dated 511 July 1958, This would 
appear from the written statement of the Opposite Party at paragraphs 2 
and 3, and also on a reference to the suid copy of the Gazette. It 18 con- 
ceded by the Opposite Party that, tecanically speaking, the adjudication 


598 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., MARCH 26, 1959 [Part I 


proceedings were pending till the 6th August 1958, 1.e., 30 days fron the 
date of the publication of the award in the Calcutta Gazette, ani Shri 
Sarkur was dismissed on 21st July 1958 without compliance of the provisions 
of section 33(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act. Shri Banerjee, on behalf of 
the Municipality, contends that the provisions of section 9103) of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act are not attracted to the facts of this case for, Shri 
Sarkar was punished with dismissal from service for an ‘‘offence’’, and 
not for a ‘misconduct’, The section applies only in the event of dismissal 
from service for a misconduct not connected with the dispute. He further 
contends that the conditions laid down in the proviso of section 33(2) of 
the said Act are to be observed, not previous to the action taken, but on some 
subsequent days, 1.e., such conditions are not precedent but subsequent, 
Misconduct has not been defined in the Industria] Disputes Act. It means 
any improper conduct, transgression, misdemeanour or illegal act. It 
includes offence, acts and omissions which have made punishable under the 
Indian Penal Code. Shri Banerjee has overlooked his own written state- 
ment on this point. The Opposite Party, im paragraph | of its written 
statement, has stated that Shri Sarkar was guilty of ‘grave misconduct’ 
and ‘negligence’ for which he was dismissed on 2186 July 1958. It ia true 
that the misconduct, for which Shri Sarkar was charge-sheeted, amounted to 
temporary defalcation of money and misappropriation of stamps which are, 
no doubt, offences punishable under the Indian Penal Code. The Company 
has punished Shri Sarkar for alleged misappropriation of the Company’s 
property, an offence under the Penal Code. Although the Penal law 
provides punishment for such offence, it does not ceuse to be a misconduct, 
as hus been specifically stated in this case, nor does the provision affect the 
right of the Opposite Party to dismiss its employee for such misconduct., 
The decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal, in Assem Oil Co. Ltd. vs. 
L. N. Mahanti & ors., reported in 1952, L.A.C., p. 488, is a case to the 
point. Jt Jends support to the finding that this is a misconduct for which 
the Opposite Party can punish although it amounts to an offence as well. 


The last objection taken by Shri Banerjee that the conditions laid down 
in the proviso to section 353(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act are condi- 
tions subsequent and not precedent is not sound. It is true taat no period 
of limitation for filing of the application for approval is stated in the Act. 
And an approval of an action necessarily implies, in the context of 
what has been provided for in the foregoing sub-section, that the applica- 
tion may he filed after the action has been taken. But it should be filed 
within a very reasonable period of time. But then. there is no warrant 
for ascribing a meuning as suggested by Shri Banerjee, to tae other pro- 
visions of the said sub-section, viz., for payment of'a month’s wages. The 
Jaw requires that this payment, or offer of it, should he made hefore the 
action 1s taken. In any event, the provisions of section 33(2) of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, which applies to the facts of the case, were not complied 
with by the Opposite Party at the time of dismissing the compluinant from 
service. Therefore, there has been contravention of the provisions of section 
33, Industrial Disputes Act, and this complaint under section 338A lies to 
this Tribunal. It is, in my opinion, maintainable. 


The scope of enquiry on 0 complaint of this description is the same as 
in a case on o regular reference under section 10(1) of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act, The complainant's story is that he was wrongfully dismissed 
on charges of wuich he was not guilty. He was duly charge-sheeted by 
the Opposite Party, and he replied to the charges. Since then, there was 
no enquiry and, as such, the employer was guilty of the violation of the 
principles of natural justice. 


THE CAL. GAZ, EXTRY., MARCH 26, 1959 599‏ (ا سط 


থপ পলাশ সপ‏ ہے جح SE‏ و شش وج شش شا 


Tribunal, in‏ ٭امالصر(رظھ appears that the decision of the Lahour‏ )ا 
Buck@gham and Carnatic Co. Lid., 1952, [.A.C., p. 490, received (ae‏ 
approval of their Lordshrps of the Supreme Court in Indian Iron & Steel‏ 
Co, Litd., and another es. their workmen reported in 1958, 1.0.3. 1, p. 260-‏ 
FUR, p. 891. This taken along with the decision of the Supreme‏ .18 
Court 111. Lakshini Devi Sugar Milla Ltd. oe. Ram = Sarup and others,‏ 
reported in Wor, LL. 1, p. 17, leave no room for doubt thai on an indus‏ 
trin] dispute being raised by a workman, after his wrougful distnissal from‏ 
service, an Industrial Tribunal ou a reterence of that dispute, is entitled‏ 
to scrutinise every fact und circumstance leading to tae dismissal, and to‏ 
give the workman appropriate relief in the case.‏ 


Turning to the merits of the case, it is evident from a reading of the 
charge-sheet, and the complainant's reply thereto that the complainant was, 
on his own admission, guilty of a temporary defalcation of money, and 
misappropriation of stamps. The Municipality held an elaborate enquiry 
before the issue of a charge-sheet. It appears that there was no enquiry 
after the explauation was submitted by Shri Sarkar. 


Question is whether this amounted to a denial of natural justice? 
Natural justice does not imply unfettered liberty to a litigant to determine 
and direct the course of hearing of a matter. 41] that 16 impiles is that 
no man should be condemned unheard. In other words, it means that the 
party whose civil rights are affected must have reasonable notire of the 
case he had to meet and an opportunity of stating his case. In my opinion, 
the complainant had both reasonable notice of the cuse, he was culled 
upon to meet and also an opportunity of stating his case. The authority 
concerned was in full possession of facts and knew what the complainant 
had anid on them. It found the explanation 80 manifestly unbelievable, 
that it was not necessary to direct further enquiry into the case. In my 
opinion, the absence of any further enquiry in this matter in the 
circumstances of the case does not amount to any violation of the principles 
of natural justice. This Tribunal, therefore, will not interfere with the 
decision of the Municipality to dismiss the complainant trom service. 


Further, the materinls on which the complainant, relied in support of 
his explanation, are before this Tribunal. A careful consideration of these 
materials cannot but impress the Tribunal that the decision taken by the 
Municipality is n possible view of the evidence before it, His explanation 
cannot be accepted in view of admissions made therein, from which 
juference of guilt can reasonably be made. In view of the complainant's 
previous record of service, the extreme punishment of dismissal from 
service cannot be said to be unduly harsh or excessive. I am, therefore, 
unable to aay that the order of dismissal of Shri Surkar was unjustified or 
that it was wrongful. Shri Sarkar is, therefore, not entitled to any relief 
in this case. The complaint is dismissed.

and evidently the corrigendum has not been drafted in the like manner, 
just like the original order of reference which is the standard form of 
reference of an industrial dispute by the (10562117062) to the Industrial 
Triunals and Laour Courts for adjudication. Shrijut Maitra argued that 
the oribinal order of reference is defective and is bad in law. The corri- 
gendum is also defective aud has not been drafted in the proper manner 
and the Court of law which is to adjudicate into the matter, cannot ignore 
11018 vital question and cannot proceed to adjudicate on a reference which 
is defective and bad in law and is not maiitainable. 


The learned Advocate Shri K. ظط‎ Maiira had referred to me a Supreme 
Court decision reported in 14.11.0.5 1958, Volume 11) page 630 (between 
State of Bihar and 1). N. Ganguly and others). where the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court says: 


“that after the dispute is referred to the Tribunal, during the continu- 
ance of the reference proceeding, it is the Tribunal which is seized 
of the dispute and which can exercise jurisdiction in respect of 
16. (Page 639, L.L.J., Volume IT, 1958.) 


So the appropriate Government cannot issue any further Teference or 
corrigendum at the last moment and is expected to remain neutral so long 


Pant 1] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., MARCH 26, 1959 607 


the Tribunal does not submit its award. Shrijut Maitre had further argued 
that 01005 this power 1s taken away by the (iovernment from the Law Court 
and the T'ribunal, it will create o dangerous precedent and the voice of 
justice will «ry in agony, wonder the pressure of exccutive high-handedness. 
Let us take a concrete instance. A big and influential industrialist or a 
big influential trade Union is, may approach the Government during the 
continuance of the proceedings, and may cry that the corrigendum be 
issued and the issues be changed or that the case be transferred to some 
other Tribunal under section 33(b) of the amended Industriul Jisputes 
Act. What will tae Governinent dof Will the Government concede to 
the request und issue fresh corrigendum? And if the Clovernment issues 
subsequent votification or corrigendum it may always not be bona fide and 
the (tovernment may do it for the suke of expediency and the very founda- 
tion of justice will be at stake. In 1947 (176) L.T. 312-1948, A.C. 87, 
it has been observed (Franklin versus Minister of Planning): 


“On the other hand, decision of the administrative authorities are 
usually subjective in the sense they are reached without applying 
any standard at all except that of expediency.”’ 


11 the Giovernment thinks it expedient, they nay issue further corrigendum 
or even transfer the case but whether such issue of subsequent notification 
or corrigendum will be valid or legal is a matter of decision by the Law 
Courts and of Law Courts alone. ‘‘The vulidity of an executive act, to 
be tested by a mind free from executive bias’, has been observed by Shri M. 
C. Sitalvad, Attorney-General of India, in the International Congress of 
Jurist, that was opened in New Delhi in January, 1959. If that be ৪০, 
1 am inclined to think it is the Tribunal who is to determine the validity 
of the executive act, 


I confess, there is much 10619 in the argument of learned Advocate 
Shrijut Maitra but we shal] have to go deep into the mutter and see whether 
the issue of corrigendum vitally affects the case or not or whether there is 
bona fie on the part of the Government for issue of such corrigendum. 
After all, ‘‘to err is human” and the Government means (tovernment 
officials and for a technical error on the part of the Government or of the 
Union official who supplied the address, the case caunot be dismissed and 
the Court of Law cannot deny justice to the puor aggrieved workmen. J 
am quoting below relevant portion of the Hon'ble Supreme Court decision 
reported in L.L.J., 1958, Volume IT, page 638: 


“Tt is not im every case where the parties allege the existence of an 
industrial dispute that a reference would be made under section 
10(1); it is only where the test of subjective satisfaction of the 
appropriate Government is satisfied that the reference con be 
made, Thus it is clear that the appropriate Government is given 
an important voice in the matter of permitting industrial disputes 
to seek adjudication by reference to the Industrial Tribunal. 
But once an order in writing is made by the appropriate Govern- 
ment referring an industrial dispute to the Tribunal for adjudica- 
tion under section 10(1), proceedings before the Tribunal are 
deemed to huve commenced and they are deemed to have concluded 
on the day on which the award made by the Tribunal becomes 
enforceable under section 174A. ‘This ia the effect of section 20(8 
of the Act. This provision saows that atter the dispute is referre 
to the Tribunal, during the continuance of the reference proceed- 
ings, it in the Tribunal which is seized of the dispute and which

can exercise jurisdiction in respect of it. The appropriate (igeern- 
ment can act m respect of a reference pending adjudication before 
a Tribunal only under section 10(5) of the Act, which authorises 
it to add other parties to the pending dispute subject to the con- 
ditiona mentioned in the said provisions.” (vide L..J., Vol. 11. 
page 638.) 


Viewed from this context, as [ have noted above, T cannot offhand reject 
the case saying that the reference is bad in law. I should think that 
it was a technical error on the part of the Government in issuing the original 
acference and in issuing the subsequent corrigendum and that the corrigen- 
dum has not been drafted in the proper way but merely because there was 
dechniceal error, ] cannot dismiss the cuse as 1 do not find any substantial 
error دہ‎ the part of the Giovernment und Jack of bona fide. In principle, 
] quite agree with the learned Advocate Shri K. K. Mattra, but since each 
ease is to be decided on its own merit, so far as this case is concerned | 
cunnot dismiss the case on tae prelimimary ground. Reference or corrizen- 
dum should only be ignored if there is substantial fampering of justice or 
lack of bona 116 on the part of (he Government or if the Government does 
it af the instance of either party, tot whieh there is no provision in the 
Industrial Disputes Act. 


Learned Advocate Shri .کا‎ K. Mattern lad further argued taat this case 
would have been a fit case under the Payment of Wages Act but so far as 
the Tribunal is concerned, this Court has ono jurisdiction to deal with 
deduction of wages and non-payment of earned wages thereof. Shrijut 
Maitra had further argued to me that in the writteu statement submitted 
by the Union it is stated that the employer iWlegully deducted the wages 
of the workman Shri Singh and thus illegally effected the change in the 
conditions of service applicable to the workman. Shri Singh is entitled to 
wages of Ka. 4-8 for the above two days and Rs. 49 a8 compensation tor 
illegal deduction. Regarding three other workmen who were not given 
wager for their respective days us they came very late, the Union had 
stated in their written statement thut the three workmen were not given 
any notice or opportunity of hearing and the workmen are entitled to 
wager of Ra. 2-4, Rs, 1-14-6 and Rs, 2-9, respectively and Rs, 22-8, Ra. 19-1 
and Rs. 25-10 as compensation for illegal deduction. Shrijut Maitra 
argued that the Union used the word ‘‘deduction’’ and even prayed for 
compensation at 10 times for the deducted wages, as is provided in the 
Payment of Wages Act and where a special statute for wages is there, this 
Court cannot adjudicate into the matter. Shrijut Maitra had further 
referred to me to page 17 of Shri Chakraborty’s Laws of Industrial 
সা ৬ in India, First Edition, wherein the learned author had 
stated : 


16018177107 arrear wages: A claim for recovery of arrears of wages 
only while in service or on discharge cannot be an industrial 
dispute. Such a claim can be made if it be connected with a 
dispute and covered by the language of section 2(k). The 
recovery can be made by un application under the Payment of 
Wages Act or by a suit, where the Payment of Wages Act does 
not apply.”’ 


Learned Advocate of the Union Shri .ث‎ K. Dhar had referred to me 
section 2(k) of the Industrial Dispuies Act which runs as follows: 

‘Industrial dispute’’ means any dispute or difference between employers 

and employers, or between employers and workmen, or between 

workmen and workmen, which is connected with the employment 


Part J] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., MARCH 26, 1959 609 


ere eer ethene nee ror anemia 


or non-employment or the terms of employment or with the condi- 
tion of labour, of any person;”’. 

Learned Advocate Shrijut Dhar had also argued that non-payment of 
wages is always a term of employment and the Union can raise an industrial 
dispute over term of employment. It is to be noticed that the dispute 
has been ruised over the terms of employment although deduction of wages 
is at accidental feature. In A.I.R. (36) 1949, Federal Court, page 150, 
Shamnagore Jute Factory versus S. N. Modak, it has been held: 


“The Tribunal contemplated by section 15, Payment of Wages Act, 
18 not, in our opinion, one which could affect the jurisdiction of 
the Tribunal set up under section 7, Industrial Disputes Act and 
to which a reference could be made under section 10 of that 
Act. The Tribunal set up under the Industrial Disputes Act has 
a much wider jurisdiction. In our opinion the two Acts are not 
in part materia and the contention that the jurisdiction of the 
Tribunal set up under the Industrial Disputes Act is excluded 
by the provisions of the Payment of Wages Act is unwarranted.” 


Viewing from this context of the matter, I accept the argument pro- 
,»nunded by the learned Advocate Shrijut Dhar in this respect. I should 
1910 that the Industrial Tribunal had much wider jurisdiction and can 
11101010869 even any matter over wages provided that it raises an industrial 
dispute as contemplated in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Acct. 


Now let us enter into the merits of the case. 


15586 No. 1: Whether Shri Nandalal ro is entitled to wages for 
283: and 24th January 1958.—It is to be noted that Nandalal Singh was 
absent on 22nd January 1958. He was not paid wages for the day. This 
was the day just preceding 23rd January, when it was closed for festival 
holidays (Netaji’s birthday) and 24th January (Saraswati Puja) and it is 
the practice of the company that in order to earn wages for the festival 
holidays one should remain present just on the day preceding. Learned 
Advocate of the Union argued that there was no standing order of, the com- 
pony, neither the company published his rule in the Notice Board and as 
such the company is bound to pay wages for the festival holidays. Although 
it 13 doubtful if this rule has been published in the Notice Board, it 
appears that the workmen must be apprised of this rule. Long years of 
custum and convention forms the basis of contract and surely there was 
unimplied contract of service between the workmen and the employer over 
the custom and convention that in order to earn wage for the festival holi- 
days, one should have to remain present and work the whole day preceding 
such holidays. This has also been further corroborated from an examina- 
tion of the attendance register produced as exhibit where workers 
have not been paid for আপস holidays, being absent on the preceding 
day. This has also been provided in the Cotton Textile Award made by 
Shri M. C, Banerjee, published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated June 10). 
1958 In page 2090, the learned Judge has said “‘that with regard to the 
enjoyment of festival holidays, religious or national, on full pay, the 
following conditiens shall apply: 


In order to qualify for a festival holiday with full pay an employee 
will be required to work the full normally scheduled hours durimg 
the working day immediately preceding the holiday.’’ 


So this is corrohorated by the principles of natural justice and I regret I 
am unable to allow two days’ wages for the festival leave to the workman 
concerned in view of the fact that he did not attend just on the day 


610 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., MARCH 26, 1989 [Part 1 


لئ مسجھہٹھیےغوچسے سےوسے 


preceding the festival holidays. 1 would therefore disallow the claim of 
festival holidays of Shri Nandalal Singh. 


Issue No. 2: Whether the following workmen are entitled to wages. 
fur the days mentioned against their names :— 


i) Shri Rawen Chakraborty—2oth Uctober 1997. 
(ii) Shri Kaloo Patra—26th October 1981. 
(iii) Shri Bharat Natya—2nd December 1967. 


4৯৬ regards the second issue whether the workmen are entitled to wages 
for the days mentioned against their names, viz., Ramen Chakraborty for 
25th Uctuber 1957, Kaloo Patra for 26th October 1947 and Shn Bharat 
Natya for 2nd December 1957, the learned Advocate of the Union had 
argued that these three workmen were late by few minutes and that they 
are not habitual late comers. How the company could lock them out and 
refuse them admittance when they came late by few minutes only? It is 
in evidence that the company closed their factory gate at 8-10 a.m. and 
the uatial hour of attendance is 8 a.m. and 10 minutes grace is wllowed to 
enable the workers to come within the schedule hours. The Union contends 
thal befvre the formation of the Union, the workers were late in attendance 
even half an hour or one hour and there was no fixed principle and while 
some were allowed late attendance of half an hour, some were not allowed 
late. attendance of 10 minutes only. It is in evidence that these workers 
are not habitual late comers. It was on a particular day that they came 
late and while they contend that they came 15 or 20 minutes Jate than 8-10 
a.m. the schedule hour including grace, the company contends that they 
were late for more thun half an hour. Even assuming that they came 
Jate by half an hour, what right the company had to shut them out to 
enter into the factory which is more or less considered to be a public 
institution (for, the factury does not belong tu employer only hut to the 
employees also and now when we hear so much of partnership in the 
business concern)." The company could mark them late, they could even 
mark them absent, but even in spite of that, if the workers are agreeable 
10 work for the day, how could the company stop the workers from entering 
into the tactory after the schedule hour of 8-10 a.m.’ Here the company 
ie overzealous and suffering from the punctuality complex of 8 a.m. 
Punctuality is a good virtue, no doubt, but so many factors are to be 
considered as, for example, climatic condition, transport difficulties on the 
way and specially when the workers are not habitual late comers. I am 
inclined to think that the company should not have been so overzealous and 
should have condoned the late attendance only for the single day, in case 
of each of the three workmen concerned. 1 do not find any motive of 
victimisation on the part of the company as alleged by the Union. I would 
therefore allow these workers their respective wager, viz., to Ramen 
Chakraborty Re. 2-4, for Kaloo Patra Rs, 1-14-6 and Bharat Natya Rs. 2-9 
for the day. I will not allow them any compensation, neither I can allow 
them 10 times compensation for their deducted wages as provided in the 
Payment of Wages Act. After all, these workers came late and I am 
prepared to give them one day's wages for the day under the special 
circumstances but further if any compensation is allowed, it will be putting 
Tremium to indiscipline in the industry. While I would allow each of the 
three workers named above their one day's wages, I will disallow them any 
cor.pensation under the Industrial Disputes Act. The payment mentioned 
ebove should be made within seven days from the date of publication of the 
award in the Calcutta Gazette.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 


DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH 


Public Health 


NOTIFICATION 
No. P.W. /1552/21-22/59.—26th March 1959.—Whereas the Governor 
18 aotisfied that the district of 24-Parganas is threntened with an outbreak 
of small-pox; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by section 2 of the 
Epidemie Diseases Act, 1897 (111 of 1897), the Governor is pleased to 
prescribe the following temporary regulations for the prevention and control 
01 small-pox and for the medical inspection, isolation, observation and 
surveillance of persons suffering from, or suspected of being infected with 
sinall-pox in the said district for a period of six months ہے‎ 


TEMPORARY RECULATIONS FOR THE PREVENTION AND 
CONTROL OF SMALL-POX. 


1. In these regulations, unless there is anything repugnant in the 
subject or context,— 

(a) ‘‘Health Officer’? means the Health Officer of the district appointed 
by the State Government, the Chief Medical Officer of 1198161) of 
the district, or the Subdivisional 116816]) Officer of any of the 
subdivisions of the district within their respective subdivisions; 

(b) “Sanitary Inspector” means a Sanitary Inspector appointed by the 
State Government;

(c) “Union Buard’’ means a union board constituted under the Bengal 
Village Self-Government Act, 1919; 


(4) “Smull-pox’? means any disease accompanied by an eruption of 
vesicles or pustules; 


(6) ‘‘Patient’’ means a person suffering from or suspected to be 
suffering from small-pox; 


(f) ‘‘Medical practitioner’? means any person practising the medical 
profession. 


Notices 


2. ]1 in any case the Health Officer considers that the issue of a notice 
under these regulations is likely to lead to such an amount of delay دس‎ 
might facilitate the spread of small-pox he may forthwith take such steps 
as he may think fit for carrying out the work, and shall thereafter, as soon 
as possible, issue a notice on the person concerned stating the reasons why 
such work has been carried out. 


3. If any measure which the Health Officer has by a notice issued 
under these regulations, required to be carried out, be not carried out to his 
sulisfaction within the time stated in the notice the Health Officer shall 
he entitled to carry out the measure. 


Costs and compensation 


4. (1) All expenses incurred in carrying out any work in pursuance of 
un order issued under these regulations shall be paid by the State (dovern- 
ment except in any case where the order directs a person to carry out any 
work in relation to property in his possession, in which case the expensea 
shall be paid by such person: 


Provided that where the conditions which led the Health (fficer to 
pass such an order, are not attributable to any act or default of the person 
in possession of the property, the State Government may pay to such person 
_ whole or a part of the expenses incurred by him in carrying out the 
order, 


(2) The State Government may recover all expenses incurred by the 
Health Officer in carrying out the measure under regulation 3 from the 
person or persons to whom the notice was originally issued, 


6, The State Government shall pay adequate compensation to any person, 
who has sustained substantial losa or damage by reason of anything done 
under these regulations: 


Provided that no person shall receive any eompensation for anything 
done or suffered under these regulations if he has failed to carry out an order 
issied under these regulations. He shall not direct the patient to be 
removed from the house unless it is, in his opinion, impossible to make 
proper arrangements for his isolation therein within the time specified in 
the order and to the satisfaction of the Health Officer. 


Location of disease 


6. When a case of amall-pox occura in a house, the nearest male 
relative in attendance upon the patient, or in the absence of any such relative 
the occupier of the house, or 1f the occupier be the patient, the senior male

. (1) Every medical practitioner called in to attend upon any case of 
small-pox shall forthwith give notice of the case by a special messenger to 
the nearest Sanitary Inspector or to the Health Officer by post and the cust 
of such messenger in each case shall be defrayed by the State Government. 


۳) The doctor-in-charge of a hospital or a dispensary within the 01861105

8. Presidents of union boards in union board areas and thuna officers 
in non-union board areas shall supply to the Health Officer such periodical 
oe . cuses of smuall-pox as he may from time to time call upon them 
te furnish. 


9. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector muy examine any person 
who is, or suspected to be, suffering from small-pox or who, in his opinion, 
may be infected with or likely to spread small-pox. 


isolation of patients 


10. When the Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector considers that 
the isvlation of any patient is a precaution necessary for the protection of 
the neighbouring population, he shall order the patient to observe isolation 
and may order the nearest relative in attendance on the putient, or the 
occupier of the house in which the patient is staying, to arrange for the 
isolation of the patient in such a manner and for such a time as may be 
approved by the Health Officer. 


11. The Wealth Officer or o Sanitary Inspector may order that any 
person, who has been in contact with a person found to be suffering from 
sinall-pox, shall be segregated for a period not exceeding a fortnight in 
ہ8‎ manner and in a place to he approved by the Health Officer. 


12. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may order that any 
person Who has been in contact with a person found to be suffering from 
small-pox shall be vaccinated or re-vaccinated within a time to be specified 
in the order. 


18. No person shall enter uny place wherein a patient is isolated under 
regulation 10, without the permission of the Health Officer or a Sanitary 
Juspector, 


14. When a patient has been removed from a house for isolation under 
regulation 10, the State Government shall provide for him free of charge 
a suitable place, with necessary attendants, diet, etc. 


15. No person, who is or has been suffering from small-pox, shall leave 
the place where he has been staying until he has received from the Healta 
Officer or a Sanitary Inspector written permission to do so. 


16, No person while suffering from evident symptoms of amall-pox vr 
in the convalescent state of the disease with scabs of pocks on his body shull 
expose himself in any street, road, public place, shop, bazar or any place

used in common by persons other than members of the family or household 
to which such infected person belongs or shall move from place to place 
unless he is proceeding to a hospital for admission and treatment. 


17. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector authorised by the Health 
Officer in writing in that behalf may, during the prevalence of any outbreak 
of small-pox, order that any bazar, shop or other public place shall remain 
closed for such time as may appear to him to be necessary and may forbid

18, The Health Officer or a Sanitary Luspector may require any peraon

he specified in the order, such measures for the disinfection of any premises

Necessary. 


19. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may «direct the owner 
or occupier of any premises to take steps to have vaccinated or re- 
vaccinated within a time to be apecified in the order any person residing 
on such premises and under the contro) of such owner or occupier if che 
Health Officer is of opinion that such person has been in contact with any 
one suffering from small-pox. 


20. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may forbid any person 
who has been a patient or who has tu his knowledge been in contact with a 
patient to act as vendor of any article for such period as may be specified 
in the order. 


21. No person shall sell any article which has been in contact with & 
patient until it has been disinfected to the satisfaction of the Health Officer 
or a Sanitary Inspector. 


22. The Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector may issue general 
orders that by a specified date certain sanitary precautions of a simple 
nature, such as lime-washing of houses, clearing of latrines or the removal 
of filth or rubbish shal] be carried out to his satisfaction. 


23. The Ilealth (fficer or a Sanitary Inspector may prohibit persons 
from retaining or selling clothes taken from the bodies of persons who have 
died of small-pox and may cause any auch clothes to be destroyed. 


24. No person shall carry or permit to be carried in a public conveyance 
৪ patient except in the case where a patient is carried to a hospital with the 
following precautions against spreading the disease, namely سے‎
